conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What is the clinical hallmark of a myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Symmetrical PROXIMAL muscle weakness — difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs and combing hair — usually WITHOUT sensory loss, with preserved/reduced reflexes and no fasciculations.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How does the weakness pattern of a myopathy differ from a peripheral neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Myopathy = symmetrical PROXIMAL weakness with NO sensory loss
  • Neuropathy = DISTAL (length-dependent) weakness WITH sensory loss (glove & stocking) and reduced reflexes

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How does myopathy differ from a neuromuscular junction disorder (e.g. myasthenia gravis)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Myopathy = fixed proximal weakness, no sensory loss
  • NMJ disease = FATIGABLE weakness (worse with use/end of day), often ocular/bulbar; reflexes and sensation normal

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What is the single most useful screening blood test for myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Creatine kinase (CK) — raised in most myopathies (and very high in rhabdomyolysis), but characteristically NORMAL in steroid/Cushing's myopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What are the associated clues that localise the CAUSE of a myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Skin rash → dermatomyositis
  • endocrine features → thyroid/Cushing's
  • drug history (statin) → drug-induced
  • exercise-induced cramps/dark urine → metabolic
  • ptosis + ophthalmoplegia → mitochondrial

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How does polymyositis present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Adults with proximal symmetrical muscle weakness and raised CK, but NO rash. It is a T-cell mediated inflammatory myopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What skin signs characterise dermatomyositis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Heliotrope rash (violaceous/purple discolouration of the eyelids)
  • Gottron's papules (scaly plaques over the knuckles/MCP-PIP joints)
  • shawl sign (rash over upper back/shoulders)
  • and photosensitivity

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Why must you screen for malignancy in adult dermatomyositis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Dermatomyositis is often PARANEOPLASTIC — associated with underlying malignancy (e.g. ovarian, lung, GI, breast). The rash can precede the cancer, so a new adult case mandates a cancer screen. Risk is highest in the first few years around diagnosis, so a negative initial screen does not exclude cancer — stay vigilant and re-screen if new symptoms appear or the disease is refractory.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How does inclusion body myositis (IBM) differ from poly/dermatomyositis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: IBM affects OLDER patients (>50), is more DISTAL and ASYMMETRIC (classically finger flexors and quadriceps), progresses slowly, and responds POORLY to steroids. Dysphagia is common, with an aspiration risk. Consider IBM in any 'polymyositis' that fails to respond to steroids.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Which autoantibody in inflammatory myopathy is linked to interstitial lung disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Anti-Jo-1 (an antisynthetase antibody) — antisynthetase syndrome with interstitial lung disease, arthritis and mechanic's hands.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Which myositis autoantibody flags malignancy risk, and which does NOT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Anti-TIF1γ (anti-p155/140), and anti-NXP2, are the antibodies associated with cancer in adult dermatomyositis. Anti-Mi-2 is the opposite: it marks classic dermatomyositis skin signs with a good steroid response and a LOWER malignancy risk. Anti-Jo-1 points to antisynthetase syndrome with interstitial lung disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What investigation is diagnostic in inflammatory myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
Muscle biopsy. Supporting tests:
  • raised CK
  • myopathic EMG
  • MRI muscle (to guide biopsy)
  • and myositis autoantibodies

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What is the management of inflammatory myopathy (polymyositis/dermatomyositis)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Corticosteroids first-line, plus a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant (azathioprine or methotrexate); IVIG for refractory disease. Screen for malignancy in dermatomyositis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What are the features of hypothyroid myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Proximal weakness
  • myalgia and cramps
  • RAISED CK
  • and classically slow-relaxing (“hung-up”) reflexes

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Why is CK a key discriminator in Cushing's / steroid myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Steroid (glucocorticoid) myopathy causes proximal weakness with a NORMAL CK — the muscle atrophies rather than breaks down. Most other myopathies raise CK.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Name endocrine causes of a proximal myopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Hypothyroidism
  • hyperthyroidism
  • Cushing's syndrome (steroid myopathy)
  • acromegaly
  • osteomalacia/vitamin D deficiency
  • and Addison's disease

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What is McArdle disease and its classic clinical clue?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: A glycogen storage disorder (myophosphorylase deficiency) causing exercise-induced cramps/pain and myoglobinuria, with the classic 'SECOND-WIND' phenomenon — symptoms ease if the patient briefly rests then continues exercising. Diagnosis is by genetic testing first-line; the non-ischaemic forearm exercise test shows a flat lactate with a rising ammonia. The old ISCHAEMIC version of the test is avoided because it has caused compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What are the key features of mitochondrial myopathies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes) and CPEO (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — ptosis + ophthalmoplegia). Biopsy shows ragged-red fibres; lactate is often raised. Mitochondrial DNA disorders are MATERNALLY inherited — an affected mother passes it to all her children, an affected father to none.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What pattern suggests a metabolic myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
Exercise intolerance with cramps ± rhabdomyolysis (myoglobinuria). Examples:
  • glycogen storage (McArdle)
  • lipid storage (carnitine deficiency)
  • and mitochondrial myopathies

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Which drug is the commonest cause of drug-induced myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Statins — spectrum from myalgia to myopathy to (rarely) rhabdomyolysis. Muscle symptoms on a statin: check CK and renal function and exclude other causes. Broadly, CK below about 5x the upper limit of normal with tolerable symptoms is usually managed by continuing, or by stopping and rechallenging at a lower dose or with a different statin; CK above about 5x ULN means stop; CK above about 10x ULN, or dark urine or AKI, is treated as rhabdomyolysis. Risk rises with high dose, hypothyroidism, renal impairment and interacting drugs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: List drugs that cause myopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Statins
  • corticosteroids (steroid myopathy — normal CK)
  • alcohol
  • colchicine
  • and antiretrovirals (e.g. zidovudine)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What defines rhabdomyolysis biochemically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
Muscle breakdown releasing contents into blood →
  • VERY high CK
  • myoglobinuria (dark/tea-coloured urine; dipstick positive for blood but no red cells)
  • hyperkalaemia
  • and acute kidney injury (AKI)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: What are the common causes of rhabdomyolysis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Crush injury
  • prolonged immobility (long lie)
  • statins
  • extreme exertion
  • seizures
  • alcohol
  • hyperthermia
  • recreational drugs (cocaine, MDMA)
  • and neuroleptic malignant syndrome

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How is rhabdomyolysis managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• Aggressive IV crystalloid titrated to a urine output of about 200–300 mL/hour
  • monitor and treat hyperkalaemia
  • monitor renal function, CK and calcium
  • remove the underlying cause
  • and check for compartment syndrome after a crush injury or long lie
Urinary alkalinisation (bicarbonate) and mannitol are NOT routine. Dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Which investigations are used to work up a myopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
• CK (key)
  • U&E (AKI/K+)
  • TFTs
  • calcium/vitamin D
  • cortisol
  • ESR/CRP
  • myositis autoantibodies
  • EMG
  • muscle biopsy
  • MRI muscle
  • urine myoglobin
  • and genetics for inherited/metabolic disease

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: Why is the finding of a NORMAL CK with proximal weakness clinically important?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: It points away from most inflammatory/dystrophic myopathies (which raise CK) and towards STEROID (Cushing's) myopathy — particularly in a patient on long-term glucocorticoids.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: How do the inherited muscular dystrophies fit into the myopathy picture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are INHERITED (X-linked, dystrophin gene) myopathies covered separately. This topic focuses on the ACQUIRED myopathies — inflammatory, endocrine, metabolic and drug-induced.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.front: A patient develops proximal weakness and dark urine after starting a statin. What is the concern and first action?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.back:
Statin-induced myopathy tipping into rhabdomyolysis.
  • Check CK and renal function (U&E)
  • stop the statin
  • and give IV fluids if rhabdomyolysis is confirmed
If the weakness and high CK persist or worsen AFTER stopping the statin, think statin-induced immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (anti-HMGCR) — it does not resolve on withdrawal and needs immunosuppression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Define dystonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often twisting, repetitive movements and/or postures. It is a hyperkinetic movement disorder of basal-ganglia origin.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What causes the characteristic twisting posture in dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Simultaneous co-activation of agonist and antagonist muscles.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is a sensory trick (geste antagoniste)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: A light touch to the affected body part that transiently relieves the dystonia (e.g. touching the chin straightens the neck in cervical dystonia). It is almost pathognomonic of dystonia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: How does dystonia differ from chorea?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Dystonia is patterned, twisting and directional (the same muscles pull the same way each time) with a sensory trick; chorea is random, flitting and non-repetitive.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is task-specific dystonia? Give an example.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Dystonia triggered only by a particular skilled action, with the same muscles working normally for other tasks. Example: writer's cramp (or musician's dystonia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What are the two axes of the modern dystonia classification?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Axis I — CLINICAL, chiefly age of onset (younger onset → more likely genetic and to generalise) and body distribution (focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonia, generalised)
  • Axis II — AETIOLOGICAL (inherited, acquired, or idiopathic)
Age of onset and distribution are the two descriptors within the clinical axis, not the two axes themselves.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Define the distribution categories of dystonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Focal = one region
  • segmental = ≥2 contiguous regions
  • multifocal = ≥2 non-contiguous regions
  • hemidystonia = one side of the body
  • generalised = trunk plus ≥2 other regions

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is the significance of hemidystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: It implies a structural lesion of the contralateral basal ganglia → image the brain (MRI).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is the commonest focal dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is blepharospasm?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Focal dystonia causing involuntary forced eye closure from orbicularis oculi contraction; can cause functional blindness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is Meige syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: A segmental cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is spasmodic dysphonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Laryngeal (vocal-cord) dystonia producing a strained/strangled voice (adductor type) or a breathy voice (abductor type).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Name the patterns of head posturing in cervical dystonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Torticollis (turn)
  • laterocollis (tilt)
  • antecollis (flexion)
  • and retrocollis (extension)
it is often painful.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What genetic dystonia classically causes early-onset generalised dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: DYT1 (TOR1A gene) early-onset generalised dystonia — autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance, so the family history is often negative. It typically starts in a limb in childhood or adolescence and generalises.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa syndrome)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: A childhood-onset dystonia (often starting in the legs/gait) with diurnal variation (worse in the evening) and a dramatic response to low-dose levodopa. A must-not-miss treatable cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Which treatable metabolic disease must always be excluded in young-onset dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
Wilson's disease — screen with
  • serum caeruloplasmin (low)
  • 24-hour urinary copper (high)
  • and slit-lamp for Kayser–Fleischer rings
Note serum copper alone is unreliable: it may be low, normal or high.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Name the 'treatable three' causes to consider in young-onset dystonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Dopa-responsive dystonia (levodopa trial)
  • Wilson's disease (copper screen)
  • and drug-induced dystonia (dopamine antagonists)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Which drugs classically cause an acute dystonic reaction?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Dopamine-antagonist antiemetics and antipsychotics — e.g. metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: How does an acute dystonic reaction present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Sudden onset — usually in a young male within 48 hours of being given a dopamine blocker — of oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus, tongue protrusion or laryngospasm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: How is an acute dystonic reaction treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Stop the offending drug and give an anticholinergic — procyclidine — with rapid, often dramatic resolution; give it parenterally if the swallow or airway is compromised, otherwise orally. Watch the airway if there is laryngeal involvement. Continue an oral anticholinergic for about 48–72 hours, because the culprit drug outlasts a single dose and symptoms otherwise recur.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is tardive dystonia and how does it differ from an acute dystonic reaction?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Tardive dystonia is dystonia after months–years of antipsychotic use and is often persistent; the acute dystonic reaction occurs within hours–days and resolves rapidly with an anticholinergic. Do not reach for an anticholinergic in a tardive presentation — tardive dystonia needs review or switch of the antipsychotic with specialist input, and anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: List secondary (non-drug) causes of dystonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Perinatal injury/cerebral palsy
  • stroke
  • structural brain lesions
  • and neurodegeneration such as Huntington's disease and PKAN (pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: How is dystonia diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Clinically — by recognising the phenomenology (patterned twisting posture, sensory trick, task specificity) and classifying it along the two axes. Investigations are reserved for young/atypical/secondary-suspicious cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What investigations are indicated in young or atypical dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• MRI brain
  • Wilson's screen (caeruloplasmin, 24h urinary copper, slit-lamp for KF rings)
  • genetic testing (e.g. DYT1/TOR1A)
  • and a levodopa trial

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is the first-line treatment for focal dystonias?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Botulinum toxin injections (e.g. for cervical dystonia and blepharospasm), repeated approximately every 3 months.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Which oral agents are used in dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back:
• Anticholinergics (e.g. trihexyphenidyl)
  • baclofen
  • benzodiazepines (e.g. clonazepam)
  • and levodopa if the dystonia is dopa-responsive

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What surgical option is used for severe or generalised refractory dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus internus (GPi DBS), particularly effective in severe generalised dystonia such as DYT1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: Why is a levodopa trial important in childhood-onset dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: To detect dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa), which responds dramatically to low-dose levodopa and would otherwise be missed and left untreated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is 'overflow' in dystonia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: Spread of the abnormal contraction beyond the intended muscles; mirror movements (dystonia appearing when the opposite limb performs a task) are a related feature.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.front: What is dystonic tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Dy.back: A jerky, position-sensitive tremor occurring in the dystonic body part, e.g. a 'no-no' head tremor in cervical dystonia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the organising principle of brainstem lesions ("crossed signs")?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: An IPSILATERAL cranial nerve palsy (nucleus/fascicle hit before it exits) PLUS CONTRALATERAL long-tract (motor/sensory) signs (tracts not yet decussated). The cranial nerve gives the level; the long tracts confirm it is in the brainstem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which cranial nerves localise to each brainstem level?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Midbrain = CN III & IV
  • Pons = CN V, VI, VII, VIII
  • Medulla = CN IX, X, XI, XII
Two caveats: the spinal trigeminal nucleus (V) descends through the medulla, which is why a lateral medullary infarct causes facial sensory loss; and CN XI arises largely from the upper cervical cord.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why do brainstem lesions produce CONTRALATERAL motor/sensory signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The corticospinal tract decussates at the medullary pyramids (below the lesion) and the spinothalamic tract has crossed in the cord, so their signs appear on the opposite side of the body; the cranial nerve, struck at its nucleus/exit, is affected on the same side.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which artery is affected in lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar artery) or the vertebral artery, causing a lateral medullary infarct.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: List the features of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Ipsilateral: facial pain/temperature loss (CN V spinal nucleus), Horner's syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, bulbar signs (dysphagia, hoarse voice, absent gag - CN IX/X), vertigo & nystagmus
  • Contralateral: body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic)
Typically NO limb weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In Wallenberg syndrome, where is sensory loss on the face versus the body?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Pain/temperature loss is IPSILATERAL on the face (CN V spinal nucleus) but CONTRALATERAL on the body (spinothalamic tract) - the classic "crossed" sensory pattern.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why is there usually NO limb weakness in Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The infarct is lateral and spares the medial corticospinal tract (pyramids), so motor power is preserved. It is a sensory/cerebellar/bulbar syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the features of medial medullary syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal tract)
  • contralateral loss of proprioception/vibration (medial lemniscus)
  • and ipsilateral tongue deviation (CN XII)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which artery is involved in medial medullary syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The anterior spinal artery (or vertebral artery).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In medial medullary syndrome, which way does the tongue deviate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Towards the side of the lesion (ipsilateral), because of the CN XII (hypoglossal) palsy - the tongue points to the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is Weber syndrome and where is the lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A midbrain (ventral) syndrome: ipsilateral CN III (oculomotor) palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is Millard-Gubler syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A ventral pontine syndrome: ipsilateral CN VI (abducens) and CN VII (facial) palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What defines locked-in syndrome and where is the lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A ventral pontine lesion (usually basilar artery occlusion) causing quadriplegia and anarthria with PRESERVED consciousness; only vertical eye movements and blinking are spared, allowing communication by blinking.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is locked-in syndrome distinguished from a vegetative state?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Locked-in: fully AWARE but unable to move except vertical gaze/blinking (ventral pons)
  • Vegetative state: wakeful but UNAWARE — now grouped with the minimally conscious state as a prolonged disorder of consciousness (RCP)
Management, prognosis and ethics differ entirely.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which cranial nerves are affected in cavernous sinus syndrome, and what else is seen?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: CN III, IV, VI and V1 (± V2) — V1 is the division usually involved — giving ophthalmoplegia, ptosis and facial (V1 ± V2) sensory loss, plus PROPTOSIS (± chemosis).Causes include cavernous sinus thrombosis, carotico-cavernous fistula, tumour and pituitary apoplexy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which cranial nerves are involved in a cerebellopontine angle (CPA) lesion, and what is the classic cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: CN VIII, VII and V. The classic cause is a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), giving unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus (VIII) first, then a reduced corneal reflex and facial numbness (V). Facial weakness (VII) is a LATE feature — an early, prominent facial palsy makes a schwannoma less likely.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What investigation is used for a suspected cerebellopontine angle lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Pure-tone audiometry first, to demonstrate asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss, then MRI of the internal auditory meatus (IAM).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which cranial nerves are affected in jugular foramen syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: CN IX, X and XI - giving dysphagia, dysphonia/hoarseness, absent gag and weakness of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (shoulder shrug).Causes include glomus tumour and skull-base lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the signs of a CN III (oculomotor) palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A "down-and-out" eye (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), ptosis and diplopia; the pupil may or may not be involved.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How do you distinguish a "surgical" from a "medical" third nerve palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Surgical: pupil INVOLVED (fixed, dilated/'blown') due to COMPRESSION of the surface pupillary fibres — e.g. PCom aneurysm or uncal herniation (emergency)
  • Medical: pupil SPARED due to microvascular ISCHAEMIA of the nerve core — e.g. diabetes/hypertension
Caveat: pupil sparing only reassures in a COMPLETE, isolated palsy in a vasculopath over about 50 — ischaemic palsies involve the pupil in up to a fifth of cases, and early compression can spare it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why does compression involve the pupil while ischaemia spares it in a CN III palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the OUTER surface of the oculomotor nerve, so they are hit early by external compression but relatively protected from microvascular ischaemia (which affects the core).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: A painful CN III palsy with a dilated pupil - what must be excluded urgently?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm — risk of catastrophic subarachnoid haemorrhage. Arrange urgent CT/CT angiography.Note pain does not discriminate: microvascular third-nerve palsies are often painful too, so judge on the pupil, the completeness of the palsy, age and vascular risk factors. Image any palsy that is partial, progressive, under about 50, or has other neurological signs, whatever the pupil is doing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which brainstem stroke syndrome gives ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Weber syndrome (midbrain).Mnemonic: "Weber = III + contralateral weakness."

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (mentioned in passing)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causing failure of adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye; classically bilateral in multiple sclerosis (covered in its own resource).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the investigation of choice for brainstem and cranial-nerve syndromes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: MRI brain focused on the posterior fossa — best for the brainstem, CPA and small infarcts. But early DWI can be falsely negative for a small brainstem infarct: a normal scan in the first 24 hours does not exclude one, so if the picture fits, treat as stroke and repeat imaging.CT/CT angiography is used acutely for stroke and to assess the vertebrobasilar circulation and aneurysms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why are acute brainstem signs a stroke emergency, and why easily missed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: They usually represent posterior-circulation (basilar/vertebral) stroke requiring urgent imaging and the thrombolysis/thrombectomy pathway, but are often FAST-negative and therefore a classic missed diagnosis.Basilar occlusion in particular is often stuttering and fluctuating before it completes, and can present with reduced consciousness rather than a hemiparesis, with very high untreated mortality.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What immediate concern arises with reduced GCS or respiratory compromise in a brainstem lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The brainstem controls breathing and airway reflexes, so airway protection is the priority - secure the airway and involve ITU immediately.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does the direction of tongue deviation localise a hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The tongue deviates TOWARDS the side of a lower motor neuron / nuclear CN XII lesion (as in medial medullary syndrome) because the genioglossus on that side is weak - "the tongue points to the lesion."

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the general principles of managing brainstem/cranial-nerve syndromes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
Treat the underlying cause — the acute stroke pathway, with thrombectomy for a confirmed proximal posterior-circulation (basilar) occlusion considered up to 24 hours from last known well where imaging shows salvageable brain (NICE); tumour, aneurysm or infection as appropriate. Supportive MDT care:
  • nil by mouth until a bedside swallow screen is passed (including oral medication), then SALT assessment and NG feeding if unsafe
  • VTE prophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression in immobile patients, not anti-embolism stockings (NICE)
  • physiotherapy and OT
  • communication aids in locked-in syndrome

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which two crossed brainstem syndromes both feature contralateral hemiparesis but differ by cranial nerve level?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Weber (midbrain, ipsilateral CN III) and Millard-Gubler (ventral pons, ipsilateral CN VI + VII) - both with contralateral hemiparesis.The cranial nerve involved gives the level.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What are the three main functions of the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Coordination of movement
  • balance
  • and posture.
It fine-tunes (does not initiate) movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Are cerebellar signs ipsilateral or contralateral to the lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: IPSILATERAL — a right cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces right-sided limb signs. (Due to double-crossing of the pathways.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What pattern does a vermis / midline cerebellar lesion produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Truncal and gait ataxia (wide-based staggering gait, falls, inability to sit unsupported).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What pattern does a cerebellar hemisphere lesion produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Ipsilateral LIMB ataxia — dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What does the mnemonic DANISH stand for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Dysdiadochokinesia
  • Ataxia (gait + limb)
  • Nystagmus
  • Intention tremor
  • Slurred/Staccato (scanning) speech
  • Hypotonia/Heel-shin incoordination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is dysdiadochokinesia and how is it tested?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Impaired rapid alternating movements — tested by rapidly patting the palm and back of one hand against the other; movements are clumsy and irregular.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which way does the fast phase of cerebellar nystagmus beat?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Gaze-evoked, horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase TOWARDS the side of the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is intention tremor and how is it elicited?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: A tremor that worsens as the finger approaches the target on finger-nose testing; associated with past-pointing (dysmetria).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What speech pattern is characteristic of cerebellar disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Scanning (staccato) dysarthria — slurred speech broken into syllables with irregular volume.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Name three additional cerebellar signs beyond DANISH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Dysmetria/past-pointing
  • rebound phenomenon (overshoot when a displaced arm is released)
  • and pendular reflexes / broad-based ataxic gait.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Is Romberg's test positive or negative in pure cerebellar ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: NEGATIVE — the patient is unsteady with eyes both open and closed (they do not rely on vision to stay upright).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: A positive Romberg test (steady with eyes open, falls with eyes closed) indicates what type of ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Sensory ataxia — loss of proprioception (dorsal column / peripheral nerve disease), NOT cerebellar disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: How do you distinguish cerebellar from sensory ataxia at the bedside?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Romberg negative + DANISH signs = cerebellar
  • Romberg positive + absent proprioception/vibration + stamping gait = sensory ataxia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which bedside tests assess limb ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Finger-nose test (intention tremor, past-pointing)
  • and heel-shin test (legs)
  • rapid alternating movements for dysdiadochokinesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which posterior circulation stroke syndrome includes ipsilateral cerebellar signs, and which artery is involved?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or the vertebral artery — vertebral occlusion is in fact the commoner cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: How does chronic alcohol cause cerebellar syndrome, and what pattern predominates?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Chronic alcohol causes vermian (midline) degeneration, producing predominantly gait/truncal ataxia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Name two drugs whose toxicity causes cerebellar signs.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Phenytoin and lithium (also carbamazepine). Phenytoin toxicity runs nystagmus → ataxia → dysarthria and is dose-related and reversible, but long exposure can leave permanent cerebellar atrophy; lithium can also leave permanent signs. Check drug levels.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What are the commonest posterior fossa tumours causing cerebellar signs in children?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Medulloblastoma and pilocytic astrocytoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the inheritance and genetic defect in Friedreich's ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Autosomal recessive; a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: List the key neurological features of Friedreich's ataxia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Cerebellar ataxia + absent lower-limb reflexes + upgoing plantars — a mixed picture of upper motor neurone plantars with a peripheral sensory neuropathy and dorsal column loss, so Romberg is often POSITIVE. Plus pes cavus and scoliosis. Onset is usually in the teens (before 25).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What are the important systemic (non-neurological) features of Friedreich's ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (main cause of death) and diabetes mellitus; also optic atrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which paraneoplastic antibody causes cerebellar degeneration, and with which cancers?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Anti-Yo, associated with ovarian and breast cancer (paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Name three reversible systemic causes of cerebellar ataxia worth screening for.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Hypothyroidism
  • coeliac disease
  • and vitamin E deficiency (plus drug toxicity).
Note vitamin B12 deficiency causes mainly a SENSORY ataxia from dorsal column loss, with a POSITIVE Romberg, rather than a cerebellar syndrome — but it is still a key reversible mimic to screen for.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the investigation of choice for cerebellar syndrome and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: MRI brain (DWI) — it best images the posterior fossa (infarct, tumour, atrophy, MS plaques). CT comes first in the emergency, but only to exclude haemorrhage and show hydrocephalus or mass effect: CT is degraded by bone artefact and a normal CT never excludes a cerebellar stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which blood tests are useful in the ataxia work-up?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• B12
  • TFTs
  • drug levels (phenytoin/lithium)
  • coeliac serology
  • paraneoplastic antibodies (anti-Yo)
  • and alcohol markers (γGT).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why is an acute cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage a neurosurgical emergency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Swelling in the tight posterior fossa can cause obstructive hydrocephalus (4th ventricle compression) and brainstem compression/coning — rapidly fatal but treatable with urgent CT and neurosurgery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What red-flag combination suggests a compressive cerebellar stroke/haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Acute cerebellar signs + headache + vomiting + reduced GCS → urgent CT head and immediate neurosurgical referral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why are cerebellar signs ipsilateral while cerebral cortical lesions cause contralateral signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Cerebellar output crosses to the contralateral motor cortex, but the corticospinal tract then crosses back in the medulla — the double crossing makes cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is dysmetria?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Inaccurate targeting of movement — over- or under-shooting a target (past-pointing), seen on finger-nose testing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Describe the gait of cerebellar ataxia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Broad-based, staggering and unsteady; with a unilateral lesion the patient tends to fall towards the side of the lesion. A midline/vermian lesion gives non-directional truncal unsteadiness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What supportive/MDT management is offered in chronic cerebellar ataxia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Treat the cause
  • plus physiotherapy (balance/falls)
  • occupational therapy (aids/adaptations)
  • and SALT (speech and swallow)
  • genetic counselling in inherited disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What are visual field defects?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Loss of part of the visual field, produced by lesions anywhere along the visual pathway — from the retina to the occipital cortex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What is the core organising principle of visual field defects?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: The site of the lesion produces a characteristic, predictable field defect, so the defect localises the lesion — and the single organising landmark is the optic chiasm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: State the 'before/at/after the chiasm' framework.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• Before the chiasm (optic nerve) → monocular loss
  • at the chiasm → bitemporal loss (crossing nasal fibres)
  • after the chiasm → homonymous loss (contralateral field of both eyes)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: Trace the visual pathway.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Retina → optic nerve (one eye) → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations (temporal = Meyer's loop; parietal) → occipital (visual) cortex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: Explain the crossing rule at the optic chiasm.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Fibres from the nasal retina (which see the temporal field) cross to the other side; the temporal retinal fibres stay uncrossed — so after the chiasm each optic tract carries the same half of the visual field from both eyes, giving a homonymous defect for post-chiasmal lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does an optic nerve or retinal (pre-chiasmal) lesion cause, and what are the typical causes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
MONOCULAR field loss — a central scotoma (optic neuritis), an altitudinal defect (ischaemic optic neuropathy), an arcuate defect, or complete loss of that eye. Causes include
  • optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis)
  • ischaemic optic neuropathy
  • giant cell arteritis
  • and retinal artery/vein occlusion
  • glaucoma too, though glaucoma is usually bilateral and asymmetric rather than one whole eye

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does an optic chiasm lesion cause, and typical causes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
A bitemporal hemianopia; causes include
  • a pituitary tumour
  • and a craniopharyngioma

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does an optic tract lesion cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: A contralateral homonymous hemianopia — e.g. 'a left homonymous hemianopia = a right optic tract lesion'; causes include stroke and tumour.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does a temporal-lobe (Meyer's loop) optic radiation lesion cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: A contralateral SUPERIOR homonymous quadrantanopia (from a temporal lobe lesion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does a parietal-lobe optic radiation lesion cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: A contralateral INFERIOR homonymous quadrantanopia (from a parietal lobe lesion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What field defect does an occipital cortex lesion cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: A homonymous hemianopia with MACULAR SPARING — classically from a PCA stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: State the PITS rule for homonymous quadrantanopias.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• Parietal = Inferior defect
  • Temporal (Meyer's loop) = Superior defect

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: Explain the logic behind PITS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• Meyer's loop (temporal) fibres loop down and forward through the temporal lobe and carry the superior field → a temporal lesion causes a superior quadrantanopia ('can't see the sky')
  • parietal fibres carry the inferior field → a parietal lesion causes an inferior quadrantanopia ('can't see the ground')

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What is a bitemporal hemianopia, and where does it localise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Loss of both temporal (outer) fields from compression of the crossing nasal fibres at the optic chiasm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: In a bitemporal hemianopia, what does 'upper quadrants worse' indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Inferior compression (from below) — a pituitary tumour (more common in adults).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: In a bitemporal hemianopia, what does 'lower quadrants worse' indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Superior compression (from above) — a craniopharyngioma (classically in children, though there is a second adult peak).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: Explain the logic of upper- vs lower-quadrant bitemporal defects.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
The chiasm sits above the pituitary;
  • a pituitary tumour grows UP and compresses the lower chiasmal fibres first → the superior field goes first (upper quadrants worse)
  • a craniopharyngioma presses DOWN → the inferior field goes first (lower quadrants worse)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What does the number of eyes involved tell you about the lesion location?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• One eye (monocular) → a lesion anterior to the chiasm (optic nerve/retina)
  • both eyes (binocular) → a lesion at or behind the chiasm

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: For a binocular defect, how do bitemporal and homonymous patterns localise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• Bitemporal (outer fields of both eyes) → the chiasm
  • homonymous (the same side of both eyes) → behind the chiasm (tract/radiation/cortex)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: For a homonymous defect, how does hemianopia vs quadrantanopia localise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• A complete hemianopia → the optic tract (incongruous), a complete optic radiation lesion, or the occipital cortex (congruous, with macular sparing)
  • a quadrantanopia → the optic radiation (localise by PITS)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What do macular sparing and congruency tell you?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Macular sparing localises to the occipital cortex (thought to be due to the large cortical representation of the macula, and possibly a dual blood supply → spared in a PCA stroke). Congruency: optic TRACT lesions are characteristically INCONGRUOUS, and defects become more congruent the further back the lesion, with the occipital cortex the most congruent — which is how you separate a tract lesion from an occipital one.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What is amaurosis fugax?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back: Transient monocular vision loss from a RETINAL TIA — an embolus to the central retinal or ophthalmic artery, usually carotid in origin. It is not an optic nerve lesion. Give aspirin 300 mg immediately and refer for specialist assessment within 24 hours; the patient must not drive for 1 month.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.front: What investigations are used for visual field defects?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Vi.back:
• Confrontation visual field testing at the bedside then formal perimetry (to map the defect)
  • fundoscopy (papilloedema, optic atrophy) and pupils (an RAPD in optic nerve lesions)
  • and neuroimaging — urgent pituitary MRI for bitemporal defects, brain imaging for homonymous defects
A SUDDEN homonymous hemianopia is an acute stroke until proven otherwise: emergency stroke pathway and immediate CT head, remembering that isolated field loss is often FAST-negative.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Compression of the neurovascular bundle (the brachial plexus, subclavian artery and/or subclavian vein) as it passes through the thoracic outlet at the root of the neck.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What is the 'core concept' of TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Three structures pass through the same narrow region, but by slightly different routes — the brachial plexus and subclavian artery through the scalene triangle (behind anterior scalene), while the subclavian vein runs in FRONT of anterior scalene in the costoclavicular space. So TOS splits into three syndromes depending on which is compressed: neurogenic (~95%), venous (~3–5%) or arterial (~1%).
Compression of the brachial plexus (nerve) causing arm/hand pain, paraesthesia, weakness and wasting — especially in the C8/T1 (ulnar) distribution; it is the commonest form.
Compression of the subclavian vein causing painful, diffuse arm swelling with distended (dilated) veins and a cyanotic arm; rarer.

Compression of the subclavian artery — almost always with a cervical rib or anomalous first rib — causing stenosis with a post-stenotic aneurysm, mural thrombus and distal embolisation. Presents with painful arm claudication, pallor, coldness and a weak pulse, OR embolically as unilateral digital ischaemia with blue painful fingers, sometimes with a palpable radial pulse. The rarest (~1%) but most serious form: limb-threatening, needing emergency vascular referral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What are the three potential compression points of the thoracic outlet?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back:
• The scalene triangle (between anterior and middle scalene),
  • the costoclavicular space (between clavicle and first rib),
  • and the subcoracoid/pectoralis minor space.

• A cervical rib (the classic bony anomaly),
  • neck trauma (often the precipitant),
  • anatomical variations (fibrous bands, abnormal first rib, scalene hypertrophy),
  • repetitive overhead activity (athletes/manual workers) and
  • poor posture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What is the classic anatomical predisposition to TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: A cervical rib — an extra rib arising from C7. It is the classic predisposition, but most cervical ribs are asymptomatic incidental findings, so one on X-ray supports the diagnosis without making it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What are the clinical features of neurogenic TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Arm/hand pain, paraesthesia and numbness, often in the ulnar (C8/T1) distribution (medial arm, ring and little fingers); hand weakness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles in chronic cases. Because the lesion is at the lower trunk (C8/T1), proximal to the median/ulnar division, BOTH median- and ulnar-supplied intrinsics waste — characteristically with disproportionate thenar wasting (the 'Gilliatt-Sumner hand') even though the sensory loss stays ulnar. Symptoms are worse with overhead arm positions/activity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What are the features of venous TOS, and its key complication?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Painful, diffuse arm swelling with distended (prominent) veins and a cyanotic arm; it risks subclavian vein thrombosis — Paget–Schroetter syndrome ('effort thrombosis') — often after vigorous arm use in young, active people.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What are the features of arterial TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Painful arm claudication (pain/fatigue on use), pallor, coldness and a weak/absent pulse — but it often presents embolically instead, as unilateral digital ischaemia or blue painful fingers, sometimes with a palpable radial pulse. The rarest but most serious (limb-threatening) form; acute ischaemia needs emergency vascular referral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What are the provocation tests for TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Adson's test (neck extension + head turn + deep breath → the radial pulse diminishes) and the Roos test (EAST — arms abducted 90°, externally rotated, with repeated hand clenching for 3 minutes → reproduces symptoms). Both have high false-positive rates — they are often positive in normal people and in carpal tunnel syndrome — so loss of the pulse alone means little, and a test only counts if it reproduces the patient's own symptoms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What should the examination in suspected TOS include?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back:
• Radial pulses in both arms,
  • arm colour/temperature/swelling,
  • a neurological exam (C8/T1 sensory loss, wasting), and
  • palpation for a cervical rib.

• Chest and cervical spine plain radiographs (identify a cervical rib or bony abnormality, AND exclude an apical Pancoast tumour);
  • duplex ultrasound FIRST and same-day if venous TOS is suspected, then venography/CT angiography;
  • nerve conduction studies/EMG — usually NORMAL in neurogenic TOS, so a normal study does not exclude it, and their real job is to exclude ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and C8/T1 radiculopathy;
  • MRI/CT for soft-tissue causes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What is the differential diagnosis of TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back:
• Cervical radiculopathy (C8/T1 — dermatomal, neck pain, root tension signs),
  • ulnar/cubital tunnel syndrome (localised to the elbow),
  • carpal tunnel syndrome (median distribution), and
  • Raynaud's/vascular disease.
The red flag is an apical lung (Pancoast) tumour — progressive C8/T1 wasting with Horner's syndrome, weight loss, a smoking history or a supraclavicular mass — which must be excluded before symptoms are attributed to TOS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What is the overarching management principle in TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Conservative treatment first; surgical decompression if conservative treatment fails or for significant vascular compromise.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What is the first-line conservative management of TOS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: Physiotherapy (posture correction, scalene/pectoral stretching, strengthening), activity modification (avoiding provoking positions) and analgesia — most neurogenic TOS responds.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.front: What surgical options exist for TOS, and when are they used?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Th.back: First rib resection ± cervical rib removal, scalenectomy, or release of fibrous bands — for failed conservative treatment, a significant neurological deficit, or vascular TOS.

Venous TOS with thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) is urgent: same-day duplex ultrasound, then anticoagulation (apixaban or rivaroxaban, at least 3 months), with catheter-directed thrombolysis most effective within about 2 weeks of symptom onset, followed by decompression. Remember upper-limb DVT can cause pulmonary embolism, and that most upper-limb DVT is secondary (central line, pacemaker lead, malignancy) rather than effort thrombosis. Arterial TOS → emergency vascular referral for repair/decompression (limb-threatening).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: A sudden neurological deficit due to a vascular cause, lasting >24 hours (or leading to death) — either ischaemic (~85%, blocked artery) or haemorrhagic (~15%, ruptured vessel).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define TIA.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: The same process as stroke but transient — focal ischaemia WITHOUT infarction (tissue-based: symptoms resolve, usually <1 hour, with no infarct on imaging).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the 'core concept' that management pivots on?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: One question answered by an urgent CT — is it ischaemic or haemorrhagic? — because the treatments are opposite; and 'time is brain' (a time-critical emergency).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Give the mechanism and causes of ischaemic stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
A blocked artery (thrombosis/embolism); causes include
  • atherosclerosis
  • AF (cardioembolic)
  • small-vessel disease and
  • carotid stenosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Give the mechanism and causes of haemorrhagic stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
A ruptured vessel bleeding into the brain; causes include
  • hypertension (commonest)
  • aneurysm
  • AVM
  • anticoagulation and
  • amyloid angiopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: How do ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke appear on non-contrast CT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Ischaemic may be normal early (low density later); haemorrhagic shows hyperdense (bright) blood immediately.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the high-yield rule about the first investigation in stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Urgent non-contrast CT head FIRST — it reliably shows/excludes blood; never thrombolyse or give aspirin until haemorrhage is excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What does the FAST tool screen for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• Face (droop)
  • Arm (weakness/drift)
  • Speech (slurred/aphasic)
  • Time (call 999).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the ROSIER score?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: The in-hospital stroke recognition tool (which excludes hypoglycaemia and scores face/arm/leg/speech/visual).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Why must glucose always be checked in a suspected stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
Hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic — check and correct it immediately; other mimics include
  • seizure (Todd's paresis)
  • migraine with aura
  • tumour
  • functional disorder and
  • Bell's palsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What three features does the Oxford (Bamford) classification use?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• (1) Unilateral weakness/sensory deficit
  • (2) homonymous hemianopia
  • (3) higher cortical dysfunction (dysphasia, neglect).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define a total anterior circulation stroke (TACS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: All 3 Bamford features — a large MCA + ACA territory stroke (worst prognosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define a partial anterior circulation stroke (PACS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: 2 of the 3 features (or higher cortical dysfunction alone) — a branch of the MCA/ACA.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define a lacunar stroke (LACS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor or ataxic hemiparesis with NO higher cortical/visual signs — from small perforators (internal capsule, pons, basal ganglia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Define a posterior circulation stroke (POCS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Cerebellar/brainstem signs, an isolated hemianopia, or cranial nerve palsies — vertebrobasilar territory.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Describe an MCA (middle cerebral artery) stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: The commonest — contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss (face + arm > leg), homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant hemisphere) and neglect (non-dominant hemisphere).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Describe an ACA (anterior cerebral artery) stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Contralateral leg > arm weakness and behavioural change.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Describe a PCA (posterior cerebral artery) stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Homonymous hemianopia (with macular sparing) and visual agnosia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Describe vertebrobasilar/brainstem stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Cerebellar signs, cranial nerve palsies, crossed signs, 'locked-in' syndrome (basilar), and the lateral medullary (Wallenberg — PICA) syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the immediate investigation in stroke, and its limitation in ischaemia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Non-contrast CT head — excludes haemorrhage (and mimics); it may be normal early in ischaemia but still allows thrombolysis if within the window and no bleed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What roles do CT/MR angiography and perfusion imaging play?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Angiography identifies a large-vessel occlusion (for thrombectomy); perfusion imaging identifies salvageable penumbra (extending the treatment window). MRI (DWI) is most sensitive for early ischaemia/infarct.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What other investigations are done in stroke, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• Glucose (mimic), FBC, coagulation, U&E, lipids
  • ECG (AF)
  • echocardiogram and carotid Doppler to find the source (cardioembolic vs carotid stenosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the principle of acute ischaemic stroke management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Exclude haemorrhage → reperfuse (thrombolysis ± thrombectomy) fast → then antiplatelet and supportive care — 'time is brain'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the thrombolysis window and agent in ischaemic stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Within 4.5 hours of known onset with alteplase or tenecteplase, after excluding haemorrhage and contraindications; the extended window (4.5–9 hours, or wake-up stroke) applies if perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue (mismatch).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: When is mechanical thrombectomy used in ischaemic stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: For a proximal large-vessel occlusion. Anterior circulation — up to 6 hours (with thrombolysis if eligible), and up to 24 hours in selected patients with salvageable tissue on perfusion imaging. Posterior circulation (basilar or posterior cerebral artery) is also considered up to 24 hours with salvageable tissue — a basilar occlusion carries the highest mortality, so a fluctuating brainstem syndrome warrants urgent CT angiography.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: How and when is aspirin used in acute ischaemic stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Aspirin 300 mg as soon as possible, and certainly within 24 hours, once haemorrhage has been excluded — orally, or rectally/by enteral tube if there is dysphagia, so the swallow assessment does not delay it. After thrombolysis it is delayed until 24 hours, with a repeat CT first. Continue 300 mg until 2 weeks after onset (or discharge, whichever is sooner), then long-term antiplatelet.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What supportive ('stroke unit') measures are used in ischaemic stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• Admit to a stroke unit
  • maintain glucose/oxygenation/hydration
  • swallow assessment (NBM until assessed — aspiration risk)
  • permissive hypertension (do not lower BP acutely — the exception is a thrombolysis candidate, who must be below 185/110 mmHg first)
  • and VTE prophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression (not early heparin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Outline the acute management of haemorrhagic stroke.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• Stop and reverse anticoagulation (warfarin → vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate; dabigatran → idarucizumab; apixaban/rivaroxaban → PCC)
  • lower the blood pressure — if within 6 hours with a systolic of 150–220 mmHg, aim for 130–140 mmHg within 1 hour and maintain it for at least 7 days (not if there is an underlying structural cause)
  • and refer to neurosurgery.
NO thrombolysis, NO antiplatelets/anticoagulants.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Outline the acute management of a TIA.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Give aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated) and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours — ABCD² is not used to decide referral urgency, so all suspected TIAs are seen urgently. Arrange carotid imaging and an ECG (AF); do not routinely CT a suspected TIA — MRI after specialist assessment is the imaging of choice. No driving for 1 month.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Why is a TIA a medical urgency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: It is a warning of impending stroke (high early stroke risk) → aspirin + urgent specialist review within 24 hours and start secondary prevention.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the antiplatelet strategy for secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke or TIA?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: After a high-risk TIA or minor ischaemic stroke (non-cardioembolic, haemorrhage excluded, confirmed by a stroke specialist): clopidogrel plus aspirin for 21 days, then clopidogrel alone. Otherwise clopidogrel 75 mg daily is first-line long-term, with aspirin + dipyridamole if clopidogrel is unsuitable.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What is the secondary-prevention antithrombotic if the stroke is cardioembolic (AF)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
Anticoagulation (a DOAC) instead of an antiplatelet. Timing balances recurrence against haemorrhagic transformation:
  • after a TIA, start immediately once imaging has excluded a bleed
  • after a mild stroke, within about 5 days
  • after a moderate-to-severe stroke, from about 5–14 days.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: What statin, BP and surgical measures are used in secondary prevention?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back:
• A high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg, started after ~48h)
  • BP control (the biggest modifiable risk factor), diabetes control, smoking cessation and lifestyle
  • and carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis of 50–99% on the relevant side — referred urgently, aiming for surgery within 14 days.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.front: Why is aspirin/thrombolysis absolutely avoided until a CT is done?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.back: Because a haemorrhagic stroke would be worsened catastrophically — the treatments for ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke are opposite, so haemorrhage must be excluded first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What do spinal cord disorders affect, and what is the key clinical skill?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Disorders affecting the spinal cord (and, for cauda equina, the lumbosacral nerve roots below it); the skill is reading the pattern of motor, sensory and sphincter signs to localise the lesion (which tract, which level), then finding the cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the organising principle of a cord lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A cord lesion gives UMN signs below the level (hyperreflexia, ↑tone, upgoing plantars) + a sensory level + sphincter involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What are the three main tracts and their functions/laterality?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Corticospinal (motor, same side below the lesion)
  • dorsal columns (fine touch/proprioception/vibration, same side)
  • and spinothalamic (pain/temperature, opposite side).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss with contralateral pain/temperature loss; classic cause is a penetrating injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe central cord syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Upper limb weakness worse than lower limb ('man in a barrel'), typically after a hyperextension injury on a cervical spondylotic canal. Sensory loss below the level is variable — note the 'cape' pattern of dissociated sensory loss belongs to syringomyelia, not to traumatic central cord syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe dorsal column syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Loss of proprioception/vibration with sensory ataxia; causes include B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) and tabes dorsalis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How is cauda equina different from a cord syndrome in principle?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: It is a nerve-root (not cord) lesion, giving LMN signs, saddle anaesthesia and bladder/bowel involvement; classically from a large disc prolapse.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Where does the spinal cord end, and how does this separate cord from cauda equina lesions?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The cord ends at ~L1/L2 (conus medullaris); lesions above give UMN signs (spastic, hyperreflexic), while lesions below (cauda equina) give LMN signs (flaccid, areflexic) with saddle anaesthesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Which spinal cord/root problems are surgical emergencies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Cauda equina syndrome and acute cord compression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is spinal cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Compression of the spinal cord by a mass, causing progressive neurological deficit — a neurosurgical/oncological emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the 'core concept' of cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The cord is squeezed within the rigid spinal canal and the priority is time; the deficit is an UMN pattern BELOW the lesion + a sensory level; the commonest serious cause is metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Contrast cord compression with cauda equina syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Cord compression = above L1/L2, UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars), a sensory level, with late (spastic) bladder involvement.
  • Cauda equina = below L1/L2, LMN signs (flaccid, hyporeflexic), saddle anaesthesia, with early bladder/bowel dysfunction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe malignant cord compression (MSCC).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The commonest serious cause. It affects up to about 5% of people with cancer over the course of their disease (not per year) and is the initial manifestation of malignancy in ~20% — it can be the first sign of cancer. Commonest primaries: breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid and myeloma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List the non-malignant causes of cord compression.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Disc prolapse/herniation
  • vertebral fracture (trauma/osteoporosis)
  • spinal stenosis
  • epidural abscess/haematoma
  • and degenerative cervical myelopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the back pain of cord compression.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The earliest and commonest feature — often preceding neurology by weeks; red-flag pain is worse on lying down, at night and on coughing/straining/Valsalva; thoracic or band-like pain is suggestive. New/progressive back pain in a cancer patient is MSCC until proven otherwise.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the motor and sensory features of cord compression.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Motor: progressive limb weakness below the level in a UMN pattern (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) — may be flaccid acutely in spinal shock.
  • Sensory: a sensory level (sensation lost below a specific dermatome), which localises the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the bladder/bowel involvement in cord compression, and how the level localises.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Bladder/bowel symptoms are later (hesitancy/retention then incontinence — a late, ominous sign). Localisation: cervical → arms + legs (tetra); thoracic → legs (para) + a trunk sensory level.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the investigation of choice in suspected cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Whole-spine MRI, reported within 24 hours — the whole spine because multiple levels of compression are common. If MRI is contraindicated or inadequate, CT with three-plane reconstruction is the alternative; the value there is bony detail, not contrast.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What are the NICE timing rules for MRI in suspected MSCC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours for spinal pain suggestive of metastases WITH neurology suggestive of MSCC
  • within 1 week if pain suggestive of metastases WITHOUT neurology.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How is the primary tumour identified if cord compression is the first sign of cancer?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
  • a myeloma screen
  • PSA and biopsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the immediate medical management of MSCC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: For anyone with neurological symptoms or signs, offer 16 mg of oral dexamethasone (or the equivalent parenteral dose) as soon as possible, then 16 mg daily while awaiting surgery or radiotherapy, with gastroprotection and glucose monitoring. Do not forget the other end: after treatment, reduce it gradually until stopped, continuing only if symptoms return as you reduce — and if imaging rules MSCC out, stop the dexamethasone that was started beforehand.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: If lymphoma is suspected in cord compression, should steroids be withheld?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Not from a patient who already has neurological signs. Dexamethasone 16 mg is given as soon as possible where there are neurological symptoms or signs of cord compression (NICE) — an established deficit is what you cannot get back. A seriously suspected haematological malignancy is a reason to get urgent senior oncology or haematology advice before steroids, because they can render the biopsy non-diagnostic — and that caveat bites in the patient with no neurology, not the one who is already weak.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What supportive measures are used in cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Thromboprophylaxis, analgesia, and urgent contact with the MSCC coordinator — that is the referral, not just a way of booking the scan. On mobilisation: the old blanket rule of flat bed rest for everyone has gone. Immobilise without delay only if there are symptoms or signs of spinal instability; otherwise, where imaging suggests the spine is stable, test it with graded sitting then weight bearing, watching neurology and pain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the definitive treatment of MSCC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Within 24 hours of confirmation — surgery is first-line in suitable patients (decompression ± stabilisation) followed by radiotherapy
  • radiotherapy within 24 hours for those unsuitable for surgery
  • best supportive care where the prognosis is poor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the key prognostic factor in cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Pre-treatment neurological status — patients with no motor function for over 48 hours are unlikely to recover useful function, so treat early before paralysis is established.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is degenerative cervical myelopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Chronic cord compression in the cervical spine from degenerative change (spondylosis, disc, ligament hypertrophy) — the commonest cause of cord dysfunction in older adults.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What are the features and management of degenerative cervical myelopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Pain, loss of motor function in both upper limbs, gait disturbance, clumsy hands, sensory loss, bladder symptoms and UMN signs in the legs; Hoffman's sign is positive; MRI cervical spine is the gold standard, and urgent decompressive surgery is done to halt progression (deficits often don't fully reverse).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is Hoffman's sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Flick the distal phalanx of the middle finger — a positive sign is reflex flexion of the thumb (often with the index finger). It is a UMN sign of cervical myelopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is spinal cord injury (SCI)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Traumatic (or acute) damage to the spinal cord causing loss of motor, sensory and autonomic function below the level of injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What two features define the clinical picture of a spinal cord injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The LEVEL (tetraplegia vs paraplegia; whether breathing/autonomic control is affected) and whether it is COMPLETE or INCOMPLETE — with the added acute complications of spinal shock, neurogenic shock and autonomic dysreflexia.
