conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Contrast a complete and an incomplete cord injury.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Complete = total loss of motor and sensory function below the level (including sacral), no sacral sparing, poor prognosis.
  • Incomplete = some preserved function below the level, sacral sparing present, better prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is 'sacral sparing', and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Preserved perianal sensation and/or voluntary anal contraction — it indicates an incomplete injury (better prognosis), so always examine the perineum / do a PR.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What does the ASIA classification grade?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: It grades the injury from A (complete) to E (normal) using motor and sensory testing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the 'neurological level' of a spinal cord injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The lowest level with normal motor and sensory function; it determines what is lost.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why are high cervical cord injuries immediately life-threatening?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5. A lesion at or above C3 abolishes diaphragmatic function, so the patient cannot breathe and is ventilator-dependent; lesions at C4–C5 impair it partially.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How does the level determine the pattern of paralysis and complication risk?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Cervical → tetraplegia (all four limbs); thoracic/lumbar → paraplegia (legs) + trunk. Injuries above T6 risk autonomic dysreflexia and neurogenic shock.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the pattern of Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Ipsilateral weakness below the lesion (corticospinal)
  • ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns)
  • and contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Explain the mechanism behind the Brown-Séquard pattern.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The dorsal columns and corticospinal tract are ipsilateral (they cross higher up/in the medulla), giving same-side deficits; the spinothalamic tract crosses at the level of entry, so its damage causes contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe central cord syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Weakness that is worse in the arms than the legs ('man in a barrel') with sacral sparing — the commonest incomplete syndrome — typically from a hyperextension injury in an elderly patient with a spondylotic spine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe anterior cord syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Loss of motor function and pain/temperature with the dorsal columns spared (vibration/proprioception preserved); from an anterior spinal artery infarct or flexion injury; poor prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is spinal shock?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A transient loss of ALL cord function below the lesion (a reflex phenomenon) — flaccid paralysis, areflexia and reduced tone — that resolves over days–weeks, after which the flaccidity becomes spastic (UMN).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is neurogenic shock, and its mechanism?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A distributive (circulatory) shock from loss of sympathetic outflow (injury above T6) with unopposed vagal tone, causing hypotension, BRADYCARDIA and warm peripheries.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the key discriminator of neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Neurogenic shock causes hypotension WITH bradycardia (loss of sympathetic tone), whereas hypovolaemic shock causes hypotension with tachycardia — critical in trauma (don't miss a bleed, but recognise neurogenic shock).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: In which patients does autonomic dysreflexia occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Patients with a spinal cord injury at or above T6.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Explain the mechanism of autonomic dysreflexia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A noxious stimulus below the level triggers a massive reflex sympathetic surge → severe vasoconstriction and hypertension below the lesion; compensatory vagal bradycardia/vasodilation above the lesion cannot override it (the sympathetic outflow is disconnected from higher control) → dangerous hypertension.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What are the triggers and features of autonomic dysreflexia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Triggers: urinary retention (commonest — blocked catheter/full bladder), faecal impaction, pressure sores, ingrown nails.
  • Features: extreme hypertension, flushing and sweating ABOVE the level, a pounding headache, and haemorrhagic stroke in extreme cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How is autonomic dysreflexia managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Remove the stimulus (unblock the catheter, relieve retention/impaction — the priority) and treat the blood pressure (sit the patient up, antihypertensives if needed).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Outline the acute assessment and management of spinal cord injury.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Immobilise + ABCDE: manual in-line stabilisation, then head blocks and tape, ideally on a vacuum mattress or scoop stretcher — a long spinal board is an extrication device only and the patient comes off it as soon as possible. Airway with C-spine control; breathing — ventilate if the injury is high cervical; circulation — distinguish neurogenic from haemorrhagic shock. Then neurological assessment of level and completeness, and imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Are high-dose steroids used in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: No — they are not given. Management centres on immobilisation, preventing secondary injury by avoiding hypotension and hypoxia, surgery where indicated, and MDT rehabilitation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is cauda equina syndrome (CES)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Compression of the cauda equina — the bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord — a surgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the 'core concept' of cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The cord ends at ~L1 (conus medullaris); below that the canal holds only nerve roots (the 'horse's tail'), so CES is a lower motor neurone (LMN), root-level problem (unlike cord compression, which is UMN); these roots carry bladder, bowel, sexual, saddle-sensory and leg function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Contrast cauda equina syndrome with cord compression.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• CES = below L1/L2 (roots), LMN signs (flaccid, reduced tone/reflexes), saddle anaesthesia, and early/prominent bladder & bowel dysfunction
  • Cord compression = above L1 (cord), UMN signs (spastic, increased tone/reflexes, upgoing plantars), a sensory level, and later bladder involvement

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What picture does a conus medullaris (L1) lesion give?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A mixed UMN/LMN picture — it is the transition zone between the cord and the cauda equina.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the relevant anatomy of the cauda equina.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The spinal cord tapers to the conus medullaris at ~L1; the roots below (travelling in the canal after L2/3) form the cauda equina, supplying the lower limbs, perineum, bladder and rectum (sensory, motor to the anal/urethral sphincters, and parasympathetic to the bladder/rectum).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why do the red flags of CES map directly onto the anatomy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Because the roots carry saddle sensation, sphincter motor control and bladder/bowel parasympathetics, their compression causes saddle anaesthesia + incontinence/retention + leg weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the commonest cause of cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A large central lumbar disc herniation (typically L4/5 or L5/S1) compressing the roots.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List other causes of cauda equina syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Tumours (especially metastases)
  • spondylolisthesis
  • epidural abscess
  • and trauma

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List the red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Saddle anaesthesia (loss of perineal sensation)
  • loss of bladder/rectal sensation
  • urinary retention or incontinence (painless retention with overflow is a late, ominous sign)
  • faecal incontinence
  • bilateral sciatica
  • bilateral/severe leg weakness
  • and reduced anal tone on PR

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the screening approach for CES in suspicious back pain?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Ask about bladder, bowel, saddle and sexual symptoms, and do a PR for anal tone plus perineal sensation. Crucially, ask about the EARLY bladder symptoms — loss of awareness of the bladder filling, loss of the desire to void, altered sensation of urine passing, a poor stream or needing to strain. Those are what should trigger the scan.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Is urinary retention a good screening finding for cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: No — it is a LATE finding, and waiting for it means waiting until the damage is largely done. The findings to act on are the early bladder symptoms, altered saddle sensation, bilateral leg symptoms and sexual dysfunction.Note too that normal anal tone and a normal post-void residual do NOT exclude cauda equina syndrome: if the history has red flags, the patient still needs the MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Distinguish CES-I from CES-R.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• CES-I (incomplete) = altered urinary sensation/difficulty — the window to intervene
  • CES-R (retention) = established painless retention with overflow — a worse prognosis

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the investigation of choice in suspected cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Immediate hospital admission and an emergency MRI, plus a bladder scan. The operational rule that decides outcomes: the scan happens at the hospital the patient presents to, on the same day, out of hours if necessary — not deferred to the morning list or to a transfer. Image the whole spine if there are any UMN signs, because a thoracic or conus lesion can imitate cauda equina.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the definitive management of cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Emergency surgical decompression (lumbar decompression/discectomy) as soon as possible to relieve pressure on the roots.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why is the timing of surgery so important in cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Outcomes — especially bladder/bowel and sexual function — depend on how early decompression happens; once complete (painless retention) develops, recovery is much less likely, so operate before that point.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How are the underlying causes and complications of CES managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Treat the cause — dexamethasone + radiotherapy/surgery if malignant, antibiotics + drainage for an abscess; plus supportive care (bladder/bowel management, physiotherapy, pressure-area care, psychological support).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Degeneration of specific spinal cord tracts due to vitamin B12 deficiency — affecting the dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts and spinocerebellar tracts.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the 'core concept' of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: 'Combined' means multiple tracts degenerate together, giving a mixed picture — dorsal column sensory loss + corticospinal UMN signs + spinocerebellar ataxia — because B12 is needed for myelin integrity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What deficit results from dorsal column involvement in SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Distal, symmetrical tingling/burning/sensory loss (legs > arms) with impaired proprioception and vibration (and fine touch).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What deficit results from lateral corticospinal tract involvement in SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: UMN signs — motor weakness, hyperreflexia and spasticity (legs first), with brisk knee reflexes and upgoing plantars.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What deficit results from spinocerebellar tract involvement in SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Dorsal columns — loss of CONSCIOUS proprioception and vibration, which is what produces sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg's sign (the patient falls when the eyes close). The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception; their loss gives a cerebellar-type unsteadiness that is present with the eyes open too, and so is NOT Romberg-positive.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the signature mixed UMN/LMN 'paradox' of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Absent ankle jerks (LMN) together with upgoing plantars and brisk knee jerks (UMN) — because B12 deficiency causes a peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle jerks) alongside corticospinal disease (upgoing plantars).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why is Romberg's sign positive in SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Loss of proprioception (dorsal columns) means the patient falls when they close their eyes — a sensory ataxia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List the causes of the B12 deficiency underlying SACD.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor — the commonest)
  • gastrectomy/ileal disease/Crohn's
  • a vegan diet
  • and malabsorption

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why is nitrous oxide a 'trap' cause of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Nitrous oxide (recreational 'laughing gas') inactivates B12 by oxidising its cobalt, so it can precipitate SACD even with normal B12 stores — increasingly seen in young people.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why must folate not be given before B12 in suspected B12 deficiency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Folate drives new red-cell production that consumes already-low B12 stores, precipitating or worsening SACD — so always replace B12 before (or with) folate.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Describe the sensory and motor clinical features of SACD.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
Symmetrical, distal, legs > arms:
  • sensory — distal tingling/burning/paraesthesia and numbness with loss of proprioception/vibration → sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg's
  • motor — progressive leg weakness and spasticity (UMN) with later gait difficulty

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What other (non-neurological) B12-deficiency features may accompany SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia — though the neurology can occur WITHOUT anaemia — glossitis, and cognitive/psychiatric change ('megaloblastic madness'); progression is subacute (weeks–months) and untreated deficits become permanent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List the key differentials for SACD.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Multiple sclerosis (relapsing, CNS lesions in space/time, optic neuritis)
  • cord compression (UMN + sensory level, structural cause on MRI)
  • tabes dorsalis/neurosyphilis (dorsal column loss + Argyll Robertson pupils)
  • peripheral neuropathy (no UMN/myelopathy)
  • and copper deficiency (an almost identical myelopathy mimic)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the key investigation in SACD, and the supporting blood findings?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Serum vitamin B12 (low) — the key test; plus folate, FBC and blood film showing a megaloblastic/macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Which more sensitive markers help if the B12 level is borderline?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine (both raised in B12 deficiency).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What further tests confirm the cause and support the diagnosis of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies (for pernicious anaemia)
  • MRI spine may show increased signal in the dorsal/lateral columns (the 'inverted V'/'rabbit ears' sign)
  • and ask about nitrous oxide use and a vegan diet

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the management of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Urgent IM B12 replacement (hydroxocobalamin) — often alternate-day loading then maintenance, with more intensive loading for neurological cases; critically, give B12 BEFORE folate; and treat the cause (lifelong B12 in pernicious anaemia, stop nitrous oxide, dietary advice, treat malabsorption).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the prognosis of SACD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Early treatment allows recovery/improvement, but delayed treatment leads to permanent deficit — so treat urgently; physio/OT help residual deficits.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A fluid-filled cavity (a 'syrinx') within the spinal cord — a collection of CSF-like fluid inside the cord substance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the 'core concept' of syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The syrinx forms centrally and expands outward, so it hits the crossing spinothalamic fibres (pain + temperature) FIRST, sparing the peripheral dorsal columns until later.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the hallmark clinical finding of syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A 'dissociated' sensory loss — pain and temperature lost but light touch, proprioception and vibration preserved — classically in a 'cape' distribution (neck, shoulders, arms).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the memory hook for syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: 'Syringomyelia = Superman — a cape, and can't feel pain' (a cape distribution of sensory loss + loss of pain).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Explain the mechanism of the dissociated sensory loss in syringomyelia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The spinothalamic tract (pain + temperature) decussates in the anterior (white) commissure at the centre of the cord; a central syrinx expands outward and destroys these crossing fibres first (losing pain/temperature), while the dorsal columns run peripherally and are spared early — hence the dissociation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why is the sensory loss of syringomyelia in a 'cape' distribution?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The syrinx is typically cervical/upper thoracic, so it affects the segments supplying the neck, shoulders and arms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the classic clinical clue of syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: The patient burns or injures their hands without realising (they can't feel pain/temperature) → painless burns/injuries and Charcot joints.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: List the causes of syringomyelia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Chiari malformation (the commonest association — cerebellar tonsils bulging through the foramen magnum, disrupting CSF flow)
  • trauma (post-traumatic syrinx)
  • spinal cord tumours
  • and idiopathic

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the key association to image for in syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A Chiari I malformation (low cerebellar tonsils) at the craniocervical junction — always image the brain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What UMN feature develops as a syrinx expands?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Spastic weakness (especially of the legs) with upgoing plantars, from corticospinal tract involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: Why can a cervical syrinx cause Horner's syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: It can involve the sympathetic outflow (T1), producing ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What other features occur as a syrinx expands?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Bladder/bowel dysfunction (autonomic tracts)
  • scoliosis (asymmetric paraspinal muscle involvement)
  • and hand wasting/LMN signs (anterior horn cell involvement — claw hand, wasting)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is syringobulbia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Extension of the syrinx into the brainstem (medulla), causing cranial nerve signs, tongue wasting and nystagmus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the key investigation in syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Full spine MRI with contrast — visualises the syrinx (contrast excludes a tumour or tethered cord); plus brain MRI to exclude a Chiari malformation at the craniocervical junction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How does MRI guide management in syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: It both confirms the syrinx and identifies the cause (Chiari, tumour, tethered cord), which determines management.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: What is the overarching management principle in syringomyelia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: Treat the underlying cause of the syrinx, and shunt a persistent/symptomatic syrinx.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How is the cause of a syrinx treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back:
• Surgical decompression of a Chiari malformation (foramen magnum decompression restores CSF flow and can collapse the syrinx)
  • resecting a tumour
  • or releasing a tethered cord

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.front: How is a persistent/symptomatic syrinx managed, and what supportive care is needed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.back: A shunt is placed into the syrinx (syringo-subarachnoid/pleural/peritoneal) to drain it; supportive care includes neuropathic pain management, physiotherapy, skin/joint protection (preventing burns, injuries and Charcot joints), and serial MRI to monitor progression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What is restless legs syndrome (RLS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Also called Willis-Ekbom disease — a sensorimotor disorder characterised by an uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest and in the evening/night, and relieved by movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What is the defining four-part pattern of RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Urge to move the legs + worse at rest + worse in the evening + relieved by movement — an essentially diagnostic pattern.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: State the 'URGE' diagnostic criteria for RLS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• (1) Urge to move the legs (usually with uncomfortable sensations)
  • (2) worse at Rest
  • (3) relieved by movement (Getting up/walking)
  • (4) worse in the Evening/night

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What are the two clinical priorities in RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Check ferritin — iron deficiency is a common, treatable cause, and the RLS threshold for replacing iron is higher than for diagnosing anaemia — and, if drug treatment is needed, start an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin or pregabalin) FIRST-LINE.Dopamine agonists are no longer first-line.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: Contrast primary and secondary RLS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Primary = idiopathic, often familial (positive family history), often younger onset
  • Secondary = due to an underlying condition, often with later onset

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: List the key secondary causes of RLS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Iron deficiency (± anaemia)
  • pregnancy
  • chronic kidney disease/uraemia
  • diabetes/peripheral neuropathy
  • and drugs

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: Which drugs worsen RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Antidepressants (SSRIs/TCAs/mirtazapine)
  • antipsychotics
  • antihistamines
  • and dopamine antagonists (e.g. metoclopramide)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: Explain the iron/dopamine link in RLS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: There is central dopaminergic dysfunction, and iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis (tyrosine hydroxylase), so low brain iron impairs dopamine function — explaining why iron deficiency causes RLS and why dopamine agonists treat it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What are the clinical features of RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• An uncontrollable urge to move the legs, usually at night and at rest, relieved by voluntary movement
  • crawling or throbbing paraesthesia
  • and periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS) — repetitive leg jerks in sleep, often noticed by the partner

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: Which single feature is defining for RLS versus other leg complaints?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Relief by movement (with worsening at rest) — the defining discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What are the consequences of RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Sleep disturbance/insomnia (difficulty falling asleep)
  • and daytime fatigue

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: How is RLS distinguished from drug-induced akathisia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Akathisia is a generalised inner restlessness, NOT confined to the legs, and follows starting or increasing an antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or an SSRI. Crucially there is no evening/night pattern — akathisia is also worse sitting still and eased by moving, so 'relief by movement' does not separate them.The discriminators are leg-confined versus whole-body, the circadian pattern, and the drug history.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: How is RLS distinguished from peripheral neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory loss/burning that is NOT relieved by movement, unlike RLS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: How is RLS distinguished from nocturnal leg cramps and vascular claudication?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Leg cramps are painful muscle contractions, not an urge
  • peripheral vascular disease causes claudication that is worse on exertion and relieved by rest — the opposite of RLS

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: How is RLS diagnosed and investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Clinically, from the characteristic (URGE) pattern. Ferritin is the key investigation — and not simply to exclude iron deficiency: offer iron replacement if ferritin is 75 micrograms/L or below, or transferrin saturation is under 20%, even with a normal full blood count. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant so can be falsely normal. Then work out WHY the iron is low — a low ferritin in a man or postmenopausal woman warrants GI investigation. Also consider U&E (chronic kidney disease), glucose/HbA1c, a pregnancy test and a drug review.Polysomnography only if there is diagnostic doubt or to assess PLMS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What is the overarching management principle in RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Treat any underlying iron deficiency and address triggers, then — if drug treatment is needed — an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin or pregabalin) first-line.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What non-drug and cause-directed measures are used in RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back:
• Treat iron deficiency with oral iron (ferrous sulfate or fumarate) if the ferritin is low — this alone can resolve the RLS, and IV iron is a specialist option
  • manage chronic kidney disease
  • review and STOP the aggravating drug (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide), which is often curative on its own
  • and lifestyle measures — sleep hygiene, avoiding evening caffeine/alcohol/nicotine, moderate exercise, leg massage/stretching
In pregnancy, RLS is usually third-trimester, linked to iron and folate deficiency, and settles within days of delivery — manage non-pharmacologically plus iron, and avoid dopamine agonists and pregabalin.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What pharmacological options are used for troublesome RLS symptoms?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: FIRST-LINE is an alpha-2-delta ligand — gabapentin or pregabalin — especially where there is pain or neuropathy. Both are off-label for RLS and are Schedule 3 controlled drugs, need dose reduction in renal impairment, carry an MHRA warning about severe respiratory depression (especially with opioids and in the elderly), and pregabalin should be avoided in pregnancy. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine patch) are NO LONGER first-line because of augmentation and impulse-control disorders.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: What is 'augmentation' in RLS, and how does it affect management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Long-term dopamine agonists can cause augmentation — symptoms become earlier, more intense and spread (a paradoxical worsening) — which is why NICE now recommends gabapentin or pregabalin first-line and says dopamine agonists should not be. If augmentation happens, do NOT increase the dose: reduce and withdraw the dopamine agonist slowly with specialist advice and switch to an alpha-2-delta ligand.Dopamine agonists also cause impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating — warn the family and ask at every review) and sudden onset of sleep.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.front: Why must ferritin be checked in RLS even without anaemia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.back: Iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, so low brain iron impairs dopamine function. The RLS threshold is deliberately higher than for anaemia: replace iron if ferritin is 75 micrograms/L or below, or transferrin saturation is under 20%, even with a normal FBC — replacement can resolve the RLS.Then establish why the iron is low.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is raised intracranial pressure (ICP), and what is the normal range?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: An increase in the pressure inside the skull above normal (normal ICP = 5–15 mmHg) — a neurological emergency because the brain is enclosed in a rigid box.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: State the Monro-Kellie doctrine.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: The rigid skull holds three components in equilibrium — brain (~1400 mL) + CSF (~150 mL) + blood (~150 mL) — so any increase in one must be offset by a decrease in another, or ICP rises.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Which components are displaced first to compensate for a rising volume, and how?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: CSF (pushed into the spinal theca) and venous blood (squeezed out) are displaced first, keeping ICP normal at first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe the intracranial compliance curve.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Compensation works up to a point; once the CSF/venous reserve is exhausted, small further volume increases cause large ICP rises (the curve is flat, then steep) → decompensation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the equation for cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: CPP = MAP − ICP; as ICP rises, CPP falls → cerebral ischaemia, which drives the Cushing's response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: At what rate is CSF produced, and how does disrupting this raise ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: ~500 mL/day in a normal production–absorption equilibrium; disrupting it (obstruction/impaired absorption) causes hydrocephalus and raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: List the mass-lesion and oedema causes of raised ICP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Mass lesions — tumour (primary/mets), haematoma (extradural/subdural/intracerebral), abscess
  • Cerebral oedema — traumatic brain injury, ischaemic stroke, hypoxic injury, hepatic encephalopathy

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: List the CSF/venous and idiopathic causes of raised ICP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• ↑CSF (hydrocephalus) from obstruction to CSF flow or impaired absorption
  • ↑venous volume from cerebral venous sinus thrombosis/obstruction
  • and idiopathic intracranial hypertension

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What are the early clinical features of raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Headache (worse on waking, lying flat, coughing or straining)
  • effortless or projectile vomiting
  • drowsiness and a falling GCS
  • papilloedema
  • and a CN VI palsy as a false localising sign
A unilateral dilated pupil is NOT early — it means uncal herniation and is a pre-terminal emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Why is the raised-ICP headache worse in the morning and positionally?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: It is worse on waking, lying down, bending over and with coughing/straining/Valsalva, because lying flat and raised intrathoracic pressure further raise ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is characteristic about the vomiting of raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: It is often effortless or projectile and may occur without preceding nausea — but the presence of nausea does not exclude raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Explain the mechanism of papilloedema in raised ICP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Blurred disc margins with an elevated disc. The optic nerve sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space, so raised CSF pressure is transmitted along it and the disc bulges forward. Important caveat: papilloedema takes hours to days to develop, so a normal fundus does not exclude acutely raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Why is a CN VI (abducens) palsy a 'false localising sign' in raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to stretch, so failure of abduction/diplopia occurs without indicating the site of the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is Cushing's reflex?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: The physiological response to dangerously raised ICP → hypertension + bradycardia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Explain the logic of Cushing's reflex.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: If ICP is high, MAP must rise to maintain CPP (CPP = MAP − ICP), so the body drives up blood pressure (hypertension); the hypertension then triggers a reflex bradycardia via the baroreceptors.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is Cushing's triad, and what does it signify?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Hypertension (widened pulse pressure) + bradycardia + irregular breathing (from brainstem compression of the respiratory centre) — a pre-terminal sign of critically raised ICP with herniation imminent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe uncal (transtentorial) herniation.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: The uncus compresses CN III → a fixed, dilated pupil and a 'down-and-out' eye on the affected side, ± contralateral hemiparesis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe tonsillar herniation ('coning').
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: The cerebellar tonsils herniate through the foramen magnum → brainstem (respiratory centre) compression → respiratory arrest and death.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is subfalcine herniation?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Herniation of the cingulate gyrus under the falx cerebri.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What does a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in a deteriorating patient indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Uncal herniation compressing CN III — an emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Why is lumbar puncture contraindicated in raised ICP with a mass lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Removing CSF from below can precipitate tonsillar herniation (coning), so CT imaging must be done first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What investigations are used in raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Removing CSF from below a pressure gradient can precipitate tonsillar herniation (coning). Image first — but the trap is that a NORMAL CT does not make an LP safe: if the clinical signs of raised ICP are present (a falling GCS, new focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, abnormal posturing, bradycardia with hypertension), the LP is still contraindicated whatever the scan shows.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the overarching management principle for raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Treat the underlying cause + emergency measures to lower ICP + protect cerebral perfusion — a neurosurgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: How is the underlying cause of raised ICP treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Evacuate a haematoma
  • resect/debulk a tumour
  • shunt hydrocephalus
  • or anticoagulate cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What positioning and osmotic measures lower ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Nurse head-up about 30° with a neutral neck, which aids venous drainage. Give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline to draw fluid out of the brain — hypertonic saline is often preferred if the patient is hypovolaemic or hypotensive, because mannitol's osmotic diuresis can drop the MAP and so the CPP.Monitor sodium and osmolality, and remember this is temporising: it buys time, it is not the treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the role of controlled ventilation and supportive measures in raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Intubate and keep the PaCO2 at 4.5–5.0 kPa — the low end of normal, not lower. Hyperventilating below that does lower ICP, but by reducing cerebral blood flow, and sustained hypocapnia causes ischaemia and worsens outcome; deeper hyperventilation is a short-term rescue only, for impending herniation. Add sedation and analgesia, treat fever and seizures, and drain CSF via an EVD if there is hydrocephalus. Never use hypotonic fluids (5% dextrose, 0.45% saline) — they worsen cerebral oedema.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: When are corticosteroids used in raised ICP, and when are they not?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Dexamethasone is used for vasogenic oedema around tumours/abscesses — but NOT for traumatic or ischaemic (stroke) oedema.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the surgical last resort for refractory raised ICP, and how is perfusion protected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Decompressive craniectomy. Cerebral perfusion is protected by aiming for a CPP of 60–70 mmHg and treating a sustained ICP above 20–22 mmHg, supporting the MAP and avoiding hypotension and hypoxia.Escalate early: discuss immediately with neurosurgery if the GCS is 8 or less after resuscitation, if it deteriorates at any point, or if imaging shows a surgically significant lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is a radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve ROOT (as it exits the spine) causing pain, sensory disturbance, weakness and reflex loss in that root's dermatome/myotome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the 'core concept' of a radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: It is a root-level (dermatomal) problem — the deficit follows a single nerve root's dermatome and myotome — distinguishing it from a peripheral nerve palsy (nerve territory) and a cord/central lesion (UMN signs).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the commonest cause of a radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: A prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc compressing the exiting nerve root.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Distinguish radiculopathy, peripheral nerve palsy and myelopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Radiculopathy = dermatome + myotome of a single root (LMN signs, radicular pain)
  • peripheral nerve palsy = a nerve's territory (LMN)
  • myelopathy = signs below the level (long tracts) with UMN signs (↑tone, ↑reflexes, upgoing plantars) + a sensory level

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: List the causes of radiculopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Prolapsed disc (commonest)
  • degenerative disease (spondylosis, osteophytes, foraminal stenosis — commoner in older patients)
  • trauma
  • tumour (spinal metastases)
  • infection (abscess, herpes zoster → dermatomal)
  • and spondylolisthesis

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe the clinical features of a prolapsed-disc radiculopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Dermatomal leg pain (usually worse than the back pain), often worse on sitting, that is radicular — shooting/electric, radiating down the dermatome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What three components make up the root deficit?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Dermatomal sensory disturbance
  • myotomal weakness (muscles that root supplies)
  • and a reduced/absent reflex (if the root subserves one)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What are the nerve root tension signs, and which roots do they test?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Straight leg raise (SLR) reproduces radicular pain in lower lumbar (L5/S1) radiculopathy
  • the femoral stretch test is used for upper lumbar (L3/L4)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: State the reflex root levels.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Ankle = S1–2
  • knee = L3–4
  • biceps = C5–6
  • triceps = C7–8

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Give the upper-limb dermatome landmarks (C5–T1).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• C5 = lateral arm, the 'regimental badge' (shoulder abduction, elbow flexion; biceps jerk)
  • C6 = thumb + index (elbow flexion, wrist extension)
  • C7 = middle finger + palm (elbow extension, wrist flexion; triceps jerk)
  • C8 = ring + little finger (finger flexion)
  • T1 = medial forearm and arm (finger abduction)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Give the trunk dermatome landmarks (T4, T10, L1).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• T4 = nipples
  • T10 = umbilicus
  • L1 = inguinal ligament

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Give the lower-limb dermatome landmarks (L4, L5, S1).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• L4 = medial shin / medial malleolus, below the knee (L3 is the knee itself)
  • L5 = big toe/dorsum of foot
  • S1 = little toe/lateral foot and sole

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe an L3/L4 radiculopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Sensory: anterior thigh/medial knee and shin
  • Motor: knee extension (quadriceps)
  • Reflex: reduced knee jerk (L3–4)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe an L5 radiculopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Sensory: big toe/dorsum of foot, lateral shin
  • Motor: weak dorsiflexion of the foot and big toe (EHL) → foot drop, and weak hip abduction
  • No easily-tested reflex

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: Describe an S1 radiculopathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Sensory: little toe/lateral foot and sole
  • Motor: weak plantarflexion (gastrocnemius) and foot eversion
  • Reflex: reduced ankle jerk (S1–2)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is 'sciatica', and which roots usually cause it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Radicular pain down the back of the leg, usually from an L5 or S1 root.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is cauda equina syndrome (CES)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Compression of the cauda equina nerve roots (below L1/L2) — a surgical emergency that can cause permanent paralysis and incontinence.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: List the red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
Bladder change, and the EARLY changes are what matter:
  • loss of the sensation of bladder filling
  • loss of the urge to void
  • loss of awareness of urinary flow
  • a poor stream or straining
Painless retention with overflow incontinence is a LATE sign with a far worse prognosis — waiting for it is the classic error.
  • Also faecal incontinence
  • sexual dysfunction (loss of genital sensation, new erectile/ejaculatory failure)
  • bilateral sciatica
  • bilateral or severe leg weakness
  • and saddle (perineal) anaesthesia
Do NOT rely on a digital rectal examination: normal anal tone does not exclude cauda equina and must never delay the MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the immediate action for suspected cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Immediate hospital admission → emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine, within 4 hours of request and done at the presenting hospital before transfer → immediate spinal surgical referral with the images.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: State the high-yield rule for cauda equina.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Any radiculopathy with bladder/bowel dysfunction or saddle anaesthesia is cauda equina until proven otherwise → emergency MRI. New bilateral sciatica WITHOUT those features warrants urgent (2-week) spinal/MSK referral with cauda equina safety-netting — and emergency referral the moment any of them appears.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: List the other 'sinister' back-pain red flags.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Age <20 or >50 with new onset
  • trauma
  • a cancer history
  • fever/weight loss
  • immunosuppression or IV drug use or recent bacterial infection (spinal infection)
  • long-term corticosteroids/osteoporosis (fracture)
  • night pain
  • thoracic pain
  • and progressive neurology
No single red flag is diagnostic — it is the pattern that counts.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: How is a radiculopathy diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Clinically — the history plus the dermatome/myotome/reflex examination localises the root, with SLR/femoral stretch for tension signs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: When is MRI of the spine indicated in radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: Do NOT routinely image in a non-specialist setting. MRI belongs in a specialist setting where the result would change management (considering injection or surgery), or where there are red flags or a severe/progressive deficit; emergency MRI if cauda equina is suspected. Most simple radiculopathies do not need immediate imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the overarching management principle for radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Most improve with conservative management
  • escalate for red flags or persistent/severe deficit
  • and perform emergency surgery for cauda equina

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the first-line conservative management of most radiculopathies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Stay active and avoid bed rest
  • NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (codeine ± paracetamol short-term only if NSAIDs are unsuitable, and no opioids for chronic sciatica)
  • and physiotherapy
NICE says do NOT offer gabapentinoids, other anticonvulsants, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica — no overall evidence of benefit and evidence of harm. Most disc-related radiculopathies resolve over weeks. Safety-net every patient about cauda equina.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the role of epidural injection in sciatica?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: An epidural injection of local anaesthetic and steroid is considered in ACUTE and SEVERE sciatica — it is not an escalation step for chronic persistent pain, and spinal injections are not offered for low back pain alone.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: When is surgery (discectomy/decompression) indicated in radiculopathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back: For a severe/progressive neurological deficit, or symptoms refractory to conservative treatment; emergency decompression is required for cauda equina syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.front: What is the reflex-level mnemonic for the four main reflexes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.back:
• Ankle S1–2 ('buckle my shoe')
  • knee L3–4 ('kick the door')
  • biceps C5–6 ('pick up sticks')
  • triceps C7–8 ('lay them straight')

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What is a peripheral nerve injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Damage to an individual peripheral nerve (or the brachial plexus) causing a lower motor neurone (LMN) pattern of weakness and sensory loss in that nerve's territory (wasting, hyporeflexia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What is the 'core concept' of peripheral nerve palsies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Each nerve has a predictable motor + sensory territory and a characteristic mechanism of injury (a specific fracture or compression point), so the deficit localises the lesion — pattern recognition is the whole skill.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Give the three quick 'deficit → nerve' localisers.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• Wrist drop → radial nerve
  • claw hand → ulnar nerve
  • foot drop → common peroneal nerve

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the axillary nerve (roots, motor, sensory, mechanism).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• C5–6
  • motor: shoulder abduction (deltoid)
  • sensory: 'regimental badge' over the inferior deltoid
  • injured by a humeral neck fracture/shoulder dislocation → a flattened deltoid

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the radial nerve (roots, motor, sensory, mechanism).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
C5–T1. Motor: extension — triceps at the elbow, then wrist, fingers and thumb; where the lesion sits decides what is lost.
  • Axilla (crutch palsy) → triceps AND wrist/finger extension lost
  • Spiral groove (midshaft humerus) → triceps SPARED, wrist drop
  • Posterior interosseous → finger drop with wrist extension largely preserved and no sensory loss
Sensory: the dorsal first web space.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the median nerve (roots, motor, sensory, mechanism).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• C6–T1
  • Motor: the LOAF muscles at the wrist (and pronation plus weak wrist flexion if injured at the elbow)
  • sensory: the palmar surface of the lateral 3½ fingers — but the palm and thenar eminence are SPARED in carpal tunnel syndrome, because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves above the wrist and passes over the flexor retinaculum
  • A wrist lesion → carpal tunnel syndrome

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the ulnar nerve (roots, motor, sensory, mechanism).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• C8, T1
  • motor: the intrinsic hand muscles except LOAF (and wrist flexion)
  • sensory: medial 1½ fingers
  • a medial epicondyle fracture → CLAW HAND

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the long thoracic nerve.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• C5–7
  • supplies serratus anterior
  • injured by a blow to the ribs (sport) or mastectomy → a WINGED SCAPULA

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: State the high-yield fracture–nerve pairs.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• Surgical neck of humerus / shoulder dislocation → axillary
  • midshaft humerus → radial (wrist drop)
  • medial epicondyle → ulnar (claw hand)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What are the LOAF muscles, and which nerve supplies them?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Lumbricals (lateral 2), Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis — supplied by the MEDIAN nerve; the ULNAR nerve supplies all the other intrinsic hand muscles.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What is carpal tunnel syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Compression of the median nerve as it passes under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What are the features of carpal tunnel syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Pain and tingling/numbness of the palmar surface of the lateral 3½ fingers, worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand; in chronic cases thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction and opposition. The localising point: the PALM AND THENAR EMINENCE ARE SPARED, because the palmar cutaneous branch passes over the flexor retinaculum rather than through the tunnel.Numbness that includes the palm means the lesion is proximal to the tunnel, or is a C6 root problem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What are the two bedside signs of carpal tunnel syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Tinel's sign (tapping over the nerve → tingling) and Phalen's test (sustained wrist flexion → symptoms).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What are the causes/associations of carpal tunnel syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• Idiopathic (commonest)
  • pregnancy
  • hypothyroidism
  • diabetes
  • rheumatoid arthritis
  • acromegaly and obesity

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: How is carpal tunnel syndrome managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: For mild or intermittent symptoms: a night wrist splint in the neutral position, activity modification, and a corticosteroid injection if that is not enough. Refer for decompression (flexor retinaculum release) if symptoms are severe or constant, if there is a progressive or established motor or sensory deficit — thenar wasting or weakness — or if there is no improvement after about 3 months of conservative treatment.Do not splint a patient who already has thenar wasting: that is axonal loss, and thenar bulk recovers poorly after late surgery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What is cubital tunnel syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Compression of the ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow) — tingling/numbness of the 4th/5th fingers worse on elbow flexion, with wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles → claw hand.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Explain the 'ulnar paradox'.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: A more proximal (elbow) ulnar lesion produces a LESS obvious claw than a distal (wrist) lesion, because the proximal lesion also knocks out the ulnar-supplied flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little finger, so those fingers flex less.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe Erb's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: An upper trunk (C5, C6) brachial plexus injury from shoulder dystocia at birth or traction → the 'waiter's tip' posture (arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated), with C5–6 sensory loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe Klumpke's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: A lower trunk (C8, T1) brachial plexus injury from traction on an ABDUCTED arm — classically breech delivery with the arm above the head, or an adult grabbing something to break a fall. It gives a claw hand from intrinsic muscle paralysis, ± Horner's syndrome (T1 sympathetic fibres).Horner's in a neonate indicates a T1 root avulsion — the worst prognostic group, needing early specialist referral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Contrast Erb's and Klumpke's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• Erb's = upper (C5–6) = waiter's tip, from downward traction on the head with the shoulder fixed — the shoulder dystocia mechanism
  • Klumpke's = lower (C8–T1) = claw hand ± Horner's, from traction on an ABDUCTED arm (breech delivery, or grabbing to break a fall)
The mechanisms are different, and that is the discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe the common peroneal (fibular) nerve injury.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: The nerve winds around the neck of the fibula (superficial and vulnerable); injured by a fibular neck fracture, a tight plaster cast, prolonged leg crossing/squatting, or compression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What are the features of a common peroneal nerve palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Foot drop (weak dorsiflexion and eversion) → a high-stepping gait, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral shin.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Name other lower-limb nerve injuries and their features.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
• Sciatic (hip dislocation, misplaced IM injection)
  • tibial (tarsal tunnel)
  • femoral (weak knee extension, absent knee jerk)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: What is the differential for foot drop?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back:
Common peroneal nerve palsy, L5 radiculopathy, a sciatic nerve lesion, and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease. Separate them with two things.
  • INVERSION (tibialis posterior — a tibial-nerve muscle but an L5 myotome): preserved in common peroneal palsy, weak in L5 radiculopathy or a sciatic lesion
  • ANKLE JERK (S1): preserved in both common peroneal palsy and L5 radiculopathy, lost in a sciatic lesion
So normal inversion and normal ankle jerk = common peroneal; weak inversion with a normal ankle jerk = L5 root (ask about back pain, saddle sensation and bladder); weak inversion with an absent ankle jerk = sciatic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe neurapraxia (Seddon classification).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: A temporary conduction block (myelin injury) with the axon intact → full recovery over days–weeks (the best prognosis) — e.g. 'Saturday night palsy' (radial nerve compression while asleep).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe axonotmesis (Seddon classification).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: The axon is severed but the connective tissue sheath is intact → recovery by axonal regrowth at ~1 mm/day.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: Describe neurotmesis (Seddon classification).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Complete nerve transection → poor recovery; it needs surgical repair.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: How are peripheral nerve injuries assessed and investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Characterise the motor + sensory deficit to localise the nerve, identify the mechanism, and examine for the classic sign (wrist drop, claw hand, winged scapula, foot drop); nerve conduction studies/EMG confirm, localise and grade the lesion, with imaging for any underlying fracture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: How are compression/neurapraxic nerve injuries managed conservatively?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Remove the cause, splinting, physiotherapy, and treat the underlying cause; corticosteroid injection (e.g. in carpal tunnel) — many recover.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.front: When is surgery indicated in peripheral nerve injury, and what supports recovery in wrist/foot drop?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.back: Decompression (carpal/cubital tunnel) or nerve repair/grafting for transection (neurotmesis); splints/orthoses (an ankle-foot orthosis for foot drop) plus physiotherapy support function while awaiting recovery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) → dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia → a movement disorder.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the 'core concept' of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: It is fundamentally a dopamine-deficiency state in the nigrostriatal pathway; losing that dopamine tips the basal ganglia toward excess inhibition of movement → the motor triad of bradykinesia + rigidity + resting tremor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the classic motor triad of Parkinson's disease (TRAP)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Tremor (resting)
  • Rigidity
  • Akinesia/bradykinesia
  • and Postural instability.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Describe the tremor of Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• A resting tremor
  • ~4–6 Hz
  • 'pill-rolling'
  • asymmetric
  • worse at rest/with distraction
  • and improving with movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Describe the rigidity of Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: 'Cogwheel' rigidity — a tremor superimposed on lead-pipe rigidity — with increased tone throughout the range of movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Describe the bradykinesia of Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
Slowness and poverty of movement — the core diagnostic feature — with
  • micrographia
  • reduced arm swing
  • a shuffling festinant gait
  • difficulty initiating movement and hypomimia (mask-like face).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Why is bradykinesia so important in diagnosing Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Bradykinesia is essential for the diagnosis — a resting tremor alone is not Parkinson's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Why is asymmetry a key feature of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Parkinson's characteristically starts on one side (asymmetric onset) — a key discriminator from the mimics, which are often symmetric.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the gait of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Stooped posture
  • reduced arm swing
  • a shuffling/festinating gait
  • freezing and difficulty turning
  • postural instability (a later feature) leads to falls.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Explain the dopamine/basal ganglia mechanism in Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Loss of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurones reduces dopamine to the striatum; dopamine normally facilitates movement (exciting the direct pathway via D1, inhibiting the indirect pathway via D2), so its loss lets the movement-suppressing indirect pathway dominate → excess inhibition → reduced movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Lewy bodies — intracellular α-synuclein aggregates — in surviving neurones (shared with Lewy body dementia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: State the therapeutic corollary of the dopamine mechanism.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Restore dopamine → improve symptoms (levodopa etc.)
  • block dopamine (antipsychotics) → worsen Parkinson's/parkinsonism
  • abruptly withdraw dopaminergic drugs → NMS/parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What non-motor features often precede the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Anosmia (loss of smell)
  • REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams)
  • constipation and depression/anxiety.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What autonomic non-motor features occur in Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Postural hypotension, urinary symptoms and erectile dysfunction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What cognitive features occur in Parkinson's disease, and how do they relate to Lewy body dementia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Dementia is a late feature (Parkinson's dementia) with hallucinations; if dementia is early/prominent, the diagnosis is Lewy body dementia instead.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the prodrome of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Anosmia + REM sleep behaviour disorder + constipation + depression, which can predate the motor diagnosis by years.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Distinguish 'parkinsonism' from Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Parkinsonism is the syndrome (bradykinesia + rigidity + tremor); Parkinson's disease is its commonest cause, but the mimics must be excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What features discriminate idiopathic Parkinson's disease from its mimics?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Parkinson's = asymmetric onset, prominent resting tremor and a good levodopa response; mimics are often symmetric, with an absent/atypical tremor and a poor levodopa response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: How is essential tremor distinguished from Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor, symmetric, improves with alcohol and has no bradykinesia; Parkinson's has a resting tremor with bradykinesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: How is drug-induced parkinsonism recognised?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: It is symmetric and temporally related to a dopamine antagonist (antipsychotic/metoclopramide) — always review the drug chart.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What are the 'Parkinson's plus' red flags suggesting an atypical syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Early falls and vertical gaze palsy (PSP)
  • early autonomic failure (MSA)
  • early dementia/visual hallucinations (Lewy body dementia)
  • symmetry
  • and a poor levodopa response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: How is Parkinson's disease diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Clinically, using the UK Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria — bradykinesia plus at least one of rigidity/resting tremor/postural instability, with supportive features and no red flags for a mimic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the role of imaging in diagnosing Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Do not routinely image. A DaTSCAN answers one question only: is this parkinsonism or essential tremor? (uptake reduced in Parkinson's, normal in essential tremor). It does NOT separate Parkinson's from a Parkinson-plus syndrome — uptake is reduced in PSP, MSA and Lewy body dementia too, because all of them destroy the same presynaptic neurones.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Should a levodopa trial be used to diagnose Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: No. NICE says do not use acute levodopa or apomorphine challenge tests in the differential diagnosis of parkinsonian syndromes. Suspected Parkinson's is referred to a specialist quickly and untreated. A sustained response to levodopa is a supporting feature observed over time once treatment has been started, not a diagnostic test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the overarching management principle in Parkinson's disease (NICE)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Dopaminergic therapy titrated to symptoms plus MDT care
  • the first-line choice depends on whether motor symptoms affect quality of life
  • and Parkinson's drugs are never stopped abruptly.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the NICE first-line pharmacotherapy split in Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• If motor symptoms affect quality of life → offer levodopa (most effective, but more long-term motor complications)
  • If they don't yet affect quality of life → a choice of levodopa, a non-ergot dopamine agonist, or a MAO-B inhibitor (less motor improvement, fewer motor complications).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Describe levodopa therapy in Parkinson's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (co-careldopa/co-beneldopa; carbidopa/benserazide prevents peripheral conversion, reducing nausea) — the most effective drug, but long-term use causes motor complications.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: Describe dopamine agonists in Parkinson's disease and their key caution.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Non-ergot agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine) cause fewer motor complications than levodopa, but carry the highest risk of impulse-control disorders — gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive shopping. These can occur with ANY dopaminergic drug, so warn every patient and their family, and ask at every review. They also cause hallucinations and excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden onset of sleep, so such patients must not drive and must tell the DVLA.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What is the current role of anticholinergics such as procyclidine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: Not for idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Their role is drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonic reactions. Do not use them where there is dyskinesia or motor fluctuation, and avoid them in the elderly because of confusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What are the long-term motor complications of levodopa?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: 'Wearing off' (benefit fades before the next dose), 'on-off' fluctuations, and dyskinesias (involuntary movements at peak dose) — managed with adjuncts, dose fractionation or advanced therapies.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What advanced therapies exist for Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back:
• Deep brain stimulation (DBS) for motor fluctuations/dyskinesia refractory to medication
  • subcutaneous apomorphine and intrajejunal levodopa gel for advanced disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.front: What are the critical safety points in Parkinson's disease management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.back: NEVER stop Parkinson's medication abruptly, and never let doses be missed — the risk is acute akinesia and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, an NMS-like emergency. In hospital these are TIME-CRITICAL drugs: give levodopa within 30 minutes of the patient's own prescribed times, record their home timings on admission, and let them self-administer where appropriate. If they cannot swallow or are nil by mouth, do not simply omit doses — convert to dispersible co-beneldopa down an NG tube, or to a transdermal rotigotine patch, with specialist input. Avoid dopamine blockers: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, cinnarizine, and typical antipsychotics. Use cyclizine or ondansetron for nausea; domperidone is an option but prolongs the QT interval. If an antipsychotic is needed, first reduce the responsible dopaminergic drug, then consider quetiapine, and clozapine if that fails; never olanzapine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorders, and which two must you know?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Disorders of transmission across the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness; the two to know are myasthenia gravis (MG) and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the organising principle contrasting MG and LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG is postsynaptic (antibodies block ACh receptors) → weakness worsens with use (fatigability)
  • LEMS is presynaptic (antibodies block voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → less ACh release) → weakness improves briefly with use.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the site and antibody in MG versus LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG = postsynaptic, anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies (± anti-MuSK)
  • LEMS = presynaptic, anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies reducing ACh release.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How does weakness behave with use in MG versus LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG worsens with use (fatigability — worse through the day)
  • LEMS improves transiently with use (post-exercise facilitation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the pattern of weakness in MG and LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG affects the eyes first (ptosis, diplopia), then bulbar and proximal limb muscles
  • LEMS affects the proximal legs first (gait), with ocular/bulbar involvement less prominent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the reflexes and autonomic features of MG and LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG: reflexes normal, no autonomic features
  • LEMS: hyporeflexia (reflexes may return after exercise) and autonomic features (e.g. dry mouth).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the key disease associations of MG and LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG is associated with thymoma/thymic hyperplasia
  • LEMS is associated with small-cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the key treatments of MG and LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG: pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy
  • LEMS: treat the underlying cancer and 3,4-diaminopyridine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Give the one-line summary contrasting MG and LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• MG = fatigues with use, postsynaptic (AChR), thymoma
  • LEMS = improves with use, presynaptic (VGCC), small-cell lung cancer + hyporeflexia + autonomic features.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is myasthenia gravis (MG)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction — antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) impair neuromuscular transmission, causing fatigable muscle weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the hallmark/core concept of MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Fatigability — weakness that worsens with use (towards the end of the day) and improves with rest, because repeated activity progressively fails transmission and rest allows recovery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the pathophysiology of MG.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Autoantibodies against the postsynaptic AChR (present in ~85% of generalised MG) block, cross-link and destroy AChRs (complement-mediated) → fewer functional receptors → a smaller endplate potential → transmission fails with repeated use → fatigable weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are anti-MuSK antibodies in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Antibodies to muscle-specific kinase, found in some AChR-negative patients; they cause more bulbar/respiratory disease and respond less well to pyridostigmine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the thymus link in MG, and its practical consequence?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: The thymus is abnormal in most MG — thymic hyperplasia (around 70% of early-onset AChR-positive disease, nearer half across all MG) or thymoma (~10–15%) — and drives the autoimmunity, so ALL MG patients need CT or MRI of the chest to look for a thymoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the demographics of MG.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Bimodal — young women and older men; it is associated with other autoimmune diseases (especially thyroid disease).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the ocular features of MG, and why do they matter?
