conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Ptosis (worse on sustained upgaze) and diplopia (extraocular muscle weakness), often the presenting feature — eye involvement is characteristic and a key contrast with MND (which spares the eyes).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the bulbar features of MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Dysarthria
  • dysphagia
  • fatigable chewing and facial weakness (the myasthenic 'snarl').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the limb and respiratory features of MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Proximal limb weakness that worsens with repetition, and respiratory muscle weakness that can progress to myasthenic crisis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the signs of fatigability in MG, and how many stay purely ocular?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Ptosis worsens on sustained upgaze and weakness worsens on repeated testing, recovering with rest; about 15% remain purely ocular (ocular MG), while the rest generalise.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Which antibody tests are used in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Anti-AChR antibodies (positive in ~85% of generalised MG — the key test)
  • anti-MuSK antibodies if AChR-negative.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What electrophysiological findings support MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
  • single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Why is CT/MRI chest essential in all MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: To look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, given the strong thymus association.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the ice-pack test in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Ice held on a ptotic lid for about 2 minutes improves the ptosis by more than 2 mm, because cooling slows acetylcholinesterase so ACh lingers in the cleft.The edrophonium (Tensilon) test is now largely historical.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is a myasthenic crisis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Severe weakness involving the respiratory muscles causing respiratory failure — a life-threatening emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What can trigger a myasthenic crisis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Infection
  • surgery
  • stress
  • pregnancy
  • tapering or stopping immunosuppression
  • and — importantly — STARTING or rapidly escalating corticosteroids, which transiently worsen myasthenia.
Drugs that worsen MG: aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, quinine, IV magnesium and penicillamine (which can actually cause myasthenia), plus phenytoin, procainamide and lithium.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How is a myasthenic crisis managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Monitor SERIAL FVC (not peak flow) and watch the trend: below about 20 mL/kg (roughly 1–1.5 L in an adult) means ITU, below about 15 mL/kg means intubation; a single-breath count under 20 is worrying at the bedside. The trap: oxygen saturations and the blood gas stay NORMAL until the patient is about to arrest, so they are terminal signs, not triggers to act. Give IVIG or plasma exchange as rapid rescue, support ventilation, and treat the trigger.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the first-line symptomatic treatment of MG, and how does it work?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Pyridostigmine — an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases ACh at the NMJ, improving transmission. Typically 30–60 mg four to six times a day, titrated to response. Its muscarinic side effects are dose-limiting — abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, salivation, sweating, lacrimation, bradycardia — and pushing past them is what produces cholinergic crisis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What immunosuppression is used in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Corticosteroids (prednisolone) for more than mild disease, usually with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine or mycophenolate) — check TPMT activity before starting azathioprine, then monitor FBC and LFTs. Critically, starting steroids causes a transient but severe worsening in the first week or two that can precipitate myasthenic crisis, so start LOW and increase slowly, and start in hospital if there is bulbar or respiratory involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: When is thymectomy indicated in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: If a thymoma is present (any MG); it is also beneficial in AChR-positive generalised MG up to ~65 years (improving outcomes and reducing medication) even without a thymoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the rescue and refractory treatment options in MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: IVIG or plasma exchange for myasthenic crisis, severe exacerbation or pre-operative stabilisation; rituximab (especially MuSK MG), with newer biologic therapies available for refractory disease under specialist care.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Which drugs should be avoided in myasthenia gravis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Aminoglycosides (gentamicin)
  • macrolides (clarithromycin)
  • and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin)
  • beta-blockers
  • quinine
  • IV magnesium — a real trap, since magnesium sulfate is the treatment for eclampsia in exactly the young women who get myasthenia
  • and penicillamine, which can actually cause myasthenia.
Also phenytoin, procainamide and lithium.Flag myasthenia before any operation too: these patients are markedly sensitive to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An autoimmune disorder of the PRESYNAPTIC neuromuscular junction — antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) reduce acetylcholine release, causing muscle weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the 'core concept' of LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: It is the presynaptic mirror-image of myasthenia gravis — blocking the presynaptic calcium channel that triggers ACh release; this explains its two signatures: weakness that IMPROVES with use, and its strong link to small-cell lung cancer.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How common is a paraneoplastic cause in LEMS, and what is the tumour?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: About 50–60% of LEMS is paraneoplastic, associated with small-cell lung cancer (SCLC); the rest are primary autoimmune.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What clues suggest paraneoplastic (SCLC-related) LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Older age, a smoker, weight loss and cough — prompting a hunt for the tumour; primary autoimmune LEMS tends to be younger with other autoimmune disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Why does every LEMS patient need a hunt for SCLC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Because 50–60% are paraneoplastic; CT chest with or without PET is done, with ongoing surveillance, as LEMS can precede the cancer by months to years.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the single best discriminator between LEMS and MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• LEMS IMPROVES with repeated use (post-exercise facilitation)
  • MG WORSENS with use (fatigability).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Besides the response to use, what other clues point to LEMS over MG?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Reduced/absent reflexes and autonomic dysfunction — both typically absent in MG.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Explain the pathophysiology of LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Antibodies destroy presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels; less Ca²⁺ influx when the impulse arrives means less ACh vesicle release into the synapse → reduced muscle contraction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Explain why LEMS weakness improves with use (facilitation).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: With repeated/sustained stimulation, calcium accumulates in the presynaptic terminal → progressively more ACh is released → weakness (and reflexes) temporarily improve after brief exercise — the signature of a presynaptic disorder.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the pattern of weakness in LEMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Proximal muscle weakness (legs > arms) — difficulty climbing stairs, standing from a seat, raising the arms — which improves transiently with exercise then fatigues with sustained effort.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What autonomic features occur in LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Dry mouth (commonest)
  • blurred vision
  • impotence/erectile dysfunction
  • constipation
  • and postural hypotension.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What happens to the tendon reflexes in LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: They are reduced or absent, but may return/increase after brief exercise (post-exercise facilitation of reflexes).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How prominent is eye/bulbar involvement in LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Usually mild — a contrast with MG, where ocular/bulbar involvement is prominent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the classic triad of LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Proximal weakness (legs > arms)
  • autonomic dysfunction (e.g. dry mouth)
  • reduced/absent reflexes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the specific antibody test for LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (anti-VGCC) antibodies.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the electrophysiological hallmark of LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: A low baseline amplitude that INCREMENTS (increases) with high-frequency repetitive stimulation or after exercise — the opposite of MG's decremental response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the overarching management principle in LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Treat the underlying SCLC
  • enhance ACh release
  • immunosuppression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the first-line symptomatic drug in LEMS, and how does it work?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine) — it blocks presynaptic potassium channels, prolonging depolarisation → more Ca²⁺ influx → more ACh release; pyridostigmine may be added (less effective than in MG).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What immunosuppression is used in LEMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Corticosteroids with steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine)
  • IVIG or plasma exchange for severe cases
  • and treating the SCLC, which often improves the LEMS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: A rare but life-threatening reaction to dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics) — or to sudden withdrawal of dopaminergic drugs (e.g. levodopa) — characterised by fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental state.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the 'core concept' of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: It is fundamentally a state of acute dopamine deficiency/blockade in the CNS, from which the whole tetrad follows; the danger is hyperthermia + rhabdomyolysis, which can cause AKI and death.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Which drugs can cause NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Any dopamine antagonist. Commoner with typical than atypical antipsychotics, but every atypical causes it too (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, clozapine) — and atypical-associated NMS may have milder rigidity and less fever, so do not exclude it on that basis. Also the antiemetics metoclopramide and prochlorperazine (a phenothiazine, very widely prescribed). Finally, sudden withdrawal of levodopa or a dopamine agonist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the tetrad of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Fever (hyperthermia)
  • generalised 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity
  • autonomic instability
  • and altered mental state.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What does the 'FEVER' mnemonic for NMS stand for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Fever
  • Encephalopathy (altered mental state)
  • Vitals unstable (autonomic instability)
  • Elevated CK/enzymes
  • and Rigidity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the typical onset of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Most cases occur within about 2 weeks of starting, increasing or switching an antipsychotic — but NMS can happen at any point, including after months or years on a stable dose, so do not exclude it because the drug is not new. Once it starts it evolves over 1–3 days (contrast serotonin syndrome, which builds over hours).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How does dopamine blockade cause the hyperthermia of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Blockade of hypothalamic dopamine impairs thermoregulation → hyperthermia (worsened by heat generated by the rigidity).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How does dopamine blockade cause the rigidity of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Blockade of dopamine in the basal ganglia/nigrostriatal pathway causes muscle rigidity; the sustained rigidity itself generates heat, worsening the hyperthermia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How does levodopa withdrawal cause an NMS-like picture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Suddenly stopping levodopa (or a dopamine agonist) in a Parkinson's patient produces the same acute dopamine-deficient state → an NMS-like syndrome ('parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the rigidity → rhabdomyolysis cascade in NMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Sustained muscle rigidity → muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) → markedly raised CK → myoglobin release → acute kidney injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the triggers of NMS and serotonin syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NMS = a dopamine antagonist (antipsychotic) or levodopa withdrawal; serotonin syndrome = a serotonergic drug (SSRI, MAOI, triptan, tramadol).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the onset of NMS and serotonin syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NMS is slow (days); serotonin syndrome is rapid (hours).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast the neuromuscular findings of NMS and serotonin syndrome.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NMS = 'lead-pipe' rigidity with HYPOreflexia; serotonin syndrome = clonus, HYPERreflexia and myoclonus (± mydriasis and diarrhoea).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Which specific drugs are used for NMS versus serotonin syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NMS → dantrolene/bromocriptine; serotonin syndrome → cyproheptadine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: List the other mimics to exclude in suspected NMS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Malignant hyperthermia — triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium, with onset within minutes of induction, masseter spasm and a rising end-tidal CO₂ (also treated with dantrolene). Also sepsis/CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis), anticholinergic toxicity, and thyroid storm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What investigations support a diagnosis of NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: A raised CK is the key supporting test — typically at least 4× the upper limit of normal and often in the thousands, though it can lag behind the rigidity, so a normal early CK does not exclude NMS. Also leucocytosis, and AKI from myoglobinuria (check U&E and creatinine). Check the potassium urgently and do an ECG: rhabdomyolysis causes hyperkalaemia, which kills before the AKI does. Sepsis is commoner and cannot be excluded quickly — take cultures and treat for it in parallel.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How is NMS diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Clinically — a recent dopamine antagonist (or levodopa withdrawal) plus the tetrad and supporting labs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the immediate, essential first step in managing NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Stop the offending antipsychotic — and every other dopamine antagonist, antiemetics included (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine). Do NOT treat the agitation or delirium with an antipsychotic; use a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam. If NMS is due to levodopa withdrawal, restart the dopaminergic drug. A depot antipsychotic cannot be stopped, so supportive care must continue for weeks rather than days.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the supportive mainstay of NMS management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Generous IV fluids titrated to a urine output of about 1–2 mL/kg/hour (protecting the kidneys from myoglobin)
  • active cooling for hyperthermia
  • a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam for agitation
  • HDU/ICU care
  • urgent correction of hyperkalaemia and other electrolytes
  • and VTE prophylaxis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What specific pharmacotherapy is used in severe NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Dantrolene (a muscle relaxant reducing rigidity and heat generation, given intravenously in critical care) and bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist restoring dopaminergic tone) — in severe cases only. The evidence for both is weak and supportive care remains the mainstay.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the advice on antipsychotic rechallenge after NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
Mortality is now around 5–10%. Rechallenge only cautiously:
  • wait at least 2 weeks after complete resolution (longer after a depot)
  • choose an agent structurally unrelated to the culprit
  • start at a very low dose
  • titrate slowly
  • and monitor temperature, pulse, BP and CK.
Recurrence risk on rechallenge is roughly 30%.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome (phakomatosis) causing benign nerve-sheath tumours (neurofibromas) throughout the nervous system, plus characteristic skin, eye and bone features.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the 'core concept' of NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: It is a tumour-suppressor disorder — loss of neurofibromin leads to unchecked cell growth along nerves; a multisystem clinical diagnosis needing lifelong surveillance for complications.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the genetic basis of NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Autosomal dominant, from a mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17 (coding for neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor); ~50% are new spontaneous mutations (no family history), with variable expressivity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast NF1 and NF2.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• NF1 = chromosome 17, neurofibromin, café-au-lait/skin features and neurofibromas.
  • NF2 = chromosome 22, merlin, and bilateral acoustic neuromas (schwannomas).
Memory hook: NF2 → chromosome 22, '2 ears' = bilateral acoustic neuromas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: List the CRABBING diagnostic criteria for NF1.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Café-au-lait macules (≥6, each >5 mm before puberty or >15 mm after puberty)
  • Relative (first-degree) with NF1
  • Axillary freckling (Crowe's sign) or inguinal freckling
  • Bony dysplasia
  • Iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules)
  • Neurofibromas (≥2 of any type, OR a single plexiform neurofibroma)
  • Glioma of the optic pathway.
≥2 criteria = NF1 — and a pathogenic NF1 variant is now itself a criterion, with the child of an affected parent needing only one other.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the café-au-lait spots of NF1.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Flat, coffee-coloured macules — ≥6, each >5 mm before puberty or >15 mm after puberty, is one of the diagnostic criteria. The paediatric threshold matters, because NF1 is diagnosed in childhood.Pigmentary features alone, with no family history, should raise Legius syndrome rather than settling on NF1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is Crowe's sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Axillary freckling.The diagnostic criterion is freckling in the axillary OR inguinal region, but 'Crowe's sign' refers to the axillary freckling specifically.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are Lisch nodules?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Iris hamartomas — yellow-brown spots on the iris, seen on slit-lamp examination.They are among the features most specific to NF1, and are present in over 90% of adults with it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are neurofibromas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Skin-coloured raised nodules/papules (benign nerve-sheath tumours). The criterion is ≥2 of ANY type, OR a single plexiform neurofibroma — a large, diffuse 'bag of worms' tumour along a nerve trunk, of which one alone is enough.Plexiform and deep nodular lesions are the ones that can turn malignant.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the optic-pathway lesion of NF1, and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An optic pathway (optic nerve) glioma — one of the two most specific features and a cause of vision loss, so visual surveillance is important.A chiasmal/hypothalamic one can also present with precocious puberty.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Which two features are the most specific for NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma — both rare outside NF1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the bony dysplasia seen in NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Bowing of a long bone or sphenoid wing dysplasia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the diagnostic threshold for NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: ≥2 of the CRABBING criteria — it is a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the malignancy complications of NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour — arising in a PLEXIFORM or deep nodular neurofibroma rather than an ordinary cutaneous one, which is why plexiform lesions are the ones imaged and monitored.Also gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), optic glioma, and an increased leukaemia risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: When should malignant transformation be suspected in NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: When a neurofibroma becomes painful, rapidly growing or hard — or causes a new or progressive neurological deficit → suspect a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and arrange urgent assessment.The risk sits with plexiform and deep nodular lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Why must blood pressure always be checked in NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NF1 causes secondary hypertension — from renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma — so BP should be checked and hypertension investigated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: List the neurological and skeletal complications of NF1.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Epilepsy, learning disabilities, brain tumours and migraines
  • scoliosis and bony dysplasia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How is NF1 investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Clinical diagnosis (≥2 CRABBING criteria)
  • examination of skin, eyes (Lisch nodules, acuity/fields for optic glioma), BP, spine and development
  • genetic testing (NF1 gene) for atypical cases/family planning
  • MRI if optic glioma/brain tumour/plexiform neurofibroma suspected
  • investigate hypertension (renal artery imaging, plasma metanephrines).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the overarching management principle in NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: No cure → monitoring, managing symptoms, and treating complications, with genetic counselling.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What surveillance is recommended in NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Annual review — skin, BP, visual assessment (optic glioma), growth and pubertal status (precocious puberty can signal a chiasmal optic pathway glioma), spine (scoliosis), development/learning, and watching for malignant change.Women with NF1 are also eligible for enhanced breast screening: annual mammography between 40 and 50.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How are the complications of NF1 treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Optic glioma → ophthalmology/oncology
  • malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour → urgent oncology (surgery ± chemo/radiotherapy)
  • hypertension → investigate and treat the cause
  • scoliosis → orthopaedics
  • learning difficulties/epilepsy → support/treatment
  • symptomatic/disfiguring neurofibromas → surgical excision, and a symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibroma in a child aged 3 or over → selumetinib, a MEK inhibitor (NICE)
  • plus genetic counselling (50% risk to offspring) and MDT care.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome causing multiple benign nervous-system tumours, especially schwannomas, with bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) as its hallmark.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the 'core concept' of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NF2 = schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas — above all BILATERAL acoustic neuromas (essentially pathognomonic); where NF1 is a 'skin + café-au-lait' disease, NF2 is a 'hearing loss + intracranial/spinal tumour' disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the genetic basis of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring), with a high rate of new mutations (~50%); the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 codes for merlin (schwannomin), a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells — loss drives schwannomas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Explain the merlin → Schwann cell link in NF2.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Merlin is key in Schwann cells (which myelinate cranial/peripheral nerves), so its loss drives schwannomas — explaining why vestibular nerve (CN VIII) tumours dominate.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Contrast NF2 and NF1.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• NF2 = chromosome 22, merlin, bilateral acoustic neuromas (schwannomas), few skin features.
  • NF1 = chromosome 17, neurofibromin, café-au-lait/neurofibromas.
Memory hook: NF2 → '2 ears' → bilateral acoustic neuromas → chromosome 22.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the hallmark presentation of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas causing bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (often the presenting feature, typically in early adulthood), with tinnitus and imbalance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What happens as the acoustic neuromas of NF2 enlarge?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: They compress adjacent structures — CN VII (facial palsy), CN V (loss of the corneal reflex), and the brainstem/cerebellum.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What other tumours occur in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Meningiomas (often multiple)
  • schwannomas of other cranial/spinal/peripheral nerves
  • and ependymomas/gliomas (spinal cord).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the ophthalmic features of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts and retinal hamartomas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How do the skin features of NF2 compare with NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: NF2 has few skin features (some skin schwannomas/plaques); café-au-lait spots may occur but are fewer and less prominent than in NF1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the key diagnostic criterion for NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas — or a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral acoustic neuroma, or two other NF2-associated lesions: meningioma, schwannoma, ependymoma, or a juvenile posterior subcapsular cataract (a lens opacity rather than a tumour).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the key investigation in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: MRI of the brain + internal auditory meati + whole spine (with contrast) — to detect bilateral acoustic neuromas, meningiomas and spinal schwannomas/ependymomas; the mainstay of diagnosis and surveillance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What other investigations are used in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Audiometry (sensorineural hearing loss)
  • genetic testing (NF2 gene, chromosome 22)
  • and ophthalmology (cataracts, retinal lesions).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the overarching management principle in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: No cure → lifelong surveillance and treating tumours while preserving hearing and neurological function, via a specialist MDT.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What surveillance is used in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Regular MRI (brain + spine) and audiometry to monitor tumour growth.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How are the acoustic neuromas/schwannomas of NF2 treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Observation (small/stable), surgery, or stereotactic radiosurgery — timed to balance tumour growth against preserving hearing and the facial nerve.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the role of bevacizumab in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) can shrink vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in NF2.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What hearing and wider management options are used in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Hearing rehabilitation (hearing aids, auditory brainstem/cochlear implants given the bilateral deafness risk)
  • meningiomas/ependymomas → surgery/radiotherapy
  • genetic counselling (autosomal dominant) and screening of at-risk relatives
  • MDT (neurosurgery, ENT/skull base, neurology, audiology, genetics, ophthalmology).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: An autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome (phakomatosis) causing benign tumours (hamartomas) in multiple organs — brain, skin, kidneys, heart, eyes and lungs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the 'core concept' of TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: A multisystem hamartoma disorder — loss of a tumour suppressor → overactive mTOR pathway → unchecked growth → benign tumours across many organs at once.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the signature triad of TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Epilepsy + learning disability + facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) — the classic 'Vogt triad', though incomplete in many.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the genetic basis of TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Autosomal dominant (~2/3 arise as de novo mutations), with variable expressivity; two genes — TSC1 on chromosome 9 (hamartin) and TSC2 on chromosome 16 (tuberin) — either of which causes TSC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Explain the mechanism linking the TSC genes to hamartomas.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Hamartin and tuberin normally inhibit the mTOR pathway; loss of either causes mTOR overactivity → uncontrolled cell growth → hamartomas — which is why mTOR inhibitors are a targeted treatment (everolimus for SEGA and angiomyolipoma; sirolimus for LAM).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe ash-leaf macules.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Hypopigmented oval/leaf-shaped patches, accentuated under a Wood's (UV) lamp — they do not fluoresce; the surrounding skin absorbs the UV so the pale patch stands out.Present at birth or in infancy, and often the earliest CUTANEOUS sign (a cardiac rhabdomyoma may be seen even earlier on antenatal scanning).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe shagreen patches.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Roughened, thickened 'orange-peel' skin, usually over the lower back.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum) in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Red/pink papules over the butterfly/malar area of the face.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are subungual/periungual fibromas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Fibromas around the nails, a cutaneous feature of TSC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: Describe the epilepsy of TSC.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Very common — classically infantile spasms (West syndrome) in infancy, then other seizure types.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What are the neurodevelopmental features of TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Learning disability and developmental delay, with autism/behavioural problems.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What brain lesions occur in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs) — which can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What renal lesions occur in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Angiomyolipomas (which can bleed → haematuria/haemorrhage) and renal cysts.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What cardiac lesion occurs in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Rhabdomyomas — often detected antenatally or in infancy and usually regress.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What pulmonary complication occurs in TSC, and in whom?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — cystic lung disease, especially in women.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What ocular lesion occurs in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Retinal hamartomas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How is TSC diagnosed and investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
Clinically (major + minor criteria); genetics supports it, and a pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant is on its own sufficient for the diagnosis whatever the clinical features. Investigations:
  • skin exam (Wood's lamp for ash-leaf macules)
  • eyes
  • MRI brain (tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA)
  • renal imaging (angiomyolipomas/cysts)
  • echocardiogram (rhabdomyomas)
  • EEG (seizures)
  • genetic testing (TSC1/TSC2)
  • and developmental assessment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the first-line treatment for infantile spasms in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Vigabatrin (a specific high-yield point in TSC — for spasms NOT due to TSC, prednisolone is combined with it). But vigabatrin causes visual field constriction in up to a third of patients and it is usually IRREVERSIBLE, so visual assessment is needed before starting and 6-monthly after (electroretinography in infants who cannot do perimetry). Suspected infantile spasms need urgent referral to a paediatric neurologist within 24 hours — delay worsens neurodevelopmental outcome.Standard antiseizure medication for other seizure types, with epilepsy surgery in selected cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What is the role of mTOR inhibitors in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back: Everolimus and sirolimus are targeted therapy, shrinking lesions by acting directly on the overactive mTOR pathway — everolimus for SEGA and renal angiomyolipoma, sirolimus for LAM.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: What surveillance and organ-specific management are used in TSC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• Regular MRI brain (SEGA), renal imaging (angiomyolipoma), skin, eyes, BP and developmental review
  • SEGA → mTOR inhibitor or surgery if obstructing CSF
  • renal angiomyolipoma → mTOR inhibitor/embolisation if large/bleeding
  • LAM → mTOR inhibitor
  • educational/behavioural support
  • genetic counselling (AD, 50% risk to offspring).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.front: How is TSC distinguished from the other neurocutaneous syndromes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.back:
• TSC = ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches, angiofibromas + epilepsy + learning disability + renal/cardiac hamartomas.
  • NF1 = café-au-lait/neurofibromas/Lisch nodules
  • NF2 = bilateral acoustic neuromas
  • Sturge–Weber = port-wine stain + seizures
  • von Hippel–Lindau = retinal/cerebellar haemangioblastomas, RCC, phaeochromocytoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What are the muscular dystrophies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: A group of inherited disorders causing progressive muscle weakness and wasting, due to genetic defects in muscle structural proteins (most importantly dystrophin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the 'core concept' of muscular dystrophies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: They are primary muscle (myopathic) diseases — the defect is in the muscle fibre itself, not the nerve.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the prototype muscular dystrophy and its classic presentation?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) — absent dystrophin producing a young boy with
  • progressive proximal weakness
  • calf pseudohypertrophy
  • Gower's sign
  • and a very high CK.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the genetic basis of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: An X-linked recessive defect in the dystrophin gene; dystrophin normally anchors the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the membrane, so without it fibres are damaged by contraction and degenerate. It affects boys — about two-thirds inherit it from a carrier mother and about a third are new (de novo) mutations, so a negative family history does NOT exclude it. Some female carriers are symptomatic ('manifesting carriers').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe the onset and course of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Symptoms usually start at 2–3 years — delayed walking, toe-walking, frequent falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, waddling gait, often with speech/language delay — though diagnosis is commonly delayed to about 4–5 years. Loss of ambulation is around 10 years untreated but typically 13–15 years on daily corticosteroids; median survival is in the mid-to-late 20s, extending into the 30s with nocturnal ventilation and cardioprotection.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is calf pseudohypertrophy in DMD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Calves that look bulky but are replaced by fat/fibrous tissue rather than true muscle.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is Gower's sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: The child 'walks up' their own legs with their hands to stand from the floor — a classic sign of proximal/pelvic-girdle weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What are the key associations and prognosis-determining complications of DMD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: About a third have learning difficulties, and speech and language delay is common — often the earliest clue of all. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the commonest association, and cardiac plus respiratory (diaphragm) involvement determines prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is Duchenne muscular dystrophy investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: A very high CK (10–100× normal, leaked from damaged muscle); the definitive test is genetic testing of the dystrophin gene. Muscle biopsy for dystrophin is now rarely needed — only if genetic testing is non-diagnostic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is Duchenne muscular dystrophy managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Supportive — no cure. Corticosteroids (prednisolone or deflazacort; vamorolone is a NICE-approved alternative) slow progression, but cause weight gain, growth suppression, vertebral fractures and adrenal suppression — so every boy needs a steroid emergency card, sick-day rules and stress dosing, and must never stop abruptly. Plus MDT care (physiotherapy, respiratory support/NIV, cardiac surveillance and an ACE inhibitor, orthopaedic care). ANAESTHETIC ALERT: suxamethonium is contraindicated (rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest) and volatile agents can trigger rhabdomyolysis — use total intravenous anaesthesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How do Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy differ genetically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
Same gene (dystrophin), different mutation:
  • DMD = frameshift → NO dystrophin → severe/early
  • Becker = in-frame → some partially functional dystrophin → milder/later.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe the features of Becker muscular dystrophy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Like DMD but presenting later (teens/adulthood), slower progression, often ambulant into adulthood with longer life expectancy; cardiac involvement (dilated cardiomyopathy) still occurs and can be significant even when skeletal weakness is mild.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the genetic basis of myotonic dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Autosomal dominant, a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK gene, showing anticipation (earlier onset/worse down generations).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the hallmark of myotonic dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Myotonia — delayed muscle relaxation (e.g. unable to release a handshake/grip, or slow eye opening after forced closure).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe the distinctive multisystem features of myotonic dystrophy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Distal and facial weakness (facial weakness, ptosis, temporalis/masseter wasting → 'hatchet face', frontal balding)
  • cataracts
  • cardiac conduction defects/arrhythmias
  • endocrine features (diabetes, hypogonadism/testicular atrophy)
  • cognitive changes and daytime somnolence.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Which is the commonest adult-onset muscular dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Myotonic dystrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is myotonic dystrophy managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
Supportively —
  • monitor and treat cardiac conduction defects (pacemaker risk)
  • cataract surgery
  • and manage the systemic features (diabetes, somnolence).
Anaesthetic alert: marked sensitivity to opioids, sedatives and anaesthetic agents with delayed postoperative apnoea, and avoid suxamethonium (masseter spasm) — even mildly affected patients are high risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the myopathic pattern that suggests a dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Proximal (shoulder/pelvic-girdle) weakness with muscle wasting (± pseudohypertrophy), NORMAL sensation, and a very high CK in Duchenne/Becker — though note the CK is normal or only mildly raised in myotonic dystrophy, where the weakness is distal and facial.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is a myopathy/dystrophy distinguished from motor neurone disease and neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• MND has fasciculations and mixed UMN/LMN signs, with a CK that is normal or only mildly raised (up to a few hundred in about half of patients) — the discriminator is the MAGNITUDE, since a dystrophy raises it 10–100×.
  • Neuropathy has distal weakness and abnormal sensation.
  • A dystrophy has proximal weakness and normal sensation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is a dystrophy distinguished from myasthenia gravis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness with ocular/bulbar involvement and a normal CK
  • a dystrophy causes fixed weakness — proximal with a very high CK in Duchenne/Becker, but distal and facial with a normal or only mildly raised CK in myotonic dystrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the overarching management principle for the muscular dystrophies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• No cure → multidisciplinary supportive care
  • anticipate and treat the cardiac and respiratory complications (leading causes of death)
  • and provide genetic counselling.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What cardiac and respiratory surveillance is needed in muscular dystrophies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Cardiac: in DMD/BMD, ECG and echo (or cardiac MRI) at diagnosis and at least annually, starting an ACE inhibitor (± beta-blocker) by around age 10 REGARDLESS of ejection fraction — do not wait for heart failure, because fibrosis precedes any fall in EF.
  • In myotonic dystrophy the problem is conduction disease, and that is where the pacemaker belongs.
  • Respiratory: monitor FVC and watch for nocturnal hypoventilation (morning headache, daytime sleepiness) prompting a sleep study; non-invasive ventilation is what has most extended survival.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What genetic counselling issues apply to the muscular dystrophies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: DMD/BMD are X-linked recessive (carrier mothers, 50% of sons affected) — but about a third of cases are de novo, so a negative family history does not exclude it. Carriers are not just transmitters: around 1 in 10 develop a dilated cardiomyopathy themselves, so offer them cardiac surveillance (ECG/echo every 3–5 years from early adulthood). Myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant with anticipation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What disease-modifying drugs exist for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in the UK?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Beyond corticosteroids, ataluren (for nonsense-mutation Duchenne), vamorolone and givinostat are available in the UK. Exon-skipping and gene therapies remain investigational here.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is multiple sclerosis (MS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: A chronic, autoimmune, inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (brain, spinal cord and optic nerves) — immune-mediated destruction of CNS myelin (oligodendrocytes), driven by both T cells and B cells, which is why the most effective drugs are B-cell depleting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the core diagnostic concept of MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Lesions disseminated in SPACE and TIME — ≥2 different CNS sites affected on ≥2 different occasions (plaques scattered across the CNS, occurring as separate episodes over time).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Which part of the nervous system does MS affect, and what does it spare?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: The CNS only (oligodendrocytes — brain, cord, optic nerves); it spares the peripheral nerves (contrast with Guillain–Barré syndrome and CMT).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe the typical demographics and geography of MS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Typically a young woman aged 20–40 — women are affected about three times as often as men. Risk rises with distance from the equator (the latitude/low vitamin D link), and the strongest associations are with previous Epstein–Barr virus infection and smoking.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: The commonest pattern (~85%) — discrete relapses followed by remission (partial or full recovery), with no progression between relapses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe secondary progressive MS (SPMS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Begins as RRMS then evolves into steady progression, ± superimposed relapses; many RRMS patients eventually convert.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Describe primary progressive MS (PPMS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Progressive from the outset with no distinct relapses/remissions (~10–15%); patients are older with a more equal sex ratio.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What defines a relapse in MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: New neurological symptoms lasting >24 hours, in the absence of infection/fever, developing over days and recovering over weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the classic first presentation of MS, and what is the trap in treating it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Optic neuritis — subacute unilateral visual loss with painful eye movements, red (colour) desaturation and a relative afferent pupillary defect. It needs urgent ophthalmology/neurology assessment. Steroids speed recovery but do not change the final visual acuity, so they are used selectively — and standard-dose oral prednisolone must NOT be used, because it does not help and increases the recurrence rate.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What are the spinal cord features of MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Sensory disturbance
  • limb weakness (UMN)
  • bladder dysfunction
  • Lhermitte's sign
  • and transverse myelitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is Lhermitte's sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: An electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion, reflecting dorsal column demyelination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What are the brainstem features of MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Diplopia
  • internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
  • vertigo
  • and facial sensory loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), and why is it relevant to MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) causing impaired adduction of one eye with nystagmus in the other; bilateral INO in a young person is very suggestive of MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What are the cerebellar features of MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Ataxia
  • intention tremor
  • and dysarthria.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is Uhthoff's phenomenon?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Worsening of MS symptoms with heat (a hot bath, exercise or fever).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: List the McDonald criteria for dissemination in space.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
≥2 separate CNS locations affected —
  • periventricular
  • juxtacortical/cortical
  • infratentorial
  • and spinal cord.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: List the ways dissemination in time can be shown in MS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• ≥2 separate clinical episodes
  • OR MRI lesions of different ages (simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing lesions)
  • OR CSF oligoclonal bands as a substitute for dissemination in time.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is a clinically isolated syndrome (CIS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: A first clinical episode of CNS demyelination lasting more than 24 hours that does not yet meet the criteria for MS. It may be monofocal or multifocal — what defines it is that there has only been one episode. It may or may not go on to become MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is the key investigation in MS, and its findings?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: MRI brain + spinal cord (with contrast) — T2/FLAIR hyperintense demyelinating plaques in characteristic sites (periventricular 'Dawson's fingers', juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord); gadolinium enhancement indicates active/new lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What CSF finding supports MS, and what is its significance?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Oligoclonal bands (IgG) present in CSF but NOT in serum → evidence of intrathecal (CNS) inflammation, which can substitute for dissemination in time.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What do visual evoked potentials show in MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Delayed responses → evidence of previous optic nerve demyelination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: List important mimics of MS to exclude.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin-4 antibodies) and MOG-antibody disease — test for both in severe, bilateral or non-recovering optic neuritis, because both are treated differently and can be worsened by MS drugs. Also ADEM, B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), SLE/vasculitis, sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, HIV and CNS lymphoma. In an acute myelopathy, always exclude structural cord compression with urgent MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: How is an acute MS relapse managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: First confirm it is a relapse: rule out infection (a UTI or chest infection can unmask old deficits — a pseudorelapse), and distinguish a relapse from a fluctuation or from steady progression. Not every relapse needs treating, so discuss with an MS specialist. If steroids are indicated, NICE says offer oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days; IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days is the alternative where oral has failed or is not tolerated, or where the person needs admission. Never use a lower dose, and never give patients steroids to keep at home for future relapses. Steroids shorten the relapse but do not change long-term disability. Plasma exchange is for severe steroid-refractory relapses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: What is disease-modifying therapy (DMT) in MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Treatment that reduces relapse frequency and slows disability. It is specialist-started and monitored, is for active relapsing disease, and does NOT treat an acute relapse. Treatment escalates from moderate-efficacy agents (injectables such as interferon-beta and glatiramer acetate, and orals) to high-efficacy monoclonals such as ocrelizumab and natalizumab. Two safety points: natalizumab carries a risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, stratified by JC virus serostatus; and several DMTs, teriflunomide and fingolimod in particular, are contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Which disease-modifying therapies are used in progressive MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back: Ocrelizumab for early primary progressive MS with imaging evidence of inflammatory activity; siponimod for active secondary progressive MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.front: Outline the symptomatic management of MS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.back:
• Spasticity → baclofen first-line, gabapentin second-line if baclofen is not tolerated or not enough (avoid the two together — risk of severe respiratory depression), with physiotherapy
  • Fatigue → exercise, amantadine, energy management
  • Bladder → assess residual volume, then anticholinergics or catheterisation
  • Neuropathic pain → a choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin; trigeminal neuralgia in MS is treated with carbamazepine
  • Treat depression; physio/OT for mobility; MDT care.
Note that NICE says do not offer vitamin D solely to treat MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What is motor neurone disease (MND)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: A group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders selectively affecting motor neurones — upper (UMN) and/or lower (LMN) — with NO sensory involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What is the core diagnostic signature of MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: Combined UMN + LMN signs, WITHOUT sensory loss and WITHOUT eye-movement involvement — a combination almost unique to MND.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Describe amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: The commonest subtype of MND, with BOTH UMN and LMN signs (the classic mix).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Describe progressive bulbar palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: The second commonest MND subtype and the worst prognosis; it affects the muscles of talking and swallowing (bulbar, CN IX–XII).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Describe progressive muscular atrophy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: An MND subtype with LMN signs only (anterior horn cells), carrying a better prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Describe primary lateral sclerosis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: An MND subtype with UMN signs only; it is the slowest-progressing form.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: List the lower motor neurone (LMN) signs.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Muscle wasting
  • reduced tone
  • reduced reflexes
  • and fasciculations (muscle twitches).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: List the upper motor neurone (UMN) signs.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Increased tone/spasticity
  • brisk (hyper) reflexes
  • and an upgoing plantar (Babinski).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Explain the mechanism of mixed UMN/LMN signs in MND.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• UMNs normally inhibit LMNs, so UMN damage disinhibits LMNs → hyper signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia)
  • LMN damage removes the muscle's supply → wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia.
In ALS both coexist (e.g. a wasted, fasciculating limb with brisk reflexes).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What are the crucial negative features that support MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• No sensory symptoms or signs (vs neuropathy, radiculopathy, MS)
  • extraocular muscles spared (vs myasthenia gravis)
  • and sphincters spared until late.
Note that cognition is NOT reliably spared: around 10–15% have frontotemporal dementia and up to about half have milder cognitive or behavioural change — which matters for capacity to make gastrostomy, ventilation and advance-care decisions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Describe the typical patient and early presentation of MND.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
Late middle age, ± family history, with insidious progressive painless weakness spreading through the body; early complaints include
  • clumsiness
  • dropping things
  • tripping
  • fatigue on exercise
  • and slurred speech.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What are the bulbar features of MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Dysarthria
  • dysphagia
  • nasal speech
  • tongue wasting with fasciculations
  • and aspiration risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What is the usual cause of death in MND, and its mechanism?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: Type 2 respiratory failure (or pneumonia) from progressive respiratory muscle weakness — presenting with breathlessness and orthopnoea.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: How is MND distinguished from myasthenia gravis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness WITH eye involvement (ptosis/diplopia)
  • MND spares the eye movements.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: How is MND distinguished from cervical myelopathy/cord compression?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: Cord compression produces a sensory level and sphincter signs, whereas MND has no sensory loss — MRI is done to exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: List other mimics of MND and their discriminators.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Multiple sclerosis (sensory symptoms, relapsing-remitting)
  • peripheral neuropathy (sensory involvement)
  • and Lambert–Eaton/myopathy (no UMN signs, no fasciculations).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Which features should make you doubt MND and look for a mimic?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: Sensory signs, eye involvement, or early sphincter involvement — MND is pure motor, eye-sparing and sphincter-sparing until late. Also think again if there is conduction block on nerve conduction studies, which points to multifocal motor neuropathy — a purely lower motor neurone, asymmetric, IVIG-responsive mimic that must not be missed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: How is MND diagnosed and investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
• Clinically — the characteristic progressive UMN + LMN pattern, supported by EMG and with mimics excluded.
  • Nerve conduction studies show NORMAL SENSORY responses (this is what excludes a neuropathy); motor conduction velocities are normal, though amplitudes fall as axons are lost, and you look specifically for conduction block, the signature of multifocal motor neuropathy.
  • EMG shows a reduced number of action potentials with increased amplitude (denervation and reinnervation).
  • MRI excludes cord compression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What EMG finding supports MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: A reduced number of motor action potentials with increased amplitude — reflecting denervation and reinnervation (fewer, larger motor units).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What is the role of riluzole in MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back: Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor (reducing excitotoxicity), 50 mg twice daily, for the ALS form of MND. Be precise about the benefit: it extends survival, or the time to mechanical ventilation, by around 3 months. It does not slow symptomatic progression, improve strength, or reverse anything. It is hepatotoxic and can cause severe neutropenia — monitor LFTs monthly for 3 months, then 3-monthly for the rest of the first year, then annually, and tell the patient to report febrile illness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: What is the role of non-invasive ventilation in MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
NIV (usually BiPAP) improves survival and quality of life, most clearly in those without severe bulbar involvement. Do not wait for symptoms to declare themselves: measure oxygen saturation on air plus FVC (or VC), or SNIP/MIP, at diagnosis and every 2–3 months. Refer for NIV
  • when FVC falls below 50% predicted
  • or below 80% with symptoms or signs (especially orthopnoea)
  • or when SNIP/MIP falls below 40 cmH2O.
A PaCO2 above 6 kPa needs urgent referral, to be seen within a week. Remember the trap: respiratory failure here is ventilatory, so oxygen alone worsens CO2 retention.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: How and when is gastrostomy managed in MND?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
Discuss it EARLY and revisit it regularly — do not wait for dysphagia to become severe. Timing is the point: once respiratory function has fallen, the procedure carries much higher morbidity and mortality, so early placement is safer than late. Weigh
  • swallowing
  • weight loss
  • respiratory function
  • the effort of eating
  • and choking risk.
Route follows respiratory function — PEG while it is preserved, RIG once FVC is below about 50% predicted. Malnutrition worsens prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.front: Outline the supportive/palliative management of MND.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.back:
Multidisciplinary care (neurology, specialist nurse, physiotherapy, OT, SALT, dietitian, respiratory, palliative) improves survival and quality of life. Know the specific first choices:
  • muscle cramps → quinine first-line, baclofen second
  • spasticity → an exercise programme plus baclofen
  • drooling → an antimuscarinic, with glycopyrronium preferred if there is cognitive impairment, and botulinum toxin A by referral if that fails
  • thick secretions → carbocisteine
  • emotional lability → amitriptyline or an SSRI.
Plan ahead while capacity allows: ventilation wishes, an advance decision to refuse treatment, DNACPR, preferred place of death. For breathlessness at the end of life, consider opioids, and a benzodiazepine if anxiety is driving it. Prognosis is usually death within 2–4 years.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: Define meningitis and encephalitis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Meningitis = inflammation of the meninges (the membranes covering the brain/spinal cord), usually infective (bacterial or viral). Encephalitis = inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself, usually viral (classically HSV).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the crucial clinical distinction between meningitis and encephalitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Meningitis affects the coverings → meningism (headache, neck stiffness, photophobia); encephalitis affects the brain substance → altered brain function (confusion, personality/behaviour change, seizures, focal deficits).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What are the two treatment reflexes for meningitis and encephalitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Bacterial meningitis → immediate antibiotics; encephalitis → immediate IV aciclovir. They overlap (meningoencephalitis) — if in doubt, cover both.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: Contrast bacterial and viral meningitis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• Bacterial = severe/life-threatening, rapid onset (hours), commonly meningococcus or pneumococcus.
  • Viral = usually self-limiting, more gradual, commonly enteroviruses (also HSV, mumps).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: List the common bacterial causes of meningitis by age group.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• Under 3 months: Group B Strep (much the commonest), then E. coli and Listeria.
  • Children/young adults: Strep pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis — since the MenB and MenACWY programmes, pneumococcus is the commoner of the two in the UK; think Haemophilus influenzae type b in an unimmunised child.
  • Aged 60 and over, pregnant or immunocompromised: the above PLUS Listeria monocytogenes (→ add amoxicillin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the classic triad of meningitis, and what caveat applies?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status — but all three occur in only a minority, so don't wait for the full triad before treating.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What are the meningism features and meningeal signs of meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Meningism: headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea/vomiting. Signs: Kernig's (pain on knee extension with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski's (neck flexion causing involuntary hip/knee flexion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: How does meningitis present in infants?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Non-specifically — fever, lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the significance of a non-blanching rash in suspected meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: A non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (doesn't fade under a glass — the 'tumbler test') indicates meningococcal septicaemia — a life-threatening emergency that can occur with or without meningitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What initial blood tests are done in suspected meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• Blood cultures
  • FBC
  • CRP
  • whole-blood PCR (for meningococcal/pneumococcal DNA)
  • glucose (for the CSF:blood ratio)
  • U&E and clotting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the key diagnostic test in meningitis, and what is sent?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Lumbar puncture for CSF — cell count/differential, protein, glucose (with paired blood glucose), Gram stain, culture and PCR (viral/bacterial).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the CSF picture in bacterial meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Turbid/cloudy appearance, ↑↑ neutrophils (polymorphs), ↑↑ protein, and ↓↓ glucose (CSF:blood ratio <0.5).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the CSF picture in viral meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Clear appearance, ↑ lymphocytes, normal/mildly raised protein, and normal glucose.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the CSF picture in TB/fungal meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: A fibrin web, ↑ lymphocytes, ↑↑ protein, and low glucose.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: Before a lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis, what are the two separate questions to ask?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• (1) Does this patient need imaging first? Most do not — image first only for signs of raised ICP, new focal neurology (including seizures or posturing), GCS of 9 or less, or a progressive/rapid fall in consciousness. A normal CT does not make an LP safe if those clinical signs are present.
  • (2) Is the LP safe to do at all right now? Shock, respiratory compromise, coagulopathy or infection over the site mean you defer the LP until corrected — a CT does not help with any of those.
Neither question ever delays antibiotics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the community/pre-hospital treatment of suspected meningococcal disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
IM or IV benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) immediately, especially with a non-blanching rash:
  • under 1 year 300 mg
  • 1–9 years 600 mg
  • 10 years and over, including adults, 1.2 g.
The overriding rule is that it must not delay transfer to hospital.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the hospital empirical antibiotic for bacterial meningitis (NICE)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: IV ceftriaxone, started within 1 hour, at any age. Use cefotaxime instead in a neonate who is jaundiced, acidotic or hypoalbuminaemic, who is pre-term, or who is receiving a calcium-containing infusion. Every baby under 3 months also gets IV amoxicillin for Listeria.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: When is amoxicillin added in bacterial meningitis, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: For babies under 3 months (automatically), adults aged 60 and over, pregnancy, and the immunocompromised — including diabetes, chronic liver or kidney disease and alcohol excess. Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria monocytogenes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the role of dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: IV dexamethasone 10 mg (children 0.15 mg/kg, max 10 mg) 6-hourly for 4 days, given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, in anyone over 3 months. It reduces neurological complications, especially hearing loss, with the greatest benefit in pneumococcal meningitis. It can still be given up to 12 hours late, and must never delay antibiotics. The exception: do NOT routinely give corticosteroids in meningococcal disease — they do not help and have been associated with higher mortality.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What are the public-health actions for meningitis/meningococcal disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Acute meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia are NOTIFIABLE — inform public health at once. Chemoprophylaxis is for close contacts of meningococcal disease (and of Hib) only: a single dose of ciprofloxacin, suitable at any age including pregnancy, ideally within 24 hours; rifampicin is the alternative. Contacts are also offered vaccination where the serogroup is vaccine-preventable. Contacts of pneumococcal, group B streptococcal and viral meningitis need no prophylaxis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: List the complications of bacterial meningitis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• Sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — needs audiology follow-up)
  • seizures/epilepsy
  • hydrocephalus
  • focal deficits
  • cognitive impairment and death
  • Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage) in meningococcal septicaemia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is encephalitis, and what is the key treatable cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma, usually viral; the crucial treatable cause is herpes simplex virus (HSV-1).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: List the causes of encephalitis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• HSV-1 (the key treatable cause)
  • other herpesviruses (VZV, CMV, EBV)
  • enteroviruses
  • and autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor — the key non-infective cause).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: Describe the clinical features of encephalitis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• Altered mental state/reduced consciousness
  • confusion
  • personality and behaviour change
  • fever
  • headache
  • seizures and focal neurology (dysphasia, hemiparesis)
HSV targets the temporal lobes → memory/behaviour/psychiatric features (can mimic psychiatric illness).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What are the investigation findings in HSV encephalitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back:
• CSF: a lymphocytic picture with raised protein and normal glucose; HSV PCR is the diagnostic test (but can be negative very early).
  • MRI: temporal lobe changes (oedema/hyperintensity).
  • EEG: temporal lobe abnormalities.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: What is the management reflex for suspected encephalitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Start IV aciclovir NOW, 10 mg/kg 8-hourly, empirically — do not wait for the PCR. It stays intravenous throughout; the course is 14 days in confirmed HSV encephalitis, or 21 days if immunocompromised. In a febrile patient who is confused or seizing, give antibiotics as well: you cannot separate meningitis from encephalitis at the bedside, so cover both.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.front: How is autoimmune encephalitis recognised and what happens next?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.back: Suspect it in a subacute encephalopathy with prominent psychiatric or behavioural change, movement disorder and seizures, particularly in a young woman (anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis). It is a specialist diagnosis — refer for immunotherapy and a search for an underlying tumour.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: A chronic inner-ear disorder — the triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, with aural fullness — caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the inner ear).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Endolymphatic hydrops — excess endolymph accumulates in the membranous labyrinth (impaired reabsorption/drainage) → distension → episodic dysfunction of the cochlea (hearing loss + tinnitus) and vestibular apparatus (vertigo).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the classic clinical picture of Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: The triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, plus aural fullness, in attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: Describe the attack pattern and demographics of Ménière's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Attacks last 20 minutes to 12 hours and recur in clusters over weeks with periods of remission; typically middle-aged adults, usually unilateral initially, with hearing progressively declining over years.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: Describe the vertigo of Ménière's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Recurrent attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours (typically 2-3 hours), often with nausea/vomiting — the most disabling feature. Shorter than 20 minutes or longer than 12 hours, think again (BPPV or a posterior-circulation TIA; vestibular migraine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: Describe the hearing loss of Ménière's disease.
