conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Sensorineural, fluctuating initially (typically low- to mid-frequency) and becoming progressive and permanent; usually unilateral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What are the tinnitus and aural fullness of Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Tinnitus in the affected ear and a sense of pressure/fullness in the same ear.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What later-disease features occur in Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Nystagmus during attacks, and drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) — sudden falls without warning.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How do you distinguish peripheral from central vertigo?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Duration does NOT separate them: peripheral causes range from seconds (BPPV) to 20 minutes-12 hours (Ménière's) to days (neuronitis/labyrinthitis), while central vertigo is usually continuous but is episodic in vestibular migraine and TIA. What does separate them: peripheral = hearing loss/tinnitus common, coordination intact, no other neurology; central = ataxia, diplopia, cranial nerve or limb signs. Important caveat — new hearing loss does NOT exclude a stroke, because AICA infarction causes vertigo with sudden deafness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the HINTS examination, and what pattern is reassuringly peripheral?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew — valid ONLY when the vertigo is continuous and present as you examine, so it is useless between attacks and does not apply to a Ménière's patient who is currently well. A peripheral picture = an abnormal head impulse (corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, and no skew; a normal head impulse suggests a central cause. A 'peripheral' result never overrules other neurological signs or new hearing loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the 'must-not-miss' central cause of vertigo?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: A posterior circulation stroke (also consider tumour, MS and vestibular migraine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How does BPPV differ from Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: BPPV causes brief (seconds) vertigo triggered by head position, with NO hearing loss; Dix-Hallpike is positive and it is treated with the Epley manoeuvre.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How does vestibular neuronitis differ from Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Vestibular neuronitis causes acute prolonged vertigo (lasting days) after a viral illness, with NO hearing loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How does labyrinthitis differ from vestibular neuronitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Labyrinthitis is like vestibular neuronitis but WITH hearing loss, because the labyrinth (cochlea) is also involved.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How does an acoustic neuroma differ from Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: An acoustic neuroma causes gradual, progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance, rather than the episodic attacks of Ménière's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How is Ménière's disease diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Clinically — the characteristic triad and episodic pattern, usually a specialist (ENT) diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the key confirmatory investigation in Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Audiometry — confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low- to mid-frequency and fluctuating early). Rinne/Weber at the bedside may only suggest the pattern; audiometry is what confirms it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the role of MRI in suspected Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: To exclude an acoustic neuroma (unilateral SNHL) and central causes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: How is an acute attack of Ménière's disease managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: A short course of a vestibular sedative/antiemetic — prochlorperazine (fast relief of vertigo/nausea) or an antihistamine (cyclizine, cinnarizine) — for a maximum of 7 days: longer use delays central vestibular compensation and worsens the chronic imbalance. Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine, so warn about extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia, oculogyric crisis, parkinsonism), especially in the young and elderly. All are sedating, so advise not to drive.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What is the prophylaxis for Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Betahistine (a histamine analogue licensed for Ménière's; 16 mg three times daily initially) is the usual UK prophylactic, given as a trial to reduce attack frequency — though the trial evidence for benefit is weak. Avoid in phaeochromocytoma; caution in asthma and peptic ulcer. Plus lifestyle measures: a low-salt diet and reducing caffeine/alcohol (widely advised, though trial evidence is lacking). Diuretics are not routinely used in the UK.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What are the options for refractory Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Specialist treatments — intratympanic steroids or intratympanic gentamicin (ablates vestibular function but is ototoxic, with a hearing-loss risk), and surgery (endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.front: What supportive measures and driving advice apply in Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.back: Hearing aids for progressive SNHL, vestibular rehabilitation and tinnitus support; patients must inform the DVLA and stop driving during active disease (sudden, unpredictable vertigo) until symptoms are controlled.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: How are intracranial haemorrhages classified?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: By the anatomical space the blood occupies — extradural, subdural and subarachnoid are the surgical/traumatic haemorrhages (intracerebral/intraparenchymal is covered under Stroke/TIA).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the organising principle linking CT shape to the space?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
The CT shape tells you the space:
  • extradural = lens/biconvex (doesn't cross sutures)
  • subdural = crescent/banana (crosses sutures)
  • subarachnoid = blood in the sulci/basal cisterns
Match shape → space → vessel → cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Give the vessel of origin for extradural, subdural and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Extradural = middle meningeal artery (arterial)
  • subdural = bridging veins (venous)
  • subarachnoid = berry aneurysm rupture (arterial)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Give the typical patient/cause for each of the three haemorrhages.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Extradural = trauma to the temporal/pterion region in a young adult
  • subdural = elderly/alcohol/anticoagulated, often minor or forgotten trauma
  • subarachnoid = spontaneous, with hypertension, polycystic kidney disease or connective tissue disease

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Give the classic history for extradural, subdural and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Extradural = lucid interval then rapid deterioration
  • subdural = fluctuating consciousness/gradual (especially chronic)
  • subarachnoid = thunderclap 'worst-ever' headache with meningism

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Give the key management for each of the three haemorrhages.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Extradural = urgent neurosurgery (clot evacuation)
  • subdural = surgical (acute) vs conservative/burr hole (chronic)
  • subarachnoid = nimodipine + coiling/clipping, with LP if CT is negative

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is an extradural (epidural) haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Blood in the potential space between the skull and the dura mater — almost always traumatic and classically arterial.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the defining clinical story of an extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: The 'lucid interval' — the patient is knocked out, briefly recovers (talks/walks, seems fine), then rapidly deteriorates as the arterial bleed expands ('talk and die').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the classic cause of an extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A temporal skull fracture rupturing the middle meningeal artery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Which patients typically get extradural haemorrhage, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Young adults — because the dura is more firmly adherent to the skull in the elderly, making extradural bleeding less likely with age.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the anatomy relevant to extradural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner skull at the pterion — the thin bone at the temple where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the mechanism of an extradural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Trauma to the temple → a temporal/parietal skull fracture → rupture of the middle meningeal artery → arterial blood strips the dura off the skull → an expanding biconvex haematoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Why does the lucid interval occur in extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: The initial impact causes brief concussion (loss of consciousness); the patient then recovers (lucid interval) before the arterial haematoma expands over minutes–hours → rising ICP → deterioration.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the CT appearance of an extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection that does NOT cross suture lines (though it can cross the midline); ± skull fracture, midline shift and effacement of ventricles/cisterns.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: State the suture/midline rules for extradural vs subdural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Extradural does NOT cross suture lines, because the dura is fused to bone at the sutures, but it CAN cross the midline. Subdural crosses sutures but NOT the midline, because the falx stops it. Learn the mechanism — these are strong rules of thumb rather than absolutes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Outline the clinical phases of an extradural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Initial brief loss of consciousness (concussion) → lucid interval (temporary recovery) → deterioration (worsening headache, vomiting, falling GCS, drowsiness) → raised ICP/herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the 'blown pupil' in extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: An ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil from uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve — a sign of impending coning and a surgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What are the late signs of raised ICP/herniation in extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• An ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III)
  • contralateral hemiparesis
  • and Cushing's reflex (rising BP + bradycardia + irregular breathing)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the investigation of choice in extradural haemorrhage, and what are the NICE CT triggers?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
Urgent non-contrast CT head. NICE triggers a CT within 1 hour for:
  • GCS 12 or less on arrival
  • GCS below 15 at 2 hours after injury
  • suspected open or depressed skull fracture
  • any sign of a basal skull fracture
  • a post-traumatic seizure
  • a focal neurological deficit
  • more than one episode of vomiting
Separately, consider a CT within 8 hours in anyone on an anticoagulant or an antiplatelet other than aspirin alone, even without those features. Also check FBC, clotting and group & save.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Why must you not perform a lumbar puncture in extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Because the raised intracranial pressure means removing CSF risks coning (herniation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Outline the immediate (ABCDE) management of extradural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Airway with C-spine control, oxygenation, and avoiding hypoxia/hypotension; if GCS ≤8, intubate. Correct coagulopathy/reverse anticoagulation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the definitive management of an extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Urgent craniotomy with evacuation of the haematoma and control of the bleeding vessel; manage raised ICP (head-up positioning, mannitol or hypertonic saline, treat seizures).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the prognosis of extradural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Excellent if evacuated promptly before herniation (the underlying brain is often uninjured), but catastrophic if missed or late — 'talk and die' is preventable, and time is brain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is a subdural haemorrhage (SDH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Blood in the space between the dura and the arachnoid mater — classically a venous bleed from the bridging veins.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the 'core concept' of subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: The slow, venous, crescent-shaped bleed — the counterpart to the fast, arterial, biconvex extradural; being low-pressure venous, it can accumulate slowly, giving both acute and chronic forms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Contrast subdural and extradural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Subdural = venous (bridging veins), crescent (crosses sutures, not the midline), slow/may be chronic, in the elderly/alcoholic/anticoagulated/infant
  • Extradural = arterial (middle meningeal), biconvex (doesn't cross sutures), fast (lucid interval), young + temporal trauma

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Distinguish acute from chronic subdural haemorrhage by timing.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Acute = within ~72 hours of trauma; chronic = weeks to months after (often trivial/forgotten) trauma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: How does CT density indicate the age of a subdural bleed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Acute = hyperdense (bright)
  • chronic = hypodense (dark, old blood)
  • acute-on-chronic = mixed density

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the anatomy/mechanism of subdural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Bridging veins cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural sinuses; trauma tears these veins, causing a slow venous bleed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Why are the elderly and alcoholics prone to subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins taut, so they tear easily even with minor or forgotten trauma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Why are anticoagulated patients prone to subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Impaired clotting (warfarin, DOACs, antiplatelets) makes any bleed larger and more likely.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Why is a subdural haemorrhage a red flag in infants?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: It suggests abusive head trauma (non-accidental injury) — torn bridging veins from shaking, often bilateral and with retinal haemorrhages, which prompts safeguarding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the features of acute subdural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Significant head trauma followed by a falling GCS, headache and focal neurology; may deteriorate rapidly (like extradural but usually less abrupt).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the features of chronic subdural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Insidious onset over weeks of confusion, cognitive decline, drowsiness, headache, unsteadiness/falls and focal weakness — often fluctuating, with an absent/forgotten trauma history → mimics dementia, stroke or delirium.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What signs indicate raised ICP/deterioration in subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Worsening headache
  • vomiting
  • falling GCS
  • a fixed dilated pupil (CN III)
  • contralateral hemiparesis
  • and Cushing's reflex

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the investigation of choice in subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Non-contrast CT head — a crescent-shaped (concave) collection crossing suture lines but not the midline, with density indicating age; also FBC, clotting and group & save. Do NOT perform an LP (coning risk).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What additional workup is needed if non-accidental injury is suspected in an infant with SDH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A safeguarding workup — skeletal survey and ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhages.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Outline the immediate management of subdural haemorrhage.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
ABCDE with C-spine control, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, intubate if GCS is 8 or less, and reverse anticoagulation:
  • warfarin with prothrombin complex concentrate + vitamin K
  • dabigatran with idarucizumab
  • and apixaban or rivaroxaban with PCC

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the definitive management of an acute (symptomatic) subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Craniotomy and evacuation — the acute clot is solid.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the management of a symptomatic chronic subdural haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Burr-hole drainage — the liquefied old blood drains through burr holes, often with dramatic improvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: When is a subdural haemorrhage managed conservatively, and what else should be addressed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Small, asymptomatic subdurals with a good GCS → observation and serial CT; also address the cause (falls assessment, review anticoagulation/alcohol, safeguarding in infants), manage raised ICP, and give antiepileptics for seizures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is a subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space (between the arachnoid and pia, where CSF flows) — most often spontaneous, from a ruptured 'berry' (saccular) aneurysm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the defining presentation of SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A thunderclap headache — sudden, severe, 'worst-ever', peaking within seconds to minutes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What are the three management priorities in SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• (1) Diagnose it fast (the CT → LP pathway)
  • (2) secure the aneurysm early to prevent the catastrophic rebleed (highest risk in the first 24h)
  • and (3) prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (days 3–14) with nimodipine

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the demographics and vascular risk factors for SAH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Commoner in women and middle age; associated with hypertension, smoking, excess alcohol and family history.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the commonest cause and site of SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm (~85%) at branch points of the Circle of Willis; the commonest site is the anterior communicating artery (also posterior communicating and MCA bifurcation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Name causes of SAH other than a berry aneurysm.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage (benign, better prognosis)
  • arteriovenous malformation
  • and trauma

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Which genetic/connective-tissue conditions predispose to SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
  • Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
  • and coarctation of the aorta
also a positive family history.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the differential for a thunderclap headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: SAH until proven otherwise; also cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, arterial dissection, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, pituitary apoplexy (and benign cough/exertional/coital headache, migraine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: State the rule for any sudden severe headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Any sudden severe headache peaking within 1–5 minutes is SAH until excluded → urgent CT.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Describe the thunderclap headache of SAH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Sudden, severe, 'worst headache of my life', typically occipital, peaking in seconds to minutes — the hallmark.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What are the meningism features of SAH, and why do they occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Neck stiffness and photophobia (blood irritates the meninges), developing over hours, with nausea and vomiting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the significance of a painful CN III palsy in SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A painful third-nerve palsy (fixed dilated pupil, ptosis, 'down-and-out' eye) suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III — a classic link.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is a 'sentinel' (herald) bleed in SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: A preceding 'warning' thunderclap headache, days to weeks before the main event — a chance to make the diagnosis before the catastrophic bleed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the first-line investigation for SAH and its time-sensitivity?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Urgent non-contrast CT head — hyperdense blood in the subarachnoid space (sulci, basal cisterns — 'star-shaped'); CT within 6 hours of onset is ~100% sensitive, so a normal CT within 6h effectively rules out SAH, but sensitivity falls after 6 hours.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: When and why is a lumbar puncture done in suspected SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: If CT is negative but suspicion remains, perform LP ≥12 hours after onset (to allow bilirubin to form) and look for xanthochromia (yellow CSF from bilirubin on spectrophotometry), which distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap. Per NICE, if a CT within 6h is negative and radiologist-reported, LP is not routinely needed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: After confirming SAH, what imaging locates the aneurysm?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Vascular imaging — CT angiography (CTA) and/or digital subtraction angiography (DSA, the gold standard); if negative, it is repeated later (~1–6 weeks).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What systemic effects can SAH cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: ECG changes (ST/T-wave changes, arrhythmias) and hyponatraemia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: Outline the immediate management of SAH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• ABCDE
  • prompt transfer to a neurosciences centre with both endovascular and neurosurgical capability
  • effective analgesia (paracetamol escalating to an opioid — treating the pain often settles the blood pressure)
  • blood-pressure control avoiding extremes
  • and reversal of anticoagulation

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: How is the aneurysm secured in SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Endovascular coiling is first-line in most cases (less invasive, better outcomes); surgical clipping is used if the aneurysm is unsuitable for coiling — done early to prevent rebleeding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: What is the role of nimodipine in SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back: Nimodipine is a calcium channel blocker given 60 mg enterally, 4-hourly, for 21 days, started within 4 days (96 hours) of the bleed. It reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia and improves outcome. Hypotension is the dose-limiting effect — reduce the dose rather than stopping it. It does NOT treat rebleeding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.front: List the key complications of SAH and their timing.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.back:
• Rebleeding (highest risk in the first 24h → secure the aneurysm early)
  • vasospasm → delayed cerebral ischaemia (days 3–14 → nimodipine prevents it; treat with euvolaemia + BP support)
  • hydrocephalus (blood blocks CSF flow → EVD/shunt)
  • and hyponatraemia (SIADH/cerebral salt wasting)
seizures are treated with antiepileptics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Raised intracranial pressure with NO identifiable cause (no mass, no hydrocephalus, no venous thrombosis), causing headache and papilloedema with a normal CSF composition — formerly 'benign intracranial hypertension'; also called 'pseudotumour cerebri'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the core concept of IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Raised ICP without a space-occupying lesion — it mimics a brain tumour clinically (headache + papilloedema) but imaging is normal; it is a diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Who is the classic patient with IIH, and what is the overriding priority?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: A young, obese woman; the overriding priority is protecting VISION, as untreated papilloedema can cause permanent visual loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: State the modified Dandy criteria for IIH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• Raised CSF opening pressure
  • papilloedema
  • NORMAL neuroimaging
  • NORMAL CSF composition, with no other identifiable cause of raised ICP

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Which secondary causes of raised ICP must be excluded before diagnosing IIH, and how?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• Space-occupying lesion (MRI)
  • hydrocephalus (imaging — ventricles not dilated)
  • cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (MR/CT venography)
  • and meningitis (normal CSF)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the key mimic of IIH, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — it shares the same demographic (young woman, COCP, pregnancy), so venography must always be done to exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: List the drug and hormonal risk factors for IIH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• Tetracyclines
  • retinoids (isotretinoin)
  • lithium
  • excess vitamin A
  • and corticosteroid WITHDRAWAL
  • also pregnancy
The COCP is not an established cause of IIH — it is a risk factor for the key mimic, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Which drug culprits should you specifically think of in a young woman with IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: The 'acne' drugs — tetracyclines (acne antibiotics) and retinoids (isotretinoin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the single most important risk factor for IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Obesity (in a young woman) — IIH is increasingly common as obesity rises.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Describe the headache of IIH.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: A raised-ICP headache — worse in the morning and on coughing, straining or lying down.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the key clinical sign of IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Bilateral papilloedema (optic disc swelling) — the sign that puts vision at risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What visual symptoms occur in IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• Blurred vision
  • transient visual obscurations (brief greying of vision with posture change)
  • an enlarged blind spot
  • and progressive visual field loss

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the significance of a CN VI palsy in IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: It is a false-localising sign (causing horizontal diplopia), not evidence of a focal lesion — due to the abducens nerve's long intracranial course.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Which characteristic auditory symptom occurs in IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Pulsatile tinnitus — a 'whooshing' sound in the ears.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Describe the visual prognosis if IIH is untreated.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Papilloedema → enlarged blind spot → progressive visual field loss → permanent blindness — which is why IIH needs urgent treatment despite the old 'benign' label.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: Which neurological findings should make you doubt a diagnosis of IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Any focal neurological deficit other than a CN VI palsy (which is a false localising sign), plus drowsiness or seizures — these point away from IIH and towards a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the correct order of investigations in suspected IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Neuroimaging FIRST (MRI + MR venography — normal, and excludes venous sinus thrombosis) BEFORE lumbar puncture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What are the lumbar puncture findings in IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: A raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmH₂O) — the diagnostic finding — with a normal CSF composition (distinguishing it from meningitis). Removing CSF transiently lowers the pressure, but the effect wears off within hours, so repeated 'therapeutic' LPs are not used as ongoing management — only as a holding measure while urgent surgery is arranged.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What ophthalmological assessments are essential in IIH, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Fundoscopy (papilloedema), visual fields/perimetry, visual acuity and OCT — to monitor vision, the key outcome measure, throughout treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the key conservative management of IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• Weight loss (the key disease-modifying step — a sustained loss of around 10% of body weight can resolve papilloedema and can be curative)
  • stop the causative drug (tetracyclines, retinoids, lithium) and avoid abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What is the first-line drug for IIH, and how does it work?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: Acetazolamide — a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production; typically 250–500 mg twice daily titrated up as tolerated, with paraesthesiae, altered taste, fatigue and nausea as common dose-limiting side effects (it is unlicensed for this indication). Topiramate is an alternative (it also causes weight loss) but is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA); furosemide is a further option.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What surgical options exist for sight-threatening or refractory IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back:
• CSF diversion (VP or lumboperitoneal shunt)
  • optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF — protects the optic nerve, preferred if vision-threatening without severe headache)
  • and venous sinus stenting for selected transverse sinus stenosis with a pressure gradient

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.front: What emerging treatments are relevant to IIH given the central role of obesity?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.back: GLP-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery for weight management.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: An accumulation of CSF within the cerebral ventricles causing ventricular dilatation, from a mismatch between CSF production, flow and absorption → raised ICP → brain injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Outline the normal CSF circulation.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: CSF is produced by the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles, and is absorbed by the arachnoid granulations/villi into venous blood.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Trace the CSF flow pathway through the ventricular system.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid space.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What are the three broad mechanisms of hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Obstruction of CSF flow, impaired absorption, or (rarely) overproduction — the site of the problem defines the type.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Define obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus and give causes.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
A blockage of CSF flow within the ventricular system so CSF can't get out of the ventricles; causes include
  • an obstructing tumour or cyst
  • congenital aqueduct stenosis
  • and Dandy-Walker malformation (obstruction of the fourth-ventricle outflow foramina)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Define non-obstructive (communicating) hydrocephalus and give causes.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
Impaired absorption at the arachnoid villi (or rarely overproduction); causes include
  • post-meningitis
  • post-subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • and head injury
NPH is the chronic idiopathic form. (Dandy-Walker is obstructive, not communicating.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Why must you NOT perform an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Removing CSF from below the block risks coning/herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: List the features of raised ICP in hydrocephalus.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
• Headache worse in the morning (after lying supine overnight) and on coughing/bending
  • nausea and vomiting
  • papilloedema
  • reduced consciousness
  • and a CN VI (abducens) palsy as a false-localising sign

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Why is the headache of raised ICP typically worse in the morning?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: It follows prolonged supine lying overnight, which raises intracranial pressure; it is also worse on coughing or bending.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What are the features of hydrocephalus in infants (open sutures)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
• Head circumference crossing centiles on the growth chart
  • a bulging fontanelle
  • 'sunset eyes' (upward gaze palsy)
  • irritability and poor feeding
While the fontanelle is open, cranial ultrasound through it is the first-line scan.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Ventricular dilatation with NORMAL CSF pressure, mostly idiopathic — an important, potentially reversible cause of neurological decline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: State the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
'Wet, Wobbly and Wacky':
  • urinary incontinence (wet)
  • gait abnormality (wobbly — magnetic, shuffling, wide-based apraxic gait, often earliest/most responsive)
  • and dementia (wacky)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Why is NPH clinically important?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: It is a potentially reversible cause of dementia plus gait disturbance that must be distinguished from Alzheimer's/other dementias and can improve with CSF shunting — though it is the gait that improves most reliably; cognitive recovery is much less predictable.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What are the imaging findings of NPH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Ventriculomegaly WITHOUT sulcal enlargement — the ventricles are disproportionately large, unlike the generalised atrophy of Alzheimer's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is the first-line imaging in hydrocephalus and its findings?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
CT head — shows
  • ventricular enlargement
  • loss of the sulcal/gyral pattern
  • and periventricular lucency (transependymal CSF exudation)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is the role of MRI in hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: Better detail — to identify the level of obstruction (e.g. aqueduct stenosis) and the underlying cause (e.g. tumour).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is the role of lumbar puncture in hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: It is diagnostic and therapeutic (measures pressure; removing CSF can help) — but always image FIRST, because you cannot know it is non-obstructive until you have. Never do an LP in obstructive hydrocephalus (coning risk), nor in anyone with a possibly blocked shunt.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What is the NPH 'tap test'?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: A large-volume LP that transiently improves gait predicts a good response to shunting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Outline the acute management of hydrocephalus with raised ICP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back: An external ventricular drain (EVD) to reduce ICP temporarily, then definitive CSF diversion. There is no effective medical treatment: acetazolamide and furosemide do not work and are not recommended (in the randomised trial in infants they increased shunt rates and disability), and must never be allowed to delay CSF diversion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: Outline the definitive management of hydrocephalus.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
• Treat the underlying cause (e.g. debulk a resectable obstructing tumour)
  • a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is the mainstay for chronic disease and NPH
  • endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is an alternative for obstructive hydrocephalus (creates a new drainage route bypassing the block)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.front: What are the recognised complications of a CSF shunt?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.back:
• Blockage → returning raised-ICP symptoms
  • over-drainage → the opposite picture, a postural headache worse on standing, with a risk of subdural haematoma
  • infection → fever, malaise, meningism, redness along the shunt tract or abdominal pain
Headache, vomiting or drowsiness in a shunted patient means a blocked shunt until proven otherwise — urgent CT and immediate neurosurgical discussion, and a normal CT does NOT exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back:
An autosomal dominant, progressive neurodegenerative disorder causing a triad of
  • movement disorder (chorea)
  • cognitive decline
  • and psychiatric disturbance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is the genetic basis of Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: A CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, producing an abnormal, toxic huntingtin protein that causes neurodegeneration.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is the inheritance pattern and offspring risk in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Autosomal dominant — a single copy causes disease, with a 50% risk to each offspring.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is anticipation, and how does it manifest in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: A feature of trinucleotide-repeat disorders where successive generations have more repeats → earlier onset down the generations; expansion occurs especially through the paternal line — which is why juvenile HD (onset under 20, presenting with rigidity and bradykinesia rather than chorea) is almost always inherited from an affected father.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: How does the number of CAG repeats relate to the disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back:
The repeat number decides whether disease occurs and largely sets the age of onset:
  • 26 or fewer is normal
  • 27–35 is intermediate (no disease in the carrier, but unstable and can expand into the pathogenic range on paternal transmission)
  • 36–39 is reduced penetrance
  • 40 or more is full penetrance.
Above the threshold, more repeats means earlier onset — but it does NOT reliably predict severity or rate of progression, and is not used to predict onset age for an individual.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: Which part of the brain degenerates in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: The striatum (caudate and putamen) — especially loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is the imaging correlate of the pathology in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Caudate atrophy → enlarged frontal horns of the lateral ventricles ('boxcar ventricles'); MRI may show caudate/striatal atrophy (supportive, not diagnostic).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: Explain the mechanism of chorea in Huntington's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Loss of the indirect pathway (which normally suppresses unwanted movement) → disinhibition of the thalamus → excess unwanted movement (chorea) — the opposite imbalance to Parkinson's disease.
Involuntary, random, irregular, 'dance-like' movements — the hallmark hyperkinetic feature of Huntington's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is the typical age and pattern of onset in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Insidious, progressive onset typically at 30–50 years, often beginning with cognitive/psychiatric or mood problems, followed by the movement disorder.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What are the psychiatric and cognitive features of Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back:
• Psychiatric (often first): personality change, depression, irritability, anxiety, apathy, psychosis, and a high suicide risk.
  • Cognitive: progressive subcortical dementia (slowed thinking, executive dysfunction).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What movement features occur in Huntington's disease beyond chorea?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Dystonia, rigidity, eye-movement disorders, dysarthria and dysphagia; rigidity/bradykinesia tend to emerge as the disease progresses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: What is the common cause of death in Huntington's disease, and the prognosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Aspiration/pneumonia (from dysphagia); life expectancy is roughly 15–20 years from symptom onset (range about 10–25).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: How is Huntington's disease diagnosed, and what must accompany testing?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: By genetic testing confirming the CAG repeat expansion in HTT. Predictive testing in at-risk relatives is offered only to adults (18 or over) with capacity who ask for it themselves, after structured pre- and post-test counselling; asymptomatic children are NOT tested. A result is never private to one person — it can reveal a relative's status without their consent. Under the UK Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance, HD is the only condition for which insurers may ask about a predictive result, and only for life cover above 500,000 pounds, so applicants are usually advised to arrange cover before testing. Reproductive options include prenatal diagnosis and pre-implantation genetic testing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: How is chorea treated in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back: Tetrabenazine (a dopamine-depleting agent) for troublesome chorea — but it can cause or worsen depression and suicidal ideation, and is contraindicated in untreated or inadequately treated depression and in anyone actively suicidal. In a disease defined by depression and a high suicide rate, screen for and treat depression first, monitor closely, and warn the patient and family. An antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone or sulpiride) is often preferred where depression, psychosis or agitation coexist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: Outline the overall management of Huntington's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back:
No cure — multidisciplinary supportive care:
  • tetrabenazine for chorea (contraindicated in untreated depression or active suicidality; an antipsychotic is often preferred then)
  • antidepressants/antipsychotics for mood and psychosis, asking directly about suicidal thoughts at every review
  • SALT for dysarthria and swallowing/aspiration
  • palliative/end-of-life care
  • MDT (neurology, physio, OT, dietitian, social care)
  • genetic counselling for the family
  • and DVLA notification with reassessment of fitness to drive as it progresses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.front: List the main differentials for chorea besides Huntington's disease.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.back:
• Sydenham's chorea (post-streptococcal, children)
  • drug-induced (levodopa, antipsychotics/tardive dyskinesia, stimulants)
  • Wilson's disease (young + liver disease + Kayser–Fleischer rings)
  • SLE/antiphospholipid (autoimmune)
  • and chorea gravidarum (pregnancy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: The commonest movement disorder — a chronic, slowly progressive, bilateral POSTURAL + ACTION (kinetic) tremor, usually of the hands/arms, worse with sustained posture and voluntary (kinetic) movement but WITHOUT the target-worsening of a cerebellar intention tremor, often improved by alcohol, with a strong family history.(The old label 'benign essential tremor' is no longer used — it is frequently disabling.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What is the core concept distinguishing essential tremor from Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Essential tremor is an ACTION tremor — it appears when the hands are doing something (holding a posture, reaching, writing, holding a cup) and is absent or much reduced at rest; Parkinson's is a REST tremor, worst when still and improving with movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What is the single most useful question when assessing a tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: 'When is the tremor worst — using the hands, or resting them?'Action/postural = essential tremor; at rest = Parkinson's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What are the key hallmarks that clinch a diagnosis of essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back:
• Typically symmetrical
  • positive family history (autosomal dominant)
  • relieved by alcohol
  • with NO other Parkinsonian features (no bradykinesia, rigidity or gait disturbance)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: Compare the symmetry and frequency of essential tremor vs Parkinson's tremor.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back:
• Essential tremor is symmetrical (bilateral) and faster (~4–12 Hz, typically 6–12, fine)
  • Parkinson's is asymmetrical (starts one side) and slower (~4–6 Hz, 'pill-rolling')
Note the frequencies overlap in older patients, so action-versus-rest is the better discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: How does alcohol affect essential tremor versus Parkinson's tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Alcohol improves essential tremor in about half to two-thirds of patients — a supportive feature, but its absence does not exclude the diagnosis, and alcohol also relieves dystonic tremor. It has no effect on Parkinson's tremor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What other body sites are commonly involved in essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: A head tremor (titubation — 'yes-yes'/'no-no') and a voice tremor (quavering); less often the jaw, tongue or legs.These are uncommon in Parkinson's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What manoeuvres bring out the tremor of essential tremor on examination?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back:
• Holding the arms outstretched
  • holding a cup
  • writing
  • pouring
  • and moving a spoon to the mouth
it is absent/reduced at rest and worse with anxiety, caffeine and fatigue.
Clinically — a characteristic postural/action tremor with no other neurological signs and a positive family history; investigations are done to EXCLUDE mimics, not to confirm it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What reversible causes/mimics should be excluded in suspected essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Thyroid function (hyperthyroidism) and a drug/substance review — caffeine, β-agonists (salbutamol), levothyroxine, lithium, valproate, SSRIs, stimulants; consider Wilson's disease in the young (copper studies).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: When is a DaT scan indicated in a tremor work-up?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Only if Parkinson's disease is in question (a rest tremor or other Parkinsonian features) — not for typical essential tremor, which is a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: How is a cerebellar (intention) tremor distinguished from essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: A cerebellar tremor worsens as the hand approaches a target (past-pointing) and is accompanied by ataxia, nystagmus and dysdiadochokinesis; essential tremor is a postural/action tremor without these signs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: When should essential tremor be treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Only if it causes functional or psychosocial impairment — many patients need only reassurance; reduce caffeine, review aggravating drugs, and avoid relying on alcohol(it helps transiently but is not a treatment).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What are the first-line drug treatments for essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back:
• Propranolol (a beta-blocker; effective in ~50–70%; start 40 mg two to three times daily, usual maintenance 80–160 mg daily; regular or situational)
  • or primidone (a barbiturate anticonvulsant; start 62.5 mg at NIGHT and increase slowly over 4–6 weeks to a usual effective 250–750 mg daily in divided doses) — primidone is the first-line alternative, especially where propranolol is contraindicated (e.g. asthma)
The two can be combined.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What are the key cautions with propranolol and primidone in essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back:
• Propranolol — avoid in asthma, bradycardia, heart block and uncontrolled heart failure
  • Primidone — start at 62.5 mg at night and titrate slowly over 4–6 weeks, because of sedation and a notorious acute first-dose reaction; it is also teratogenic
Both are relevant to driving: the patient must notify the DVLA if the tremor affects safe vehicle control, and primidone is sedating.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.front: What are the second-line and refractory treatment options for essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.back: Second-line: topiramate — contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA) — gabapentin, or a benzodiazepine such as clonazepam (dependence risk); botulinum toxin for head/voice tremor. Refractory/severe: deep brain stimulation (thalamic/VIM) or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is headache broadly classified, with examples?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Primary (no structural cause — migraine, tension-type, cluster) vs secondary (an underlying cause — SAH, GCA, raised ICP, meningitis, medication-overuse). The first job in any headache is to screen for red flags of a secondary cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the classic profile of migraine (character, duration, associations, acute treatment, prevention).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Unilateral, throbbing/pulsatile
  • 4–72 hours
  • photophobia, nausea, ± aura, worse with activity
  • acute = a triptan + NSAID/paracetamol
  • prevention = propranolol/topiramate/amitriptyline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the classic profile of a tension-type headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Bilateral, 'tight band'/pressing
  • 30 minutes–days
  • no prominent associated features
  • acute = simple analgesia
  • prevention (if frequent) = amitriptyline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the classic profile of a cluster headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Unilateral, severe, around the eye
  • 15 minutes–3 hours in clusters
  • prominent ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, red eye, rhinorrhoea, ptosis/miosis) with restlessness
  • acute = high-flow oxygen + SC triptan
  • prevention = verapamil.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: List key headache red flags and what each suggests.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Thunderclap ('worst ever') → SAH
  • new headache with scalp tenderness/jaw claudication in a patient >50 → giant cell arteritis
  • worse on waking/lying/Valsalva with papilloedema → raised ICP
  • fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → meningitis
  • focal neurology/reduced GCS/cancer/immunosuppression/pregnancy → a serious secondary cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is medication-overuse headache, and how is it managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A secondary headache caused by regular use of acute headache medication for 3 months or more — triptans, opioids, ergots or combination analgesics on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month. Management is to stop all the overused drugs abruptly for at least a month.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Define migraine.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A primary headache disorder: recurrent, moderate–severe, often unilateral, pulsating headaches lasting 4–72 hours, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, ± aura.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Describe the epidemiology of migraine.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• One of the commonest disabling conditions
  • commoner in women
  • strong genetic component
  • onset often in adolescence/young adulthood.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the four phases of a migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Prodrome (mood/appetite change, yawning, fatigue)
  • aura (in ~one-third)
  • headache (4–72 hours)
  • and postdrome ('migraine hangover' — fatigue, poor concentration).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Describe migraine aura.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Fully reversible neurological symptoms developing over 5–20 minutes and lasting <60 minutes — classically visual (zigzag/fortification lines, scintillating scotoma, flashing lights); can also be sensory or dysphasic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: State the diagnostic criteria for migraine without aura.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: At least 5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours, with >=2 of (unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe, aggravated by activity) AND >=1 of (nausea/vomiting, or photophobia + phonophobia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the POUND mnemonic for migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Pulsatile
  • O = 4–72 hOurs
  • Unilateral
  • Nausea
  • Disabling
— the more features present, the more likely it is migraine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is migraine investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: It is a clinical diagnosis (characteristic pattern + no red flags); a headache diary helps. No investigations are needed in typical migraine with a normal examination — image only if there are red flags. Examine fundi, visual fields and neurology, and check BP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the NICE first-line acute treatment of a migraine attack?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Taken early: a triptan PLUS an NSAID, or a triptan plus paracetamol. Triptans (e.g. sumatriptan) are 5-HT1 agonists causing cranial vasoconstriction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What adjunct is added for nausea in migraine, and which drug class is avoided?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Add an antiemetic (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine — which also aid absorption), even without vomiting. Avoid opioids (ineffective and a cause of medication-overuse headache).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the critical contraindications to triptans?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Ischaemic heart disease
  • uncontrolled hypertension
  • and previous stroke/TIA
(triptans cause vasoconstriction).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the medication-overuse limits to advise in migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Keep triptans, opioids, ergots and combination analgesics to fewer than 10 days a month, and simple analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) to fewer than 15 days a month.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: When is migraine prophylaxis offered, and what are the first-line options?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
If migraines are frequent/disabling (e.g. >=4 migraine days/month):
  • propranolol
  • topiramate
  • or amitriptyline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give a key caveat for propranolol and for topiramate used as migraine prophylaxis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Propranolol — avoid in asthma, and take care in someone with depression because it is dangerous in overdose
  • Topiramate — contraindicated in pregnancy for migraine prophylaxis, and contraindicated in women and girls able to have children unless all the conditions of a pregnancy prevention programme are met; in-utero exposure also carries a 2–3 times higher risk of intellectual disability, autism and ADHD.
It reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the options for refractory/chronic migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) or gepants (rimegepant) after >=3 preventives have failed; botulinum toxin for chronic migraine (specialist).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the critical rule about migraine, aura and the combined pill?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Migraine WITH aura + combined hormonal contraception = contraindicated (UKMEC 4) because both raise ischaemic stroke risk. Use a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method. Migraine without aura is UKMEC 2/3 (relative).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is hemiplegic migraine, and the key action?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A migraine in which the aura includes motor weakness, mimicking a stroke — exclude stroke first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is migraine managed in pregnancy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Paracetamol first-line for an acute attack. A triptan or an NSAID may still be considered after discussing the need for treatment against the risks — sumatriptan has the largest safety dataset, and NSAIDs are avoided in the third trimester. Topiramate is contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy. Involve a specialist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is menstrual migraine managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Triptans + NSAIDs (e.g. mefenamic acid); consider perimenstrual prophylaxis (e.g. frovatriptan); review prophylaxis after ~6 months.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is a cluster headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A severe, strictly unilateral headache around the eye/temple, occurring in clusters (bouts) with prominent ipsilateral cranial autonomic features — one of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Describe the demographics of cluster headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Commoner in men and smokers; onset typically in the 20s–40s; the clustering time-pattern is the diagnostic signature.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the two almost-unique management priorities in cluster headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: High-flow 100% oxygen (acute) and verapamil (prophylaxis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the duration and timing pattern of cluster headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Attacks last 15 minutes–3 hours, are often nocturnal / at the same time each day, and occur in clusters (e.g. 3–4 a day for weeks, then remission for months–years).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the ipsilateral autonomic features of cluster headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• A red, swollen, watering eye
  • miosis
  • ptosis
  • nasal congestion/discharge
  • and facial sweating
— the eye and nose 'run' on the same side as the pain (a partial Horner's-like picture).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the characteristic behaviour in cluster headache, and why is it useful?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: The patient is restless/agitated and paces — a classic bedside discriminator from migraine, in which the patient lies still in the dark.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Contrast cluster headache with migraine.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Cluster = shorter (15 min–3 h), prominent autonomic features, restless, in clusters. Migraine = longer (4–72 h), nausea/photophobia, lies still.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Contrast cluster headache with trigeminal neuralgia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Cluster = 15 min–3 h peri-orbital pain with autonomic features. Trigeminal neuralgia = seconds-long, shock-like paroxysms in the trigeminal (V2/V3) distribution, without autonomic features.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is cluster headache diagnosed, and what imaging is considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Clinically (peri-orbital pain + ipsilateral autonomic features + clustering + restlessness); consider MRI brain (including pituitary/cavernous sinus), especially at first presentation or if atypical.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Which other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia must be distinguished, and how?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Paroxysmal hemicrania — shorter and more frequent attacks that respond completely to indomethacin.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the acute treatment of a cluster attack?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: High-flow 100% oxygen at at least 12 L/min, through a non-rebreathing mask with a reservoir bag, PLUS subcutaneous sumatriptan (the formulation licensed for cluster) or a nasal triptan. The oxygen has to be prescribed as home and ambulatory oxygen or the patient cannot use it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Why are oral triptans and simple analgesics not used to abort a cluster attack?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: The attacks are too short and fast for oral absorption to act in time, so oral triptans and simple analgesics are ineffective.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the first-line prophylaxis for cluster headache during a bout, and its key monitoring?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Verapamil (a calcium-channel blocker) — monitor the ECG because of the risk of heart block / PR prolongation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give other prophylactic and lifestyle measures for cluster headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• An occipital nerve block
  • a short course of prednisolone to break a bout while verapamil takes effect (seek specialist advice before starting either verapamil or a corticosteroid)
  • avoid alcohol during a bout
  • and smoking cessation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is tension-type headache (TTH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: The commonest primary headache — a mild-to-moderate, bilateral, band-like 'pressure/tightness' headache without the disabling features of migraine or the autonomic features of cluster.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the 'core concept' that defines tension-type headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: It is defined largely by what it lacks: featureless, non-throbbing, non-disabling, no aura, no significant nausea, no autonomic signs, and not worsened by routine activity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Describe the character and site of tension-type headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A bilateral, band-like / 'vice-like' pressure or tightness that develops and resolves gradually; it is non-pulsatile and mild-to-moderate in severity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How does activity affect tension-type headache versus migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: TTH is NOT worsened by routine physical activity, whereas migraine characteristically is aggravated by activity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What associated features distinguish tension-type headache from migraine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: TTH has no aura and no significant nausea (at most mild photophobia OR phonophobia); migraine has nausea, photophobia AND phonophobia, ± aura.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What examination sign may be present in tension-type headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Pericranial (scalp/neck muscle) tenderness may be present; otherwise examination is normal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: List common triggers/associations for tension-type headache.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Stress, depression, alcohol, skipping meals and dehydration — plus poor posture, fatigue, eye strain and sleep disturbance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is tension-type headache classified by frequency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Episodic = <15 days/month; chronic = ≥15 days/month for >3 months. Chronic TTH overlaps with medication-overuse headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is medication-overuse headache (MOH)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A chronic daily headache (present ≥15 days/month) that develops or worsens while taking regular symptomatic analgesia, with non-specific tension-like features.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is medication-overuse headache managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Stop ALL the overused acute medications abruptly, not gradually, for at least 1 month — simple analgesics, triptans and opioids alike. Warn that the headache usually worsens for a week or two before it improves. Consider specialist referral or inpatient withdrawal for people on strong opioids, those with relevant comorbidities, and those in whom previous attempts have failed. Review 4–8 weeks after withdrawal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the key question to ask in any chronic daily 'tension' headache, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Ask about analgesic frequency — because the treatment for medication-overuse headache is to STOP the overused analgesic, not add more.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the acute/episodic treatment of tension-type headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Reassurance plus a simple analgesic — aspirin, paracetamol, or an oral NSAID (ibuprofen); avoid opioids, and limit acute analgesic use to <15 days/month to avoid medication-overuse headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the prophylaxis for chronic/frequent tension-type headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: NICE recommends a course of up to 10 sessions of acupuncture over 5–8 weeks. Low-dose amitriptyline is widely used in practice but is off-label for this indication and is not a NICE recommendation. Also address triggers and lifestyle — stress, sleep, hydration, meals, posture, and comorbid depression or anxiety.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Why is reassurance central to managing tension-type headache?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: It is a benign condition — explaining the mechanism reassures the patient and helps avoid over-investigation, once red flags, migraine and medication-overuse headache have been excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Before diagnosing tension-type headache, what must always be excluded?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Red-flag features pointing to a secondary cause, and medication-overuse headache in anyone with a chronic daily headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is trigeminal neuralgia (TN)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A disorder of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) causing sudden, severe, brief, 'electric-shock'-like unilateral facial pain in a trigeminal distribution.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the signature pattern of trigeminal neuralgia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Paroxysms of stabbing/electric-shock pain lasting seconds, triggered by innocuous stimuli (touch, chewing, cold, wind), in one or more trigeminal divisions, with the patient pain-free between attacks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Which trigeminal divisions are usually affected in TN, and on which side?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Unilateral, usually V2 (maxillary) and/or V3 (mandibular); V1 (ophthalmic) is less commonly involved.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the two management priorities in trigeminal neuralgia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• (1) Exclude a secondary cause (MS, tumour, or a compressing vessel — via MRI)
  • and (2) treat with carbamazepine, because the pain is neuropathic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Describe the typical demographics and cause of classic trigeminal neuralgia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Commoner in older adults and women; usually idiopathic/vascular — neurovascular compression of the trigeminal root near the pons (typically by an aberrant superior cerebellar artery).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the red flags suggesting SECONDARY trigeminal neuralgia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Age <40, bilateral pain, sensory loss, or other neurology — these suggest MS (a pontine demyelinating plaque) or a tumour, and should prompt MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What proportion of trigeminal neuralgia is due to multiple sclerosis, and what feature should raise suspicion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: ~2–4% is due to an MS plaque on the trigeminal root; bilateral or young-onset TN should prompt investigation for MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Explain the pathophysiology of classic trigeminal neuralgia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: An aberrant vascular loop (usually the superior cerebellar artery) compresses the trigeminal root near the pons → demyelination → abnormal firing → paroxysmal pain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the typical triggers of trigeminal neuralgia attacks?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
Innocuous stimuli —
  • light touch
  • washing/shaving
  • chewing
  • talking
  • brushing teeth
  • and cold wind.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is trigeminal neuralgia diagnosed and investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Diagnosis is clinical (paroxysmal, seconds-long, shock-like triggered pain with a normal neurological exam in classic TN)
  • MRI brain excludes secondary causes (neurovascular compression, MS plaques, tumours)
  • consider ESR/CRP to exclude GCA.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is trigeminal neuralgia distinguished from cluster headache and migraine by duration?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• TN = seconds (shock-like, touch-triggered)
  • cluster = 15 min–3 h (peri-orbital, autonomic, restless)
  • migraine = 4–72 h (throbbing, nausea/photophobia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the first-line drug treatment of trigeminal neuralgia, and why not simple analgesia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Carbamazepine (an anticonvulsant / sodium-channel blocker), titrated to effect — the pain is neuropathic, so standard analgesics, NSAIDs and opioids do not work.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the key side effects of carbamazepine to monitor for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Dizziness
  • drowsiness
  • diplopia
  • ataxia
  • hyponatraemia (SIADH)
  • rash (rarely Stevens–Johnson)
  • and enzyme induction (reducing contraceptive efficacy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is done if carbamazepine fails or is not tolerated in TN?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Refer to a specialist. Nothing other than carbamazepine should be started outside a specialist setting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What surgical options exist for refractory trigeminal neuralgia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Microvascular decompression is the procedure of choice for classic TN with neurovascular compression, giving the best long-term relief. Ablative and radiosurgical options exist for those unfit for, or unwilling to have, open surgery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What does the GCS measure, its range, and its three components?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Level of consciousness, scored 3 (worst) to 15 (best): Eyes (/4), Verbal (/5), Motor (/6).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the eye-opening responses (E, /4).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• 4 spontaneous
  • 3 to speech
  • 2 to pain
  • 1 none.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the verbal responses (V, /5).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• 5 orientated
  • 4 confused
  • 3 inappropriate words
  • 2 incomprehensible sounds
  • 1 none.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the motor responses (M, /6).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• 6 obeys commands
  • 5 localises to pain
  • 4 withdraws
  • 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate)
  • 2 extension (decerebrate)
  • 1 none.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the significance of a GCS of 8 or less?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Coma — the patient cannot protect their airway → intubate ('GCS 8, intubate').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Which GCS component is most prognostic, and how do flexion and extension compare?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Motor is the most prognostically important; extension (decerebrate) is worse than flexion (decorticate) — it reflects deeper/lower brainstem involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Give the GCS severity bands for head injury.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Mild 13–15
  • moderate 9–12
  • severe 8 or less.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is the GCS recorded and reported?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Record the BEST response in each category; report as E_V_M_ (e.g. E3V4M5 = 12).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the Monro-Kellie doctrine, and why does it matter in head injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: The skull is a fixed box, so an expanding haematoma/oedema raises ICP → herniation → death. This is why time-critical detection of a treatable bleed matters.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: List the NICE indications for CT head within 1 hour.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• GCS <13 on initial assessment
  • GCS <15 at 2 hours
  • suspected open/depressed skull fracture
  • any sign of basal skull fracture
  • post-traumatic seizure
  • focal neurological deficit
