  • more than one episode of vomiting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the signs of a basal skull fracture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Haemotympanum
  • 'panda'/raccoon eyes
  • CSF leak from ear/nose
  • and Battle's sign (mastoid bruising).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: List the NICE indications for CT head within 8 hours.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
Some loss of consciousness or amnesia PLUS any of:
  • age 65 or over
  • any CURRENT bleeding or clotting disorder
  • a dangerous mechanism
  • or more than 30 minutes of retrograde amnesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the NICE anticoagulant/antiplatelet CT rule?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A head injury with no other CT indication but the patient is on an anticoagulant (warfarin/DOAC/heparin) or antiplatelet (excluding aspirin monotherapy) → CT within 8 hours (or within 1 hour if presenting more than 8 hours after injury).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the classic features of an extradural haematoma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A lucid interval then rapid deterioration; biconvex (lens-shaped) on CT; middle meningeal artery (often temporal trauma) — a neurosurgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the classic features of a subdural haematoma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Crescent-shaped on CT; typically elderly/alcoholic/anticoagulated patients (bridging veins); can be acute or chronic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What other traumatic intracranial bleeds may CT show?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage and intracerebral haemorrhage/contusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is a 'lucid interval', and what does it classically indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A brief recovery of consciousness after the injury followed by deterioration — classic for an extradural (arterial) haematoma expanding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the single most important sign of neurological deterioration?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: A falling GCS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is Cushing's reflex, and what does it signify?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing — a late, ominous sign of raised ICP and impending herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What does a fixed, dilated ('blown') pupil indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Third cranial nerve compression from uncal (transtentorial) herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the immediate ABCDE priorities in head injury, and what worsens outcome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Airway with C-spine immobilisation, oxygenation, and circulation — avoid hypoxia and hypotension, which worsen secondary brain injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is the airway rule for a severe head injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: GCS 8 or less → intubate (the patient cannot protect the airway).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: When and how is tranexamic acid used in head injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: For a head injury with GCS <=12 and no suspected active extracranial bleeding → IV tranexamic acid (2 g) as soon as possible, within 2 hours of injury, before imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is anticoagulation reversed if there is an intracranial bleed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Warfarin → prothrombin complex concentrate + vitamin K.
  • Dabigatran → idarucizumab.
  • Apixaban or rivaroxaban → PCC, discussing urgently with haematology — there is no NICE-recommended specific antidote for factor Xa inhibitors in intracranial bleeding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What are the indications for neurosurgical referral?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Significant bleeds (evacuation of extradural/subdural haematoma)
  • depressed skull fractures
  • and raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: How is raised ICP managed acutely?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• Head-up positioning
  • avoiding hypoxia and hypercapnia
  • and neurosurgical measures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: Who should be admitted for observation after a head injury?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back:
• A new clinically important abnormality on imaging
  • GCS not back to 15 (or the pre-injury baseline) after imaging, whatever the scan shows
  • CT indicated but not obtainable in time
  • continuing worrying symptoms (persistent vomiting, severe headache, seizures)
  • or other sources of concern — drug or alcohol intoxication, other injuries, shock, suspected non-accidental injury, meningism, a CSF leak.
Note what is NOT on the list: being on an anticoagulant is not by itself a reason to admit. NICE looked at this and found no clinically important excess of delayed bleeding, so a patient on a DOAC with GCS 15, a normal CT and nothing else of concern can go home with head-injury advice.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.front: What is concussion, and what is post-concussion syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.back: Concussion = a transient disturbance of brain function (brief confusion, headache, dizziness, amnesia). It is a CLINICAL diagnosis — most concussed patients never meet the CT criteria and are never scanned, so a scan is neither needed to make it nor able to exclude it. Post-concussion syndrome = persistent headache, dizziness, poor concentration and mood or sleep disturbance for weeks to months. For sport: if in doubt, sit them out — no return to play that day, then a graduated return, with a minimum of 21 days before any match involving possible contact.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: A seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise neurologically normal child, without CNS infection or another identifiable cause. It is a provoked seizure — NOT epilepsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What is the typical epidemiology of febrile convulsions?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Common (~3% of children), age 6 months–5 years, occurring early in a fever — often before anyone has noticed it — usually from a viral infection.

• <15 minutes
  • generalised (tonic-clonic)
  • no recurrence within 24 h
  • and complete recovery (<1 hour).

At least one of:
  • lasting more than 15 minutes (there is no upper limit)
  • focal features
  • recurrence within 24 hours or within the same febrile illness
  • or incomplete recovery within 1 hour.

A febrile seizure lasting >30 minutes. It is a prolonged COMPLEX febrile seizure, not a separate third category — so it triggers every 'complex' rule (admission, considering LP, higher epilepsy risk).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: Why does the simple vs complex distinction matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Complex febrile convulsions carry a higher risk of recurrence and a (slightly) higher risk of later epilepsy — so they warrant more caution/investigation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What are the typical clinical features of a febrile convulsion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Occur early in a febrile illness — often as the first sign the child is unwell, so the seizure may come before anyone notices the fever (a higher peak temperature makes one more likely); usually tonic-clonic; last <5 minutes; often a family history; the child is developmentally normal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What is the critical 'must-not-miss' differential, and its red flags?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back:
Meningitis/encephalitis —
  • neck stiffness
  • a non-blanching rash
  • a bulging fontanelle
  • drowsiness/altered consciousness
  • focal neurology
  • or failure to recover.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: Besides CNS infection, what else must be excluded?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back:
• Other serious infection ('red' features)
  • metabolic causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia)
  • and epilepsy (seizure without fever, or afebrile recurrences).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What age caveat should heighten suspicion of another cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: A seizure with fever <6 months or >5 years is unusual for a febrile convulsion — scrutinise for another cause. Meningitis signs are subtle in infants (<18 months).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What investigations does a simple febrile convulsion need?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Often none beyond identifying the fever source — examine thoroughly, do a urine dip/culture (occult UTI), and check blood glucose.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: When is a lumbar puncture indicated in a child with a febrile seizure?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: If meningitis/encephalitis is suspected — complex features, failure to recover, or red flags. Signs of meningitis are unreliable under 18 months, so have a much lower threshold there. But stabilise first and defer the LP if there is shock, a non-blanching rash or any sign of raised intracranial pressure, and never let it delay antibiotics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: Which investigations are NOT routinely needed for a simple febrile convulsion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back:
• EEG
  • neuroimaging
  • and routine bloods — over-investigation is a common error.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: When should a child with a febrile convulsion be admitted?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back:
• A first febrile convulsion
  • complex features
  • diagnostic uncertainty
  • an unwell child
  • age <18 months
  • no identified focus for the fever
  • or the child is currently or recently on antibiotics (which can mask the signs of meningitis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: Outline the acute management of a febrile seizure.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back:
• Protect from injury, recovery position once the seizure has stopped, oxygen if needed
  • call 999 if it lasts >5 minutes
  • benzodiazepine rescue if one has been supplied — buccal midazolam is the UK first choice, rectal diazepam if that is unsuitable — given at 5 minutes
  • and treat the underlying infection.
If meningitis or meningococcal disease is suspected, give empirical IV ceftriaxone immediately and do NOT delay it for a lumbar puncture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What is the role of antipyretics and anticonvulsant prophylaxis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) are for comfort only — they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions. No routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis for simple FCs.

~1 in 3 chance of recurrence; very low epilepsy risk (reassure). For a future seizure:
  • time it
  • protect the head
  • do NOT restrain the child and do NOT put anything in their mouth
  • recovery position once it has stopped
  • call 999 if it lasts >5 minutes.
Seek urgent help for a non-blanching rash, drowsiness or difficulty waking, another seizure in the same illness, or failure to recover as expected.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.front: What is the prognosis of febrile convulsions?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.back: Recurrence ~1 in 3 — higher if under 18 months at the first seizure, a family history of febrile convulsions, a lower peak temperature, or a short fever before the seizure. Epilepsy risk very low: about 1–2% absolute after a simple FC, against roughly 0.5–1% in the general population; higher with complex features, neurodevelopmental abnormality or a family history of epilepsy. No effect on development or intelligence — reassure strongly.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: An acute, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy causing rapidly progressive ascending flaccid paralysis, usually following an infection. Most UK cases are demyelinating (AIDP), but the AMAN variant is axonal — so 'demyelinating' alone is too narrow.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What weakness pattern does GBS produce, and the hallmark sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: An acute, ascending, symmetrical, LMN (flaccid) weakness with areflexia. It is the commonest cause of acute flaccid paralysis since polio control.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What two features make GBS an emergency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• Respiratory muscle failure (the leading cause of death — monitor FVC)
  • and autonomic instability.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: A post-infectious autoimmune process: infection triggers antibodies that cross-react with peripheral nerve myelin (molecular mimicry) — causing demyelination of peripheral nerves and roots.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the classic infective trigger of GBS, and its significance?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis — the commonest identified precedent, associated with more severe/axonal disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: Name other GBS triggers and the timing of weakness onset.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• CMV
  • EBV
  • Mycoplasma
  • HIV
  • influenza/viral URTIs.
Weakness begins ~1–3 weeks after the infection.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What are the main subtypes of GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• AIDP (commonest in the West)
  • AMAN (acute motor axonal — Campylobacter-associated)
  • and the Miller Fisher variant.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: Describe the weakness in typical GBS.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Symmetrical and ascending — starting in the legs and ascending to arms/trunk over days; the nadir is usually reached within 4 weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What reflex finding is characteristic of GBS, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Areflexia/hyporeflexia — a key LMN sign, reflecting peripheral nerve/root demyelination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the sensory involvement in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Often paraesthesia/pain (may precede weakness), but objective sensory loss is mild — it is predominantly motor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What cranial-nerve features occur in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Bilateral facial weakness and bulbar involvement (difficulty swallowing/speaking).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: Why is respiratory function critical in GBS, and how is it monitored?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Diaphragm/intercostal weakness causes ventilatory failure (the leading cause of death). Monitor with serial forced vital capacity (FVC).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What autonomic features occur in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• Arrhythmias
  • labile blood pressure
  • tachy- or bradycardia
  • urinary retention and ileus.
The practical hazard: tracheal suctioning, laryngoscopy, turning and straining can provoke profound bradycardia or even asystole — pre-oxygenate, keep atropine to hand, and treat hypertension only with short-acting agents, because these patients swing violently into hypotension.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is Miller Fisher syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: A GBS variant with the triad ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia, with cranial-nerve onset and without the typical limb weakness; associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies in the great majority. Usually a good prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the key differential to exclude in GBS, and how does it differ?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Spinal cord compression — a surgical emergency with UMN signs, a sensory level and bladder/sphincter involvement (GBS gives LMN signs and no sensory level).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: Name other differentials of acute weakness besides cord compression.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• Transverse myelitis
  • myasthenia gravis (fatiguable, ocular)
  • botulism (descending, with fixed dilated pupils)
  • hypokalaemia and other electrolyte disturbance
  • acute intermittent porphyria
  • and organophosphate poisoning.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the classic CSF finding in GBS, and its caveat?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Albuminocytologic dissociation — raised protein with a normal white cell count. Caveat: it may be normal in the first week, so an early normal LP does not exclude GBS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What do nerve conduction studies show in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Slowed conduction / conduction block (demyelination); they may be normal early.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: Which antibody supports Miller Fisher syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Anti-GQ1b (anti-ganglioside antibodies; not routine in typical GBS).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the most important monitoring investigation in GBS, and the key rule?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Serial FVC every few hours in a progressing patient. Two thresholds: below 20 mL/kg, or a rapidly falling trend, means critical-care review and ITU-level monitoring; below 15 mL/kg, or bulbar failure with an ineffective cough, means intubate. NIV is generally avoided in neuromuscular respiratory failure with bulbar involvement, because the airway is not protected. Do not wait for hypoxia or a rising CO2 — the saturations and blood gas stay normal until the patient is about to arrest.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the first-line immunotherapy for GBS, and the alternative?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: IV immunoglobulin first-line — 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 consecutive days, 2 g/kg in total — OR plasma exchange, which is equally effective. Give one, not both. Treat patients who cannot walk 10 m unaided, or who have respiratory or bulbar involvement, or who are progressing rapidly, and start within 2 weeks of the onset of weakness; a mildly affected patient still walking independently is monitored rather than treated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What are two critical treatment 'don'ts' in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back: Give ONE, not both — do not give plasma exchange after IVIG (it removes the immunoglobulin). And corticosteroids are NOT effective in GBS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What supportive care is the mainstay of GBS management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• Respiratory monitoring (serial FVC, ventilate if failing)
  • cardiac and autonomic monitoring
  • VTE prophylaxis
  • catheter and bowel care
  • neuropathic pain control
  • physiotherapy and OT
  • and nutrition if there is bulbar involvement.
Note on the pain: gabapentin and pregabalin work, but the MHRA warns of respiratory depression in exactly this group — compromised respiratory function, neurological disease, the elderly, renal impairment, other CNS depressants — so start low and monitor. The same applies to opioids.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: When is ICU admission indicated in GBS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
• Severe/rapidly progressing weakness
  • a falling FVC
  • bulbar involvement
  • or autonomic instability.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.front: What is the prognosis of GBS, and the chronic counterpart?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.back:
Usually monophasic, though it recurs in roughly 2–5%, and about 1 in 10 have a treatment-related fluctuation — a transient deterioration after initial improvement, which is treatable and does not mean the diagnosis was wrong. Most recover over weeks to months, but about 20% are still unable to walk unaided at 6 months and mortality is around 3–7%; residual fatigue, pain and distal paraesthesiae are much commoner than that. A small proportion develop CIDP (chronic, over 8 weeks). Poor prognostic factors:
  • older age
  • rapid onset
  • the axonal subtype
  • needing a ventilator
  • and a preceding Campylobacter illness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Define epilepsy and a seizure.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Epilepsy = a tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, OR 1 unprovoked seizure with a high recurrence risk (e.g. a structural cause). A seizure = a transient episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronous cortical electrical activity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are the three management 'pillars' of epilepsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• (1) Classify the seizure (focal vs generalised — it determines the drug)
  • (2) treat the acute prolonged seizure (status epilepticus = emergency)
  • (3) advise on practical consequences (DVLA, safety, pregnancy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What is the first question the ILAE classification asks, and the two answers?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: 'Where does the seizure start?' → Focal (one part of one hemisphere) vs generalised (both hemispheres from the start).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: How are focal seizures sub-classified by awareness, and what can they evolve to?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Focal aware (conscious) or focal impaired awareness. A focal seizure can evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: List the generalised seizure types.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Tonic-clonic
  • absence
  • myoclonic
  • tonic
  • and atonic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are the features of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
Tonic (stiffening) → clonic (jerking)
  • loss of consciousness
  • tongue-biting
  • incontinence
  • and post-ictal drowsiness/confusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are the features of absence seizures?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Brief (typically 5–20 seconds) vacant staring/'blank', with NO post-ictal phase; typically children; 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are myoclonic seizures, and a classic syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Sudden, brief, shock-like jerks — e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Contrast tonic and atonic seizures.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Tonic = sudden stiffening → fall; atonic = sudden loss of tone → 'drop attack'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are temporal-lobe focal seizure features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Aura (déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, fear)
  • automatisms (lip-smacking, fidgeting)
  • and altered awareness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are frontal-lobe focal seizure features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Motor features — Jacksonian march, posturing, and Todd's paresis (post-ictal weakness).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are parietal and occipital focal seizure features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Parietal = sensory (tingling, numbness); occipital = visual (flashes, patterns).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What is Todd's paresis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Transient post-ictal focal weakness that can mimic a stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What is a Jacksonian march?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Motor seizure activity 'marching' along the body as it spreads across the motor cortex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What is the single most important part of diagnosing epilepsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: It is a clinical diagnosis — a detailed eyewitness account (aura, event, tongue-biting, incontinence, post-ictal confusion, duration) is the most important thing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Name key provoking causes to exclude before diagnosing epilepsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Hypoglycaemia
  • hyponatraemia
  • hypocalcaemia
  • alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
  • drugs
  • infection (meningitis/encephalitis)
  • eclampsia
  • head injury
  • hypoxia.
A provoked seizure is not epilepsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Name key seizure mimics.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Syncope (vasovagal/cardiac — brief, quick recovery, situational)
  • non-epileptic attack disorder (NEAD/functional)
  • TIA
  • migraine
  • panic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What is the role and the key caveat of EEG in epilepsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: It supports classification (e.g. 3 Hz spike-wave = absence). Caveat: a normal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy, and an abnormal one does not confirm it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: When is MRI brain indicated, and what other tests are done?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: MRI to find a structural cause (especially focal seizures or new-onset in adults — exclude tumour/AVM/malformation). Also glucose, U&E, calcium, magnesium, FBC (provoked causes) and ECG (cardiac syncope).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: When are antiseizure medications usually started, and what is the aim?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Usually after a SECOND seizure — or after a first if there is a structural lesion, an unequivocal epileptic EEG, or high judged risk. Aim for monotherapy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: NICE first-line for generalised tonic-clonic and focal seizures?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Generalised tonic-clonic → sodium valproate in boys and men, and women unable to have children; lamotrigine or levetiracetam in girls and women able to have children.
  • Focal → lamotrigine or levetiracetam, whatever the sex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: NICE first-line for absence and myoclonic seizures?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Absence → ethosuximide first-line for everyone; second-line is valproate (boys/men, women unable to have children) or lamotrigine/levetiracetam. Avoid carbamazepine, which worsens absence.
  • Myoclonic → sodium valproate in boys/men and women unable to have children, levetiracetam in girls and women able to have children; avoid carbamazepine, and lamotrigine may worsen it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: NICE first-line for tonic/atonic seizures?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Sodium valproate in boys and men, and women unable to have children; lamotrigine in girls and women able to have children.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Summarise the valproate restrictions.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: Valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects): it must NOT be used in women and girls of childbearing potential unless a pregnancy-prevention programme is in place and there is no alternative. MHRA: do not START valproate in anyone under 55, male or female, unless two specialists independently document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or that there are compelling reasons the reproductive risks do not apply. In men, the man and his partner should use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after stopping, because of a possible small increase in neurodevelopmental disorders in children they father.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Key points about carbamazepine.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Enzyme inducer
  • can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures (avoid in generalised epilepsy)
  • causes SIADH/hyponatraemia
  • reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception — as do oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone and topiramate.
The copper coil, hormonal coil and depot injection are unaffected. Note the interaction runs the other way for lamotrigine: the combined pill roughly halves lamotrigine levels.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Key points about lamotrigine, levetiracetam and phenytoin.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Lamotrigine — slow titration (Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk); lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the most reassuring pregnancy data.
  • Levetiracetam — neuropsychiatric effects (irritability, low mood).
  • Phenytoin — narrow therapeutic index needing level monitoring, gum hyperplasia; used mainly in status now.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: When and how is antiseizure medication withdrawal considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: After ≥2 years seizure-free, with specialist input, tapering slowly.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Define status epilepticus.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back: A seizure lasting ≥5 minutes, OR ≥2 seizures without recovery of consciousness in between. A medical emergency (neuronal injury, hypoxia, death).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: Outline the stepwise management of status epilepticus.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• (1) ABCDE, secure airway, high-flow O2, check glucose (treat hypoglycaemia), IV access, thiamine if alcohol-dependent or malnourished.
  • (2) First-line: IV lorazepam 4 mg, repeated once after 5–10 minutes; no IV access → buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam. Give a maximum of TWO benzodiazepine doses in total — and count any dose already given before arrival by paramedics, family or carers.
  • (3) Second-line: IV levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate.
  • (4) Third-line: phenobarbital, or general anaesthesia with intubation in ICU.
Look for and treat the cause throughout.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.front: What are the DVLA rules for epilepsy (Group 1 and 2), and who informs the DVLA?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ep.back:
• Group 1 (car): first unprovoked seizure = 6 months off (12 months if there is a structural or EEG abnormality); established epilepsy = 12 months seizure-free; medication withdrawal = stop during and for 6 months after.
  • Sleep-only seizures: a 1-year established pattern if there has never been an awake seizure, or 3 years if there has.
  • Group 2 (HGV/bus): first seizure = 5 years seizure-free off medication; epilepsy = 10 years off medication.
The PATIENT (not the doctor) must inform the DVLA, and the doctor advises them to and to stop driving — but if they cannot be persuaded, or keep driving against advice, and that puts others at risk of death or serious harm, tell them you intend to disclose and then contact the DVLA yourself.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is diabetic neuropathy, and how common/significant is it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Nerve damage caused by chronic hyperglycaemia. It is the commonest complication of diabetes and the commonest cause of peripheral neuropathy in the developed world — one of the three microvascular complications (with retinopathy and nephropathy). Risk rises with duration of diabetes and poor glycaemic control.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the four main patterns of diabetic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• (1) Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy, sensory > motor (commonest);
  • (2) autonomic neuropathy;
  • (3) mononeuropathy / mononeuritis multiplex;
  • (4) diabetic amyotrophy (proximal motor).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is the classic/commonest form of diabetic neuropathy, and its distribution?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Distal symmetrical sensory 'glove-and-stocking' polyneuropathy — length-dependent, so the feet are affected first (stocking), then the hands (glove) as it progresses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: By what mechanisms does chronic hyperglycaemia damage nerves?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum; the polyol/sorbitol pathway (osmotic + oxidative stress); advanced glycation end-products (AGEs); and oxidative stress → predominantly axonal damage, with some secondary demyelination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Why is diabetic neuropathy distal and symmetrical, and how does the fibre pattern differ from Charcot-Marie-Tooth?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: It is length-dependent — the longest nerves fail first (feet → hands). It is sensory > motor, in contrast to Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, which is motor-predominant.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the positive sensory symptoms of the classic form?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Burning, tingling, 'electric-shock' and shooting pain — often worse at night (neuropathic pain).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the negative sensory symptoms, and which is the most dangerous?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Numbness and loss of sensation — critically the loss of protective sensation, which is the key risk factor for foot ulceration.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What examination signs are found in the classic distal sensory form?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• Loss of vibration and proprioception (large-fibre / dorsal column),
  • reduced or absent ankle reflexes, and
  • reduced pinprick sensation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Why is loss of protective sensation so dangerous?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: It leads to unnoticed trauma → foot ulcers → infection → amputation. The diabetic foot is the major clinical concern.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is Charcot foot?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Neuropathy → repeated unnoticed trauma → progressive destruction and deformity of the foot joints (a 'rocker-bottom' foot). Recognise it ACUTELY, before the deformity: a hot, swollen, red foot with intact or bounding pulses and little or no pain, skin unbroken, afebrile, inflammatory markers near-normal — and the X-ray may be normal early. Suspect it even with no deformity, keep the patient non-weight-bearing, and refer to the multidisciplinary foot service within 1 working day.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the cardiovascular features of diabetic autonomic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• Postural (orthostatic) hypotension,
  • resting tachycardia, and
  • silent (painless) myocardial ischaemia/infarction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Why does autonomic neuropathy cause 'silent' MIs, and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: It blunts pain perception, so diabetics can have painless MIs — keep a low threshold to investigate atypical presentations.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the gastrointestinal features of diabetic autonomic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Gastroparesis (early satiety, bloating, vomiting, erratic glycaemic control) and altered bowel habit (diarrhoea/constipation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What are the genitourinary features of diabetic autonomic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Erectile dysfunction (often the earliest sign) and neurogenic bladder (retention, incontinence).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Give two 'other' autonomic features of diabetic neuropathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Gustatory sweating (facial sweating triggered by food) and hypoglycaemia unawareness (loss of the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia — dangerous).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Give examples of diabetic mononeuropathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• CN III (oculomotor) palsy that is pupil-sparing;
  • carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve);
  • and foot drop (common peroneal nerve).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is diabetic amyotrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: A lumbosacral plexus neuropathy causing painful, asymmetrical, proximal (thigh) weakness and wasting — typically in older type 2 diabetics; usually recovers gradually.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is done at the diabetic foot check, and how often?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• 10 g monofilament (protective sensation),
  • 128 Hz tuning fork (vibration),
  • ankle reflexes,
  • pinprick,
  • foot inspection (deformity/ulcers), and
  • pedal pulses (also screening for peripheral arterial disease).
At least annually if low risk, but every 3 to 6 months if moderate risk and every 1 to 2 months if high risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What investigations complete the assessment of diabetic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• Lying + standing BP (postural drop);
  • nerve conduction studies only if there is diagnostic doubt or an atypical picture;
  • and exclude other causes of neuropathy — B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, alcohol, drugs.
Also assess for retinopathy and nephropathy (they cluster).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: What is the single most important disease-modifying step in diabetic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: Optimising glycaemic control — it slows/prevents progression (best evidence in type 1 diabetes). Also address BP, lipids and smoking.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: Outline the NICE approach to painful diabetic neuropathy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back: First-line is one of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin — NICE does not rank them, it is a free choice. In UK practice duloxetine is often chosen in diabetes because it is licensed for diabetic neuropathic pain; amitriptyline is used off-label (start 10 mg at night) and worsens postural hypotension and urinary retention. Gabapentin and pregabalin are controlled drugs (Class C, Schedule 3) with MHRA warnings about misuse and severe respiratory depression, especially with opioids, and both need dose reduction in CKD. If ineffective or not tolerated, SWITCH to another of the four rather than adding on. Tramadol is for acute rescue only — do not start long-term tramadol or strong opioids outside a specialist pain service. Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia specifically, not for diabetic neuropathy. Neuropathic pain does NOT respond to standard analgesics/NSAIDs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.front: How are the autonomic features and the foot managed in diabetic neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Di.back:
• Postural hypotension → first review drugs that worsen it (antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, tricyclics), then conservative measures ± fludrocortisone/midodrine;
  • gastroparesis → dietary measures plus a prokinetic, alternating erythromycin and metoclopramide (metoclopramide max 5 days at a time), with domperidone only exceptionally because of its cardiac risk;
  • erectile dysfunction → PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil).
Foot → MDT diabetic foot service, podiatry, patient education (daily foot checks, appropriate footwear) — and any active foot problem (ulcer, spreading infection, critical ischaemia, gangrene, suspected Charcot) is referred to the MDT foot service within 1 working day.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: A rapidly progressive, invariably fatal neurodegenerative disease — the prototypical human prion disease (a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is a prion, and how does it cause disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: A misfolded form of the normal cellular prion protein (PrPᶜ → PrPˢᶜ). It contains no nucleic acid, yet is 'infectious': the abnormal protein templates conversion of normal PrP into more misfolded protein → accumulation → neuronal death.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the characteristic neuropathology of CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Spongiform (vacuolar) change in grey matter, neuronal loss, and astrocytic gliosis — crucially with no inflammatory infiltrate (unlike infection). ± amyloid plaques (especially vCJD).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the four main types of CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• Sporadic (~85%, commonest)
  • Variant (vCJD)
  • Familial/genetic
  • and Iatrogenic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: Describe sporadic CJD (epidemiology and course).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• The commonest form (~85%), at about 1–2 per million per year in the UK
  • typically older adults, with a UK median age at onset of 67
  • rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months
  • median survival about 4 months, with most dead within a year.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the key clinical features of sporadic CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• Rapidly progressive dementia
  • myoclonus (often startle-induced)
  • cerebellar ataxia
  • visual disturbance/cortical blindness
  • extrapyramidal and pyramidal signs
  • and akinetic mutism terminally.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What causes variant CJD (vCJD)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Ingestion of beef contaminated with BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy) prions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: How does vCJD differ from sporadic CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• Younger patients (~late 20s)
  • early psychiatric/behavioural symptoms plus painful sensory symptoms
  • a longer course (~14 months)
  • the MRI pulvinar sign
  • and usually no periodic EEG complexes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the routes of iatrogenic CJD transmission?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater grafts, corneal transplants, and cadaveric (human-derived) pituitary growth hormone — prions resist standard sterilisation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the inheritance and gene in familial CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Autosomal dominant mutation in the PRNP gene (chromosome 20). Related inherited prion diseases include GSS and fatal familial insomnia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the classic EEG finding in sporadic CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Periodic sharp-wave (triphasic) complexes, ~1–2 Hz. (Typically absent in vCJD.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the MRI findings in sporadic CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: DWI/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cortex ('cortical ribboning') and basal ganglia (caudate/putamen).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What MRI sign is characteristic of vCJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: The pulvinar sign — bilateral posterior thalamic (pulvinar) hyperintensity ('hockey-stick' sign).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What CSF marker supports a diagnosis of CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Elevated 14-3-3 protein (released by rapid neuronal destruction — supportive but not specific).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the most specific and sensitive CSF test for sporadic CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) — it detects the misfolded prion protein with high sensitivity and specificity in SPORADIC CJD. Important caveat: CSF RT-QuIC is usually NEGATIVE in variant CJD, so a negative CSF panel does not exclude vCJD — tonsil biopsy is the ante-mortem test there.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: How is CJD definitively diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Brain biopsy or post-mortem histology (spongiform change plus prion protein immunostaining). In practice diagnosis is usually clinical plus investigations; biopsy is rarely done. In suspected variant CJD, tonsil biopsy detects prion protein in lymphoreticular tissue and is a highly sensitive and specific ante-mortem test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the management of CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: No cure; it is uniformly fatal. Supportive and palliative care (e.g. clonazepam/valproate for myoclonus), with MDT and family support.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the public health and infection-control points in CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Two separate notification duties: CJD is a notifiable disease, so notify UKHSA / your local health protection team ON SUSPICION; and separately refer and discuss every suspected case with the National CJD Research & Surveillance Unit in Edinburgh, which runs surveillance and provides the specialist tests. Infection control: prions survive standard autoclaving AND formalin fixation, so instruments used on high-infectivity tissue are quarantined pending the diagnosis and destroyed if confirmed, never simply reprocessed; use single-use LP needles. ALL forms are potentially transmissible by inoculation, not just vCJD — but CJD is NOT spread by casual contact or routine nursing care, so no isolation is needed. Patients with CJD, or at increased risk of it, must never donate blood, tissue or organs, and must tell surgical and dental teams before invasive procedures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What is the prognosis of CJD?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: Uniformly fatal — sporadic CJD median survival ~4–6 months (most <1 year); vCJD ~14 months.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: Why is the dementia pattern a key clue to CJD versus Alzheimer's?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back: CJD causes rapid decline over weeks–months with early myoclonus; Alzheimer's declines gradually over years without early myoclonus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: Which treatable mimics must be excluded in rapidly progressive dementia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• Autoimmune/limbic encephalitis
  • Hashimoto's encephalopathy
  • CNS infection
  • paraneoplastic syndromes
  • Wernicke's encephalopathy
  • and metabolic causes — some are reversible.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.front: What are the other human and animal prion diseases?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Cr.back:
• Human: kuru (ritual cannibalism), GSS, and fatal familial insomnia.
  • Animal: BSE (cattle) and scrapie (sheep).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT), and what else is it called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: An inherited (hereditary) peripheral neuropathy affecting motor and sensory peripheral nerves — also called hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the core concept of CMT (pattern, course, cure)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: CMT is a length-dependent, predominantly motor peripheral neuropathy — so it hits the longest nerves first (the feet/legs), producing the classic distal wasting + foot deformity + high-stepping gait picture. It's the commonest inherited neuropathy, is slowly progressive, and has no cure — management is supportive.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: When does CMT usually present, what is its inheritance, and what neuron pattern?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Usually presents in childhood/adolescence (CMT2 often presents later, in adulthood); mostly autosomal dominant, though CMTX is the second commonest form; a lower motor neuron (LMN) pattern (it's a peripheral nerve disease).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: Which features point to CMT (inherited) rather than an acquired neuropathy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back:
• Family history (autosomal dominant)
  • very slow onset (years), from childhood
  • marked foot deformity (pes cavus, hammer toes) implying long-standing disease
  • symmetrical, distal, predominantly motor
  • normal until you look for the pattern.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: Which features point to an acquired neuropathy rather than CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back:
• No family history
  • subacute/acute onset
  • less deformity
  • pattern varies (e.g. diabetic = sensory)
  • an identifiable cause (diabetes, B12, alcohol, drugs).
The one that really matters is CIDP — subacute over weeks to months, often asymmetric with proximal as well as distal weakness, no pes cavus, and patchy slowing with conduction block on nerve conduction studies — because it is TREATABLE and CMT is not.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: State the rule for identifying CMT and the key caveat.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Pes cavus + a positive family history + slow distal weakness = CMT; the foot deformity implies a long-standing (hence inherited) neuropathy. Always exclude acquired causes first (diabetes, B12 deficiency, alcohol, drugs, thyroid) — all axonal. And always consider CIDP, the treatable demyelinating mimic: an atypical or rapidly progressive 'CMT' needs urgent neurology referral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What causes CMT at the molecular level, and what are the two main subtypes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Mutations affecting peripheral nerve myelin or axons → demyelinating (CMT1 — commonest, e.g. PMP22 duplication) or axonal (CMT2) subtypes. It is predominantly motor — motor > sensory involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the length-dependent principle in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: The longest nerves are affected first → symptoms start in the feet/legs, then progress to the hands ('stocking then glove') → this explains the distal-first pattern.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is pes cavus in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: High foot arches — the classic deformity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: Why does foot drop occur in CMT, and what gait results?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Weak dorsiflexion → a high-stepping gait as compensation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What are 'inverted champagne bottle legs' in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Distal muscle wasting + weakness — thin lower legs with preserved thighs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What reflex and tone findings occur in CMT, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Areflexia, or marked hyporeflexia — LMN signs; reflexes are typically absent, and tone is reduced or normal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the sensory involvement like in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Distal sensory loss — milder (stocking distribution).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the signature CMT tetrad?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Pes cavus + 'inverted champagne bottle' legs + high-stepping (foot drop) gait + areflexia = the classic CMT tetrad.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: Why does CMT produce an LMN pattern, and what additional features occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back:
Because CMT is a peripheral nerve (LMN) disease, it produces LMN signs — wasting, absent or markedly reduced reflexes, and reduced or normal tone (not the increased tone/hyperreflexia of a UMN lesion). Also:
  • distal hand wasting/weakness (later)
  • foot ulcers (sensory loss)
  • palpably thickened nerves (demyelinating types).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: How is CMT diagnosed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Diagnosis is clinical (characteristic picture + family history), supported by nerve conduction studies — slowed conduction velocity in demyelinating CMT1, reduced amplitudes in axonal CMT2 — and confirmed by genetic testing (e.g. the PMP22 duplication in CMT1A).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What do nerve conduction studies (NCS) show in CMT, and what do they confirm?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Slowed conduction (demyelinating CMT1) or reduced amplitudes (axonal CMT2); they confirm a peripheral neuropathy and its type.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What does genetic testing do in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Confirms the diagnosis + subtype (e.g. PMP22 duplication in CMT1A).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What does nerve biopsy show in CMT, and how often is it needed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: 'Onion bulb' formation in demyelinating types — rarely needed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What investigations exclude acquired causes in a suspected CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Glucose/HbA1c (diabetes), B12/folate, TFTs, U&E, LFT — all of which cause AXONAL neuropathies. If the picture is demyelinating but atypical for CMT (subacute, asymmetric, proximal weakness, no pes cavus, conduction block), think CIDP, which is treatable with steroids, IVIg or plasma exchange.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the overarching management principle for CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: No cure → multidisciplinary supportive care to maintain function and mobility.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the role of physiotherapy and occupational therapy in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back:
• Physiotherapy — maintain strength, range of movement, mobility
  • Occupational therapy — aids and adaptations.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What orthotics and podiatry are used in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back:
• Orthotics — ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) for foot drop, special footwear for pes cavus
  • Podiatry — foot care (deformity, ulcer prevention from sensory loss).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What analgesia and surgery are used in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: For neuropathic pain, NICE offers a free choice of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin, switching to another if one fails — note gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs with an MHRA warning about respiratory depression. Orthopaedic surgery for severe foot deformity or contractures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: Why is genetic counselling offered in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Most CMT is autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring) — but CMTX is the second commonest form: X-linked, males more severely affected, and an affected father transmits it to ALL his daughters and NONE of his sons. Recessive forms exist too, so the recurrence risk depends on the confirmed genotype.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.front: What is the key safety point about drugs in CMT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ch.back: Vincristine is CONTRAINDICATED in demyelinating CMT — not merely cautioned. One or two doses can cause severe, sometimes irreversible deterioration, and it can unmask previously undiagnosed CMT, so ask about foot deformity and family history before giving a vinca alkaloid. Paclitaxel/taxanes are the only other agent with good evidence of added risk; use nitrofurantoin, prolonged metronidazole, amiodarone and platinum agents with care.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: A thrombus in the cerebral venous sinuses (or cerebral veins) obstructing venous drainage of the brain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the core concept of CVST, and how does it differ from arterial stroke?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Unlike arterial stroke (which cuts off supply), CVST obstructs venous drainage → venous congestion → raised pressure → cerebral oedema, raised ICP, and venous (often haemorrhagic) infarction. This 'backing-up' mechanism explains the headache/raised ICP, the seizures, and — critically — why anticoagulation is given even when there's a haemorrhage (the bleed is caused by the venous congestion, so treating the clot relieves it).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: In whom does CVST characteristically occur, and why is it often missed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Rare but important — a cause of stroke in young adults, women (hormonal), and pregnancy/puerperium; frequently missed/delayed because the presentation is variable.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis: frequency and features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: ~50% (the commonest); headache, raised ICP, seizures + hemiplegia, reduced consciousness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Cavernous sinus thrombosis: features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Periorbital erythema + oedema
  • ophthalmoplegia
  • eye pain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Transverse/sigmoid sinus thrombosis: features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Headache, ear/mastoid involvement (can follow otitis/mastoiditis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Deep venous system (straight sinus) thrombosis: features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Severe — thalamic/deep involvement, reduced consciousness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: State the rule about which sinus is most commonly thrombosed and the distinctive subtype.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: ~50% are isolated sagittal sinus thromboses (the commonest); cavernous sinus thrombosis has a distinctive eye-centred picture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the commonest symptom of CVST and its characteristics?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Headache — the commonest symptom; may be sudden onset (can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage) or gradual/progressive; often a raised-ICP headache (worse lying down, worse on Valsalva).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Besides headache, what are the clinical features of CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Nausea + vomiting (raised ICP)
  • reduced consciousness
  • seizures (more common than in arterial stroke — a useful clue)
  • focal deficits (e.g. hemiplegia in sagittal sinus)
  • and papilloedema/visual symptoms (raised ICP).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why are seizures a useful diagnostic clue in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Seizures are more common in CVST than in arterial stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What clues point to CVST over an arterial stroke, and what can it mimic?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Clues: headache + seizures + focal signs that don't fit a single arterial territory + a young patient with thrombotic risk factors. It can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage, IIH, meningoencephalitis, and arterial stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why is cavernous sinus thrombosis an exam-favourite subtype?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Because of what runs through the cavernous sinus, producing a distinctive eye-centred syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — why periorbital erythema + oedema, and proptosis/chemosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Both result from venous congestion (of orbital drainage).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — why is CN VI affected before CN III/IV?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: CN VI runs freely through the middle of the sinus (most vulnerable); III/IV run in the wall. So the 6th nerve is affected first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — why eye pain + facial hyperaesthesia of the upper face?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Trigeminal (CN V1/V2) involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the 'CN VI-first' point in cavernous sinus thrombosis, and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: In cavernous sinus pathology the 6th nerve is affected before the 3rd/4th (it sits centrally, exposed) → early lateral rectus palsy (failure of abduction).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why is cavernous sinus thrombosis often septic, and what does this mean for treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: It is often septic — spreading from facial/sinus/dental infection (the 'danger triangle' of the face) → it needs antibiotics too.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the fundamental nature of CVST as a disorder, and what should you look for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: CVST is fundamentally a thrombotic disorder — look for a hypercoagulable state (Virchow's triad).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What are the HORMONAL risk factors for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Combined oral contraceptive pill
  • pregnancy + puerperium (postpartum — ~20% of cases)
  • HRT.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What thrombophilias are risk factors for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Factor V Leiden
  • antiphospholipid syndrome
  • protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which infective sources are risk factors for CVST, and which sinuses do they affect?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Local infection — sinusitis, otitis/mastoiditis, dental, facial → cavernous/transverse sinus; also meningitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What systemic/dehydration and 'other' risk factors are there for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Dehydration, inflammatory disease (Behçet's, IBD, SLE), nephrotic syndrome
  • malignancy (prothrombotic states)
  • head injury, recent LP/neurosurgery
  • VITT (vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia — a rare cause).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the high-yield classic context for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: A young woman on the COCP or postpartum → the classic CVST context.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the first-line investigation of choice for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: MRI venography (MRV) — visualises the thrombosed sinus and any venous infarct/oedema; CT venography is an equally good alternative.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the key pitfall regarding non-contrast CT in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Non-contrast CT head can be NORMAL in around 30% of cases — a normal CT does NOT exclude CVST → if suspected, proceed to venography.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the 'empty delta sign' in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: On contrast CT/venography, a filling defect in the (superior sagittal) sinus — contrast outlines the sinus wall but not the clot → a triangular 'empty' centre.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the role of D-dimer in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: It may support the diagnosis (often raised) but a normal D-dimer does NOT exclude CVST → don't rely on it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What investigations look for the underlying cause of CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Pregnancy test, look for infection/malignancy, and test for antiphospholipid antibodies (they change the type and duration of anticoagulation). A heritable thrombophilia screen is NOT routinely indicated just because the clot is at an unusual site — it would not change management.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the overarching management principle for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Anticoagulate — even if there's a haemorrhage — plus treat the cause, seizures, and raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the acute anticoagulation treatment for CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Anticoagulation with LMWH — low-molecular-weight heparin is first-line acute treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the long-term anticoagulation for CVST, and for how long?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Warfarin (or a DOAC) — but if the patient is pregnant neither can be used (warfarin is teratogenic, DOACs are contraindicated), so continue LMWH throughout pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks postnatally. Typical total duration is 3–12 months (3–6 months if a transient/reversible factor e.g. pregnancy/COCP; 6–12 months if idiopathic; lifelong if recurrent/persistent thrombophilia/malignancy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: How do you treat the underlying cause in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Antibiotics if septic (esp. cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/sinus infection)
  • stop the COCP
  • treat malignancy/thrombophilia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What supportive and rescue treatments are used in CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Antiepileptics for seizures
  • manage raised ICP
  • endovascular thrombectomy or decompressive surgery reserved for severe/deteriorating cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What advice applies to pregnancy/future after CVST?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception afterwards; give prophylactic LMWH in future pregnancies if prior CVST.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Explain the critical, counterintuitive anticoagulation point in CVST.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Anticoagulate EVEN IN THE PRESENCE OF INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE — the venous (haemorrhagic) infarct is caused by the venous congestion, and anticoagulation (by clearing the clot) relieves the congestion and does not worsen the bleed. This is the opposite of arterial haemorrhagic stroke (where you would never anticoagulate).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How are intracranial tumours broadly classified, and which is commonest overall in adults?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Primary (arising from CNS tissue — glioma, meningioma, pituitary, schwannoma) or secondary/metastatic. In adults, metastases are the commonest intracranial tumour overall; of the primaries, gliomas and meningiomas dominate.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the three mechanisms by which brain tumours present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Raised ICP (morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema)
  • focal deficit (by location)
  • and seizures (new-onset seizure in an adult → image the brain)
The cell of origin + location define the specific tumour.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Glioma (incl. glioblastoma): origin and key points?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: glial cells (astrocytes). Key points: commonest malignant primary; GBM = grade 4, poor prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Meningioma: origin and key points?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: meninges (arachnoid). Key points: commonest benign primary; extra-axial, dural-based; often slow/incidental.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Pituitary adenoma: origin and key points?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: anterior pituitary. Key points: bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm); hormone excess (prolactin) or hypopituitarism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): origin and key points?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: Schwann cells of CN VIII. Key points: cerebellopontine angle; unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + balance problems; bilateral → NF2.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Metastases: origin and key points?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: extracranial primary. Key points: commonest overall; from lung, breast, melanoma, renal, GI; often multiple.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the general management principles for brain tumours?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: MRI with contrast; MDT (neurosurgery/oncology); surgery for resection or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy. Dexamethasone 4–8 mg daily (up to 16 if severe or ICP is rising), given in the morning, for SYMPTOMATIC peritumoural oedema only, tapered to the lowest effective dose. Treat seizures if they occur — but do not give prophylactic antiepileptics to someone who has not had one, and prefer levetiracetam when one is needed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are gliomas, and how are they graded?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Tumours arising from the glial (neuroepithelial support) cells of the brain/spinal cord — astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. Glial cells surround and support neurones; gliomas are graded WHO 1–4 by aggressiveness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the core concept of gliomas as a spectrum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Gliomas are the commonest primary malignant brain tumour, behaving along a spectrum from low-grade (slow, well-differentiated) to high-grade (aggressive, poorly-differentiated) — with glioblastoma the most aggressive. They present like any space-occupying lesion (seizures, focal deficit, raised ICP), and modern classification integrates molecular markers alongside histology.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Astrocytoma: origin and notes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: astrocytes. Notes: the commonest glioma; its most aggressive form = glioblastoma (grade 4).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Oligodendroglioma: origin and notes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: oligodendrocytes. Notes: often frontal; calcification; better prognosis if 1p/19q co-deleted.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Ependymoma: origin and notes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Origin: ependymal cells (line ventricles). Notes: can cause hydrocephalus; commoner in children.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Explain WHO glioma grading from Grade 1 to Grade 4, and the astrocytoma spectrum.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Grade 1 is slow-growing and well-differentiated; grade 4 is fast-growing and aggressive. Note the terminology has changed: 'anaplastic astrocytoma' no longer exists — IDH-mutant tumours are astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2, 3 or 4 — and glioblastoma is by definition IDH-wildtype, so 'secondary glioblastoma' has gone too.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is glioblastoma (GBM), its epidemiology and prognosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Grade 4 astrocytoma — the commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults; peak age 50–60; very poor prognosis (median survival ~12–15 months).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the classic imaging sign of glioblastoma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A frontal mass that crosses the corpus callosum — the 'butterfly glioma' appearance; typically ring enhancement + central necrosis + surrounding oedema.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the characteristic histology of glioblastoma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Necrosis + microvascular proliferation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What was the major change in the current WHO glioma classification?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Gliomas are now classified by molecular markers integrated with histology (current WHO classification), not histology alone.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the significance of IDH mutation status in gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: IDH-mutant = better prognosis (usually lower-grade/secondary); IDH-wildtype = worse. Glioblastoma is now defined as IDH-wildtype grade 4 astrocytoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the significance of 1p/19q co-deletion in gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Defines oligodendroglioma (+ IDH mutation); predicts better response to chemo (PCV) + radiotherapy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the significance of MGMT promoter methylation in gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Predicts better response to temozolomide + better prognosis (methylated → temozolomide works better).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Summarise how molecular markers guide modern glioma diagnosis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Modern glioma diagnosis is histology + molecular markers — IDH status, 1p/19q co-deletion, and MGMT methylation guide classification, treatment, and prognosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Glioma clinical features — what is the commonest first symptom?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Seizures — the commonest first symptom leading to diagnosis (new-onset seizure in an adult → image the brain).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Glioma clinical features — how does raised ICP present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Headache worse on waking / coughing / bending forward
  • papilloedema
  • nausea/vomiting
  • altered mental state
  • CN III/VI palsies (false localising)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Glioma clinical features — what focal deficits occur and what is the course?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Focal deficits depend on location — cranial nerve palsies, visual field defects, aphasia, hemiparesis. The course is subacute and progressive (vs stroke's sudden onset).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the two high-yield glioma clinical pearls?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The raised-ICP headache is worse on waking, coughing, bending forward + papilloedema + vomiting. New-onset seizure in an adult → think brain tumour until proven otherwise → image.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the investigation sequence for a suspected brain tumour?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: MRI with contrast is first-line for a suspected brain tumour. CT is the alternative acutely, or where MRI is contraindicated. Biopsy (or resection) gives the definitive histological and molecular diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the overarching management principle for gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Grade-directed — watch-and-wait/surgery for low grade; maximal safe resection + radiotherapy + temozolomide (Stupp protocol) for high grade.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is a low-grade glioma managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Watch and wait with radiological surveillance (serial imaging) if asymptomatic/stable; surgery (resection/debulking) if needed, with radiotherapy afterwards if residual tissue remains.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the mainstay of high-grade glioma/glioblastoma management, and the Stupp protocol?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Maximal safe surgical resection (debulking) is the mainstay. Glioblastoma → the Stupp protocol: maximal safe resection → concurrent radiotherapy + temozolomide → adjuvant temozolomide (in previously fit patients). MGMT-methylated tumours respond better to temozolomide.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted) managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Radiotherapy + PCV chemotherapy (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What supportive management is used in gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Dexamethasone for symptomatic tumour-associated oedema — 4–8 mg daily, up to 16 mg if severe, given in the morning and tapered to the lowest effective dose. Antiepileptics for seizures, but not as prophylaxis in someone who has never had one; levetiracetam is preferred because it does not induce liver enzymes, whereas carbamazepine and phenytoin interact with chemotherapy. Neuro-oncology MDT; palliative care where appropriate. And the trap: if CNS lymphoma is a possibility, get tissue BEFORE giving steroids.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is a meningioma, and where does it arise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A non-glial tumour arising from the arachnoid (meningothelial) 'cap' cells of the meninges — an extra-axial tumour (arising outside the brain parenchyma, from its coverings).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the core concept of meningiomas, and how do they contrast with gliomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Meningiomas are the commonest primary brain tumour overall. Unlike gliomas they are usually benign, slow-growing, and extra-axial — causing symptoms by compressing adjacent brain (mass effect), not invading it. Hence often incidental, frequently curable by surgery, and much better prognosis than gliomas. Commoner in women and with increasing age.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Meningioma vs glioma — contrast origin and relationship to brain.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Meningioma: arachnoid cap cells (meninges — outside brain); compresses brain from outside (mass effect)
  • Glioma: glial cells (within brain parenchyma); infiltrates brain from within
