conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Meningioma vs glioma — contrast behaviour, imaging, and prognosis.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Meningioma: usually benign, slow-growing; well-circumscribed, extra-axial, uniform enhancement, 'dural tail'; good prognosis (often curable)
  • Glioma: often malignant/infiltrative; ill-defined, intra-axial, often irregular/necrotic; worse prognosis (esp. glioblastoma)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: State the rule distinguishing meningioma from glioma.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Meningioma = extra-axial, benign, compresses; glioma = intra-axial, malignant, infiltrates — the extra-axial location + dural attachment identifies a meningioma on imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Where are meningiomas located?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
~90% are intracranial; common sites:
  • ~25% falx cerebri (parasagittal)
  • ~20% convexity (over the hemispheres)
  • ~20% sphenoid wing
Also: olfactory groove, tuberculum sellae, posterior fossa, spinal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does meningioma location determine symptoms?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Sphenoid wing → visual/eye signs
  • parasagittal → leg weakness/seizures
  • olfactory groove → anosmia

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Describe the WHO grading of meningiomas with grades, types and frequencies.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Grade 1 = meningioma (benign), ~90%, benign/slow-growing
  • Grade 2 = atypical meningioma, ~5%, abnormal cells likely to recur post-op
  • Grade 3 = anaplastic (malignant), ~5%, malignant, fast-growing, recurs post-op
The vast majority (~90%) are benign grade 1 — hence the generally good prognosis; higher grades recur and behave aggressively.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the risk factors for meningioma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Idiopathic (most)
  • increasing age
  • female sex (hormone-sensitive — express progesterone receptors)
  • previous cranial irradiation (a well-recognised risk)
  • neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) — a classic association (also causes bilateral acoustic neuromas)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does a symptomatic meningioma present via mass effect?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
Often an incidental finding. When symptomatic:
  • seizures (cortical compression)
  • raised ICP (headache worse on waking/coughing/bending, papilloedema, vomiting)
  • focal deficits (cranial nerve palsies, visual field defects, language dysfunction) — depending on location

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the high-yield point about meningioma deficits?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Because meningiomas compress rather than infiltrate, the deficit is focal and localises to the site (parasagittal → contralateral leg weakness; sphenoid wing → proptosis/visual loss; olfactory groove → anosmia).Slow growth → insidious symptoms; they can become large before presenting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the investigations for a meningioma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: MRI with contrast, as for any suspected brain tumour — a well-circumscribed ('globose') extra-axial mass with uniform enhancement and a characteristic 'dural tail'. Meningiomas are often first found incidentally on a CT done for another reason, and CT shows the calcification well, but CT is not the first-line investigation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the overarching management principle for meningioma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Observe if small/asymptomatic
  • surgical resection is the mainstay for symptomatic/growing tumours
  • radiotherapy for residual/high-grade/inoperable

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the management options for meningioma in detail?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Observation (watch-and-wait): small, asymptomatic, incidental meningiomas → serial imaging surveillance (many never need treatment)
  • Endovascular embolisation: pre-operative, to reduce vascular supply and bleeding at surgery
  • Surgical removal (mainstay for symptomatic tumours): gross total resection (curative for grade 1 if completely removed), subtotal resection, or biopsy only — depending on location/resectability
  • Radiotherapy: for residual/recurrent tumour, high-grade (2/3), or surgically inaccessible lesions; stereotactic radiosurgery for small/deep lesions
  • Supportive: dexamethasone for peritumoural oedema; antiepileptics for seizures

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is a pituitary adenoma?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A benign tumour of the anterior pituitary gland, arising within the sella turcica.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the three ways a pituitary adenoma causes problems?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• (1) Mass effect (compressing local structures, classically the optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia)
  • (2) hormone hypersecretion (a functioning adenoma → an endocrine syndrome)
  • (3) hormone hyposecretion (compressing normal gland → hypopituitarism).
Crucially, prolactinoma is treated medically first, not surgically.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why are pituitary adenomas described as sitting at a crossroads of specialties?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: They are the commonest cause of pituitary dysfunction and sit at the crossroads of neurology (mass effect), endocrinology (hormones), and ophthalmology (visual fields).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does mass effect from a pituitary adenoma present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm)
  • headache
  • cranial nerve palsies
  • hypopituitarism
  • and (rarely) CSF rhinorrhoea and pituitary apoplexy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does hormone hypersecretion from a pituitary adenoma present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: As an endocrine excess syndrome — prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing's disease, and (rarely) TSH-oma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does hormone hyposecretion from a pituitary adenoma occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Hypopituitarism — from compression of the normal gland.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: State the rule linking adenoma type to presentation.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A functioning microadenoma presents with a hormone syndrome; a non-functioning macroadenoma presents with mass effect + hypopituitarism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How are pituitary adenomas classified by size?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Microadenoma <1 cm
  • macroadenoma >1 cm
  • giant adenoma >4 cm
(any type — not restricted to prolactinomas; non-functioning giant adenomas are common).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Prolactinoma: what does it secrete and what syndrome does it cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Secretes prolactin → hyperprolactinaemia. It is the commonest functioning adenoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Somatotroph adenoma: what does it secrete and what syndrome does it cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Secretes GH → acromegaly (adults) / gigantism (children).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Corticotroph adenoma: what does it secrete and what syndrome does it cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Secretes ACTH → Cushing's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Non-functioning adenoma: what does it secrete and how does it present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Secretes none → presents with mass effect + hypopituitarism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Thyrotroph adenoma (rare): what does it secrete and what syndrome does it cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Secretes TSH → secondary hyperthyroidism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the size-function link for pituitary adenomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Microadenomas usually present via hormone hypersecretion (small but functioning); macroadenomas present via mass effect + hypopituitarism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Bitemporal hemianopia in pituitary adenoma — what is the mechanism, and which fields go first?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Compression of the optic chiasm (which sits above the pituitary) — the classic sign. Superior (upper quadrant) fields are affected first, as it compresses from below.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why does a pituitary adenoma cause non-specific headaches?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Stretching of the dura/sella.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does a pituitary adenoma cause cranial nerve palsies and diplopia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Lateral extension into the cavernous sinus (CN III, IV, VI, Va/b) → diplopia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why does a pituitary adenoma cause hypopituitarism as a mass-effect feature?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Compression of the normal anterior pituitary.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why does a pituitary adenoma rarely cause CSF rhinorrhoea?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Downward erosion through the sellar floor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is pituitary apoplexy in terms of mass-effect mechanism?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Haemorrhage/infarction of the tumour (rare, an emergency).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Explain the bitemporal hemianopia of pituitary adenoma in full (why and pattern).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The optic chiasm sits directly above the pituitary → an enlarging adenoma compresses the crossing nasal fibres → loss of both temporal (outer) visual fields (classically upper quadrants first, as it compresses from below) — the single most examined pituitary sign.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How does a prolactinoma present in women vs men?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Women: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea, infertility, reduced libido (present early → usually microadenomas).
  • Men: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia (present late → often macroadenomas).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the 'stalk effect' caveat in interpreting a raised prolactin?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Any large pituitary mass can mildly raise prolactin by compressing the stalk (dopamine can't reach the lactotrophs) — but a very high prolactin = a true prolactinoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the clinical features of acromegaly (GH excess)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Enlarged hands/feet/jaw
  • coarse features
  • sweating
  • organomegaly

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the clinical features of Cushing's disease (ACTH excess)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Central obesity
  • striae
  • hypertension
  • hyperglycaemia

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the gold-standard imaging for a pituitary adenoma, and what does it define?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: MRI (pituitary/sella with contrast) — defines size, extent, and chiasm/cavernous sinus involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which hormones should be tested in a pituitary adenoma work-up?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Test ALL pituitary hormones: prolactin, IGF-1 (GH), cortisol/ACTH (± dexamethasone suppression), TFTs, LH/FSH/oestrogen/testosterone — to identify hypersecretion and hyposecretion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What visual test is used in a pituitary adenoma, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Formal visual field testing (perimetry) — to detect/monitor bitemporal hemianopia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the main differential for a pituitary adenoma, and its features?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Craniopharyngioma — a sellar/suprasellar tumour from Rathke's pouch remnants (commoner in children, often calcified, classically lower quadrant field loss first from superior compression).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is pituitary apoplexy, and why is it an emergency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Sudden haemorrhage into or infarction of a pituitary tumour → a neurosurgical/endocrine emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the features of pituitary apoplexy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Sudden severe headache
  • visual loss/ophthalmoplegia
  • reduced consciousness
  • and acute hypopituitarism — critically an adrenal (cortisol) crisis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is pituitary apoplexy managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Urgent hydrocortisone (steroid cover for adrenal insufficiency — life-saving)
  • fluid/electrolyte support
  • urgent MRI
  • neurosurgical + endocrine input.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the overarching management principle for pituitary adenomas?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• PROLACTINOMA → dopamine agonist first-line (medical)
  • ALL OTHER symptomatic adenomas → transsphenoidal surgery first-line
  • replace deficient hormones.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why is prolactinoma the exception in management, and how is it treated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: 1st-line = dopamine agonist (cabergoline > bromocriptine) — it shrinks the tumour and normalises prolactin, so medical treatment is first-line and surgery is rarely needed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How are all other functioning + symptomatic non-functioning adenomas managed, and what are the complications?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
1st-line = transsphenoidal surgery (the sella is accessed via the nose/sphenoid sinus). Complications:
  • CSF leak
  • meningitis
  • bleeding
  • endocrine disturbance (hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is acromegaly managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Surgery first-line; if not cured → somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide), GH-receptor antagonist (pegvisomant), or dopamine agonist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is Cushing's disease managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Transsphenoidal surgery first-line; medical adrenal-blocking therapy/radiotherapy if not cured.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: When is radiotherapy used for pituitary adenomas, and what hormone replacement may be needed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
Radiotherapy for residual/recurrent/inoperable tumour. Hormone replacement for hyposecretion:
  • hydrocortisone
  • levothyroxine
  • sex steroids
  • ± desmopressin for DI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is a non-functioning, asymptomatic microadenoma managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Observe with serial imaging (incidentalomas).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A focal collection of pus within the brain parenchyma, usually bacterial, surrounded by a capsule and oedema — a neurosurgical + infective emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the core clinical concept of how a brain abscess presents?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A combination of infection (fever) + a space-occupying lesion (raised ICP, focal deficit) + seizures — but the 'classic triad' is often incomplete, so a high index of suspicion is needed, especially with a predisposing source.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of a brain abscess, and what does management combine?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: The diagnostic hallmark is a ring-enhancing lesion on imaging; management combines prolonged antibiotics + neurosurgical drainage.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why can a brain abscess be fatal, and who is at higher risk?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: It can be fatal if untreated (raised ICP → herniation); there is higher risk in the immunocompromised.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Direct/contiguous spread: what are the sources and typical organisms/location?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
Sources:
  • otitis media/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellum
  • sinusitis → frontal lobe
  • dental infection.
Organisms: streptococci — especially the Streptococcus anginosus ('milleri') group, the commonest UK isolate — anaerobes (Bacteroides), oral flora.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Haematogenous spread: what are the sources and typical organisms/location?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Sources: distant infection — endocarditis, lung abscess/bronchiectasis, skin, dental; cyanotic congenital heart disease (right-to-left shunt bypasses the lung filter). Typically multiple abscesses at the grey-white junction; streptococci, Staph aureus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Penetrating trauma/neurosurgery: source and typical organism for brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Source: open skull fracture, surgery. Typical organism: Staph aureus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Immunocompromised: sources and typical organisms for brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Sources: HIV, transplant. Organisms: Toxoplasma (HIV), fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), Nocardia, TB.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the high-yield source-to-location links for brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Otitis/mastoiditis → temporal lobe/cerebellar abscess; sinusitis → frontal lobe; cyanotic congenital heart disease → haematogenous spread (the right-to-left shunt lets bacteria bypass the pulmonary filter).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In HIV, what is a ring-enhancing lesion until proven otherwise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Toxoplasmosis — the key immunocompromised differential. It is not treated like a bacterial abscess: give pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid and repeat imaging — a response within about 2 weeks confirms the diagnosis without needing to biopsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the classic triad of a brain abscess, and how reliable is it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Fever, headache, and focal neurological deficit — but the classic triad is present in <50%, so don't rely on all three.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In the brain abscess triad, where does each feature come from?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Fever — from the infection (may be absent, an important pitfall).
  • Headache — from raised ICP/the mass (often the commonest symptom — dull, progressive, unremitting).
  • Focal neurological deficit — depends on abscess location (hemiparesis, aphasia, ataxia, visual field defect).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Beyond the triad, what other features can a brain abscess produce, and over what time course?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Seizures, nausea/vomiting, reduced consciousness/confusion, personality change, signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, worsening headache) — evolving over days to weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the key diagnostic pitfall with brain abscess presentation?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Fever is often absent and the presentation can be subacute → a brain abscess can masquerade as a tumour → the predisposing source (recent otitis/sinusitis/endocarditis) is a key clue.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the diagnostic imaging hallmark of a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Neuroimaging — contrast MRI (preferred) or CT → a RING-ENHANCING LESION with surrounding oedema and central necrosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why is MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) key in brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: A brain abscess shows restricted diffusion centrally → this distinguishes it from a necrotic tumour (which doesn't restrict) — the crucial radiological discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What blood/lab investigations are used in brain abscess, and their caveats?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Blood cultures (before antibiotics — positive in ~25%)
  • FBC/CRP (inflammatory markers, though can be normal)
  • and consider an HIV test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How do you identify the source of a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Examine ears/sinuses/teeth
  • echocardiogram (endocarditis)
  • CXR (lung source).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is definitive microbiology obtained in brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: From surgical aspiration of the abscess (send for culture — it guides targeted therapy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Why is lumbar puncture contraindicated in brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: LP is contraindicated in a space-occupying lesion with raised ICP → risk of coning (herniation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the mnemonic and differential for a ring-enhancing lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
'MAGIC DR':
  • Metastases/Malignancy
  • Abscess
  • Glioblastoma
  • Infarct (subacute)
  • Contusion
  • Demyelination (MS)
  • Radiation necrosis/Resolving haematoma
  • Toxoplasmosis (in HIV).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In the ring-enhancing differential, what are the clues for metastases vs abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Metastases/malignancy: often multiple; no DWI restriction.
  • Abscess: DWI restriction; a source of infection.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In the ring-enhancing differential, what clues point to glioblastoma, subacute infarct, and contusion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Glioblastoma: irregular, older patient.
  • Infarct (subacute): vascular territory.
  • Contusion: trauma history.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: In the ring-enhancing differential, what clues point to demyelination, radiation necrosis/resolving haematoma, and toxoplasmosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back:
• Demyelination (MS): younger patient, other lesions, incomplete ring.
  • Radiation necrosis/resolving haematoma: prior treatment/bleed.
  • Toxoplasmosis: immunocompromised (HIV).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the single DWI point that separates abscess from tumour?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Abscess restricts on DWI; tumour does not — the key distinguisher.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the overarching management principle for a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Empirical IV antibiotics + neurosurgical aspiration/drainage + treat the source + manage raised ICP — a combined medical-surgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What is the standard empirical IV antibiotic regimen for a brain abscess, and when is it started?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) + metronidazole (covers streptococci, anaerobes/Bacteroides, and Gram-negatives) — started promptly, after blood cultures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: When should vancomycin be added to the empirical regimen for a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Add vancomycin if MRSA/Staph aureus is suspected (post-trauma, post-neurosurgery, endocarditis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is antibiotic therapy for a brain abscess refined and for how long?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Tailor to culture results from aspiration; give a prolonged course: IV for ~6–8 weeks (abscesses are hard to penetrate).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: What are the neurosurgical drainage options for a brain abscess, and their dual role?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Stereotactic (CT-guided) aspiration or surgical excision — both diagnostic (get pus for culture) and therapeutic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: Which brain abscesses are drained versus managed medically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Generally abscesses >2 cm are aspirated/drained; small/multiple ones may be treated with antibiotics + monitoring.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is raised ICP managed in a brain abscess, including the role of dexamethasone?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Neurosurgical involvement; dexamethasone only if significant oedema/mass effect (used cautiously — it can reduce antibiotic penetration), and it must never delay antibiotics or drainage.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How are seizures and the source managed in a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Seizures: treat seizures that occur with an antiepileptic — routine prophylaxis is NOT recommended in a patient who has not had a seizure. Treat the source: e.g. ENT surgery for mastoiditis/sinusitis, treat endocarditis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.front: How is treatment response monitored in a brain abscess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Br.back: Monitor with serial imaging (repeat CT/MRI) to track resolution.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Define Bell's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: An acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve (CN VII) palsy — a diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the single most important clinical task in a facial palsy, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Distinguishing an LMN facial palsy (forehead involved) from an upper motor neuron (UMN) facial palsy (forehead spared → stroke). Bell's is a stroke mimic, so getting the UMN/LMN distinction right is what prevents a missed stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Why does a CN VII lesion produce a cluster of features beyond facial droop?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Because CN VII also carries fibres for taste, tears, saliva, and the stapedius, an LMN lesion produces a characteristic cluster beyond just facial droop.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: How common is Bell's palsy, and what are its key risk associations and proposed mechanism?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: It is the commonest cause of facial nerve palsy; ~3× more common in pregnancy (especially the third trimester and just after delivery), and also associated with diabetes (which predicts slower, less complete recovery); thought to involve viral reactivation (HSV) causing nerve inflammation/oedema in the facial canal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: In LMN (Bell's) vs UMN facial palsy — how is the forehead affected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: LMN (Bell's): forehead INVOLVED (can't wrinkle forehead / raise eyebrow / close eye). UMN (stroke/tumour): forehead SPARED (can still wrinkle forehead).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: In LMN vs UMN facial palsy — what is the pattern of weakness?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: LMN: whole half of the face (forehead + lower face). UMN: lower face only (spares forehead).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: In LMN vs UMN facial palsy — where is the lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: LMN: facial nerve nucleus or nerve (pons → periphery). UMN: above the nucleus (cortex / internal capsule).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: In LMN vs UMN facial palsy — what other signs help distinguish them?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: LMN: isolated CN VII (± its branches). UMN: often limb weakness and other deficits.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the mechanism behind forehead sparing in a UMN facial palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: The forehead (frontalis) has bilateral cortical innervation (input from both hemispheres). A UMN lesion on one side leaves the forehead still driven by the other hemisphere → forehead spared.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Why does an LMN lesion paralyse the whole side of the face including the forehead?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: The LMN is the final common pathway, so no input reaches the forehead → the whole side including the forehead is paralysed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: State the forehead rule for facial palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Forehead SPARED → UMN → think stroke; forehead INVOLVED → LMN → Bell's palsy (or other LMN cause). If unsure, treat as a suspected stroke and put the patient on the hyperacute stroke pathway — do not give prednisolone instead.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Describe the onset and core motor feature of Bell's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
Rapid onset (<72 hours) of unilateral facial weakness — the whole half of the face:
  • drooping mouth
  • inability to smile on that side
  • inability to close the eye or wrinkle the forehead
  • drooling.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Over what time course does Bell's palsy typically progress?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Onset is acute, typically progressing over ~24–72 hours; usually reaches maximal weakness within days.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is Bell's phenomenon?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: The eye rolls up and out on attempted closure (visible because the lid won't close).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is hyperacusis in Bell's palsy and why does it occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Sounds seem loud — due to loss of stapedius muscle dampening.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Why is there loss of taste in Bell's palsy, and where?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Loss of taste on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue, via the chorda tympani.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What other autonomic/sensory features accompany Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Reduced/altered tear and saliva production, and post-auricular pain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: A vesicular rash in the ear/palate with severe pain alongside facial palsy suggests what?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Forehead sparing, limb weakness, or other deficits with a facial palsy should make you consider what?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Stroke / a UMN lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: A gradual-onset or progressive facial palsy should raise suspicion of what?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Tumour (e.g. parotid, acoustic neuroma).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What causes should you consider in a bilateral facial palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
• Lyme disease
  • sarcoidosis
  • Guillain-Barré
  • leukaemia.
Bilateral facial palsy is never 'Bell's' — arrange same-day hospital assessment, and if Guillain-Barré is possible (ascending weakness, areflexia) monitor the FVC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Associated ear/parotid signs with a facial palsy point to which causes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
• Otitis media
  • cholesteatoma
  • parotid tumour (CN VII runs through the parotid).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Systemic features or involvement of other cranial nerves alongside facial palsy suggest what?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: A brainstem lesion or MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Describe Ramsay Hunt syndrome fully and its treatment.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Herpes zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion → LMN facial palsy + painful vesicular rash in the ear/auditory canal/palate + often vertigo/hearing loss → treat with oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (the zoster dose, much higher than the herpes simplex dose) plus prednisolone, as early as possible, with urgent ENT advice. Worse prognosis than Bell's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: How is Bell's palsy diagnosed, and are routine investigations needed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Diagnosis is clinical — an acute isolated LMN facial palsy with no other neurology and no alternative cause; routine bloods/imaging are NOT needed in typical cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: When and how should you investigate an atypical facial palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
Investigate only if red flags:
  • consider MRI (for a mass lesion, or if not recovering by ~3 months)
  • Lyme serology (exposure/geography)
  • blood glucose (diabetes)
  • and examine the ear + parotid.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What grading system documents facial nerve function severity?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: House-Brackmann grading (I–VI) is used to document facial nerve function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the overarching management principle for Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Prednisolone within 72 hours + meticulous eye protection; most recover well.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Give the details of prednisolone use in Bell's palsy.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Give oral prednisolone to those aged 16 and over presenting within 72 hours of onset — either 50 mg daily for 10 days, or 60 mg daily for 5 days then reducing by 10 mg a day to complete 10 days. Benefit is proven only within 72 hours, so treat that as the target window; beyond it the benefit is unproven rather than disproven, so take advice rather than automatically withholding. Pregnancy is not a contraindication. In diabetes, expect blood glucose to rise sharply. Under 16, steroids are not routinely recommended — refer to paediatrics/paediatric ENT rather than doing nothing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the role of antivirals in Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Antiviral alone is NOT recommended. Adding an antiviral to prednisolone may give a small extra benefit — seek specialist advice before doing so.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: Why is eye care critical in Bell's palsy, and what does it involve?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Because the eye won't close, there's a risk of exposure keratopathy / corneal damage → lubricating eye drops (daytime) + ointment + taping the eye shut at night (check the lid is fully closed before taping — tape over a partly open eye scratches the cornea). Same-day ophthalmology if there are corneal symptoms (pain, redness, visual change), or if the cornea stays exposed when they try to close the eye even without symptoms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What supportive measures are used in Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
• Reassurance (good prognosis but recovery may take weeks–months)
  • soft diet/straw if eating affected
  • facial physiotherapy/retraining for persistent weakness or synkinesis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the follow-up plan for Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Refer urgently to ENT/neurology if there is NO improvement after ~3 weeks of treatment — a referral trigger, not a watch-and-wait point. If recovery is still incomplete at ~3 months, refer for MRI to exclude a structural cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What is the overall prognosis of Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back: Most patients recover fully, the majority within weeks: about 70% recover completely without treatment, rising to ~85% with prednisolone started within 72 hours.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What features predict a worse prognosis in Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
• Complete (vs partial) palsy
  • older age
  • Ramsay Hunt (worse than Bell's)
  • and no recovery by 3 weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.front: What are the complications of Bell's palsy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Be.back:
• Incomplete recovery
  • synkinesis (aberrant reinnervation → involuntary co-movements, e.g. eye closes when smiling)
  • crocodile tears (tearing while eating)
  • and exposure keratopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is a cerebral AVM?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: An abnormal tangle of blood vessels connecting arteries directly to veins, bypassing the normal capillary bed — a high-flow, high-pressure lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: Why is the direct artery-to-vein shunt in an AVM dangerous?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: With no capillary bed to buffer the pressure, the draining veins are exposed to arterial pressure → they become fragile and prone to rupture. The whole clinical concern is the risk of haemorrhage, which is what management aims to prevent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How common/symptomatic are AVMs, and who typically presents?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Usually considered congenital, though sporadic AVMs are now attributed to post-zygotic somatic mutations. Only a minority (~10–15%) are found incidentally; the commonest symptomatic presentation is haemorrhage, frequently in young adults. Natural history: an UNRUPTURED AVM bleeds at roughly 2–3% per year, but after a first bleed the rebleed risk is much higher — around 6–15% in the first year — before falling back toward baseline. That distinction drives every treatment decision.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: Contrast normal cerebral blood flow with AVM blood flow.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Normal: artery → capillary bed (high resistance, drops the pressure) → vein. AVM: artery → direct connection (the 'nidus' — a tangle of vessels) → vein, with no capillary bed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What happens to the draining veins in an AVM, and what is the main risk?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: They receive blood at arterial pressure → become dilated, tortuous and fragile → rupture → haemorrhage (the main risk).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How can an AVM cause seizures and focal deficits without bleeding?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Through a combination of arteriovenous shunting ('steal'), venous hypertension, and gliosis with haemosiderin deposition in the surrounding brain from occult microbleeds — the gliosis and haemosiderin are now thought to be the main reason AVMs cause seizures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: State the rule for an AVM's danger.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: An AVM's danger = rupture → intracranial haemorrhage (typically intracerebral ± subarachnoid).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: Which inherited conditions are associated with brain AVMs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu) is the classic heritable association, along with capillary malformation–AVM syndrome (RASA1). Most brain AVMs are sporadic. Note that neurofibromatosis, von Hippel-Lindau and Sturge-Weber are phakomatoses but are NOT causes of brain AVM — and HHT is a vascular dysplasia, not a phakomatosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the commonest and most serious symptomatic presentation of an AVM, and its frequency?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Haemorrhage (intracerebral ± subarachnoid) — ~50%; the commonest and most serious.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: List the symptomatic presentations of AVM with their approximate frequencies.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back:
• Haemorrhage ~50%
  • seizures ~25%
  • persistent headaches ~10–15%
  • focal neurological deficit ~5-10% (mass effect, venous hypertension or vascular steal).
Only ~10–15% are incidental.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How does AVM haemorrhage present clinically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Like any intracranial bleed — sudden severe headache, focal deficit, reduced consciousness, seizures; it is a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in young adults.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What auscultatory sign may occasionally be found in an AVM?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: A pulsatile bruit may occasionally be heard over the skull (reflecting the high-flow shunt).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for an AVM and what does it define?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) — it defines the location, size, feeding arteries and draining veins (essential for planning treatment).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the first-line imaging for AVM, and the non-invasive vascular options?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: CT/MRI is first-line to detect the AVM and any haemorrhage; CT angiography (CTA) / MR angiography (MRA) for non-invasive vascular imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How is an AVM followed up after treatment, and what is the crucial imaging caveat?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Follow-up is by MRI/MRA, with catheter DSA to confirm obliteration (for example after radiosurgery). The crucial caveat: a CAVERNOMA is angiographically OCCULT — low-flow, no arteriovenous shunt, invisible on DSA — so a normal DSA does NOT exclude a vascular malformation. MRI (T2*/SWI, showing 'popcorn' mixed-age blood with a haemosiderin rim) is the test for cavernoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the imaging approach in acute AVM haemorrhage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Urgent non-contrast CT head first (to detect the bleed), then angiography to find the source.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the Spetzler-Martin grading system for, and which three features does it use?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back:
It grades the AVM to guide management and predict surgical risk, based on:
  • size
  • eloquence of adjacent brain
  • and venous drainage.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: In Spetzler-Martin grading, how is each of the three components graded?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back:
• Size: 1 point if under 3 cm, 2 for 3–6 cm, 3 if over 6 cm.
  • Eloquence of adjacent brain (whether it sits in a functionally critical area): 0 if non-eloquent, 1 if eloquent.
  • Venous drainage: 0 if superficial, 1 if deep.
The points are SUMMED to give a grade of I to V.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What does a higher Spetzler-Martin grade indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Higher surgical risk — larger, in eloquent cortex, with deep venous drainage means harder/riskier to treat.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How do the Spetzler-Ponce management classes map to the Spetzler-Martin grade?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back:
The three-tier Spetzler-PONCE classification condenses the Spetzler-Martin grades:
  • Class A = grade I–II (surgery)
  • Class B = grade III (multimodality treatment)
  • Class C = grade IV–V (usually observation).
But rupture status matters at least as much as grade — ARUBA supports conservative management for most UNRUPTURED AVMs, whatever the class.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is the overarching principle of AVM management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: The goal is to prevent haemorrhage/rupture; treatment choice is guided by the Spetzler-Martin grade (risk vs benefit).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is surgical resection (microsurgery) for AVM, and when is it best used?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Definitive removal; best for low-grade, accessible, non-eloquent AVMs (Class A).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is endovascular embolisation and how is it typically used?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Catheter-delivered occlusion of feeding vessels; often used to reduce the AVM before surgery/radiosurgery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What is stereotactic radiosurgery for AVM, and when is it used?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: E.g. Gamma Knife — for small, deep, or eloquent AVMs unsuitable for surgery; it works gradually over months–years.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: What does multimodality treatment (Class B) mean for AVM?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Combinations of the above treatments (surgery, embolisation, radiosurgery).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: When is observation / conservative management (Class C) used for AVM?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: For high-grade, high-risk AVMs where treatment risk outweighs benefit (Class C) — and, on the ARUBA evidence, for most UNRUPTURED AVMs of any grade, since medical management alone outperformed intervention for death or symptomatic stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.front: How is acute AVM haemorrhage managed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ar.back: Manage as for intracranial haemorrhage. Urgent blood-pressure lowering: if within 6 hours with a systolic of 150–220 mmHg, target a systolic of 130–139 mmHg within 1 hour, sustained for at least 7 days. Reverse anticoagulation urgently — warfarin: prothrombin complex concentrate + IV vitamin K; DOAC: the drug-specific reversal agent. Do NOT try to reverse an antiplatelet: platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated intracerebral haemorrhage caused MORE death and dependence in the randomised trial. Control seizures, consider neurosurgical evacuation, and treat the AVM definitively once stabilised. Anti-seizure medication treats seizures that occur — prophylaxis is not indicated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is aphasia (dysphasia)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: An acquired disorder of language — affecting production and/or comprehension — due to damage to the language areas of the dominant hemisphere (usually left).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What are cortical syndromes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: The characteristic deficits produced by damage to each lobe — patterns that localise the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the core concept linking cortical deficits to lesion location?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Higher cortical function is anatomically localised, so the pattern of deficit tells you where the lesion is. The clinical skill is mapping the deficit to the cortical area, which makes aphasia one of the most powerful localising signs in neurology (and a stroke red flag).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: How does aphasia differ from dysarthria?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Aphasia is a language disorder (the words/meaning are wrong); dysarthria is a motor speech disorder (articulation is slurred but language is intact) — a high-yield distinction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Which hemisphere holds language, and in whom?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: The dominant hemisphere — left in ~95% of right-handers and most left-handers.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Trace the language circuit from hearing a word to producing fluent speech.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Spoken word heard at the ear → Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) → comprehension → signal passes via the arcuate fasciculus → Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus) → generates the motor plan → fluent speech.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the function and location of Wernicke's area, and its blood supply?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Comprehension
  • located in the superior temporal gyrus
  • supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the function and location of Broca's area, and its blood supply?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Speech production
  • located in the inferior frontal gyrus
  • supplied by the superior division of the left MCA.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the arcuate fasciculus and what does it allow?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: The tract connecting Wernicke's → Broca's; it allows repetition.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Why is aphasia a high-yield vascular sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: The language areas are MCA territory, so aphasia is a classic sign of an MCA stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What three questions classify every aphasia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Is speech fluent?
  • Is comprehension intact?
  • Is repetition intact?

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Broca's (expressive) aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Non-fluent (effortful, 'BRoken')
  • comprehension intact
  • repetition impaired
  • lesion in the inferior frontal gyrus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Fluent ('Waffly', neologisms)
  • comprehension impaired
  • repetition impaired
  • lesion in the superior temporal gyrus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Conduction aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Fluent
  • comprehension intact
  • repetition POOR (the hallmark)
  • lesion in the arcuate fasciculus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Global aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Non-fluent
  • comprehension impaired
  • repetition impaired
  • large lesion (Broca's + Wernicke's — a big MCA stroke).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Transcortical motor aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Non-fluent
  • comprehension intact
  • repetition INTACT
  • lesion around Broca's, sparing it — classically a watershed/borderzone infarct after global hypoperfusion, which is why repetition survives.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Transcortical sensory aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Fluent
  • comprehension impaired
  • repetition INTACT
  • lesion around Wernicke's, sparing it — also a watershed lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Anomic aphasia: fluency, comprehension, repetition, and lesion site?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Fluent
  • comprehension intact
  • repetition intact
  • naming difficulty.
Classically the angular gyrus, but anomic aphasia is the LEAST localising type — naming failure arises across the temporo-parieto-occipital area and even in diffuse disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Memory aid: what does 'Broca's = BRoken speech' capture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Non-fluent, effortful speech, but the patient understands (frustrated because they know what they want to say) — a frontal lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Memory aid: what does 'Wernicke's = Waffly speech' capture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Fluent but nonsensical speech (word salad, neologisms); the patient doesn't understand and is unaware of the error — a temporal lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the repetition rule for distinguishing conduction from transcortical aphasias?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Repetition distinguishes conduction (impaired) from the transcortical aphasias (intact) — if comprehension and fluency seem fine but repetition is out, it's conduction aphasia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Broca's vs Wernicke's — contrast speech quality at the bedside.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Broca's: halting, effortful, telegraphic, few words. Wernicke's: fluent with normal rhythm but meaningless (neologisms, paraphasias).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Broca's vs Wernicke's — contrast comprehension and insight.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Broca's: comprehension preserved, patient is aware and frustrated. Wernicke's: comprehension impaired, patient often unaware of the deficit.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Broca's vs Wernicke's — contrast associated signs.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Broca's: often right hemiparesis (adjacent motor cortex). Wernicke's: often no hemiparesis; ± visual field defect.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the 'frustration clue' distinguishing Broca's from Wernicke's?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Broca's patients know what they want to say and are frustrated (comprehension intact); Wernicke's patients talk fluently but nonsensically and are often unaware — a useful bedside discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Distinguish aphasia, dysarthria, and dysphonia by the problem and the feature.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Aphasia = language problem (cortical): wrong words/meaning, comprehension and/or production affected
  • Dysarthria = motor articulation problem (speech muscles — UMN, cerebellar, extrapyramidal as in Parkinson's, or LMN/neuromuscular junction as in bulbar MND and myasthenia, which also carry an aspiration risk): slurred but language intact
  • Dysphonia = voice production problem (larynx/vocal cords): hoarse/quiet voice.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: State the one-line rule separating aphasia, dysarthria, and dysphonia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Aphasia = language; dysarthria = articulation; dysphonia = voice — don't conflate them.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Frontal lobe syndrome — key deficits?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Personality/behaviour change (disinhibition/apathy)
  • expressive (Broca's) aphasia if dominant
  • primitive reflexes
  • contralateral motor weakness
  • perseveration
  • anosmia
  • urinary incontinence.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Temporal lobe syndrome — key deficits?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia if dominant
  • memory impairment
  • superior quadrantanopia (Meyer's loop)
  • auditory/complex hallucinations
  • temporal lobe epilepsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Parietal lobe syndrome — key deficits?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Cortical sensory loss
  • apraxia
  • tactile agnosia (astereognosis)
  • neglect (non-dominant)
  • inferior quadrantanopia
  • Gerstmann's syndrome (dominant).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Occipital lobe syndrome — key deficits?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Visual field defects
  • cortical blindness — which requires BILATERAL occipital damage (PCA territory), with normal pupil reactions and normal fundi
  • and visual agnosia (occipitotemporal), including prosopagnosia for faces (fusiform, usually right-sided or bilateral).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What does a dominant (left) parietal lesion produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
Gerstmann's syndrome:
  • acalculia (can't calculate)
  • agraphia (can't write)
  • finger agnosia
  • left-right disorientation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What does a non-dominant (right) parietal lesion produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Neglect (of the left side/space)
  • dressing/constructional apraxia
  • anosognosia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the PITS rule for quadrantanopia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior: a parietal lesion causes inferior quadrantanopia; a temporal lesion (Meyer's loop) causes superior quadrantanopia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Define apraxia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Inability to perform learned skilled movements despite intact motor and sensory function AND intact comprehension of the task — you cannot call it apraxia if the patient did not understand the command.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Define agnosia (and name the face-specific form).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Inability to recognise or interpret despite intact senses. Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) is parietal; visual agnosia is occipitotemporal, and its face-specific form is prosopagnosia (fusiform gyrus, usually right-sided or bilateral).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Define acalculia and agraphia.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Acalculia = inability to calculate (part of Gerstmann's); agraphia = inability to write.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: Define neglect (as a cortical sign).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Failure to attend to one side of space (non-dominant parietal).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: How do you systematically test language at the bedside?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
Test the components systematically:
  • fluency (listen to spontaneous speech)
  • comprehension (follow commands)
  • repetition ('no ifs, ands, or buts')
  • naming (name objects)
  • reading + writing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: How does each bedside language component localise the aphasia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
• Fluency → Broca's vs Wernicke's
  • comprehension → receptive involvement
  • repetition → conduction vs transcortical
  • naming → anomic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: After testing language, what do you examine to localise the lobe?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Examine for associated signs — hemiparesis, visual fields, neglect — to localise the lobe.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What is the default interpretation of sudden-onset aphasia, and what else to consider?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back: Sudden-onset aphasia = stroke until proven otherwise → stroke pathway. Check the capillary glucose immediately: hypoglycaemia is the one instantly reversible mimic.Also consider tumour, abscess, MS, migraine and post-ictal (Todd's) for other tempos, and HSV encephalitis (fever + dysphasia + confusion — start aciclovir empirically), which is classically temporal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.front: What imaging and immediate steps are needed in sudden-onset aphasia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ap.back:
In SUDDEN onset the first scan is not a localisation exercise: get an immediate non-enhanced CT head to exclude haemorrhage and assess thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility. MRI comes later, for diagnostic uncertainty or non-vascular causes. Alongside it:
  • nil by mouth until a validated swallow screen within 4 hours
  • check the glucose
  • and refer early to speech and language therapy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the neuron, and what is the action potential?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The neuron is the signalling unit of the nervous system, and the action potential is the electrical signal it uses to transmit information rapidly over distance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the neuron and action potential?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A neuron maintains a resting membrane potential (a charge difference across its membrane), and an action potential is a brief, all-or-nothing reversal of that charge — driven by sequential opening of Na⁺ then K⁺ channels — that propagates along the axon. Myelination speeds this up dramatically.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: State the roles of the neuron's parts: dendrites, cell body, axon, axon terminal, myelin sheath.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Dendrites — receive incoming signals
  • cell body (soma) — integrates inputs
  • axon — conducts the action potential away
  • axon terminal — releases neurotransmitter at the synapse
  • myelin sheath — insulation (Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS), speeds conduction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield myelin point (PNS vs CNS)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Schwann cells myelinate the PNS; oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS — which is why MS (CNS, oligodendrocytes) and Guillain-Barré (PNS, Schwann cells) are different diseases of the same process.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What maintains the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
At rest the inside is negative relative to the outside (~−70 mV), maintained by:
  • Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase (pumps 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in → sets up the ion gradients, high Na⁺ outside, high K⁺ inside)
  • and K⁺ leak channels (the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest → K⁺ leaks out → leaves the inside negative).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Why is the resting potential mainly set by potassium?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest → the resting potential sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains the gradients that make this possible.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the hyperkalaemia link to the resting potential?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Changing extracellular K⁺ alters the resting potential (↑K⁺ depolarises it, ↓K⁺ hyperpolarises it) → the basis of K⁺'s effect on excitable tissue.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Action potential: describe the depolarisation phase and its ion movement.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A stimulus reaches threshold (~−55 mV) → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → rapid Na⁺ influx → membrane shoots positive (~+30 mV). Ion: Na⁺ IN.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Action potential: describe the repolarisation phase and its ion movement.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Na⁺ channels inactivate + voltage-gated K⁺ channels open → K⁺ efflux → membrane returns negative. Ion: K⁺ OUT.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Action potential: describe hyperpolarisation and return to rest.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Hyperpolarisation: K⁺ channels close slowly → brief undershoot (after-hyperpolarisation) below resting (K⁺ slow closure).
  • Return to rest: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores the ionic gradients — it is not what repolarises the membrane (that is K⁺ efflux).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the all-or-nothing principle, and how is stimulus strength coded?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Once threshold is reached, the action potential fires fully — its size doesn't vary; stimulus strength is coded by frequency of firing, not amplitude.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the threshold concept?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Subthreshold stimuli don't fire; reaching threshold triggers the positive-feedback Na⁺ influx → the all-or-nothing spike.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the absolute refractory period, and why does it occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: No new action potential is possible, however strong the stimulus, because Na⁺ channels are inactivated (can't reopen yet).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the relative refractory period, and why does it occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire, because some Na⁺ channels have recovered + there is hyperpolarisation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the functions of the refractory periods?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They ensure the AP propagates one way only (the area behind is refractory) + limit maximum firing frequency + prevent signals merging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does the action potential propagate along the axon?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The AP propagates by local depolarisation triggering the adjacent membrane to threshold → a self-propagating wave down the axon.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is saltatory conduction, and what are the nodes of Ranvier?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Myelin insulates the axon; the gaps are the nodes of Ranvier (where the Na⁺ channels are concentrated). The AP 'jumps' from node to node (saltatory conduction) → dramatically faster + more energy-efficient than continuous conduction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What factors affect conduction speed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Myelination (faster)
  • axon diameter (larger = faster)
  • temperature (cold slows conduction, which is why limbs are warmed before nerve conduction studies).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the demyelination link (the major clinical payoff)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Losing myelin → conduction slows/fails → MS (CNS) and Guillain-Barré (PNS) → neurological deficits; nerve conduction studies measure this.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do MS and Guillain-Barré differ in mechanism and presentation?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• MS: CNS demyelination (oligodendrocytes) → slowed/failed conduction → relapsing neurological deficits.
  • Guillain-Barré: PNS demyelination (Schwann cells) → ascending weakness; nerve conduction studies show slowing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do local anaesthetics (lidocaine), hyperkalaemia, and hypocalcaemia affect the action potential/excitability?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Local anaesthetics (lidocaine): block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevent depolarisation → no AP → no pain signal.
  • Hyperkalaemia: ↑extracellular K⁺ depolarises the resting potential → first more excitable, then inexcitable as Na⁺ channels inactivate (arrhythmias).
  • Hypocalcaemia: ↑neuronal excitability → tetany (Ca²⁺ stabilises the membrane).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What do nerve conduction studies measure, and what is Uhthoff's phenomenon?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Nerve conduction studies measure conduction velocity (↓ in demyelination). MS heat sensitivity (Uhthoff's): demyelinated nerves fail at higher temperatures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of synaptic transmission?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The electrical signal (AP) triggers Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release → the transmitter crosses the synaptic cleft → binds receptors on the next cell → produces an excitatory or inhibitory effect. The specific neurotransmitter + receptor determines the effect — and most neuro/psychiatric drugs act here.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: List the six steps of synaptic transmission.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• 1. AP arrives at the presynaptic terminal
  • 2. Ca²⁺ influx (depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → Ca²⁺ enters)
  • 3. vesicle fusion (Ca²⁺ triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse + release neurotransmitter by exocytosis)
  • 4. receptor binding (transmitter diffuses across the cleft → binds postsynaptic receptors)
  • 5. postsynaptic effect (excitatory/depolarise or inhibitory/hyperpolarise)
  • 6. termination (reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield Ca²⁺ point in synaptic transmission?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Calcium influx is the trigger for neurotransmitter release — which is why Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies vs presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels) impairs ACh release → weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare excitatory and inhibitory synaptic effects, including main transmitters.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Excitatory: depolarises the postsynaptic cell (toward threshold) → EPSP; main transmitter glutamate (the main excitatory CNS transmitter).
  • Inhibitory: hyperpolarises (away from threshold) → IPSP; main transmitters GABA (main inhibitory in brain) and glycine (spinal cord).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is summation, and why does it matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A single EPSP usually isn't enough — the postsynaptic cell sums many inputs (spatial + temporal summation) → fires an AP only if the net reaches threshold → this integration is how neurons 'compute'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield GABA point?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter → benzodiazepines + alcohol + barbiturates enhance GABA (→ sedation, anxiolysis); anti-epileptics often boost inhibition or reduce excitation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Acetylcholine (ACh): main roles and key clinical/drug links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Roles: neuromuscular junction, autonomic, CNS (memory).
  • Links: myasthenia gravis (antibodies vs ACh receptor); Alzheimer's (↓ACh → cholinesterase inhibitors); autonomic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Dopamine: main roles and key clinical/drug links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Roles: movement, reward, mood.
  • Links: Parkinson's (↓nigrostriatal dopamine); schizophrenia (↑mesolimbic → antipsychotics block D2); prolactin inhibition.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Glutamate, GABA, and glycine: roles and key links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Glutamate — main excitatory CNS transmitter (excitotoxicity in stroke, epilepsy).
  • GABA — main inhibitory in brain (benzodiazepines, alcohol, anti-epileptics enhance it).
  • Glycine — inhibitory in spinal cord (strychnine blocks it → spasms).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Serotonin (5-HT) and noradrenaline: roles and key links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Serotonin (5-HT) — mood, sleep, appetite; depression/anxiety → SSRIs; serotonin syndrome.
  • Noradrenaline — mood, arousal, sympathetic; depression (SNRIs), sympathetic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare ionotropic and metabotropic receptors (mechanism and speed).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels): transmitter opens an ion channel directly → fast (e.g. nicotinic ACh at NMJ, glutamate AMPA/NMDA, GABA-A).
  • Metabotropic (G-protein-coupled): transmitter triggers an intracellular cascade → slower, longer (e.g. muscarinic ACh, GABA-B, most dopamine/serotonin receptors).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the relevance of ionotropic vs metabotropic receptors?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Fast transmission (NMJ, reflexes) uses ionotropic receptors; modulatory/mood effects use metabotropic — and the receptor subtype determines drug specificity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the neuromuscular junction sequence and how the signal is terminated.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: AP → Ca²⁺ influx → ACh release → binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the muscle → depolarises → muscle contraction. ACh is broken down by acetylcholinesterase (terminates the signal).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton at the NMJ: mechanisms and (for MG) treatment.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Myasthenia gravis: antibodies block and destroy nicotinic ACh receptors → fatiguable weakness → treat with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (↑ACh).
  • Lambert-Eaton: antibodies vs presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ACh release (paraneoplastic, small cell lung cancer).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do organophosphates, non-depolarising muscle relaxants, and botulinum toxin act at the NMJ?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Organophosphates: inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ↑↑ACh → cholinergic crisis.
  • Non-depolarising muscle relaxants (rocuronium): block nicotinic receptors → paralysis (anaesthesia).
  • Botulinum toxin: blocks ACh release → paralysis (Botox).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Dopamine pathways: describe the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic pathways and their clinical links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Nigrostriatal (substantia nigra → striatum): movement — Parkinson's (degenerates → ↓dopamine → bradykinesia); antipsychotics block → extrapyramidal side effects.
  • Mesolimbic (VTA → limbic system): reward, emotion — ↑activity → positive symptoms of schizophrenia → antipsychotics (D2 block).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Dopamine pathways: describe the mesocortical and tuberoinfundibular pathways and their clinical links.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Mesocortical (VTA → prefrontal cortex): motivation, cognition — ↓activity → negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
  • Tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus → pituitary): inhibits prolactin — block (antipsychotics) → ↑prolactin → galactorrhoea.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield antipsychotic trade-off across dopamine pathways?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: D2 blockade helps the mesolimbic pathway (psychosis) but also hits the nigrostriatal (→ extrapyramidal/Parkinsonian side effects) and tuberoinfundibular (→ ↑prolactin) — which explains antipsychotic side effects.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How is the synaptic signal terminated (three mechanisms and their drug targets)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Reuptake (e.g. serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline — the SSRI/SNRI target: blocking reuptake ↑synaptic transmitter)
  • enzymatic breakdown (e.g. acetylcholinesterase for ACh; MAO (the MAOI target) and COMT for monoamines)
  • diffusion away.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do SSRIs/SNRIs and antipsychotics act synaptically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• SSRIs/SNRIs: block serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake → ↑synaptic levels (depression).
  • Antipsychotics: block dopamine D2 (mesolimbic → antipsychotic; nigrostriatal → EPS; tuberoinfundibular → ↑prolactin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how are Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and organophosphate poisoning explained synaptically?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Parkinson's: ↓nigrostriatal dopamine → levodopa/dopamine agonists.
  • Alzheimer's: ↓ACh → cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil).
  • Organophosphate poisoning: acetylcholinesterase inhibition → ↑ACh.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What do motor pathways carry, and why does understanding them matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They carry the command for movement from the brain to the muscles — and understanding them is the key to localising neurological lesions (the most examined skill in clinical neurology).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of voluntary movement and its single most important clinical distinction?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Voluntary movement travels down the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract via a two-neuron relay — upper motor neuron (UMN) then lower motor neuron (LMN) — and the single most important clinical distinction is UMN vs LMN signs, because where the lesion is determines the pattern. Modulatory systems (basal ganglia, cerebellum) fine-tune this.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare the pyramidal and extrapyramidal descending systems (tracts and function).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Pyramidal: corticospinal (body) + corticobulbar (face/head) → voluntary movement (the main motor pathway)
  • Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal → muscle tone, posture, involuntary/automatic movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the two-neuron relay of the corticospinal tract (UMN and LMN paths).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Upper motor neuron (UMN): motor cortex → internal capsule → brainstem → most fibres decussate (cross) in the medulla → descends the spinal cord → synapses on the LMN in the anterior horn
  • Lower motor neuron (LMN): anterior horn → peripheral nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield decussation point, and what does it mean for a left cortical lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Most corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla (the pyramidal decussation) → so one side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body → a left cortical/internal capsule lesion (e.g. stroke) → right-sided weakness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare UMN and LMN lesions for tone and reflexes.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
