• Tone: UMN ↑ (spasticity), LMN ↓ (flaccid)
  • Reflexes: UMN ↑ (hyperreflexia) + clonus, LMN ↓/absent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare UMN and LMN lesions for plantar response, power, wasting, and fasciculations.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Plantar response: UMN upgoing (Babinski +ve), LMN downgoing/absent
  • Power: weakness in both
  • Wasting: UMN minimal (disuse only), LMN marked (atrophy)
  • Fasciculations: UMN absent, LMN present.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the logic behind UMN vs LMN signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• The LMN is the 'final common pathway' to the muscle → losing it → flaccid, wasted, areflexic (no signal reaches the muscle)
  • Losing the UMN → removes the brain's inhibition of the cord reflexes → spastic, hyperreflexic, upgoing plantar (the cord runs unrestrained).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the memory anchor for UMN vs LMN signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• UMN = everything UP (tone ↑, reflexes ↑, plantar up)
  • LMN = everything DOWN (tone ↓, reflexes ↓) + wasting + fasciculations.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the localisation payoff of UMN vs LMN signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• UMN signs → lesion is in the brain or spinal cord (above the anterior horn)
  • LMN signs → anterior horn, root, or peripheral nerve.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Localising by pattern: what signs do a cortex/internal capsule (stroke) lesion and a spinal cord lesion produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cortex/internal capsule (stroke): contralateral UMN signs (MCA territory → face + arm more than leg; ACA territory → leg more than arm)
  • Spinal cord: UMN signs below the level + LMN signs at the level (anterior horn) + a sensory level.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Localising by pattern: what signs do anterior horn (e.g. polio), peripheral nerve, and MND lesions produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Anterior horn (polio): pure LMN signs
  • Peripheral nerve: LMN signs in that nerve's distribution
  • Motor neuron disease (MND): mixed UMN + LMN signs (degenerates both — the classic clue).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield MND point?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: MND causes both UMN and LMN signs together (e.g. a wasted, fasciculating limb with brisk reflexes) — the combination is the diagnostic clue.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield facial nerve point (UMN vs LMN facial lesion)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• A UMN facial lesion spares the forehead (the forehead gets bilateral cortical input)
  • an LMN lesion (Bell's palsy) affects the whole side including the forehead.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the two modulatory systems that fine-tune movement, and what do their lesions cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Basal ganglia: initiate/inhibit movement, set muscle tone → lesions = movement disorders (Parkinson's, Huntington's)
  • Cerebellum: coordination, balance, motor learning → lesions = ataxia, incoordination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the three-way distinction between pyramidal, basal ganglia, and cerebellar lesions?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Pyramidal lesions → weakness + UMN/LMN signs
  • basal ganglia → movement disorders (too much/little movement, tone)
  • cerebellar → incoordination (ataxia)
— three different 'flavours' of motor problem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Why does an internal capsule stroke cause a dense contralateral hemiparesis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The fibres are tightly packed there, so an internal capsule stroke → dense contralateral hemiparesis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the role of the basal ganglia in movement?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They are deep grey-matter nuclei that modulate voluntary movement — they don't initiate movement directly (the cortex does that), but they select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones, and set muscle tone.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the basal ganglia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They work through two opposing loops — the direct pathway (facilitates movement) and the indirect pathway (inhibits movement) — balanced by dopamine from the substantia nigra. Too little movement (Parkinson's) or too much (Huntington's/hemiballismus) results from tipping this balance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the basal ganglia nuclei and their roles: striatum and globus pallidus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Striatum (caudate + putamen): the main input station (receives from cortex)
  • Globus pallidus (internus GPi + externus GPe): GPi = the main output; GPe = part of the indirect loop.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the roles of the substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Substantia nigra (pars compacta SNc + reticulata SNr): SNc makes dopamine (degenerates in Parkinson's); SNr = output (with GPi)
  • Subthalamic nucleus (STN): key node of the indirect pathway.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the overall flow through the basal ganglia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Cortex → striatum (input) → [direct or indirect pathway] → GPi/SNr (output) → thalamus → back to cortex → a loop that modulates the cortex's motor output.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Direct pathway: net effect, route, and how it works.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Net effect: facilitates movement ('go')
  • Route: cortex → striatum → GPi/SNr → thalamus → cortex
  • How: striatum inhibits GPi → GPi normally inhibits the thalamus → so inhibiting GPi releases (disinhibits) the thalamus → ↑movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Indirect pathway: net effect, route, and how it works.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Net effect: inhibits movement ('stop')
  • Route: cortex → striatum → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr → thalamus → cortex
  • How: striatum → GPe → STN → excites GPi → GPi inhibits the thalamus more → ↓movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the 'brake' logic that students find tricky?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: GPi is tonically inhibitory on the thalamus (it normally 'holds the brake on'). The direct pathway takes the brake off (disinhibits the thalamus → movement happens); the indirect pathway pushes the brake harder (more inhibition → movement suppressed). The two are balanced to select wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones. Simplest summary: direct = go, indirect = stop.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does dopamine act as the balancer of the basal ganglia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta (the nigrostriatal pathway) acts on the striatum to tip the balance toward movement: it stimulates the direct pathway (D1 receptors → 'go') AND inhibits the indirect pathway (D2 receptors → less 'stop') → net effect: dopamine facilitates movement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key concept of dopamine as the 'throttle' for movement?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Dopamine is the throttle that enables movement → losing it (Parkinson's) → too little movement; excess dopamine signalling → too much movement — this single principle explains the movement disorders.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Parkinson's disease: lesion, balance change, and result.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Lesion: degeneration of SNc dopamine neurons (nigrostriatal)
  • Balance: ↓dopamine → ↓'go' + ↑'stop' → too little movement
  • Result: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor (hypokinetic) → treat by ↑dopamine (levodopa).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Huntington's disease: lesion, balance change, and result.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Lesion: degeneration of striatal neurons (indirect pathway)
  • Balance: loss of 'stop' → too much movement
  • Result: chorea (involuntary movements; hyperkinetic).
Autosomal dominant, CAG repeat.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Hemiballismus: lesion, balance change, and result.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Lesion: of the subthalamic nucleus (STN)
  • Balance: loss of indirect 'stop'
  • Result: violent flinging movements of the limbs contralateral to the lesioned STN.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the unifying logic linking hypokinetic and hyperkinetic movement disorders?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Hypokinetic disorders (Parkinson's) = too much 'stop' / too little dopamine
  • hyperkinetic disorders (Huntington's, hemiballismus) = too little 'stop' / loss of inhibition → so the direct/indirect balance predicts the disorder.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the Parkinson's treatment link?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• ↑dopamine (levodopa, dopamine agonists) restores the balance
  • STN deep brain stimulation dampens the overactive 'stop'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do antipsychotics (D2 blockers) cause movement effects?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Block striatal D2 receptors → mimic Parkinson's → extrapyramidal side effects (parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia; tardive dyskinesia is a late hyperkinetic effect of chronic blockade). The same dopamine balance lost in Parkinson's is blocked by antipsychotics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What movement effects do too much levodopa and dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide) cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Levodopa (too much): excess dopamine → dyskinesias
  • Dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide): can cause acute dystonia/parkinsonism.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does Wilson's disease relate to the basal ganglia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Copper deposition in the basal ganglia → movement disorder + liver disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does deep brain stimulation (STN) help in Parkinson's?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: High-frequency stimulation functionally suppresses the overactive subthalamic nucleus → less excitation of GPi → less inhibition of the thalamus → more movement. It dampens the overactive 'stop' pathway.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the role of the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The cerebellum is the brain's coordination centre — it doesn't initiate movement, but it fine-tunes it, making movements smooth, accurate, and well-timed, and it's essential for balance and motor learning.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It compares the intended movement (from the cortex) with the actual movement (sensory feedback) and sends corrective signals to smooth it out — a continuous error-correction system. It works ipsilaterally (each side controls the same side of the body), and its lesions produce a characteristic set of cerebellar signs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the three functions of the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Coordination — smooths + sequences movement (the main job): accurate, fluid, well-timed movement
  • Balance + posture — via vestibular input → equilibrium, gait, posture
  • Motor learning — learning + refining skilled movements (e.g. learning to ride a bike).
Do not confuse these with the three anatomical divisions: vestibulocerebellum (balance, eye movements), spinocerebellum/vermis (trunk and gait), cerebrocerebellum (skilled limb movement).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key concept of the cerebellum as a comparator/error-corrector?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It doesn't start movement (the cortex does), it makes ongoing movement accurate by comparing intention with execution and correcting the difference.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the roles of mossy fibres and climbing fibres as cerebellar inputs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Mossy fibres: relay sensory + cortical information (from spinal cord, brainstem, cortex) into the cerebellar cortex
  • Climbing fibres: from the inferior olive → powerful input to Purkinje cells (error/timing signals, motor learning).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the roles of Purkinje cells and the deep cerebellar nuclei?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Purkinje cells: the sole output of the cerebellar cortex — inhibitory (GABA); integrate the inputs
  • Deep cerebellar nuclei: the output of the cerebellum as a whole → send corrective signals back to the motor cortex (via the thalamus) + brainstem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the cerebellar loop.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Inputs (mossy + climbing fibres) → cerebellar cortex (Purkinje cells) → deep cerebellar nuclei → thalamus → motor cortex → corrective feedback that refines the movement command.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the Purkinje cell point?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory → they regulate the deep nuclei's output.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the ipsilateral rule for cerebellar signs, and why does it occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral — each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body (unlike the motor cortex, which controls the opposite side). The reason is the 'double crossing': cerebellar output crosses in the superior cerebellar peduncle to the opposite motor cortex, whose corticospinal tract then crosses back in the medulla — two crossings on the output side → net effect ipsilateral control → a left cerebellar lesion → left-sided cerebellar signs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the clinical payoff of the ipsilateral rule?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It distinguishes cerebellar lesions from cortical/corticospinal lesions (which are contralateral) → a key localising clue.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What does the DANISH mnemonic for cerebellar signs stand for (first three)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• D — Dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements)
  • A — Ataxia (unsteady, broad-based gait + trunk/limb incoordination)
  • N — Nystagmus (involuntary eye oscillations).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What does the DANISH mnemonic for cerebellar signs stand for (last three)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• I — Intention tremor (tremor worsening as the hand approaches a target, vs the resting tremor of Parkinson's)
  • S — Slurred/scanning speech (dysarthria, staccato, scanning quality)
  • H — Hypotonia / impaired heel-shin test (↓tone + impaired heel-to-shin coordination).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield intention-vs-resting tremor distinction?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cerebellar = intention tremor (worse on reaching a target)
  • Parkinson's (basal ganglia) = resting tremor (worse at rest, improves with movement) → distinguishes the two modulatory systems.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the 'drunk' analogy for cerebellar signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Cerebellar signs resemble drunkenness (ataxia, slurred speech, nystagmus) — because alcohol affects the cerebellum (a common cause).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the three modulatory 'flavours' of motor problem?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Pyramidal (corticospinal): weakness + UMN/LMN signs
  • Basal ganglia: movement disorders — too much/little movement, ↑/↓tone, resting tremor
  • Cerebellum: incoordination (ataxia) — DANISH signs, intention tremor, ipsilateral.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do cerebellar stroke and alcohol affect the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cerebellar stroke: ipsilateral cerebellar signs (DANISH) — posterior circulation
  • Alcohol: acute intoxication + chronic cerebellar degeneration (ataxia, classically the vermis — the midline strip that coordinates trunk and gait, so the picture is truncal/gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do MS, cerebellar tumours, and Friedreich's ataxia involve the cerebellum?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• MS: cerebellar involvement → ataxia, intention tremor, scanning speech
  • Cerebellar tumours: e.g. medulloblastoma (children), metastases; + raised ICP signs
  • Friedreich's ataxia: inherited cerebellar + spinal degeneration.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the features of a posterior fossa lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cerebellar signs
  • brainstem/cranial nerve signs
  • hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What do sensory pathways carry, and why does understanding them matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They carry information from the body up to the brain — and like the motor system, understanding them is key to localising lesions (where the sensory loss is, and what type, tells you where the problem is).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the two main ascending sensory pathways and the modalities they carry?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) for fine touch/vibration/proprioception, and the spinothalamic tract for pain/temperature/crude touch. The crucial difference is where each crosses the midline, which explains dissociated sensory patterns (especially Brown-Séquard).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare the DCML and spinothalamic tracts: modalities, crossing point, and fibre type.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• DCML: fine touch, vibration, proprioception (+ two-point discrimination); crosses in the medulla (ascends first, then crosses); large, myelinated (fast) fibres.
  • Spinothalamic: pain, temperature, crude touch; crosses in the spinal cord (at/near the level of entry — crosses immediately); small (slower) fibres.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the single most important point about where the two sensory pathways cross?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The two pathways cross at different levels — DCML crosses high (in the medulla), spinothalamic crosses low (in the cord, near entry) → this is the key to understanding dissociated sensory loss and Brown-Séquard.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the three-neuron relay of the DCML pathway.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• 1st neuron: peripheral receptor → enters the cord → ascends the dorsal columns on the same side → synapses in the medulla.
  • 2nd neuron: crosses (decussates) in the medulla → ascends as the medial lemniscus → thalamus.
  • 3rd neuron: thalamus → sensory cortex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key feature of DCML crossing, and its consequence for a cord lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: DCML fibres ascend ipsilaterally first, then cross in the medulla → so a cord lesion affects DCML on the same side as the lesion (below it).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield dorsal column point (which diseases damage them and how)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) + tabes dorsalis (syphilis) damage the dorsal columns → loss of vibration + proprioception (→ sensory ataxia, positive Romberg).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the three-neuron relay of the spinothalamic tract.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• 1st neuron: receptor → enters the cord → synapses immediately (in the dorsal horn).
  • 2nd neuron: crosses (decussates) within the cord (within a segment or two of entry) → ascends the contralateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus.
  • 3rd neuron: thalamus → sensory cortex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key feature of spinothalamic crossing, and its consequence for a cord lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Spinothalamic fibres cross almost immediately → so a cord lesion affects pain/temperature on the opposite side (below the lesion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is Brown-Séquard syndrome, and what causes its dissociated pattern?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Brown-Séquard = hemisection (one half) of the spinal cord → produces a characteristic dissociated, split-sided pattern that's entirely explained by where each pathway crosses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: In Brown-Séquard, which side is affected for motor weakness and DCML loss, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Motor (UMN) weakness: ipsilateral (same side, below) — the corticospinal tract already crossed in the medulla.
  • Fine touch/vibration/proprioception (DCML) loss: ipsilateral — DCML hasn't crossed yet (crosses in the medulla, above the lesion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: In Brown-Séquard, which side is affected for pain/temperature loss, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic): contralateral (opposite side, below) — spinothalamic already crossed in the cord (below the lesion).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the whole logic of Brown-Séquard's dissociated picture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Because DCML crosses high and spinothalamic crosses low, a cord hemisection gives ipsilateral motor + fine touch/proprioception loss but contralateral pain/temperature loss → the classic dissociated picture. This is the reason the crossing levels matter (derive it, don't memorise a list).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Localising by pattern: what causes a sensory level and dissociated sensory loss?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Sensory level (loss below a dermatome): spinal cord lesion (transection) — both pathways lost below.
  • Dissociated sensory loss: selective pathway damage (e.g. syringomyelia = central cord → loss of pain/temp, sparing fine touch — 'cape' distribution).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Localising by pattern: what causes dorsal column loss, glove-and-stocking loss, and dermatomal loss?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Dorsal column loss (vibration/proprioception): B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis → sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg.
  • Glove-and-stocking: peripheral neuropathy (diabetes) — distal, length-dependent.
  • Dermatomal: nerve root lesion (e.g. shingles, radiculopathy).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield Romberg sign, and what does it distinguish?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Dorsal column (proprioception) loss → unsteady with eyes closed (Romberg +ve) — because they rely on vision to compensate; distinguishes sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia (which is unsteady eyes open or closed).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How is the sensory cortex organised, and what do cortical lesions produce?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Sensory information arrives at the primary sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), organised as a homunculus (body map — disproportionate areas for hands/face). Cortical lesions → contralateral sensory loss + higher-order deficits (e.g. neglect, astereognosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do B12 deficiency (SACD) and syringomyelia present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• B12 deficiency (SACD): dorsal column degeneration → ↓vibration/proprioception → sensory ataxia, +ve Romberg (+ cord UMN signs).
  • Syringomyelia: central cord → dissociated loss (pain/temp lost, fine touch spared) — 'cape' distribution.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do spinal cord transection, tabes dorsalis, and peripheral neuropathy present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Spinal cord transection: sensory level (all modalities lost below).
  • Tabes dorsalis: dorsal column (neurosyphilis) → sensory ataxia.
  • Peripheral neuropathy: glove-and-stocking (diabetes, B12).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the limbic system, and what does it govern?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A group of interconnected structures deep in the brain that govern emotion, memory, motivation, and behaviour — the 'emotional brain'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the limbic system?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It links sensory/cognitive information to emotional responses and memory — with the hippocampus central to memory formation and the amygdala central to emotion (especially fear). The Papez circuit is the classic hippocampal loop for memory consolidation and emotional experience (the amygdala sits outside it, in its own circuit).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the main roles of the hippocampus, amygdala, and hypothalamus in the limbic system?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Hippocampus: memory formation (converting short-term → long-term memory).
  • Amygdala: emotion — especially fear + the emotional significance of stimuli.
  • Hypothalamus: the output — drives autonomic + endocrine + behavioural responses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the roles of the cingulate gyrus, mammillary bodies, fornix, and anterior thalamic nucleus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cingulate gyrus: emotion + linking behaviour to emotion.
  • Mammillary bodies: memory relay (part of the Papez circuit; damaged in Korsakoff's).
  • Fornix: the white-matter tract connecting hippocampus → mammillary bodies.
  • Thalamus (anterior nucleus): relay within the circuit.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the 'two stars' of the limbic system?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Hippocampus = memory, amygdala = emotion (fear) — anchor these two and the rest is connecting circuitry.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the Papez circuit.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Cingulate gyrus → (cingulum → entorhinal cortex) → hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → (mammillothalamic tract) → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus (→ loop repeats). It is involved in memory consolidation (laying down long-term memories) and emotional experience.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield clinical payoff of the Papez circuit (mammillary bodies and hippocampus lesions)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Lesions anywhere in the circuit impair memory.
  • The mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei are damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (thiamine deficiency, alcohol) → anterograde and retrograde amnesia + confabulation.
  • Bilateral hippocampus damage → dense anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories) — the classic memory structure.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What does the amygdala do?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
It processes the emotional significance of stimuli and generates emotional + autonomic responses, especially fear:
  • it links sensory input → emotional response (e.g. seeing a threat → fear → fight-or-flight)
  • drives the fear response via connections to the hypothalamus + brainstem → autonomic fight-or-flight (↑HR, ↑BP, sweating)
  • attaches emotional memory (links with the hippocampus).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is Klüver-Bucy syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Bilateral anterior temporal lobe damage (the amygdala being the key component) →
  • loss of fear
  • placidity
  • hyperorality
  • hypersexuality
  • visual agnosia ('psychic blindness')
  • and hypermetamorphosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the hippocampus's role in memory, and the effect of bilateral damage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It is essential for forming new long-term (declarative) memories, converting short-term → long-term memory (consolidation). Bilateral hippocampal damage → anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories; remote memories preserved, though there is usually graded retrograde loss for the years just before the injury).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Distinguish declarative/explicit from procedural/implicit memory.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Declarative/explicit (facts/events) — hippocampus-dependent.
  • Procedural/implicit (skills) — basal ganglia/cerebellum, hippocampus-independent.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield Alzheimer's link to the hippocampus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Alzheimer's disease affects the hippocampus early → early memory loss is the hallmark.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does the limbic system produce a bodily response (its outputs)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Via the hypothalamus → autonomic (fight-or-flight) + endocrine (HPA stress axis) + behavioural drives (hunger, thirst, sexual); and via the brainstem/autonomic → the physical signs of emotion (↑HR, sweating, pupil dilation). The integrating idea: emotional/cognitive input → autonomic, endocrine, and behavioural outputs (e.g. fear → fight-or-flight via the hypothalamus + sympathetic system).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how are Alzheimer's, Wernicke-Korsakoff, and anterograde amnesia explained by the limbic system?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Alzheimer's: early hippocampal involvement → early memory loss.
  • Wernicke-Korsakoff: thiamine deficiency → mammillary body and dorsomedial thalamic damage → anterograde and retrograde amnesia + confabulation.
  • Anterograde amnesia: bilateral hippocampal damage → can't form new memories.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how are temporal lobe epilepsy, Klüver-Bucy, and PTSD explained by the limbic system?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Temporal lobe epilepsy: seizures from the limbic/temporal region → déjà vu, emotional/autonomic auras, memory disturbance.
  • Klüver-Bucy: bilateral anterior temporal/amygdala damage → loss of fear, placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, visual agnosia.
  • PTSD: amygdala/hippocampus dysregulation (emotional memory).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What does the autonomic nervous system (ANS) control?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The body's involuntary functions — heart rate, blood pressure, digestion, glands, pupils, bladder — running automatically in the background.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the ANS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It has two opposing divisions — sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest') — that work in balance, acting via specific neurotransmitters (ACh, noradrenaline) and receptors (adrenergic, cholinergic). Knowing the receptors is the key that unlocks a huge swathe of pharmacology.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare the overall role and origin of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Sympathetic ('fight or flight'): mobilises the body for stress/activity; origin thoracolumbar (T1–L2 spinal cord).
  • Parasympathetic ('rest and digest'): conserves energy, restores calm; origin craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X; sacral S2–4).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic effects: heart, lungs, and pupils.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Heart: sympathetic ↑rate + contractility, parasympathetic ↓rate.
  • Lungs: sympathetic bronchodilation, parasympathetic bronchoconstriction.
  • Pupils: sympathetic dilate (mydriasis), parasympathetic constrict (miosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Sympathetic vs parasympathetic effects: gut and other (glucose/secretions/bladder).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Gut: sympathetic ↓motility/secretion, parasympathetic ↑motility/secretion (digestion).
  • Other: sympathetic ↑glucose, sweating, vasoconstriction; parasympathetic ↑secretions, bladder emptying.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield vagus point?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries most parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs and gut as far as the distal transverse colon (the hindgut, bladder and genitalia come from S2-S4) → 'vagal tone' slows the heart (which is why atropine speeds the heart).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the two-neuron layout of the ANS, and the transmitters used by each division?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Both divisions use a two-neuron relay (preganglionic → ganglion → postganglionic → target).
  • Sympathetic: preganglionic ACh (nicotinic) → postganglionic noradrenaline (mostly, acting on adrenergic receptors).
  • Parasympathetic: preganglionic ACh (nicotinic) → postganglionic ACh (acting on muscarinic receptors).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the key exceptions to the standard ANS transmitter layout?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Adrenal medulla: sympathetic preganglionic fibres go straight to it → it releases adrenaline (~80%) and noradrenaline (~20%) into the blood (a modified ganglion).
  • Sweat glands: sympathetic but use ACh (muscarinic) — the exception to 'sympathetic = noradrenaline'.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the unifying point about ANS transmitters and receptors?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: All preganglionic fibres + all parasympathetic + sweat glands = ACh; most sympathetic postganglionic = noradrenaline → this determines which receptors (and drugs) act where.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: α1 adrenergic receptor: location/effect and drug examples.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Location/effect: vasoconstriction (vessels), pupil dilation, bladder sphincter.
  • Drugs: α-blockers (doxazosin — BPH/HTN), α-agonists (vasopressors).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: α2 and β1 adrenergic receptors: location/effect and drug examples.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• α2: presynaptic feedback (↓noradrenaline) — clonidine.
  • β1: heart (↑rate + contractility), renin release — β-blockers (↓HR/BP), dobutamine (inotrope).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: β2 adrenergic receptor: location/effect and drug examples.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Location/effect: bronchodilation, vasodilation, uterine relaxation.
  • Drugs: β2-agonists (salbutamol — asthma).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Muscarinic (cholinergic) receptor: location/effect and drug examples.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Location/effect: parasympathetic effects (↓HR, ↑secretions, ↑gut, miosis, bladder), and sympathetic cholinergic sweating.
  • Drugs: antimuscarinics (atropine, ipratropium, oxybutynin); muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Nicotinic (cholinergic) receptor: location/effect and drug examples.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Location/effect: autonomic ganglia (neuronal type) + the neuromuscular junction (muscle type).
  • Drugs: NMJ blockers, which act at the muscle-type receptor only and so do not block the ganglia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the drug-mapping payoff for β1, β2, and muscarinic receptors?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• β1 in the heart → β-blockers slow it (angina, HTN, arrhythmia)
  • β2 in lungs → salbutamol dilates airways (asthma).
  • Muscarinic → atropine blocks it (↑HR, dries secretions); ipratropium (bronchodilator); oxybutynin (bladder).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the drug-mapping payoff for α1 receptors?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: α1 → vasoconstriction → α-blockers for BPH/HTN; α-agonists as vasopressors.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Autonomic control in action: how are heart rate/BP and pupils controlled?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Heart rate/BP: sympathetic ↑ (β1), parasympathetic (vagus) ↓; the baroreceptor reflex.
  • Pupils: sympathetic dilates (α1), parasympathetic constricts (CN III).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Autonomic control in action: how are airways, bladder, and fight-or-flight controlled?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Airways: sympathetic (β2, largely via circulating adrenaline) dilates, parasympathetic constricts.
  • Bladder: parasympathetic empties (detrusor contraction), sympathetic stores.
  • Fight-or-flight: sympathetic surge (+ adrenal adrenaline) → ↑HR/BP, dilated pupils, bronchodilation, ↑glucose.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: what do β-blockers, β2-agonists, and antimuscarinics do (with examples)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• β-blockers: block β1 → ↓HR/BP/contractility (angina, HTN, HF, arrhythmia).
  • β2-agonists (salbutamol): β2 → bronchodilation (asthma/COPD).
  • Antimuscarinics: atropine (↑HR, bradycardia/organophosphates), ipratropium (COPD), oxybutynin (bladder), hyoscine (secretions — palliative).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: what do α-blockers and vasopressors do (with examples)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• α-blockers: doxazosin/tamsulosin (BPH, HTN).
  • Vasopressors (noradrenaline, metaraminol): α1 vasoconstriction (shock).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is Horner's syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A break anywhere in the three-neuron oculosympathetic chain (hypothalamus → ciliospinal centre C8-T2 → superior cervical ganglion → plexus on the internal carotid) → ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. How far the anhidrosis extends depends on where the lesion sits.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does autonomic neuropathy (e.g. diabetes) present, and what happens in organophosphate poisoning?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Autonomic neuropathy (diabetes): postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction.
  • Organophosphate poisoning: ↑ACh → cholinergic crisis (muscarinic + nicotinic) → treat with atropine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is a reflex?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: An automatic, involuntary motor response to a stimulus — fast, stereotyped, and not requiring conscious thought (often not even the brain).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of reflexes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Reflexes work through a reflex arc (the basic circuit: sensor → spinal cord → effector), and crucially they're modulated by the brain — which is why reflexes change in UMN vs LMN lesions. Testing reflexes is a window into the integrity of that whole circuit.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: List the components of the reflex arc and their roles.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Receptor — detects the stimulus (e.g. muscle stretch)
  • afferent (sensory) neuron — carries the signal to the spinal cord
  • integration centre — the spinal cord (± interneurons) processes the signal
  • efferent (motor) neuron — carries the response from the cord to the muscle (the LMN)
  • effector — the muscle that responds.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key concept about where a reflex occurs and how the brain affects it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A reflex can occur at the spinal cord level without involving the brain (which is why it's fast + automatic) — but the brain normally modulates (dampens) it from above → this modulation is what's lost in UMN lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the stretch (myotatic) reflex using the knee-jerk.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The knee-jerk is the model reflex — a monosynaptic stretch reflex: tendon tap → stretches the muscle → activates the muscle spindle (stretch receptor) → afferent neuron → spinal cord → directly synapses on the LMN (monosynaptic) → muscle contracts (the jerk). Simultaneously, the antagonist muscle is inhibited (reciprocal inhibition, via an interneuron).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the function of the stretch reflex, and why is it so fast?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: It maintains muscle tone + posture (resists unexpected stretch). It's monosynaptic (one synapse, afferent → efferent) — which is why it's so fast.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do reflexes change in a UMN lesion, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Reflexes: ↑ (hyperreflexia) + clonus. Why: loss of the brain's descending inhibition → the spinal reflex arc runs unrestrained.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do reflexes change in an LMN lesion, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Reflexes: ↓/absent (hyporeflexia). Why: the reflex arc itself is broken (the efferent LMN is damaged).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key insight linking the brain's role to reflex changes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The brain normally dampens spinal reflexes from above. A UMN lesion removes that brake → reflexes become brisk (hyperreflexia) + clonus; an LMN lesion breaks the arc itself → reflexes are lost → so reflexes localise the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is clonus, and what does it indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Rhythmic involuntary muscle contractions (e.g. at the ankle) — a sign of a UMN lesion (the unrestrained, repetitive stretch reflex).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the plantar (Babinski) reflex, and what does an abnormal response indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Normal in adults = toes down (an extensor plantar is normal up to about 1 year); upgoing (Babinski +ve) = UMN lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the significance of tendon reflexes (biceps, triceps, knee, ankle)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: They test specific nerve roots (biceps + supinator C5/6, triceps C7/8, knee L3/4, ankle S1/2) → localise root lesions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the withdrawal (flexor) reflex and pupillary light reflex?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Withdrawal (flexor) reflex: polysynaptic — pull away from a painful stimulus (protective).
  • Pupillary light reflex: tests CN II (afferent) + CN III (efferent) — brainstem integrity.
Light in one eye constricts both pupils (direct + consensual); an afferent defect shows as a relative afferent pupillary defect on the swinging-light test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the significance of primitive reflexes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Normal in infants (Moro, grasp, rooting); reappearance in adults = frontal/diffuse brain pathology.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the root-localising point for tendon reflexes?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Each tendon reflex tests specific nerve roots → an absent reflex localises a root/peripheral lesion (e.g. absent ankle jerk = S1).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: what do hyperreflexia + clonus and hyporeflexia/areflexia indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Hyperreflexia + clonus: UMN lesion (loss of descending inhibition) — stroke, cord lesion, MS.
  • Hyporeflexia/areflexia: LMN lesion (broken arc) — peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, Guillain-Barré.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: what do mixed (↑ + ↓) reflexes and Hoffman's sign indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Mixed (↑ + ↓ reflexes): MND (UMN + LMN). Hoffman's sign: a UMN sign in the upper limb. (Pupillary light reflex tests CN II/III + brainstem, used in coma/brainstem assessment.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the special senses, and what do they do?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Vision, hearing, balance, taste, smell — they convert specific physical stimuli (light, sound, chemicals) into neural signals the brain can interpret.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of the special senses?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Each sense has a specialised receptor that transduces its stimulus into action potentials, then a dedicated pathway to a specific cortical area. The clinically high-yield parts are the visual pathway (lesions cause characteristic field defects) and the auditory/vestibular system (hearing loss + vertigo).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does the eye transduce light (rods vs cones)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Light → cornea + lens (focus) → retina → photoreceptors: rods (dim light, peripheral, black-and-white) + cones (bright light, central/macula, colour) → transduce light into signals → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the visual pathway.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN, thalamus) → optic radiations → primary visual cortex (occipital lobe).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What happens at the optic chiasm (the high-yield crossing point)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The fibres from the nasal (medial) half of each retina cross over (the temporal/lateral fibres stay uncrossed) → so after the chiasm, each side of the brain handles the opposite visual field.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What visual field defects result from lesions of the optic nerve, optic chiasm, and post-chiasm (tract/radiation/cortex)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Optic nerve (before chiasm): monocular blindness (that whole eye).
  • Optic chiasm (crossing fibres): bitemporal hemianopia (loss of both outer/temporal fields — classically pituitary tumour pressing on the chiasm).
  • Optic tract/radiation/occipital cortex (after chiasm): homonymous hemianopia (loss of the same-side field in both eyes — e.g. stroke); a partial radiation lesion instead gives a quadrantanopia (temporal/Meyer's loop → superior, parietal → inferior), and occipital infarcts often spare the macula.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the localising logic for visual field defects?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Before the chiasm = one eye (monocular); at the chiasm = bitemporal; after the chiasm = homonymous (same field both eyes) — derive the defect from where the lesion sits.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the high-yield pituitary point for vision?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A pituitary tumour grows up and compresses the chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How does the ear transduce sound?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Sound → outer ear (collects) → middle ear (ossicles amplify) → inner ear/cochlea → hair cells transduce vibration into neural signals → CN VIII.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the auditory pathway.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Cochlea → cochlear nuclei → superior olivary nucleus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus (MGN, thalamus) → primary auditory cortex (temporal lobe).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare conductive and sensorineural hearing loss (problem and cause examples).
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Conductive: sound can't reach the cochlea (outer/middle ear) — wax, otitis media, otosclerosis, perforation.
  • Sensorineural: cochlea or CN VIII problem — presbycusis (age), noise, ototoxic drugs, acoustic neuroma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Which bedside tests distinguish the two types of hearing loss, and what do they assess?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Rinne + Weber tests.
  • Rinne: air vs bone conduction — AC > BC is normal or sensorineural ('Rinne positive'); BC > AC means conductive loss in that ear ('Rinne negative').
  • Weber: lateralisation — the sound lateralises towards a conductive loss and away from a sensorineural loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the vestibular apparatus, and what does it do?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, which detect angular/rotational acceleration, + the otolith organs — utricle and saccule — which detect linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity) → via CN VIII → brainstem/cerebellum → maintains balance + coordinates eye movements (the vestibulo-ocular reflex).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the clinical link of vestibular dysfunction, with examples and the central-vs-peripheral distinction?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Vestibular dysfunction → vertigo (the illusion of movement) — e.g. BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière's; central (brainstem/cerebellar) vs peripheral (vestibular) vertigo.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the smell (olfaction) pathway, and what is special about it?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Chemicals → olfactory receptors (nasal epithelium) → olfactory nerve (CN I) → olfactory cortex. It's the only sense that bypasses the thalamus + links directly to the limbic system → which is why smells evoke strong memories/emotions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe the taste (gustation) pathway and the five basic tastes.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Chemicals → taste buds (anterior two-thirds of tongue → chorda tympani of CN VII; posterior third → CN IX; epiglottis/pharynx → CN X; buds also sit on the palate and pharynx) → nucleus of the solitary tract → thalamus → insular cortex. Five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the causes of anosmia (loss of smell)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• URTI
  • head trauma (shearing of olfactory fibres)
  • COVID
  • Parkinson's (early).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do papilloedema and acoustic neuroma present?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Papilloedema: raised ICP → swollen optic disc.
  • Acoustic neuroma: CN VIII tumour → sensorineural hearing loss + balance problems.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how do CN palsies (III, IV, VI) present, and what causes anosmia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• CN palsies (III, IV, VI): eye movement problems → diplopia.
  • Anosmia: head trauma, COVID, early Parkinson's.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is pain, and why can the same injury hurt differently in different circumstances?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Pain is the body's protective warning system — detecting actual or potential tissue damage — but it's also modulated at multiple levels, which is why the same injury can hurt differently in different circumstances.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the organising principle of pain physiology?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Pain signals travel from nociceptors → spinal cord → brain (the spinothalamic tract), but the signal is modulated along the way (the gate control theory, descending inhibition) — and analgesics work by targeting different points in this pathway. There are also distinct types of pain (nociceptive vs neuropathic) that respond to different drugs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the four steps of nociception (pain detection)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• 1. Transduction — tissue damage → nociceptors (free nerve endings) detect it; inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P) sensitise them.
  • 2. Transmission — the signal travels via two fibre types → dorsal horn → crosses → ascends the spinothalamic tract → thalamus → cortex.
  • 3. Perception — the cortex interprets it as pain (with emotional context via the limbic system).
  • 4. Modulation — the signal is dampened or amplified along the way.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Compare the two pain fibres (A-delta and C fibres): speed and pain quality.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• A-delta: fast, myelinated — sharp, immediate, localised ('first pain').
  • C fibres: slow, unmyelinated — dull, aching, throbbing, diffuse ('second pain').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: By which pathway does pain travel, and why does this matter?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Pain travels via the spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) — the same pathway from the sensory note, which is why it crosses in the cord (relevant to dissociated sensory loss).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is inflammatory sensitisation, and why does injured tissue hurt more?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Tissue damage releases inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, histamine) → sensitise nociceptors → lower their threshold → the area becomes hyperalgesic (exaggerated pain from a painful stimulus) and often allodynic (pain from a normally non-painful stimulus, such as light touch).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the NSAID link (the key payoff of inflammatory sensitisation)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Prostaglandins sensitise nociceptors → NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis (COX inhibition) → ↓sensitisation → analgesia (+ anti-inflammatory) — this is why NSAIDs work for inflammatory/nociceptive pain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the gate control theory of pain?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: In the dorsal horn, non-painful sensory input (e.g. touch/rubbing, via A-beta fibres) can 'close the gate' → inhibit the transmission of pain signals. This is why rubbing a sore area helps, and the basis of TENS machines (stimulate touch fibres → gate pain).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is descending inhibition of pain, and what does it explain?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The brain (periaqueductal grey, brainstem) sends descending pathways that inhibit pain at the spinal cord, using endogenous opioids (endorphins/enkephalins), serotonin, and noradrenaline. This descending system explains stress-induced analgesia (not feeling an injury in the heat of the moment).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the opioid link (the key payoff of descending inhibition)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Opioids act on opioid receptors (in the brain + spinal cord) → mimic this descending inhibition → potent analgesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Nociceptive pain: mechanism, character, and treatment.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Mechanism: nociceptor activation (tissue damage).
  • Character: sharp/aching, localised.
  • Treatment: NSAIDs, paracetamol, opioids (the WHO ladder).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Neuropathic pain: mechanism, character, and treatment.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Mechanism: nerve damage itself (not nociceptors).
  • Character: burning, shooting, electric, numb.
  • Treatment: anticonvulsants (gabapentin/pregabalin), antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine) — not standard analgesics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Inflammatory pain: mechanism, character, and treatment.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Mechanism: inflammatory sensitisation.
  • Character: aching/throbbing pain with swelling, warmth and tenderness.
  • Treatment: NSAIDs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the key distinction between nociceptive and neuropathic pain for treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Nociceptive pain responds to standard analgesics (the WHO ladder); neuropathic pain responds poorly to them and needs neuropathic agents (gabapentinoids, amitriptyline) — this is why classifying the pain type matters for treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is referred pain, and why does it occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Pain felt at a site distant from its source, because visceral + somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord neurons → the brain misattributes the visceral pain to the somatic area. Visceral pain is poorly localised because visceral afferents are sparse and share spinal segments with skin → the brain refers it to the corresponding dermatome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Referred pain: where do cardiac (MI) and diaphragmatic pain refer to?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Cardiac (MI): left arm and chest wall (T1–T4 dermatomes), also referred to the jaw and neck (upper cervical/trigeminal convergence).
  • Diaphragm: shoulder tip (C3–5, phrenic nerve).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Referred pain: where do gallbladder and early appendix pain refer to?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Gallbladder: right scapula.
  • Appendix (early): central abdomen (then localises to RIF).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Analgesic targets: where do NSAIDs, paracetamol, and local anaesthetics act?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• NSAIDs: block prostaglandins (↓nociceptor sensitisation — peripheral).
  • Paracetamol: central (mechanism incompletely understood).
  • Local anaesthetics: block Na⁺ channels → no AP → no transmission.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Analgesic targets: where do opioids, gabapentinoids/antidepressants, and TENS act?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Opioids: opioid receptors (brain + cord) → mimic descending inhibition.
  • Gabapentinoids/antidepressants: neuropathic pain (modulate nerve signalling/descending pathways).
  • TENS: gate control (touch fibres close the gate).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the multimodal principle of analgesia?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Targeting multiple points (e.g. NSAID + paracetamol + opioid) gives better pain control with lower doses of each — the principle of multimodal analgesia, which complements the stepwise escalation of the WHO ladder.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are CSF and the blood-brain barrier, and what is the organising principle?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The brain is protected by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) — a fluid cushion that surrounds and buoys it — and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) — a tight barrier controlling what reaches the brain from the blood. Organising principle: CSF is made, circulates, and is absorbed in a continuous loop — disrupting this raises pressure (hydrocephalus, raised ICP); the BBB protects the brain but also keeps many drugs out.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Describe CSF production, circulation, and absorption.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Production: the choroid plexus (in the ventricles) makes CSF (~500 mL/day, ~150 mL present at any time → turned over several times daily).
  • Circulation: lateral ventricles → (foramina of Monro) → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → (foramina of Luschka and Magendie) → subarachnoid space (around the brain + cord).
  • Absorption: arachnoid granulations → into the venous sinuses (back into the blood).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the CSF flow path (high-yield for hydrocephalus), and what happens with a blockage?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Lateral → (foramina of Monro) → 3rd → aqueduct → 4th → (foramina of Luschka and Magendie) → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → venous blood; a blockage anywhere → CSF accumulates upstream → hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the CSF balance principle?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Production = absorption keeps the volume/pressure constant; any ↑production, ↓absorption, or obstruction → ↑CSF → ↑pressure.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the functions of CSF?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Protection/cushioning (buoys the brain → protects from impact)
  • buoyancy (reduces the effective weight of the brain)
  • homeostasis (stable chemical environment, removes waste)
  • diagnostic (sampled by lumbar puncture → analysis for meningitis, SAH, MS).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is hydrocephalus, and what are the obstructive and communicating types?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Hydrocephalus = accumulation of CSF with ↑ventricular size, usually with ↑pressure, from an imbalance of production/circulation/absorption (normal pressure hydrocephalus is the exception: ventriculomegaly with normal or only intermittently raised measured pressure).
  • Obstructive (non-communicating): blockage within the ventricular system (e.g. aqueduct stenosis, tumour) → CSF can't flow out.
  • Communicating: impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations (e.g. post-meningitis, post-SAH) → CSF builds up.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), its classic triad, and treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The classic triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, wobbly') — treatable with a shunt. General hydrocephalus treatment: relieve the pressure — VP shunt (drains CSF) or treat the cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the Monro-Kellie doctrine of raised intracranial pressure?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: The skull is a fixed box: it contains brain + blood + CSF in a fixed volume → if one increases (tumour, bleed, oedema, ↑CSF), the others must compensate, and once compensation fails, pressure rises steeply.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are the signs of raised ICP, including the late ominous sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Headache (worse lying down/morning)
  • vomiting
  • papilloedema (swollen optic disc)
  • reduced consciousness
  • Cushing's reflex (↑BP + bradycardia + irregular breathing — a late, ominous sign).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the herniation danger, and why is LP contraindicated with raised ICP and a mass?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: Severe raised ICP → brain herniation (coning) → brainstem compression → death; this is why LP is contraindicated when ICP is raised with a mass (removing CSF below → pressure gradient → coning).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: CSF analysis: what is the appearance and white cell picture in bacterial vs viral vs TB/fungal meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Appearance: normal clear; bacterial cloudy/turbid; viral clear; TB/fungal fibrin web.
  • White cells: normal 0-5 lymphocytes/mm³ (opening pressure 10-20 cmH₂O); bacterial ↑↑ neutrophils; viral ↑ lymphocytes; TB/fungal ↑ lymphocytes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: CSF analysis: what is the protein and glucose picture in bacterial vs viral vs TB/fungal meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Protein (normal 0.15-0.45 g/L): bacterial ↑↑; viral normal/↑; TB/fungal ↑↑.
  • Glucose (normally at least two-thirds of serum): bacterial ↓↓ (low); viral normal; TB/fungal ↓ (low).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the pattern logic for CSF analysis in meningitis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Bacterial = neutrophils, high protein, low glucose (bacteria consume it)
  • viral = lymphocytes, normal glucose
  • TB = lymphocytes, very high protein, low glucose.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are other uses of lumbar puncture (besides meningitis)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Xanthochromia (yellow CSF from broken-down blood) in subarachnoid haemorrhage
  • oligoclonal bands in MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and how is it formed?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back: A tight barrier between the blood and the brain, formed by tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte end-feet and pericytes on a shared basement membrane. It protects the brain (keeps out toxins, pathogens, large/polar molecules, and most drugs) and is selective (lets in O₂, CO₂, glucose via transporters, and lipid-soluble small molecules, which cross easily).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What is the drug-penetration principle of the BBB?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
Lipid-soluble drugs cross the BBB; water-soluble/large ones don't, unless there is a specific carrier — glucose crosses on GLUT1, and L-dopa (a polar molecule) on the large-neutral-amino-acid transporter.
  • Crosses well: lipophilic drugs (most CNS drugs, e.g. benzodiazepines, chloramphenicol).
  • Doesn't cross well: polar or large agents such as aminoglycosides and vancomycin (why you need high doses / specific agents in meningitis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: How do meningitis and L-dopa relate to the BBB?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Meningitis: inflammation disrupts the BBB → (helpfully) lets more antibiotic in, but also allows the infection/inflammation.
  • L-dopa vs dopamine for Parkinson's: dopamine can't cross the BBB, but its precursor L-dopa can (then converted in the brain) — the reason we give L-dopa, not dopamine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: What are circumventricular organs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
A few brain regions that lack a blood-brain barrier, so they can sample the blood:
  • the area postrema → senses circulating toxins → vomiting
  • and the median eminence and subfornical organ/OVLT at the margins of the hypothalamus → sense circulating hormones and osmolality.
(The hypothalamus as a whole does have a barrier.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.front: Clinical relevance: how does papilloedema arise, and why must a CNS antibiotic cross the BBB?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fo.back:
• Papilloedema: raised ICP → swollen optic disc.
  • CNS antibiotic choice: must cross the BBB (high doses; inflammation helps penetration).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is cerebral palsy (CP)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: A disorder of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive lesion of the developing brain's motor pathways, occurring antenatally, perinatally, or in early childhood (conventionally up to about 2 years).It is the commonest cause of physical disability in children.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What are the two defining concepts of CP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: (1) The brain lesion is non-progressive — a fixed, one-off injury that does not get worse. (2) The clinical picture evolves as the child develops (motor signs become more apparent over time). A truly worsening/progressive course is NOT CP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: How is CP classified, and what does the classification tell you?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
By the predominant type of motor disorder, which localises the injury:
  • Spastic → UMN (motor cortex/pyramidal tracts)
  • Dyskinetic → basal ganglia
  • Ataxic → cerebellum
  • Mixed → multiple sites

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which is the commonest type of CP, and what is its motor abnormality?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Spastic CP (~70–90%) — increased tone (spasticity) in a UMN pattern: hypertonia, brisk reflexes, clonus, and upgoing plantars, from damage to upper motor neurons.(Extensor plantars are normal under about 1 year, so they carry little weight in infants.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Dyskinetic CP — lesion site and clinical picture?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Damage to the basal ganglia / substantia nigra → dystonia and/or choreoathetosis (slow, writhing involuntary movements) and oro-motor problems (dysarthria, feeding/drooling difficulty). Classically follows kernicterus, now rare in the UK — most cases today follow term hypoxic-ischaemic injury to the basal ganglia and thalami.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Ataxic CP — lesion site and signs?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Damage to the cerebellum → incoordination and ataxia(the cerebellar signs: dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, dysarthria, hypotonia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Name the three subtypes of spastic CP by limb distribution.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Hemiplegia — one side (arm + leg)
  • Diplegia — both legs (arms mild/spared)
  • Quadriplegia — all four limbs (most severe)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which spastic CP subtype is classically associated with prematurity, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Spastic diplegia — prematurity predisposes to periventricular leukomalacia (and intraventricular haemorrhage); the periventricular white-matter tracts to the legs run closest to the ventricles, so the legs are affected more than the arms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which spastic CP subtype is most severe and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Spastic quadriplegia — all four limbs affected, and most often accompanied by seizures, severe learning disability, and feeding problems (extensive brain injury).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: At what age is the aetiology of CP most commonly acquired?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
Antenatal causes are the commonest:
  • cerebral malformation
  • congenital infection (CMV, rubella, toxoplasmosis — TORCH)
  • placental insufficiency
  • and genetic causes

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Give the classic perinatal cause of CP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (birth asphyxia); also prematurity and low birth weight.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: List postnatal causes of CP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Meningitis/encephalitis
  • head injury (including non-accidental injury)
  • and kernicterus (severe neonatal jaundice)
Note that intraventricular haemorrhage of prematurity is a perinatal, not postnatal, cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which congenital infections cause CP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: The TORCH infections — most classically CMV, rubella, and toxoplasmosis (also others).CMV is the commonest congenital infection overall.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What early motor red flag suggests hemiplegic CP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Established hand preference before 12 months of age is abnormal and suggests a hemiplegia (the child avoids the affected hand).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: List the typical presenting features of CP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Delayed motor milestones — not sitting by 8 months or not walking by 18 months (both corrected for gestation), or hand preference before 1 year, each of which warrants referral to a child development service. Also abnormal tone (hypertonia/spasticity or early hypotonia), abnormal posture/movements and asymmetry, persistent primitive reflexes with brisk reflexes (UMN signs), and feeding difficulties.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why is CP described as 'rarely isolated'? Name key comorbidities.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
CP commonly has associated problems needing MDT care:
  • epilepsy
  • learning disability
  • visual/hearing impairment
  • speech/language difficulty
  • feeding problems/GORD and unsafe swallow (aspiration is the commonest cause of death in CP)
  • constipation
  • pain (common and under-recognised)
  • hip subluxation
  • and scoliosis

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: How is CP diagnosed, and what is the role of MRI?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Diagnosis is clinical (history + examination of tone, posture, reflexes, movement pattern). MRI brain supports the diagnosis by showing the underlying lesion (e.g. periventricular leukomalacia, malformation) and helps exclude mimics — it does not make the diagnosis, and a normal MRI does not exclude CP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What must you exclude before diagnosing CP, and why?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Progressive / neurodegenerative and metabolic conditions — because CP is by definition non-progressive.A deteriorating clinical course should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What does the GMFCS grade?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: The Gross Motor Function Classification System (I-V) grades the functional severity of gross motor impairment, guiding prognosis and management (higher grade = more dependent).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: What is the overarching principle of CP management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: There is no cure (the lesion is fixed) → multidisciplinary supportive care to maximise function and comfort, and to manage spasticity and comorbidities lifelong.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Which therapy is the cornerstone of CP management, and who else is in the MDT?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
Physiotherapy (maintain range of movement and function) is the cornerstone; plus
  • OT
  • speech & language therapy (communication + feeding)
  • dietitian
  • orthotics
  • paediatric neurology
  • and social/educational support

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Outline the options for managing spasticity in CP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back:
• Oral baclofen for a sustained effect (diazepam only for rapid, short-term relief of painful spasm — it is sedating)
  • botulinum toxin A for focal spasticity
  • intrathecal baclofen for severe generalised spasticity
  • orthopaedic surgery for contractures/hip/spine
  • and selective dorsal rhizotomy for AMBULANT children with spastic diplegia (GMFCS II–III, aged 3–9, no dystonia) — not for the most severely affected child

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Name two antenatal/perinatal interventions that reduce the risk of CP.
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Magnesium sulfate given to mothers before preterm birth for fetal neuroprotection — offered between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks and considered between 30+0 and 33+6 weeks — and therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) for term babies with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.front: Why is hip surveillance important in CP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ce.back: Every child with CP enters a hip surveillance programme from about age 2 (clinical examination + pelvic X-ray), with the frequency set by GMFCS level: displacement risk rises from near zero at GMFCS I to around 90% at GMFCS V. It is painless until advanced, so surveillance allows intervention before dislocation.(Note GMFCS III children DO walk, with a hand-held aid; non-ambulant is IV–V.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.question: A 58-year-old woman describes three months of difficulty rising from a low chair and hanging washing on a line. Her strength is the same first thing in the morning as last thing at night. Sensation, tone and plantar responses are normal, reflexes are present and symmetrical, and there is no wasting or fasciculation. At which level of the motor system is the lesion most likely to be?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.explanation: Proximal, symmetrical weakness with intact sensation, normal tone and plantars, preserved reflexes and no fasciculation points to the muscle fibre itself. Distal weakness with glove-and-stocking sensory loss indicates peripheral nerve; wasting with fasciculation indicates the anterior horn cell; increased tone with an extensor plantar indicates the corticospinal tract; junctional disease fluctuates through the day.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.question: A 45-year-old man has proximal muscle weakness and a purple discolouration of his eyelids, with scaly plaques over his knuckles. Which diagnosis is most likely?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.explanation: The heliotrope rash (violaceous eyelids) and Gottron's papules (scaly plaques over the MCP and PIP joints) are the characteristic skin signs of dermatomyositis; a shawl-distribution rash and photosensitivity may also be present. Lupus causes a photosensitive facial rash but classically spares the knuckles.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__My.question: A 60-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with dermatomyositis and treatment has been started by the rheumatology team. Which additional action is most important?
options: Monitor creatine kinase to assess treatment response
Refer for physiotherapy and graded exercise
