Timing balances recurrence against haemorrhagic transformation: after a TIA, start immediately once imaging excludes a bleed; after a mild stroke, within about 5 days; after a moderate-to-severe stroke, from about 5–14 days.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.question: Which lipid-lowering therapy is recommended for secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke?
options: A low-intensity statin, titrated up slowly over several months
No statin, as lipid lowering is of no benefit after a stroke
A fibrate, which is preferred to a statin in cerebrovascular disease
A high-intensity statin, started after about 48 hours
Ezetimibe alone, with a statin added only if the LDL stays high
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.answer: A high-intensity statin, started after about 48 hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.explanation: A high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) is started after about 48 hours as part of secondary prevention.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.question: A patient with a recent anterior circulation ischaemic stroke is found to have a 75% stenosis of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery. Which intervention is indicated?
options: Carotid endarterectomy, referred urgently and aimed for within 14 days
Bilateral carotid stenting, regardless of which side is symptomatic
Best medical therapy alone, with no surgical referral at any point
Immediate thrombolysis, repeated at the time of the operation
Elective review in twelve months with a repeat carotid duplex
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.answer: Carotid endarterectomy, referred urgently and aimed for within 14 days
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.explanation: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50–99% on the relevant side is an indication for carotid endarterectomy, alongside best medical treatment. The benefit falls away with delay, so referral is urgent and surgery is aimed for within 14 days of the event.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.question: Which VTE prophylaxis is appropriate in an immobile acute stroke patient?
options: Early low-molecular-weight heparin for every immobile patient
Aspirin 300 mg daily, which doubles as VTE prophylaxis here
Warfarin, loaded on admission and continued for three months
Intermittent pneumatic compression of the legs
Graduated compression stockings applied on admission
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.answer: Intermittent pneumatic compression of the legs
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.explanation: Intermittent pneumatic compression is used for VTE prophylaxis in immobile acute stroke patients. Early heparin is avoided because of bleeding and haemorrhagic transformation risk, and graduated compression stockings are not effective in stroke.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.question: Which statement about the definitions of stroke and TIA is correct?
options: Stroke lasts >24h or is fatal; a TIA is transient with no infarction
A stroke resolves within 24 hours whereas a TIA lasts much longer
Both stroke and TIA always show an infarct on diffusion-weighted MRI
A TIA is by definition haemorrhagic and a stroke is always ischaemic
The two are distinguished only by the severity of the initial deficit
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.answer: Stroke lasts >24h or is fatal; a TIA is transient with no infarction
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__St.explanation: Stroke is a vascular deficit lasting more than 24 hours (or leading to death); a TIA is transient focal ischaemia without infarction — the tissue-based definition, meaning no infarct on imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Following a stab wound to the back, a patient has weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception on the same side as the injury, with loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side. Which cord syndrome is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Cord hemisection gives ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss and contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature) loss — Brown-Séquard syndrome, classically from penetrating injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: After an anterior spinal artery infarct, a patient loses motor function and pain/temperature sensation but retains vibration and proprioception. Which syndrome is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Anterior cord syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory) affects the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts but spares the dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception preserved).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: An older patient with cervical spondylosis falls with neck hyperextension and develops weakness that is worse in the arms than the legs, with a 'cape' distribution of sensory loss. Which syndrome is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Central cord syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Central cord syndrome causes upper > lower limb weakness with a cape-like sensory loss, typically from hyperextension in cervical spondylosis (or a syrinx).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: How does a lesion above L1 differ from a cauda equina lesion on examination?
options: Both give lower motor neurone signs with flaccid, areflexic weakness
Both give upgoing plantars and pathologically brisk lower limb reflexes
A cord lesion gives saddle anaesthesia; cauda equina gives a sensory level
A lesion above L1 gives UMN signs and a sensory level; cauda equina gives LMN signs
Neither affects bladder function until the very late stages of the illness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: A lesion above L1 gives UMN signs and a sensory level; cauda equina gives LMN signs
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The cord ends ~L1/L2; lesions above produce UMN signs and a sensory level, while cauda equina (below L1) produces LMN signs with saddle anaesthesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which tract, when damaged in the cord, causes loss of pain and temperature on the OPPOSITE side of the body below the lesion?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Spinothalamic tract
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The spinothalamic tract carries pain/temperature and (having crossed near its entry) its damage causes contralateral loss below the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency develops loss of vibration/proprioception with a sensory (gait) ataxia. Which cord pattern does this represent?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Dorsal column dysfunction
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) affects the dorsal columns, causing loss of vibration/proprioception and sensory ataxia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A 65-year-old man with known prostate cancer has 3 weeks of worsening thoracic back pain (worse lying flat and at night) and now has progressive leg weakness with brisk reflexes and a sensory level at the umbilicus. What is the diagnosis and the immediate investigation?
options: Metastatic spinal cord compression; urgent whole-spine MRI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Metastatic spinal cord compression; urgent whole-spine MRI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: New/progressive back pain with UMN leg signs and a sensory level in a cancer patient is metastatic spinal cord compression — arrange an urgent whole-spine MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: How does spinal cord compression differ from cauda equina syndrome on examination?
options: Cord compression gives LMN signs with saddle anaesthesia and areflexia
Both give flaccid areflexia with preserved sensation below the lesion
Cord compression gives UMN signs and a sensory level; cauda equina LMN signs
Cord compression causes early incontinence whereas cauda equina causes it late
Neither affects the bladder until months after the deficit has become fixed
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Cord compression gives UMN signs and a sensory level; cauda equina LMN signs
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Cord compression (above L1) produces UMN signs and a sensory level; cauda equina (below L1) produces LMN signs with saddle anaesthesia and early bladder/bowel involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the immediate medical management once MSCC is suspected?
options: Withhold all treatment until a tissue biopsy has been obtained
Start systemic chemotherapy immediately, before any imaging
Oral simple analgesia only, with review in the morning
Urgent lumbar puncture to obtain CSF for cytology
Dexamethasone 16 mg as soon as possible, with gastroprotection
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Dexamethasone 16 mg as soon as possible, with gastroprotection
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: For anyone with neurological symptoms or signs, offer 16 mg of oral dexamethasone (or the equivalent parenteral dose) as soon as possible, then 16 mg daily awaiting surgery or radiotherapy. Note where the lymphoma caveat actually applies: it is the patient with radiologically suspected lymphoma or myeloma and NO neurology in whom you seek haematology advice before starting steroids, because steroids can render the biopsy non-diagnostic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: In a patient with suspected cord compression, when should high-dose steroids be withheld?
options: If the patient has prostate cancer
If lymphoma is suspected (steroids can mask the diagnosis)
If there is any back pain
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: If lymphoma is suspected (steroids can mask the diagnosis)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: If lymphoma is suspected, steroids are withheld because they can obscure the histological diagnosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Why should the WHOLE spine be imaged in suspected cord compression, not just the symptomatic level?
options: Because the symptomatic level is never involved
Because multiple levels of compression are common
Because MRI cannot target one level
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Because multiple levels of compression are common
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Multiple levels of metastatic compression are common, so the whole spine is imaged (CT with three-plane reconstruction if MRI is contraindicated).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: According to NICE, within what timeframe should a whole-spine MRI be performed for spinal pain suggestive of metastases WITH neurology suggestive of MSCC?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Within 24 hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: NICE recommends whole-spine MRI within 24 hours when there is spinal pain suggestive of metastases with neurology suggestive of MSCC (within 1 week if pain without neurology).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the first-line definitive treatment for MSCC in a fit patient with a good prognosis?
options: Decompressive surgery ± stabilisation, followed by radiotherapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Decompressive surgery ± stabilisation, followed by radiotherapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: In suitable patients, surgery (decompression ± stabilisation) followed by radiotherapy is first-line; radiotherapy alone is used if surgery is unsuitable.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which factor most strongly predicts neurological recovery after treatment of cord compression?
options: The patient's chronological age, independent of any other factor
The histological type of the primary tumour, taken on its own
The serum calcium at the time the compression is diagnosed
The pre-treatment neurological status when treatment begins
The choice of anaesthetic technique used for the decompression
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: The pre-treatment neurological status when treatment begins
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Pre-treatment function is the key prognostic factor — patients with no motor function for over 48 hours are unlikely to regain useful function, so early treatment is vital.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: An older man has progressive clumsiness of the hands, an unsteady gait and brisk leg reflexes; flicking his middle finger causes the other fingers to twitch (Hoffman's sign). MRI shows cervical cord compression from spondylosis. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Degenerative cervical myelopathy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Bilateral UMN signs, clumsy hands, gait disturbance and a positive Hoffman's sign with cervical cord compression indicate degenerative cervical myelopathy — the commonest cause of cord dysfunction in older adults.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which set of primary cancers most commonly cause metastatic spinal cord compression?
options: Breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid and myeloma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Breast, lung, prostate, renal, thyroid and myeloma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: MSCC is most commonly caused by breast, lung, prostate, renal and thyroid cancers and myeloma (vertebral metastases extending into the canal).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which feature of back pain is a red flag suggesting a sinister cause such as cord compression?
options: Pain worse on lying down and at night, and on coughing/straining
Pain of a few hours' duration after lifting
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Pain worse on lying down and at night, and on coughing/straining
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Pain worse on lying down, at night and on coughing/straining/Valsalva is a red flag; thoracic/band-like pain and new pain in a cancer patient are especially concerning for MSCC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A thoracic-level cord compression typically produces which pattern?
options: Paraparesis (leg weakness) with a trunk sensory level
Weakness worse in the arms than the legs
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Paraparesis (leg weakness) with a trunk sensory level
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A thoracic lesion affects the legs (paraparesis) with a sensory level on the trunk; a cervical lesion would involve the arms and legs (tetraparesis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with a traumatic cord injury has preserved perianal sensation and can voluntarily squeeze the anal sphincter on PR examination. What does this indicate?
options: A complete injury with poor prognosis
An incomplete injury (sacral sparing) with a better prognosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: An incomplete injury (sacral sparing) with a better prognosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Sacral sparing (perianal sensation/voluntary anal contraction) indicates an incomplete injury, which carries a better prognosis — always examine the perineum/PR.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient sustains a high cervical spinal cord injury above C4 and cannot breathe. Which structure's innervation is lost, and what is required?
options: The intercostals only; oxygen by mask
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: The diaphragm (C3,4,5); immediate ventilatory support
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: 'C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive' — injuries above this level paralyse the diaphragm, causing respiratory failure and requiring ventilation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: After a penetrating injury, a patient has ipsilateral leg weakness and loss of vibration/proprioception, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature. Which syndrome is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome gives ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss and contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature) loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: An elderly man with cervical spondylosis falls, hyperextending his neck, and develops weakness that is worse in the arms than the legs. Which incomplete cord syndrome is this?
options: Central cord syndrome ('man in a barrel')
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Central cord syndrome ('man in a barrel')
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Central cord syndrome — the commonest incomplete syndrome — causes arms > legs weakness ('man in a barrel'), typically from hyperextension on a spondylotic spine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient has an anterior cord syndrome. Which sensory modality is characteristically PRESERVED?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns spared)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Anterior cord syndrome spares the dorsal columns, so vibration and proprioception are preserved while motor and pain/temperature are lost.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Immediately after a spinal cord injury, a patient has flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes below the lesion, which over the following weeks becomes spastic with brisk reflexes. What explains the initial phase?
options: Spinal shock (transient loss of cord function)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Spinal shock (transient loss of cord function)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Spinal shock is a transient loss of all cord function below the lesion (flaccid areflexia) that resolves over days–weeks, after which UMN (spastic) signs emerge.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A trauma patient with a high thoracic cord injury is hypotensive with a heart rate of 50 and warm peripheries. Which type of shock is this, and what is the key clue?
options: Neurogenic shock; hypotension WITH bradycardia (and warm peripheries)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Neurogenic shock; hypotension WITH bradycardia (and warm peripheries)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone from an injury above T6) causes hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries — the bradycardia distinguishes it from hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with a spinal cord injury at T4 develops a sudden pounding headache, flushing and sweating of the face, and a blood pressure of 210/120, having not passed urine for hours. What is the diagnosis and first action?
options: Neurogenic shock; give IV fluids and consider a vasopressor
A migraine with autonomic features; give a triptan and rest
A panic attack driven by anxiety; reassure and observe him
Autonomic dysreflexia; find and remove the trigger, treat the BP
Spinal shock returning; lie him flat and monitor observations
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Autonomic dysreflexia; find and remove the trigger, treat the BP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia (injury ≥T6) is triggered by a noxious stimulus below the lesion (commonly a full/blocked bladder); the priority is to remove the trigger and control the dangerous hypertension (sit up, antihypertensives).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which is the commonest trigger of autonomic dysreflexia in a patient with a high spinal cord injury?
options: Urinary retention (a full or blocked bladder/catheter)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Urinary retention (a full or blocked bladder/catheter)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Urinary retention (full bladder/blocked catheter) is the commonest trigger; faecal impaction, pressure sores and ingrown nails are others.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: The ASIA scale is used in spinal cord injury. What does it classify?
options: The patient's level of consciousness after the initial injury
The blood-pressure response to fluid resuscitation on arrival
Severity from A (complete) to E (normal), by motor and sensory testing
The fracture pattern seen on the CT of the injured spinal segment
The rehabilitation potential alone, independent of the examination
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Severity from A (complete) to E (normal), by motor and sensory testing
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The ASIA impairment scale grades cord injury from A (complete) to E (normal) using standardised motor and sensory examination.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the correct immediate approach to a suspected traumatic spinal cord injury?
options: Sit the patient up and mobilise them early to prevent complications
Give immediate high-dose methylprednisolone to every injured patient
Lumbar puncture, to measure the CSF opening pressure below the lesion
ABCDE with airway and C-spine control, ventilating a high cervical injury
Discharge with advice if the patient is able to move their toes on request
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: ABCDE with airway and C-spine control, ventilating a high cervical injury
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Management begins with manual in-line stabilisation and ABCDE — head blocks and tape, ideally on a vacuum mattress; a long spinal board is an extrication device only, defining level/completeness and preventing secondary injury; imaging (CT + MRI) and surgery follow as indicated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the current recommendation regarding high-dose corticosteroids in acute traumatic spinal cord injury?
options: They are given routinely to every patient within 8 hours of injury
They are not given in acute traumatic spinal cord injury
They reverse the deficit if given within the first 24 hours
They are given only if the patient is also hypertensive
They replace surgical decompression in unstable injuries
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: They are not given in acute traumatic spinal cord injury
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: High-dose steroids are not given in acute traumatic spinal cord injury. Care focuses on immobilisation, preventing secondary injury by avoiding hypotension and hypoxia, surgery where indicated, and MDT rehabilitation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which statement correctly defines a complete versus incomplete spinal cord injury?
options: Complete means some sacral sparing remains; incomplete means none at all
Both types preserve some degree of sacral motor and sensory function
Incomplete injuries consistently carry the worse prognosis of the two
Complete = no sacral sparing at all; incomplete = some preserved function
Completeness is determined by the fracture pattern rather than examination
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Complete = no sacral sparing at all; incomplete = some preserved function
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A complete injury has total motor/sensory loss below the level with no sacral sparing (poor prognosis); an incomplete injury preserves some function, indicated by sacral sparing (better prognosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A 40-year-old with 2 days of severe low back pain now has bilateral leg pain, numbness when wiping after opening his bowels, difficulty passing urine, and reduced anal tone on PR. What is the diagnosis and immediate investigation?
options: Cauda equina syndrome; emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Cauda equina syndrome; emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Bilateral sciatica with saddle anaesthesia, urinary difficulty and reduced anal tone is cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency needing emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: How does cauda equina syndrome differ from cord compression on examination?
options: CES gives UMN signs with a sensory level and pathologically brisk reflexes
Both give upgoing plantars with spasticity and increased tone in the legs
CES gives LMN signs, saddle anaesthesia and early bladder/bowel involvement
CES gives a sensory level whereas cord compression gives saddle anaesthesia
Neither condition affects bladder or bowel function at any stage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: CES gives LMN signs, saddle anaesthesia and early bladder/bowel involvement
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: CES (below L1) is a root-level LMN problem with saddle anaesthesia and early bladder/bowel dysfunction; cord compression (above L1) gives UMN signs with a sensory level.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the commonest cause of cauda equina syndrome?
options: A large central lumbar disc herniation (L4/5 or L5/S1)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: A large central lumbar disc herniation (L4/5 or L5/S1)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A large central lumbar disc herniation (typically L4/5 or L5/S1) is the commonest cause of CES.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the investigation of choice for suspected cauda equina syndrome?
options: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine confirms the compression, level and cause and must not be delayed; a bladder scan provides objective evidence of retention.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the definitive treatment for cauda equina syndrome from a disc?
options: A reducing course of high-dose oral corticosteroids over two weeks
Bed rest with analgesia and review in the fracture clinic
Outpatient physiotherapy with a graded mobilisation programme
Emergency surgical decompression, as soon as it can be done
Long-term urethral catheterisation without surgical intervention
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Emergency surgical decompression, as soon as it can be done
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: CES requires emergency surgical decompression; the sooner it is done, the better the outcome for bladder/bowel and leg function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Why is early surgery emphasised in cauda equina syndrome?
options: Because outcomes depend on decompressing before retention is established
To reduce the length of the hospital stay and free up the surgical bed
Because operating becomes technically impossible once symptoms begin
Because corticosteroids are more effective once the disc is decompressed
Because the prolapsed disc will otherwise resolve spontaneously in time
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Because outcomes depend on decompressing before retention is established
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Recovery of bladder/bowel and sexual function depends on early decompression; once painless retention (CES-R) is established, recovery is much less likely.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: At what level does the spinal cord end, and what lies below it?
options: At S1, with the cord itself continuing down to the sacral hiatus
At T12, below which lies the lower end of the brainstem
At about L1; below it lie the cauda equina nerve roots
At L5, below which the canal contains only bone and ligament
At C7, below which lies the lower part of the brachial plexus
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: At about L1; below it lie the cauda equina nerve roots
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The cord ends at ~L1 (conus medullaris); below this the canal contains the lumbosacral nerve roots (the cauda equina).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which finding should trigger emergency imaging in suspected cauda equina syndrome?
options: Established painless urinary retention with a palpable bladder
Loss of the awareness of bladder filling or the desire to void
A unilateral sciatica that has been present for several weeks
Reduced ankle reflexes with normal saddle sensation on testing
Low back pain that is worse on standing and eased by sitting
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Loss of the awareness of bladder filling or the desire to void
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The early neurogenic bladder symptoms are what should trigger the scan — loss of awareness of the bladder filling, loss of the desire to void, altered sensation of urine passing, a poor stream or needing to strain — together with altered saddle sensation, bilateral leg symptoms and sexual dysfunction. Established retention is a LATE finding: by then much of the damage is done. Note also that normal anal tone and a normal post-void residual do not exclude CES.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: When assessing a patient with back pain for cauda equina, what is the best way to elicit saddle anaesthesia in the history?
options: Ask about pain radiating from the back down towards the shoulder
Ask whether wiping after opening the bowels feels normal
Ask about early morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Ask about calf pain on walking that is relieved by standing still
Ask about restriction of neck movement in all three planes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Ask whether wiping after opening the bowels feels normal
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Asking about perineal sensation — e.g. whether wiping feels normal — screens for saddle anaesthesia, a key red flag; a PR assesses anal tone.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A lesion precisely at the conus medullaris (L1) produces which pattern?
options: Pure LMN signs with no sphincter involvement
A mixed UMN/LMN picture (the transition zone)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: A mixed UMN/LMN picture (the transition zone)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The conus medullaris (L1) is the transition zone, so a lesion there gives a mixed UMN/LMN picture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient has early CES with altered urinary sensation but is still passing urine (CES-I), rather than established painless retention (CES-R). What is the significance?
options: CES-I is the window to intervene, with a far better prognosis
CES-I carries a distinctly worse prognosis than established CES-R
There is no meaningful difference in prognosis between the two stages
CES-I never requires surgery and can be managed with analgesia alone
CES-R should be managed conservatively once retention has developed
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: CES-I is the window to intervene, with a far better prognosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: CES-I (incomplete, altered sensation) is the window to operate; once CES-R (retention) is established the prognosis is worse — so decompress early.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A 55-year-old vegan has months of distal tingling in the legs, an unsteady gait, and difficulty with balance in the dark. Examination shows loss of vibration and proprioception, absent ankle jerks, but brisk knee jerks and upgoing plantars. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (B12 deficiency)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (B12 deficiency)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Dorsal-column sensory loss with the mixed UMN/LMN paradox (absent ankle jerks + upgoing plantars) in an at-risk patient is subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which three tracts are affected in subacute combined degeneration of the cord?
options: Dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal and spinocerebellar tracts
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal and spinocerebellar tracts
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: SACD affects the dorsal columns (sensory/proprioception), lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN) and spinocerebellar tracts (ataxia) — hence the 'combined' picture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What explains the paradox of absent ankle jerks together with upgoing plantars in SACD?
options: A single cord lesion producing mixed signs at different spinal levels
B12 deficiency damages peripheral nerves AND the corticospinal tracts
It indicates two entirely separate and unrelated coexisting diseases
It is an artefact of examination technique rather than a real finding
This combination does not in fact occur and should prompt a rethink
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: B12 deficiency damages peripheral nerves AND the corticospinal tracts
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: B12 deficiency produces both a peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle jerks — LMN) and corticospinal degeneration (upgoing plantars, brisk knee jerks — UMN), giving the mixed picture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A 22-year-old who regularly inhales 'laughing gas' develops a myelopathy with a normal-range B12. What is the mechanism?
options: A direct toxic effect on the cord that has nothing to do with B12
An opportunistic viral infection of the dorsal columns and tracts
Simple intoxication, which leaves no lasting neurological deficit
Nitrous oxide inactivates B12, precipitating SACD despite normal stores
An excess of dietary folate driving red-cell production and depletion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Nitrous oxide inactivates B12, precipitating SACD despite normal stores
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Nitrous oxide inactivates B12 by oxidising the cobalt, so it can cause SACD even when the measured B12 is normal — increasingly seen in young recreational users.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with macrocytic anaemia is found to be B12 and folate deficient. Why must B12 be replaced before (or with) folate?
options: Folate is directly toxic to the spinal cord in B12-deficient patients
Folate first drives red-cell production, consuming the low B12 stores
B12 competitively blocks the absorption of folate from the small bowel
Folate reliably causes a severe haemolysis in B12-deficient patients
There is no such interaction; the order of replacement does not matter
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Folate first drives red-cell production, consuming the low B12 stores
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Correcting folate before B12 can precipitate/worsen subacute combined degeneration, so B12 is always replaced first (or together, prioritising B12).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the key initial investigation in suspected SACD, and which markers help if it is borderline?
options: Serum copper first, followed by ferritin if that is equivocal
Serum calcium first, followed by parathyroid hormone if abnormal
Serum B12; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine if it is borderline
CRP first, followed by an ESR if the inflammatory markers are raised
Serum folate alone, since folate and B12 deficiency present alike
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Serum B12; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine if it is borderline
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Serum B12 is the key test; raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive markers when the B12 level is borderline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with SACD is found to have anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies. What is the underlying cause?
options: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Anti-intrinsic factor/anti-parietal cell antibodies indicate pernicious anaemia, the commonest cause of B12 deficiency (needing lifelong B12).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the appropriate management of subacute combined degeneration?
options: Urgent IM B12 (hydroxocobalamin) given BEFORE folate, and treat the cause
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Urgent IM B12 (hydroxocobalamin) given BEFORE folate, and treat the cause
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: SACD is treated with urgent IM B12 replacement (before folate) and treatment of the cause; early treatment improves recovery, delayed treatment leaves permanent deficits.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which examination sign reflects the loss of proprioception in SACD?
options: A positive Romberg's sign (falls on eye closure)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: A positive Romberg's sign (falls on eye closure)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A positive Romberg's sign — instability/falling when the eyes are closed — reflects the proprioceptive (dorsal column) loss of SACD.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient has a myelopathy clinically indistinguishable from SACD but a normal B12. Which mimic should be considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Copper deficiency (an almost identical myelopathy)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Copper deficiency causes an almost identical myelopathy and should be considered when the picture fits SACD but B12 is normal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Regarding the relationship between the anaemia and neurology of B12 deficiency, which statement is correct?
options: Neurology only occurs once severe anaemia is present
Anaemia always precedes any neurology by years
The neurological features can occur WITHOUT anaemia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: The neurological features can occur WITHOUT anaemia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: The neurological manifestations of B12 deficiency (SACD) can occur without anaemia, so a normal Hb does not exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Why is prompt treatment emphasised in subacute combined degeneration?
options: Because the condition is contagious and needs isolation of contacts
Because it resolves spontaneously if simply left alone for a while
Because treatment only becomes effective after about six months
Because early replacement allows recovery; delay leaves deficits
Because it always reverses completely, whatever the delay involved
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Because early replacement allows recovery; delay leaves deficits
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: SACD is reversible if treated early but causes permanent deficits if treatment is delayed — hence urgent B12 replacement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A 30-year-old has painless burns on both hands and, on examination, loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and arms ('cape' distribution) but preserved light touch, vibration and proprioception. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Syringomyelia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature lost, dorsal-column modalities preserved) in a cape distribution, with painless burns, is the hallmark of syringomyelia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Why does syringomyelia cause loss of pain and temperature first, sparing light touch and proprioception?
options: The dorsal columns decussate in the very centre of the cord and go first
The spinothalamic tract runs peripherally and is compressed from outside
Pain fibres are always the last modality to be affected by any lesion
The syrinx destroys the decussating fibres in the central commissure first
It affects only the peripheral nerves rather than the cord itself at all
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: The syrinx destroys the decussating fibres in the central commissure first
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A central syrinx first destroys the crossing spinothalamic fibres (pain/temperature) in the anterior commissure; the dorsal columns run peripherally and are spared early — hence the dissociation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: In syringomyelia, which sensory modalities are characteristically LOST, and which are PRESERVED early?
options: Pain and temperature lost; light touch, vibration and proprioception preserved early
Vibration and proprioception lost; pain/temperature preserved
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Pain and temperature lost; light touch, vibration and proprioception preserved early
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a dissociated loss — pain and temperature are lost (spinothalamic), while light touch, vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns) are preserved early.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Which condition is the commonest association with syringomyelia, prompting brain imaging?
options: A Chiari I malformation (low cerebellar tonsils)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: A Chiari I malformation (low cerebellar tonsils)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A Chiari I malformation is the classic association (it disrupts CSF flow), so the brain/craniocervical junction is always imaged in syringomyelia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A young patient repeatedly burns their fingers on hot objects without feeling it. Which underlying spinal cord problem does this suggest?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Syringomyelia (loss of pain/temperature sensation)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Painless burns/injuries reflect loss of pain and temperature sensation — the classic clue to syringomyelia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A patient with a cervical syrinx develops ptosis, a small pupil and reduced sweating on one side of the face. What is this, and why does it occur?
options: Horner's syndrome — the syrinx involves the T1 sympathetic outflow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Horner's syndrome — the syrinx involves the T1 sympathetic outflow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: A cervical syrinx can involve the sympathetic fibres (T1), producing Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: As a syrinx expands to involve the corticospinal tracts, which sign develops?
options: Spastic weakness (especially of the legs) with upgoing plantars
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Spastic weakness (especially of the legs) with upgoing plantars
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Corticospinal tract involvement produces UMN signs — spastic weakness (especially legs) with upgoing plantars — as the syrinx enlarges.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: What is the investigation of choice for syringomyelia?
options: Full spine MRI, plus brain MRI to exclude a Chiari malformation
Nerve conduction studies with electromyography of the affected limbs
Plain spinal radiographs in two planes of the whole vertebral column
Lumbar puncture, measuring the opening pressure and CSF protein
CT of the abdomen and pelvis to look for an underlying malignancy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Full spine MRI, plus brain MRI to exclude a Chiari malformation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Full spine MRI with contrast visualises the syrinx and excludes a tumour/tethered cord; brain MRI excludes a Chiari malformation at the craniocervical junction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A symptomatic syrinx is found to be associated with a Chiari malformation. What is the appropriate directed management?
options: Long-term opioid analgesia alone, with no surgical intervention
Amputation of any insensate digits to prevent further injury
Foramen magnum decompression, to restore CSF flow
Lumbar puncture, repeated as needed to drain the syrinx cavity
Reassurance and discharge, since a syrinx does not progress
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Foramen magnum decompression, to restore CSF flow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Treatment is directed at the cause — foramen magnum decompression of the Chiari restores CSF flow and can collapse the syrinx; a persistent/symptomatic syrinx may be shunted.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: A syrinx extends upward into the medulla, causing tongue wasting, nystagmus and other cranial nerve signs. What is this called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Syringobulbia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Extension of a syrinx into the brainstem (medulla) is syringobulbia, producing cranial nerve signs, tongue wasting and nystagmus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: How does the sensory loss of syringomyelia differ from that of subacute combined degeneration or tabes dorsalis?
options: The two patterns are identical and cannot be distinguished clinically
Syringomyelia loses pain and temperature; SACD loses the dorsal columns
Syringomyelia loses vibration and proprioception with preserved pain
SACD and tabes dorsalis both lose pain and temperature symmetrically
Neither condition produces any demonstrable sensory abnormality at all
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Syringomyelia loses pain and temperature; SACD loses the dorsal columns
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Syringomyelia (central) loses pain/temperature with dorsal columns spared early; SACD and tabes dorsalis affect the dorsal columns (loss of vibration/proprioception).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.question: Besides treating the cause, what supportive measures are important in syringomyelia?
options: High-dose corticosteroids continued indefinitely to shrink the syrinx
Strict bed rest with spinal precautions until the cavity has resolved
Regular therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce cord venous congestion
Neuropathic pain control, physiotherapy and protecting insensate skin
No follow-up is required once the underlying cause has been treated
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.answer: Neuropathic pain control, physiotherapy and protecting insensate skin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Sp.explanation: Supportive care matters: neuropathic pain management, physiotherapy, and protecting insensate skin and joints — patients burn themselves without noticing and can develop Charcot joints — with serial MRI monitoring.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: A 45-year-old woman describes an uncontrollable urge to move her legs, with a crawling sensation, that comes on when she sits down in the evening and at night, and is relieved by getting up and walking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: The 'URGE' pattern — urge to move, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement — is diagnostic of restless legs syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: Which is the key investigation in a patient with restless legs syndrome?
options: Nerve conduction studies of the lower limbs
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Ferritin is the key test. Note it is not simply used to 'exclude iron deficiency': in RLS the action threshold is higher, so replace iron if ferritin is 75 micrograms/L or below, or transferrin saturation is under 20%, even when the full blood count is normal — and then find out why the iron is low.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: What is the pathophysiological link that explains why iron deficiency causes RLS and dopamine agonists treat it?
options: Dopamine acts by storing iron within neurones, so low dopamine depletes brain iron
Iron directly blocks transmission at the neuromuscular junction of the leg muscles
Iron deficiency causes demyelination of the peripheral nerves supplying the legs
Iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, so low brain iron impairs dopamine
Iron deficiency raises central dopamine excessively, over-driving the motor pathways
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: Iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, so low brain iron impairs dopamine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase in dopamine synthesis; low brain iron impairs dopaminergic function — hence iron deficiency causes RLS and dopamine agonists help.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: How does the timing of symptoms in RLS differ from vascular claudication?
options: Both are relieved by rest, so the history cannot separate them at the bedside
Both are worse on exertion and settle when the patient stops to rest a while
RLS is worse at rest and relieved by movement; claudication is the reverse
RLS is only ever exertional, coming on after a fixed claudication distance
They are clinically indistinguishable and need arterial duplex to separate
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: RLS is worse at rest and relieved by movement; claudication is the reverse
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: RLS is relieved by movement and worse at rest — the opposite of vascular claudication, which is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: Which of the following is a recognised secondary cause of restless legs syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Secondary RLS is associated with iron deficiency, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease/uraemia and peripheral neuropathy, and with drugs (antidepressants including mirtazapine and SSRIs, antipsychotics, antihistamines and metoclopramide).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: A patient's restless legs syndrome worsened after starting a new medication. Which class is most likely responsible?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines and dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide) can worsen RLS and should be reviewed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: A patient with RLS is found to have a low ferritin. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Treat the iron deficiency with iron replacement (which can resolve the RLS)
Start a dopamine agonist and ignore the ferritin
Refer for polysomnography before any treatment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: Treat the iron deficiency with iron replacement (which can resolve the RLS)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Iron replacement is the first move when the ferritin is low — it can resolve the RLS outright. Replace if ferritin is 75 micrograms/L or below or transferrin saturation is under 20%, even with a normal FBC, and investigate why the iron is low.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: A patient on long-term pramipexole for RLS reports that symptoms now start earlier in the day, are more intense and have spread to the arms. What has most likely happened?
options: Augmentation — a paradoxical worsening with long-term dopamine agonists
Simple tolerance requiring a higher dose indefinitely
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: Augmentation — a paradoxical worsening with long-term dopamine agonists
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: This is augmentation — a paradoxical worsening with long-term dopamine agonists, in which symptoms start earlier, intensify and spread. Do NOT increase the dose: escalation drives it. Reduce and withdraw the dopamine agonist slowly with specialist advice and switch to an alpha-2-delta ligand.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: Because of augmentation, which drug class does NICE now recommend first-line for troublesome RLS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Because long-term dopamine agonists cause augmentation and impulse-control disorders, NICE now recommends an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentin or pregabalin) first-line and says dopamine agonists should not be used first-line. Both gabapentinoids are off-label for RLS and are Schedule 3 controlled drugs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: A partner reports that a patient with RLS makes repetitive jerking leg movements during sleep. What is this associated phenomenon called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS) — repetitive leg jerks in sleep often noticed by the partner — are commonly associated with RLS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: How does RLS differ from drug-induced akathisia?
options: Akathisia is confined to the legs and follows a clear circadian pattern
They are the same condition under two different names
Akathisia occurs only in patients who have never taken medication
RLS is leg-focused and evening-worse; akathisia is whole-body with no circadian pattern
Akathisia is characteristically relieved by sitting still and resting
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: RLS is leg-focused and evening-worse; akathisia is whole-body with no circadian pattern
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: RLS is leg-focused, rest-related and evening/night-worse. Akathisia is a generalised inner restlessness following an antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or an SSRI, with no circadian pattern. Note that akathisia is ALSO worse sitting still and eased by movement, so relief by movement does not separate them.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.question: Which feature is most essential to the diagnosis of restless legs syndrome?
options: Objective sensory loss on examination of the feet and lower legs
Relief of the urge and sensations by movement, with worsening at rest
Absent ankle reflexes bilaterally on examination with a tendon hammer
Claudication pain in the calves coming on after a fixed walking distance
A raised serum creatine kinase reflecting the repetitive leg movements
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.answer: Relief of the urge and sensations by movement, with worsening at rest
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Re.explanation: Relief by movement (with worsening at rest) is the defining feature that separates RLS from other leg complaints.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: According to the Monro-Kellie doctrine, the rigid skull contains three components in equilibrium. Which are they?
options: Grey matter, white matter and CSF
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states the fixed skull holds brain (~1400 mL) + CSF (~150 mL) + blood (~150 mL); a rise in one must be offset by a fall in another or ICP rises.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which equation defines cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: CPP = MAP − ICP; as ICP rises, CPP falls, causing cerebral ischaemia (and driving the Cushing's response).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient has headaches worst on waking and when bending over, vomiting without nausea, and bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy. What do these features indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: A morning/positional headache with vomiting (without nausea) and papilloedema is the classic syndrome of raised intracranial pressure.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: What is the mechanism of papilloedema in raised intracranial pressure?
options: Direct pressure of the raised CSF on the retinal surface itself
Occlusion of the central retinal artery by the raised pressure
Demyelination of the optic nerve behind the lamina cribrosa
A secondary rise in intraocular pressure compressing the disc
Raised CSF pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Raised CSF pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheath
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The optic nerve sheath is continuous with the subarachnoid space, so raised CSF pressure is transmitted along it, making the disc swell (papilloedema).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient with raised ICP develops horizontal diplopia due to a sixth-nerve palsy. How should this be interpreted?
options: It precisely localises the lesion to the pons
It is a false localising sign of raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: It is a false localising sign of raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: A CN VI palsy is a false localising sign of raised ICP, due to the abducens nerve's long, vulnerable intracranial course.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A head-injured patient becomes hypertensive with a widened pulse pressure, bradycardic and develops irregular breathing. What does this triad signify?
options: Cushing's triad — critically raised ICP with impending herniation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Cushing's triad — critically raised ICP with impending herniation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Cushing's triad (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing) is a pre-terminal sign of dangerously raised ICP with impending herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Why does the blood pressure rise (with a reflex bradycardia) as ICP becomes critically high?
options: MAP must rise to preserve cerebral perfusion; that triggers bradycardia
Blood loss from the injury provokes a compensatory pressor response
An adrenaline surge from the pain raises the pressure and slows the heart
Dehydration concentrates catecholamines, raising the blood pressure
Hypoxia alone drives both the hypertension and the reflex bradycardia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: MAP must rise to preserve cerebral perfusion; that triggers bradycardia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: As ICP rises, MAP must increase to preserve CPP; the induced hypertension triggers a reflex bradycardia — the basis of Cushing's reflex.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A deteriorating patient develops a fixed, dilated pupil with a 'down-and-out' eye on one side. Which herniation and nerve are involved?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Uncal herniation compresses the ipsilateral third cranial nerve, producing a fixed dilated pupil and a 'down-and-out' eye — a neurosurgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which herniation causes brainstem compression through the foramen magnum, leading to respiratory arrest and death?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Tonsillar herniation ('coning') forces the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem respiratory centre → respiratory arrest and death.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated in a patient with raised ICP and a space-occupying lesion?
options: It is technically impossible to obtain CSF when the pressure is raised
Removing CSF from below the lesion can precipitate coning
It almost invariably introduces infection and causes a meningitis
It lowers the systemic blood pressure to a dangerous degree
The CSF obtained has no diagnostic value in this clinical situation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Removing CSF from below the lesion can precipitate coning
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Removing CSF from below a pressure gradient can precipitate tonsillar herniation (coning). Image first — but note that a normal CT does not make an LP safe: if the clinical signs of raised ICP are present, the LP remains contraindicated whatever the scan shows.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Regarding the compliance of the intracranial compartment, what happens once the CSF/venous reserve is exhausted?
options: The skull expands to accommodate the volume
Small further increases in volume cause large rises in ICP (decompensation)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Small further increases in volume cause large rises in ICP (decompensation)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The compliance curve is flat then steep — once compensatory reserve is exhausted, small volume increases cause large ICP rises (decompensation).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which combination of measures is appropriate to acutely lower ICP?
options: Nurse head-up ~30° with a neutral neck, and give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline
Head-down positioning and IV fluids to raise ICP
Lie flat and restrict all analgesia
Warm the patient and allow hypercapnia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Nurse head-up ~30° with a neutral neck, and give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Head-up ~30° with a neutral neck aids venous drainage, and osmotic agents (mannitol/hypertonic saline) draw fluid out of the brain to lower ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone) reduce cerebral oedema in which situation?
options: Vasogenic oedema around a tumour or abscess
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Vasogenic oedema around a tumour or abscess
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Dexamethasone helps vasogenic oedema around tumours/abscesses but is NOT used for traumatic or ischaemic (stroke) oedema.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: What is the surgical last resort for refractory raised ICP?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Decompressive craniectomy is the surgical last resort for raised ICP refractory to medical measures; the cause is also treated and perfusion protected.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Controlled hyperventilation can transiently lower ICP. By what mechanism?
options: It increases CSF production, which displaces blood from the skull
Lowering CO2 constricts cerebral vessels, cutting blood volume
It raises the CO2, which dilates vessels and improves drainage
It removes CSF directly through the arachnoid granulations
It reduces cerebral metabolism to zero, abolishing brain demand
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Lowering CO2 constricts cerebral vessels, cutting blood volume
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Lowering the CO2 constricts cerebral vessels and reduces cerebral blood volume, so the ICP falls. But it does that by reducing cerebral blood FLOW — sustained hypocapnia causes ischaemia and worsens outcome. Keep the PaCO2 at 4.5–5.0 kPa; deeper hyperventilation is a short-term rescue only, for impending herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient with a large intracerebral haematoma and raised ICP is deteriorating. Alongside emergency ICP-lowering measures, what is the key definitive step?
options: Treat the underlying cause — e.g. surgical evacuation of the haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Treat the underlying cause — e.g. surgical evacuation of the haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Lowering ICP is temporising; the definitive step is to treat the cause (e.g. evacuate a haematoma, debulk a tumour, shunt hydrocephalus).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which set correctly groups the mechanisms of raised ICP?
options: Mass lesions, cerebral oedema, hydrocephalus and venous congestion
Only space-occupying tumours can raise the intracranial pressure
Only disorders of CSF circulation can raise the intracranial pressure
Only intracranial bleeding can raise the intracranial pressure
Cerebral oedema alone, with the other compartments unaffected
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Mass lesions, cerebral oedema, hydrocephalus and venous congestion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Raised ICP arises from mass lesions, cerebral oedema, increased CSF (hydrocephalus), increased venous volume (e.g. CVST), or is idiopathic (IIH).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: What is the normal range of intracranial pressure?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Normal ICP is 5–15 mmHg; sustained elevation above this range constitutes raised intracranial pressure.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A 45-year-old has shooting pain down the back of the leg to the sole and little toe, weak plantarflexion (can't stand on tiptoe), and an absent ankle jerk. Which nerve root is affected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Little toe/sole sensory loss, weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle jerk localise to the S1 root.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient has pain and numbness over the big toe and dorsum of the foot, weak dorsiflexion of the foot and big toe (mimicking foot drop), but normal ankle and knee jerks. Which root is affected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Big-toe/dorsal-foot sensory loss with weak dorsiflexion (and no easily-tested reflex change) is an L5 radiculopathy — a key differential for foot drop.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient has anterior thigh and medial knee pain, weak knee extension, and a reduced knee jerk. Which roots are most likely involved?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Anterior thigh/medial knee sensory symptoms, weak knee extension and a reduced knee jerk localise to L3/L4.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient has weakness with reduced reflexes and dermatomal sensory loss following a single nerve root, without any upper motor neurone signs. How is this best classified?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: A dermatomal/myotomal LMN deficit following a single root is a radiculopathy; UMN signs below a level would indicate myelopathy, and a nerve-territory deficit a peripheral nerve palsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: What is the commonest cause of a lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: A prolapsed intervertebral disc compressing the exiting root is the commonest cause of radiculopathy/sciatica.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient with back pain and bilateral leg pain has lost the urge to void, with saddle numbness and new bilateral leg weakness. What is the diagnosis and immediate action?
options: Simple sciatica; reassure and prescribe regular analgesia
Cervical myelopathy; arrange an outpatient MRI within 6 weeks
Peripheral neuropathy; check the HbA1c and B12 level
Cauda equina syndrome; emergency lumbosacral MRI and immediate spinal referral
Mechanical back pain; refer routinely for physiotherapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Cauda equina syndrome; emergency lumbosacral MRI and immediate spinal referral
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Bilateral leg pain with bladder dysfunction and saddle numbness is cauda equina syndrome. Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine within 4 hours of request, at the presenting hospital before transfer, then immediate spinal surgical referral. Note that a digital rectal examination is not relied upon — normal anal tone does not exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which reflex corresponds to the S1–2 nerve roots?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The ankle jerk tests S1–2 (knee L3–4, biceps C5–6, triceps C7–8).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which examination manoeuvre best tests for a lower lumbar (L5/S1) nerve root tension sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The straight leg raise reproduces L5/S1 radicular pain; the femoral stretch test is used for upper lumbar (L3/L4) roots.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient describes radicular pain shooting down the back of the leg from the buttock. This 'sciatica' most commonly arises from which roots?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Sciatica is radicular pain down the back of the leg, usually from an L5 or S1 root.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A cervical radiculopathy causes numbness of the middle finger. Which root is most likely affected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: The C7 dermatome covers the middle finger (C6 = thumb/index, C8 = ring/little finger).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: What is the first-line management for most disc-related lumbar radiculopathies without red flags?
options: Immediate surgical discectomy for all patients
Strict bed rest for at least six weeks
Immediate MRI and an epidural steroid injection for all
Conservative care — stay active, NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose, physiotherapy
Long-term strong opioids titrated to effect
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Conservative care — stay active, NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose, physiotherapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Most disc-related radiculopathies resolve over weeks with conservative care: staying active, NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and physiotherapy. NICE says do not offer gabapentinoids, other anticonvulsants, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which drug group does NICE specifically say should NOT be offered for sciatica?
options: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at the lowest effective dose
Topical capsaicin applied to the affected dermatome
Short-term codeine when NSAIDs are unsuitable
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: NICE says do not offer gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica — there is no overall evidence of benefit and there is evidence of harm. NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time are the usual first-line analgesia, with codeine short-term only if NSAIDs are unsuitable; opioids are not used for chronic sciatica.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: Which single finding, in a patient with sciatica, should most urgently prompt emergency imaging?
options: Unilateral calf pain radiating to the ankle
A mildly reduced ankle jerk on the affected side
Pain that is worse on prolonged sitting
A positive straight leg raise at 40 degrees
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Saddle (perineal) anaesthesia signals cauda equina syndrome and mandates emergency MRI. Do not look to a digital rectal examination to confirm or exclude it — normal anal tone does not exclude cauda equina and must never delay imaging.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: How does a myelopathy (cord compression) differ from a radiculopathy on examination?
options: Both conditions are characteristically painless and are distinguished only by imaging
Myelopathy gives lower motor neuron signs confined to a single dermatome and myotome
Myelopathy gives UMN signs below the lesion with a sensory level; radiculopathy is LMN in one root
Radiculopathy gives upgoing plantars and a spastic gait; myelopathy does not
Myelopathy follows the territory of a single named peripheral nerve, as a mononeuropathy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Myelopathy gives UMN signs below the lesion with a sensory level; radiculopathy is LMN in one root
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Myelopathy produces UMN signs below the lesion with a sensory level; a radiculopathy produces LMN signs confined to a single root's dermatome/myotome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: When is MRI of the spine indicated in a patient with a radiculopathy?
options: Only if the pain is confined to the back with no radiation into the leg
In every patient at their first presentation to primary care with sciatica
Never, because the diagnosis of radiculopathy is always purely clinical
Only after twelve months of continuous, unremitting radicular symptoms
Not routinely in a non-specialist setting — only where it would change management
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: Not routinely in a non-specialist setting — only where it would change management
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: NICE says do not routinely offer imaging in a non-specialist setting. MRI belongs in a specialist setting where the result would change management, or where there are red flags or a severe/progressive deficit — and emergency MRI if cauda equina is suspected.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient develops a painful, dermatomal band of sensory disturbance and later a vesicular rash in the same distribution. Which cause of radicular symptoms is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: Herpes zoster reactivation produces dermatomal pain/sensory disturbance followed by a vesicular rash in the same dermatome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient presents with bilateral sciatica but currently normal bladder function. How should this be regarded?
options: As benign mechanical back pain that will settle with simple analgesia
As possible cauda equina until proven otherwise — urgent assessment and MRI
As a peripheral neuropathy needing nerve conduction studies in clinic
As certainly a cord myelopathy requiring whole-spine imaging today
As requiring only reassurance, since bladder function is currently normal
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.answer: As possible cauda equina until proven otherwise — urgent assessment and MRI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: New bilateral sciatica is a red flag: it warrants urgent (2-week) spinal/MSK referral with explicit cauda equina safety-netting, and emergency referral for MRI the moment any bladder, bowel, saddle or sexual symptom appears. Do not wait for painless retention — that is a late sign.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.question: A patient with a lumbar radiculopathy has a severe, progressive foot drop despite conservative treatment. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Continue the same conservative treatment indefinitely
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ra.explanation: A severe or progressive neurological deficit (e.g. worsening foot drop) refractory to conservative care is an indication for surgical discectomy/decompression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A man sustains a midshaft humeral fracture. Afterwards he cannot extend his wrist or fingers ('wrist drop') and has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is injured?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: A midshaft humeral fracture classically injures the radial nerve, causing wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient with an anterior shoulder dislocation cannot abduct the arm and has sensory loss over the lateral ('regimental badge') area of the upper arm, with a flattened deltoid. Which nerve is injured?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The axillary nerve (C5–6) is injured in shoulder dislocation/humeral neck fracture, causing deltoid weakness/flattening and regimental-badge sensory loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus is followed by a claw-hand deformity and numbness of the little and ring fingers. Which nerve is affected?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle; injury there causes a claw hand and sensory loss over the medial 1½ fingers.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A pregnant woman has nocturnal tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand; tapping the wrist reproduces the tingling. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Median nerve compression at the flexor retinaculum causes carpal tunnel syndrome — nocturnal median-distribution paraesthesia with a positive Tinel's/Phalen's, and pregnancy is a classic association.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: Which set of conditions is classically associated with carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: Hyperthyroidism, iron-deficiency anaemia and coeliac disease
Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly
Asthma, atopic eczema and allergic rhinitis in a young adult
Gout and psoriasis, through crystal and inflammatory arthropathy
Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis and primary biliary cholangitis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome is associated with pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and obesity (most cases idiopathic).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient has carpal tunnel syndrome with constant numbness and visible thenar wasting. What is the appropriate management?
options: A night wrist splint, reviewing her again in three months' time
Refer for surgical decompression — do not delay with a splint
A corticosteroid injection, with surgery only if that fails
Reassure her, as thenar wasting resolves once the pain settles
Long-term oral corticosteroids to reduce the tunnel swelling
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Refer for surgical decompression — do not delay with a splint
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Splinting and steroid injection are for mild or intermittent symptoms. Refer for decompression if symptoms are severe or constant, if there is a progressive or established motor or sensory deficit — thenar wasting or weakness — or if there is no improvement after about 3 months of conservative treatment. Thenar wasting means axonal loss, and bulk recovers poorly after late surgery, so waiting costs her function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A rugby player takes a blow to the ribs and later the medial border of the scapula stands off the chest wall (winging), worse when pushing against a wall. Which nerve is injured?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–7) supplies serratus anterior; its injury causes a winged scapula.
