conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A newborn after a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended and forearm pronated (the 'waiter's tip' position). What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Erb's palsy is an upper trunk (C5–6) brachial plexus injury (e.g. shoulder dystocia) producing the 'waiter's tip' posture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A neonate has a claw hand and, on examination, ptosis and a constricted pupil on the same side. Which brachial plexus palsy is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1) causes a claw hand and, because T1 carries sympathetic fibres, may be accompanied by Horner's syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient develops foot drop after a period in a tight below-knee plaster cast, with weak dorsiflexion/eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured, and where?
options: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the neck of the fibula
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the neck of the fibula
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The common peroneal nerve is vulnerable as it winds around the fibular neck; compression there causes foot drop with dorsal foot sensory loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A person falls asleep with their arm over a chair after drinking and wakes with a wrist drop that fully recovers over a few weeks. Which type of nerve injury (Seddon) is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: 'Saturday night palsy' is a neurapraxia — a temporary conduction block with an intact axon — which recovers fully over days to weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A nerve is completely transected by a laceration. Which Seddon grade is this, and what does it require?
options: Axonotmesis; regrows without surgery in days
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Complete transection is neurotmesis, which has a poor prognosis and requires surgical repair/grafting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: Which statement about hand intrinsic muscle innervation is correct?
options: The ulnar nerve supplies the LOAF muscles of the thenar eminence
The radial nerve supplies all of the intrinsic muscles of the hand
Median supplies LOAF; ulnar supplies all the other intrinsics
Neither the median nor the ulnar nerve supplies the hand intrinsics
The median nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the hand
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Median supplies LOAF; ulnar supplies all the other intrinsics
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The median nerve supplies the LOAF muscles (lateral 2 lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis); the ulnar nerve supplies the remaining intrinsics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: Why does a proximal (elbow) ulnar nerve lesion produce a LESS pronounced claw than a distal (wrist) lesion — the 'ulnar paradox'?
options: Because a proximal lesion spares all of the ulnar-supplied muscles
Because the median nerve compensates for the ulnar deficit proximally
Because the degree of clawing bears no relation to the lesion level
Because it also denervates FDP, so those fingers flex less
Because a wrist lesion spares the intrinsic muscles of the hand
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Because it also denervates FDP, so those fingers flex less
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: A proximal ulnar lesion also knocks out the flexor digitorum profundus to the ring/little fingers, so they flex less at the DIPs — making the claw less obvious than with a distal lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient has numbness affecting the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger, worse when the elbow is held flexed for long periods. Which nerve and site are involved?
options: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.answer: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel (behind the medial epicondyle) causes medial 1½-finger symptoms worse on elbow flexion (cubital tunnel syndrome).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient has sensory loss over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle and lateral half of the ring finger. Which nerve supplies this territory?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar lateral 3½ fingers (thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: In axonotmesis, the axon is severed but the connective tissue sheath is intact. At roughly what rate does axonal regrowth occur?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: In axonotmesis, axonal regeneration proceeds along the intact sheath at approximately 1 mm per day.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient has a foot drop. Inversion is weak and the ankle jerk is preserved. Where is the lesion?
options: The common peroneal nerve, compressed at the neck of the fibula
The sciatic nerve, in the buttock or posterior thigh
The tibial nerve, within the tarsal tunnel at the ankle
The femoral nerve, within the pelvis or the inguinal region
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: Use two findings. Inversion (tibialis posterior — a tibial-nerve muscle but an L5 myotome) is PRESERVED in a common peroneal palsy and WEAK in an L5 root or sciatic lesion. The ankle jerk (S1) is preserved in both common peroneal palsy and L5 radiculopathy, and lost in a sciatic lesion. Weak inversion with a normal ankle jerk therefore localises to the L5 root — so ask about back pain, saddle sensation and bladder function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: A patient has weakness of knee extension and an absent knee jerk after a pelvic procedure. Which nerve is most likely injured?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The femoral nerve supplies knee extension (quadriceps) and the knee jerk; its injury causes weak knee extension and an absent knee jerk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.question: Which nerve, injured in isolation only rarely (usually as part of a brachial plexus injury), supplies elbow flexion (biceps) and forearm supination?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pe.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5–7) supplies elbow flexion (biceps) and supination, with sensation to the lateral forearm; isolated injury is rare.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A 68-year-old man has a 1-year history of a tremor in his right hand that is worst when the hand is resting in his lap and eases when he reaches for objects. His wife notes his handwriting has become tiny and his face less expressive. Examination shows cogwheel rigidity and slow finger movements, worse on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: An asymmetric resting (pill-rolling) tremor with bradykinesia (micrographia, hypomimia, slow movements) and cogwheel rigidity is classic idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: Which single clinical feature is essential for a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Bradykinesia is the obligatory feature in the UK Brain Bank criteria — it must be present, plus at least one of rigidity, a 4–6 Hz resting tremor, or postural instability.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: Parkinson's disease results from the loss of dopaminergic neurones in which structure?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta reduces striatal dopamine, producing the motor features of Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: What is the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Lewy bodies — intracellular α-synuclein aggregates — are the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease (also seen in Lewy body dementia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A 70-year-old has a bilateral, symmetric tremor that is present when holding a cup or writing, is absent at rest, improves after a glass of wine, and is not accompanied by slowness of movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: An action/postural, symmetric tremor that improves with alcohol and lacks bradykinesia is essential tremor, not Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A 60-year-old on long-term haloperidol develops a symmetric parkinsonian syndrome. What is the most important step?
options: Start levodopa immediately to relieve the motor symptoms
Arrange a DaTSCAN to confirm idiopathic Parkinson's disease
Start a non-ergot dopamine agonist such as ropinirole
Review the drug chart — this is likely drug-induced
Reassure him that this is idiopathic Parkinson's disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: Review the drug chart — this is likely drug-induced
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Symmetric parkinsonism temporally related to an antipsychotic (or metoclopramide) suggests drug-induced parkinsonism; review/stop the offending dopamine antagonist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient with a parkinsonian syndrome has prominent early falls and difficulty with vertical eye movements. Which diagnosis should be considered rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Early falls and a vertical gaze palsy are red flags for progressive supranuclear palsy, an atypical ('Parkinson's plus') syndrome with a poor levodopa response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient with parkinsonism has early, prominent autonomic failure (marked postural hypotension, bladder dysfunction). Which atypical syndrome does this suggest?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Early, prominent autonomic failure with parkinsonism suggests multiple system atrophy (MSA), a Parkinson's-plus syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A man with parkinsonism develops early dementia and vivid visual hallucinations within the first year. Which diagnosis is most likely?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Early/prominent dementia and visual hallucinations alongside parkinsonism indicate Lewy body dementia rather than idiopathic Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient has a tremor that cannot be clinically separated from essential tremor. What does a DaTSCAN add?
options: It distinguishes parkinsonism from essential tremor
It separates Parkinson's disease from PSP and MSA reliably
It confirms drug-induced parkinsonism beyond reasonable doubt
It predicts how well the patient will respond to levodopa
It grades the severity of nigrostriatal degeneration for staging
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: It distinguishes parkinsonism from essential tremor
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: A DaTSCAN answers one question: is there presynaptic nigrostriatal degeneration? Uptake is reduced in parkinsonism and normal in essential tremor. It cannot separate Parkinson's from a Parkinson-plus syndrome, because uptake is reduced in PSP, MSA and Lewy body dementia too.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: According to NICE, a newly diagnosed patient's Parkinson's motor symptoms are significantly affecting their quality of life. Which first-line drug is recommended?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: When motor symptoms affect quality of life, NICE recommends levodopa first-line as the most effective drug for motor symptoms and activities of daily living.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: Why is levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (e.g. carbidopa or benserazide)?
options: It prevents peripheral conversion, cutting nausea and boosting delivery
It increases the breakdown of levodopa within the central nervous system
It blocks dopamine receptors in the periphery to limit side effects
It acts as a centrally acting antiemetic alongside the levodopa
It prolongs the action of levodopa within the gut lumen only
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: It prevents peripheral conversion, cutting nausea and boosting delivery
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: A peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor stops levodopa being converted to dopamine outside the CNS, reducing peripheral side effects (nausea) and improving central delivery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A man on ropinirole for Parkinson's has started gambling heavily and hiding it from his wife. What is happening?
options: An impulse-control disorder from dopaminergic therapy
An unrelated primary gambling disorder needing referral
An early feature of Parkinson's disease dementia
A side effect specific to levodopa rather than agonists
A manifestation of untreated depression in Parkinson's
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: An impulse-control disorder from dopaminergic therapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Impulse-control disorders — gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive shopping — are a recognised effect of dopaminergic therapy. The risk is highest with dopamine agonists but they can occur with any dopaminergic drug, so every patient and family should be warned and asked at review. Management is gradual reduction of the agonist, watching for dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: After several years of levodopa therapy, a patient notices the benefit fades before the next dose and has involuntary movements at peak effect. What do these represent?
options: An allergic reaction to levodopa developing after chronic exposure
Progression of the disease to Lewy body dementia with fluctuations
Drug-induced parkinsonism from an interacting prescribed medicine
Long-term motor complications — wearing off and dyskinesias
Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome from erratic drug absorption
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: Long-term motor complications — wearing off and dyskinesias
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: 'Wearing off' and peak-dose dyskinesias are the long-term motor complications of levodopa, managed with adjuncts, dose fractionation or advanced therapies.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease is admitted nil-by-mouth before surgery and their levodopa is withheld. Why is this dangerous?
options: It causes only a mild and entirely self-limiting increase in tremor
Abrupt withdrawal risks acute akinesia and hyperpyrexia
It has no important consequences over a short perioperative period
It temporarily cures the disease by resetting receptor sensitivity
It commonly provokes an allergic reaction on drug reintroduction
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: Abrupt withdrawal risks acute akinesia and hyperpyrexia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Parkinson's drugs are time-critical: abrupt withdrawal or missed doses risk acute akinesia and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, an NMS-like emergency. If the patient is nil by mouth, convert to dispersible co-beneldopa via NG tube or to a rotigotine patch — do not simply omit the doses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A Parkinson's patient on the ward is vomiting and needs an antiemetic. What is appropriate?
options: Metoclopramide, which is the standard first-line antiemetic
Prochlorperazine, which is well tolerated in the elderly
Haloperidol, at a low dose, for intractable vomiting
Any antiemetic, since none affects Parkinson's disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Avoid dopamine-blocking antiemetics — metoclopramide and prochlorperazine both worsen parkinsonism, and prochlorperazine is a leading cause of drug-induced parkinsonism in older people. Cyclizine and ondansetron are safe. Domperidone is also used because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, but it prolongs the QT interval, so it is given at the lowest dose for the shortest time.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease develops psychosis requiring antipsychotic treatment. Which agents are preferred?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: If an antipsychotic is needed in Parkinson's disease, quetiapine or clozapine are preferred as they least worsen the motor features; typical antipsychotics should be avoided.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A Parkinson's patient has disabling motor fluctuations and dyskinesia despite optimised oral therapy. What are the options?
options: Stop all Parkinson's medication and restart from scratch
Add a typical antipsychotic to suppress the dyskinesia
Deep brain stimulation, apomorphine or intrajejunal levodopa
An anticholinergic as monotherapy in place of levodopa
Long-term bed rest with physiotherapy input only
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: Deep brain stimulation, apomorphine or intrajejunal levodopa
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: For motor fluctuations and dyskinesia refractory to medication, the advanced options are deep brain stimulation, subcutaneous apomorphine and intrajejunal levodopa gel. Stopping Parkinson's medication is dangerous, and dopamine-blocking drugs make parkinsonism worse.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: Which combination of non-motor symptoms is a recognised prodrome that can predate the motor diagnosis of Parkinson's disease by years?
options: Photophobia with neck stiffness and an early morning headache
Fatigable ptosis with diplopia worsening through the day
A sensory level with sphincter disturbance and back pain
Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression
Bilateral progressive hearing loss with tinnitus and vertigo
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: Anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation and depression form the recognised prodrome that can precede the motor features of Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.question: A patient on levodopa experiences 'wearing off' between doses. Which adjunct works by prolonging levodopa's action?
options: A COMT inhibitor such as entacapone
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.answer: A COMT inhibitor such as entacapone
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Pa.explanation: COMT inhibitors (entacapone) prolong levodopa's action and reduce 'wearing off'; MAO-B inhibitors are also used, and amantadine targets dyskinesia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A neuromuscular junction disorder is characterised by antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor, with weakness that worsens on repeated use. Which disorder is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Myasthenia gravis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Postsynaptic anti-AChR antibodies with fatigable weakness (worse with use) define myasthenia gravis; LEMS is presynaptic and improves with use.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient's proximal leg weakness briefly improves after a few seconds of sustained exercise, and they have hyporeflexia and a dry mouth. Which neuromuscular junction disorder is most likely?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Post-exercise facilitation (transient improvement with use), hyporeflexia and autonomic features (dry mouth) point to LEMS (presynaptic, anti-VGCC).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which disease association is correctly paired?
options: Myasthenia gravis — thymoma; Lambert-Eaton — small-cell lung cancer
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Myasthenia gravis — thymoma; Lambert-Eaton — small-cell lung cancer
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: MG is associated with thymoma/thymic hyperplasia, and LEMS with small-cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which combination of reflex and autonomic findings suggests Lambert-Eaton rather than myasthenia gravis?
options: Brisk reflexes with normal autonomic function
Normal reflexes with no autonomic features
Upgoing plantars with a spastic bladder
Hyporeflexia with autonomic features (e.g. dry mouth)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Hyporeflexia with autonomic features (e.g. dry mouth)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: LEMS characteristically shows hyporeflexia (may return after exercise) and autonomic features; MG has normal reflexes and no autonomic involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which antibody is characteristically found in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: LEMS is caused by antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC), reducing ACh release; anti-AChR (and anti-MuSK) are seen in MG.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which pattern of initial weakness best fits myasthenia gravis rather than Lambert-Eaton?
options: A sensory level with sphincter disturbance
Ocular first (ptosis and diplopia), then bulbar and proximal limb
Purely respiratory onset with no other features
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Ocular first (ptosis and diplopia), then bulbar and proximal limb
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: MG typically begins with ocular symptoms (ptosis, diplopia) then bulbar/proximal weakness; LEMS starts in the proximal legs with less prominent ocular/bulbar involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 28-year-old woman reports drooping eyelids and double vision that are mild in the morning but marked by evening, plus tiring of her jaw while chewing. Examination shows ptosis that worsens on sustained upgaze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Myasthenia gravis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Fatigable, ocular-predominant weakness (ptosis/diplopia worse with use and by evening) with fatigable chewing is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which antibody test is the key initial investigation in generalised myasthenia gravis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Anti-AChR antibodies are positive in ~85% of generalised MG and are the key test; anti-MuSK is checked if AChR-negative.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Why must every patient diagnosed with myasthenia gravis have imaging of the chest?
options: To exclude a pneumonia that might be driving the weakness
To look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia
To measure the lung volumes before starting pyridostigmine
To exclude a small cell lung cancer, as in Lambert-Eaton
To assess the heart size before starting immunosuppression
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: To look for a thymoma or thymic hyperplasia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: The thymus drives the autoimmunity in most myasthenia — hyperplasia in the majority of early-onset AChR-positive disease, and a thymoma in around 10–15%. CT or MRI of the chest is needed in everyone, because a thymoma is an indication for thymectomy. Small cell lung cancer is the tumour to hunt in Lambert-Eaton, not myasthenia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A simple bedside test for ptosis in suspected MG involves applying ice to the closed eyelid. What result supports MG, and why?
options: The ptosis worsens, because cold impairs the affected muscle
The ptosis improves, because cooling slows acetylcholinesterase
No change occurs at all, which effectively excludes myasthenia
The pupil dilates on the affected side within two minutes
The eye becomes red and watery with reflex lacrimation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: The ptosis improves, because cooling slows acetylcholinesterase
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: In the ice-pack test, ice is held on the closed ptotic lid for about 2 minutes; improvement of more than 2 mm supports myasthenia. Cooling slows acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lingers in the synaptic cleft and transmission improves.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which electrophysiological finding is characteristic of myasthenia gravis?
options: An incremental response on high-frequency repetitive stimulation
Conduction block with slowing of motor conduction velocity
A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
Myotonic discharges with a waxing and waning frequency
Fibrillation potentials with large polyphasic motor units
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation is characteristic of myasthenia, where receptors are progressively occupied and transmission fails with use. An INCREMENTAL response on high-frequency stimulation is the Lambert-Eaton pattern — the opposite, reflecting facilitation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the first-line symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis, and its mechanism?
options: Prednisolone — immunosuppression of the antibody response
Bromocriptine — a dopamine agonist acting centrally
Riluzole — a glutamate release inhibitor reducing excitotoxicity
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Pyridostigmine — an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, raises ACh at the NMJ to improve transmission and is the first-line symptomatic treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with MG has rapidly worsening weakness and breathlessness after a chest infection. Saturations are 98% on air. What is the priority?
options: Reassure her — the saturations show respiratory function is adequate
Increase the pyridostigmine dose at home and review in 48 hours
Measure serial FVC, involve ITU, and give IVIG or plasma exchange
Start a beta-blocker to control the associated sinus tachycardia
Arrange an urgent thymectomy on the same day as the admission
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Measure serial FVC, involve ITU, and give IVIG or plasma exchange
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: This is a myasthenic crisis. Monitor SERIAL FVC and the trend — below about 20 mL/kg means ITU. Normal saturations are the trap: in neuromuscular respiratory failure the saturations and blood gas stay normal until the patient is on the point of arrest. Simply increasing pyridostigmine risks tipping into cholinergic crisis instead.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis needs an antibiotic for a chest infection. Which should be avoided?
options: Amoxicillin, which blocks acetylcholine receptors directly
A cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, given intravenously
Metronidazole, which potentiates the neuromuscular block
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Clarithromycin or ciprofloxacin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Three antibiotic classes worsen myasthenia: macrolides (clarithromycin), fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and aminoglycosides (gentamicin). Penicillins and cephalosporins are safe. Beyond antibiotics, remember beta-blockers, quinine, IV magnesium and penicillamine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: In which patients with MG is thymectomy indicated or beneficial?
options: Only in patients over the age of 80 with severe generalised disease
If a thymoma is present, and in AChR-positive generalised MG
Never, because removing the thymus reliably worsens the myasthenia
Only in purely ocular myasthenia that has failed pyridostigmine
Only in anti-MuSK positive disease, where it is most effective
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: If a thymoma is present, and in AChR-positive generalised MG
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Thymectomy is indicated whenever a thymoma is present, whatever the myasthenia. It is also beneficial in AChR-positive generalised MG up to about 65 even without a thymoma, improving outcomes and reducing medication. It is not helpful in anti-MuSK disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient has clear myasthenic features but is negative for anti-AChR antibodies, with prominent bulbar and respiratory involvement and a poor response to pyridostigmine. Which antibody is most likely positive?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Anti-MuSK (muscle-specific kinase)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Anti-MuSK antibodies occur in some AChR-negative patients, with more bulbar/respiratory disease and a poorer response to pyridostigmine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: How does MG differ from motor neurone disease on examination?
options: MG is fatigable with eye involvement; MND is mixed UMN/LMN, eye-sparing
MG causes fasciculations and mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs
Both conditions prominently involve the extraocular muscles early on
MG produces a sensory level whereas MND produces distal sensory loss
MND characteristically causes fatigable ptosis worsening through the day
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: MG is fatigable with eye involvement; MND is mixed UMN/LMN, eye-sparing
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: MG is fatigable with characteristic ocular involvement and no UMN signs; MND has mixed UMN/LMN signs (with fasciculations) and characteristically spares the eyes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Beyond first-line pyridostigmine, what is the usual approach for more than mild generalised MG?
options: Long-term prophylactic antibiotics to prevent infective exacerbations
A beta-blocker, to reduce sympathetic drive at the junction
Prednisolone with a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine
A dopamine agonist, to increase neurotransmitter availability
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Prednisolone with a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Corticosteroids are used for more than mild generalised disease, usually with a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine (check TPMT first). Start the prednisolone LOW and increase slowly — steroids transiently worsen myasthenia in the first week or two and can precipitate a crisis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What proportion of MG stays purely ocular, and what is the typical course of the rest?
options: About 15% remain ocular; the rest generalise
None remain ocular; all are bulbar from the start
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: About 15% remain ocular; the rest generalise
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: About 15% of MG remains purely ocular (ocular MG); the majority generalise to bulbar, limb and respiratory involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with anti-MuSK positive MG has not responded to standard immunosuppression. What is appropriate?
options: Reduce the pyridostigmine dose and observe over several months
A macrolide antibiotic to modulate the immune response
A beta-blocker to reduce the sympathetic drive at the junction
Levodopa, to increase neurotransmitter availability generally
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Rituximab, under specialist care
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Rituximab is used for refractory myasthenia, particularly anti-MuSK positive disease, alongside IVIG or plasma exchange for crises. Newer biologic therapies are available under specialist care. Note that macrolides and beta-blockers would make the myasthenia worse.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 64-year-old smoker with weight loss reports difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs; the weakness eases briefly after activity. He has a dry mouth and absent knee reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Proximal weakness that improves with use, autonomic features (dry mouth) and hyporeflexia in an older smoker is LEMS — often paraneoplastic with SCLC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Having diagnosed LEMS, what is the most important investigation to arrange?
options: Echocardiography, to look for a cardiac source of embolism
MRI of the brain, to exclude a brainstem demyelinating lesion
CT chest, to hunt for small-cell lung cancer
Muscle biopsy, to demonstrate the characteristic fibre changes
Lumbar puncture, to look for oligoclonal bands in the CSF
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: CT chest, to hunt for small-cell lung cancer
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: About half of LEMS is paraneoplastic (SCLC), so CT chest ± PET is essential, with ongoing surveillance as LEMS can precede the cancer.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: On repetitive nerve stimulation, which finding is characteristic of LEMS?
options: A decremental response at low frequency, as receptors are occupied
A completely normal study with no decrement or increment at all
Myotonic discharges with a characteristic waxing and waning sound
An incremental response after exercise, from a low baseline
Conduction block with marked slowing of conduction velocity
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: An incremental response after exercise, from a low baseline
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: LEMS shows a low baseline amplitude that increments with high-frequency stimulation/after exercise (facilitation) — the opposite of MG's decrement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which single feature best distinguishes LEMS from myasthenia gravis on the history?
options: Weakness that is consistently worse towards the end of the day
Weakness that improves transiently with repeated use
Prominent ptosis and diplopia from the very earliest symptoms
Difficulty chewing that worsens progressively during a meal
Weakness that is confined to the bulbar and respiratory muscles
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Weakness that improves transiently with repeated use
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: LEMS improves with use (post-exercise facilitation), whereas MG worsens with use (fatigability); prominent ocular features and the ice-pack test favour MG.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the mechanism of 3,4-diaminopyridine (amifampridine), the first-line symptomatic drug in LEMS?
options: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so ACh persists in the cleft
It blocks the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor competitively
It suppresses the antibody response as an immunosuppressant
It blocks presynaptic potassium channels, raising ACh release
It is a dopamine agonist acting on presynaptic autoreceptors
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: It blocks presynaptic potassium channels, raising ACh release
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: 3,4-diaminopyridine blocks presynaptic K⁺ channels, prolonging depolarisation so more Ca²⁺ enters and more ACh is released, improving transmission.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which triad is characteristic of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
options: Proximal weakness (legs > arms), autonomic features, hyporeflexia
Ptosis, diplopia and fatigable chewing worsening through the day
Fever, muscular rigidity and an altered mental state with sweating
Sensory loss, sphincter disturbance and a well-defined sensory level
Fasciculations, muscle wasting and pathologically brisk reflexes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Proximal weakness (legs > arms), autonomic features, hyporeflexia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: The LEMS triad is proximal weakness (legs > arms), autonomic dysfunction (e.g. dry mouth) and hyporeflexia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: In a patient with paraneoplastic LEMS, which intervention often improves the neurological syndrome itself?
options: Treating the underlying small-cell lung cancer
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Treating the underlying small-cell lung cancer
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: In paraneoplastic LEMS, treating the underlying SCLC often improves the LEMS and is the priority.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Why do the reflexes and strength in LEMS improve briefly after a few seconds of sustained muscle contraction?
options: Acetylcholinesterase is transiently inhibited by muscle activity
The postsynaptic receptors are rapidly up-regulated by activity
Circulating antibodies are washed away from the junction by exercise
Calcium accumulates presynaptically, so more ACh is released
Muscle temperature falls, which improves junctional transmission
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Calcium accumulates presynaptically, so more ACh is released
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Repeated firing causes presynaptic calcium accumulation, transiently increasing ACh release — the facilitation that underlies post-exercise improvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which autonomic feature is the commonest in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Dry mouth
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Dry mouth is the commonest autonomic feature of LEMS; others include blurred vision, impotence, constipation and postural hypotension.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which statement correctly contrasts LEMS with MG?
options: LEMS is postsynaptic (anti-AChR); MG is presynaptic (anti-VGCC)
Both worsen with use and both involve the eyes prominently
LEMS is associated with thymoma, and MG with small-cell lung cancer
LEMS is presynaptic and improves with use; MG is postsynaptic
LEMS shows a decremental EMG response and MG an incremental one
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: LEMS is presynaptic and improves with use; MG is postsynaptic
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: LEMS is presynaptic (anti-VGCC), improves transiently with use, and comes with hyporeflexia and autonomic features such as a dry mouth; it is associated with small-cell lung cancer. MG is postsynaptic (anti-AChR), worsens with use, prominently involves the eyes, and is associated with thymoma. Their EMG patterns are opposite: increment in LEMS, decrement in MG.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 30-year-old man started on haloperidol three days ago becomes confused and febrile (39.5°C), with generalised 'lead-pipe' rigidity, a labile blood pressure and tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and altered mental state evolving over days after an antipsychotic is neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Note that it can occur at any point in treatment, not only after a recent start.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which combination best distinguishes NMS from serotonin syndrome?
options: NMS has clonus and hyperreflexia; serotonin syndrome has rigidity and hyporeflexia
NMS is caused by SSRIs, whereas serotonin syndrome is caused by antipsychotics
Both have identical clinical features and cannot be told apart at the bedside
NMS has lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia; serotonin syndrome has clonus and mydriasis
NMS causes diarrhoea, whereas serotonin syndrome characteristically causes constipation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: NMS has lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia; serotonin syndrome has clonus and mydriasis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NMS (dopamine antagonist, slow onset) gives rigidity + hyporeflexia; serotonin syndrome (serotonergic drug, rapid onset) gives clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which blood test most strongly supports a diagnosis of NMS and reflects its key complication?
options: A low serum sodium from inappropriate ADH secretion
A markedly raised creatine kinase, from rhabdomyolysis
A low platelet count from marrow suppression
A raised serum amylase from pancreatic involvement
A low blood glucose from increased metabolic demand
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: A markedly raised creatine kinase, from rhabdomyolysis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: A markedly raised CK reflects the rhabdomyolysis of NMS and is the key supporting test; the released myoglobin can cause AKI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Why is aggressive IV fluid therapy central to managing NMS?
options: To reverse the dopamine blockade at the receptor level
To raise the blood pressure, which is the main threat to life
To treat the underlying infection that has triggered the syndrome
To lower the creatine kinase concentration directly by dilution
To prevent acute kidney injury by clearing myoglobin and maintaining urine output
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: To prevent acute kidney injury by clearing myoglobin and maintaining urine output
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin, which causes AKI. Give generous IV fluids titrated to a urine output of about 1–2 mL/kg/hour. Check the potassium urgently too: hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis is what kills first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the fundamental mechanism underlying neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
options: A ryanodine receptor mutation unmasked by a volatile anaesthetic
Excess serotonin at central synapses following a serotonergic drug
Central dopamine blockade or deficiency (antagonist, or levodopa withdrawal)
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Excess circulating thyroid hormone driving the metabolic rate
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Central dopamine blockade or deficiency (antagonist, or levodopa withdrawal)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NMS is driven by central dopamine blockade (or acute dopamine deficiency from levodopa withdrawal), impairing thermoregulation and causing rigidity.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Beyond stopping the offending drug and giving supportive care, which drugs are used in severe NMS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Dantrolene and bromocriptine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Severe NMS may be treated with dantrolene (reduces rigidity and heat, given IV in critical care) and bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist). Both are for severe cases only, the evidence is weak, and supportive care remains the mainstay. A benzodiazepine, not another antipsychotic, is used for the agitation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient develops fever, rigidity and confusion after repeated doses of an antiemetic. Which antiemetic can precipitate NMS through dopamine antagonism?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Metoclopramide
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and, like antipsychotics, can precipitate NMS. Prochlorperazine — a phenothiazine and a very common UK prescription — does the same.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease is admitted and their levodopa is abruptly stopped; two days later they develop fever, marked rigidity and confusion. What is the most appropriate specific action?
options: Give a large dose of a beta-blocker
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics as the sole treatment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Restart the dopaminergic (levodopa) therapy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Abrupt levodopa withdrawal causes an NMS-like 'parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia' state; the specific step is to restart the dopaminergic drug, alongside supportive care.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient on an SSRI who was also given tramadol rapidly develops agitation, sweating, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, hyperreflexia and clonus. What is the diagnosis and specific antidote?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Serotonin syndrome; cyproheptadine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Rapid onset with clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis and diarrhoea after serotonergic drugs is serotonin syndrome, treated with cyproheptadine — the key contrast to NMS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the mechanism of dantrolene in the treatment of NMS?
options: It is a serotonin antagonist that blocks 5-HT2A receptors centrally
It blocks dopamine receptors, reversing the autonomic instability
It is a dopamine agonist that restores central dopaminergic tone
It is a muscle relaxant that reduces rigidity and heat generation
It blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, relaxing muscle
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: It is a muscle relaxant that reduces rigidity and heat generation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Dantrolene is a skeletal muscle relaxant that reduces the rigidity (and thus heat generation) of NMS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the rationale for using bromocriptine in NMS?
options: It is an antipsychotic that sedates the agitated, hyperthermic patient
It is a dopamine agonist, restoring dopaminergic tone against the blockade
It is an antipyretic that acts centrally on the hypothalamic set point
It is an antibiotic covering the sepsis that commonly coexists
It blocks serotonin receptors, as in the treatment of serotonin syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: It is a dopamine agonist, restoring dopaminergic tone against the blockade
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist that counters the central dopamine blockade underlying NMS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A febrile, rigid patient develops these features during a general anaesthetic using succinylcholine and volatile agents. Which diagnosis, rather than NMS, should be considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Malignant hyperthermia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics, with onset within minutes of induction, masseter spasm and a rising end-tidal CO₂. It is an important mimic of NMS, and both respond to dantrolene.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Regarding the tempo of illness, how does NMS typically present compared with serotonin syndrome?
options: NMS develops within minutes; serotonin syndrome over weeks
NMS develops slowly over days; serotonin syndrome develops rapidly over hours
NMS is always faster than serotonin syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: NMS develops slowly over days; serotonin syndrome develops rapidly over hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NMS characteristically evolves slowly over 1–3 days, whereas serotonin syndrome develops rapidly (within hours) of the serotonergic trigger.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient has recovered from an episode of NMS and still needs antipsychotic treatment for psychosis. What is the safest approach?
options: Never use any antipsychotic again under any circumstances
Restart the same drug at the same dose as soon as the fever settles
Use a high-potency typical antipsychotic at a high dose
Give the same antipsychotic, but only by the intravenous route
Wait at least 2 weeks after full recovery, then a structurally unrelated agent at low dose
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Wait at least 2 weeks after full recovery, then a structurally unrelated agent at low dose
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Recurrence risk on rechallenge is roughly 30%, so wait at least 2 weeks after complete resolution (longer after a depot), choose an agent structurally unrelated to the culprit, start at a very low dose, titrate slowly, and monitor temperature, pulse, BP and CK.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 7-year-old boy has 8 flat coffee-coloured skin patches (each 8–12 mm), freckling in both axillae, and yellow-brown spots on the irises noted on slit-lamp examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Neurofibromatosis type 1
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Six or more café-au-lait macules (each over 5 mm before puberty, or over 15 mm after), axillary freckling and Lisch nodules are three of the CRABBING criteria, and two are enough for NF1. Note the paediatric size threshold — 8–12 mm comfortably meets it in a 7-year-old.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the genetic basis of neurofibromatosis type 1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Chromosome 17, neurofibromin (a tumour suppressor)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF1 is caused by mutation of the NF1 gene on chromosome 17 encoding neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor; loss leads to tumour growth along nerves.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A young adult presents with progressive bilateral hearing loss and is found to have bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas). Which condition does this indicate, and on which chromosome is the gene?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: NF2; chromosome 22 (merlin)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Bilateral acoustic neuromas are the hallmark of NF2 (chromosome 22, merlin) — 'NF2 → 22 → 2 ears'; NF1 features skin lesions instead.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: How many of the CRABBING criteria are required to diagnose NF1?
options: Genetic testing is always required regardless
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: At least 2
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF1 is a clinical diagnosis made when ≥2 of the CRABBING criteria are present.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: On slit-lamp examination, a patient with suspected NF1 has yellow-brown raised lesions on the iris. What are these?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas and one of the two most specific features of NF1 (the other being optic pathway glioma).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with NF1 is found to be hypertensive. Which two NF1-associated causes of secondary hypertension should be investigated?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF1 causes secondary hypertension via renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma, so BP is checked and these are investigated (renal artery imaging, plasma metanephrines).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with known NF1 reports that one of their neurofibromas has become painful, hard and is enlarging rapidly. What is the most important concern?
options: Malignant transformation to a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Malignant transformation to a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: A neurofibroma that becomes painful, hard or rapidly enlarging — or that causes a new neurological deficit — raises malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and needs urgent assessment. The risk lies with plexiform and deep nodular neurofibromas rather than ordinary cutaneous ones.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which tumour is a recognised cause of vision loss in NF1 and warrants visual surveillance?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Optic pathway (optic nerve) glioma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: An optic pathway glioma is a specific NF1 feature that can cause vision loss, so visual acuity/fields are monitored.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the inheritance of NF1, and what is notable about new cases?
options: X-linked recessive, so that only boys are clinically affected by it
Autosomal recessive, with every case inherited from two carrier parents
Autosomal dominant, 50% to offspring; about half of cases are new mutations
Mitochondrial, transmitted exclusively down the maternal line
Autosomal dominant, but new spontaneous mutations never occur
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Autosomal dominant, 50% to offspring; about half of cases are new mutations
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF1 is autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring), but ~50% of cases arise from new spontaneous mutations, so many have no family history.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which pair are regarded as the two MOST specific features of NF1?
options: Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma
A first-degree relative and learning difficulty
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Lisch nodules and optic pathway glioma are the two features most specific to NF1, both being rare outside it. Café-au-lait macules, freckling and neurofibromas are commoner but far less specific.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What does routine annual surveillance in NF1 typically include?
options: Nothing at all until the patient develops symptoms of a complication
An annual whole-body MRI scan and nothing else besides
Annual echocardiography alone, to screen for cardiac lesions
Skin, blood pressure, vision, growth and puberty, spine and development
A yearly lumbar puncture to sample the cerebrospinal fluid
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Skin, blood pressure, vision, growth and puberty, spine and development
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Surveillance is clinical and annual — skin, BP, vision (optic glioma), spine and development — with vigilance for malignant change.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Besides nerve-sheath tumours, which gastrointestinal tumour is associated with NF1?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: GISTs are associated with NF1, alongside malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours, optic glioma and an increased leukaemia risk.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A parent with NF1 asks about the risk to their children. What is the most accurate advice?
options: There is no risk at all, because NF1 is not an inherited condition
Each child has a 50% risk, though severity varies widely between people
Every child will be affected, and severely so, in each generation
Only the daughters are at risk, as the gene sits on the X chromosome
The risk is 25%, since the condition is inherited recessively
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Each child has a 50% risk, though severity varies widely between people
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF1 is autosomal dominant, so each child has a 50% risk of inheriting it, with markedly variable expressivity even within a family.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 24-year-old presents with progressive hearing loss and tinnitus in both ears and unsteadiness. MRI shows bilateral vestibular schwannomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Neurofibromatosis type 2
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) causing bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in a young adult are essentially pathognomonic of NF2.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the genetic basis of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Chromosome 22, merlin (schwannomin)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF2 is caused by mutation of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, encoding merlin (schwannomin), a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which feature of NF2 most reliably distinguishes it from NF1?
options: Bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) with few skin features
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Bilateral acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas) with few skin features
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF2 (now termed NF2-related schwannomatosis) is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas, from a chromosome 22 defect in merlin, with few skin features. Café-au-lait macules, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma and axillary freckling all belong to NF1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Why do vestibular (CN VIII) schwannomas dominate in NF2?
options: Acoustic neuromas are the only kind of tumour that NF2 is able to cause
Merlin is expressed only within the cochlea and nowhere else in the body
The vestibular nerve uniquely lacks its own arterial blood supply
NF2 is a disease confined entirely to the structures of the inner ear
Merlin is a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells, which myelinate nerves
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Merlin is a tumour suppressor important in Schwann cells, which myelinate nerves
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Loss of merlin (key in Schwann cells) drives schwannomas, and the vestibular nerve schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are the dominant, hallmark feature.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which imaging is the mainstay of diagnosis and surveillance in NF2?
options: MRI of the brain, internal auditory meati and whole spine (with contrast)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: MRI of the brain, internal auditory meati and whole spine (with contrast)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Contrast MRI of the brain, internal auditory meati and whole spine detects bilateral acoustic neuromas, meningiomas and spinal tumours, and is the mainstay of diagnosis and surveillance.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which drug can shrink vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Bevacizumab (an anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody) can shrink vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in NF2.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Besides vestibular schwannomas, which tumour is characteristically multiple in NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Meningiomas
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Meningiomas (often multiple) occur in NF2, along with schwannomas of other nerves and spinal ependymomas/gliomas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which ophthalmic finding is characteristic of NF2?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts (and retinal hamartomas) occur in NF2; Lisch nodules are a feature of NF1.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the key clinical/radiological criterion for diagnosing NF2?
options: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or a relative with NF2 plus other NF2 lesions
Six or more café-au-lait macules over 15 mm in diameter
A single cutaneous neurofibroma on the trunk
Ash-leaf macules seen under a Wood's lamp
A facial port-wine stain in the V1 distribution
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or a relative with NF2 plus other NF2 lesions
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: The key criterion is bilateral vestibular schwannomas — or a first-degree relative with NF2 plus either a unilateral acoustic neuroma, or two other NF2-associated lesions (meningioma, schwannoma, ependymoma, or a juvenile posterior subcapsular cataract).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: As an acoustic neuroma in NF2 enlarges at the cerebellopontine angle, which additional cranial nerves are most likely to be affected?
options: CN VII (facial) and CN V (trigeminal — loss of corneal reflex)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: CN VII (facial) and CN V (trigeminal — loss of corneal reflex)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Enlarging acoustic neuromas compress the adjacent facial nerve (CN VII → facial palsy) and trigeminal nerve (CN V → loss of the corneal reflex), and eventually the brainstem/cerebellum.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: When deciding on surgery or radiosurgery for the acoustic neuromas of NF2, what is the central management trade-off?
options: Whether to use general or local anaesthesia
Controlling tumour growth versus preserving hearing and facial-nerve function
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Controlling tumour growth versus preserving hearing and facial-nerve function
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Interventions carry a heavy risk of permanent nerve damage, so timing balances tumour control against preserving hearing and the facial nerve; small/stable tumours may just be observed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A parent has NF2. What is the risk to each child, and how does this guide care?
options: 50% (autosomal dominant); screen at-risk relatives and offer genetic counselling
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: 50% (autosomal dominant); screen at-risk relatives and offer genetic counselling
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: NF2 is autosomal dominant with a 50% risk to offspring, so genetic counselling and screening of at-risk relatives are offered.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A 2-year-old with developmental delay has had seizures since infancy (initially infantile spasms). Examination shows several hypopigmented oval skin patches and pink papules across the cheeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Epilepsy (infantile spasms) + learning disability + ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas is the classic picture of tuberous sclerosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: What is the genetic and molecular basis of tuberous sclerosis?
options: Chromosome 22, coding for the tumour suppressor protein merlin
Chromosome 17, coding for the tumour suppressor protein neurofibromin
TSC1 (chromosome 9, hamartin) or TSC2 (chromosome 16, tuberin) → overactive mTOR
A CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion within the DMPK gene
Chromosome 3, coding for the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) protein
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: TSC1 (chromosome 9, hamartin) or TSC2 (chromosome 16, tuberin) → overactive mTOR
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: TSC is caused by TSC1 (hamartin, chr 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chr 16); loss disinhibits the mTOR pathway, driving hamartoma growth.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which examination tool helps reveal the ash-leaf macules of tuberous sclerosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: A Wood's (ultraviolet) lamp
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Ash-leaf macules are hypopigmented patches that are accentuated under a Wood's (UV) lamp — they do not fluoresce; the surrounding skin absorbs the UV so the pale patch stands out. They are present from birth or infancy and are often the earliest cutaneous sign of TSC.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: An infant with tuberous sclerosis develops infantile spasms (West syndrome). What is the first-line treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Vigabatrin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Vigabatrin is first-line for infantile spasms specifically in tuberous sclerosis — for spasms not due to TSC, prednisolone is combined with it. Warn about visual field constriction, which occurs in up to a third and is usually irreversible: visual assessment is needed before starting and 6-monthly after. Suspected infantile spasms need paediatric neurology referral within 24 hours.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient with TSC has an enlarging subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) and a large renal angiomyolipoma. Which class of drug directly targets the underlying pathway?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: mTOR inhibitors (everolimus/sirolimus)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: mTOR inhibitors act directly on the pathway left unchecked by loss of hamartin or tuberin — everolimus for SEGA and renal angiomyolipoma, sirolimus for LAM.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A child with tuberous sclerosis develops worsening headaches, vomiting and drowsiness. MRI shows an enlarging lesion near the foramen of Monro. What has most likely happened?
options: Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis has developed in the lungs
A renal angiomyolipoma has bled, causing pain and haematuria
A cardiac rhabdomyoma has enlarged and is obstructing outflow
A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is obstructing CSF flow → hydrocephalus
An ash-leaf macule has undergone malignant transformation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma is obstructing CSF flow → hydrocephalus
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: A SEGA near the foramen of Monro can obstruct CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus — presenting with raised-ICP features and needing mTOR inhibitor or surgery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which renal lesion of tuberous sclerosis characteristically risks bleeding (haematuria/haemorrhage)?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Angiomyolipoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Renal angiomyolipomas in TSC can bleed, causing haematuria or haemorrhage; large or bleeding lesions are treated with an mTOR inhibitor or embolisation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A fetus/neonate with a family history of tuberous sclerosis is found to have a cardiac tumour on echocardiography. Which tumour is this most likely to be, and what is its usual course?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Rhabdomyoma; usually regresses spontaneously
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are the characteristic cardiac lesion of TSC, often detected antenatally/in infancy and usually regressing spontaneously.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which pulmonary complication of tuberous sclerosis characteristically affects women?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — cystic lung disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a cystic lung disease, occurs in TSC especially in women, and responds to mTOR inhibitors.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A patient has roughened, thickened 'orange-peel' skin over the lower back. What is this lesion called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: A shagreen patch
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: A shagreen patch is the roughened, thickened 'orange-peel' skin (usually over the lower back) seen in tuberous sclerosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: Which triad is classically associated with tuberous sclerosis?
options: Café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules and neurofibromas
Bilateral acoustic neuromas, cataracts and meningiomas
Epilepsy, learning disability and facial angiofibromas
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Epilepsy, learning disability and facial angiofibromas
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: The classic 'Vogt triad' of tuberous sclerosis is epilepsy + learning disability + facial angiofibromas.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: How do hamartin and tuberin normally act, and what results from their loss in TSC?
options: They inhibit the mTOR pathway; loss causes mTOR overactivity and uncontrolled cell growth
They activate mTOR; loss reduces cell growth
They repair DNA; loss causes cancers only
They form part of the cell membrane; loss causes haemolysis
They transport copper; loss causes copper accumulation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: They inhibit the mTOR pathway; loss causes mTOR overactivity and uncontrolled cell growth
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: Hamartin (TSC1) and tuberin (TSC2) inhibit mTOR; their loss disinhibits mTOR, driving the hamartomatous growth of TSC — the rationale for mTOR inhibitors.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.question: A child has seizures and a facial birthmark. Which feature would point to tuberous sclerosis rather than Sturge–Weber syndrome?
options: A port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution
Hypopigmented ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas with renal angiomyolipomas
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.answer: Hypopigmented ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas with renal angiomyolipomas
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Ne.explanation: TSC features ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas and multi-organ hamartomas; Sturge–Weber is characterised by a facial port-wine stain (capillary malformation) with seizures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A 4-year-old boy has a waddling gait, difficulty climbing stairs, and stands from the floor by pushing his hands up his thighs. His calves look bulky and his CK is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: A young boy with proximal weakness, Gower's sign, calf pseudohypertrophy and a very high CK is the classic picture of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (absent dystrophin).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: What is the mode of inheritance of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Duchenne (and Becker) muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive, so each son of a carrier mother has a 50% risk. Note that about a third of cases arise de novo, so a negative family history does not exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A boy stands from the floor by 'walking' his hands up his own legs. What is this sign, and what does it indicate?
options: Trendelenburg sign; hip abductor weakness only
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Gower's sign — using the hands to climb up the legs to stand — reflects proximal/pelvic-girdle weakness, classic for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy affect the same gene. What accounts for Duchenne being the more severe?
options: Duchenne spares cardiac muscle, so patients survive far longer than in Becker
Duchenne affects a completely different structural protein of the muscle fibre
Becker is X-linked whereas Duchenne is inherited in an autosomal manner
Duchenne's frameshift leaves NO dystrophin; Becker's in-frame leaves some
Becker has absent dystrophin while Duchenne has merely reduced dystrophin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Duchenne's frameshift leaves NO dystrophin; Becker's in-frame leaves some
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Both affect dystrophin; DMD's frameshift mutation abolishes dystrophin (severe/early), whereas BMD's in-frame mutation leaves partially functional dystrophin (milder/later).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: What are the leading causes of death in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: Renal failure and haemorrhagic stroke in early adult life
Massive gastrointestinal bleeding from steroid-related ulceration
Malignancy arising within the degenerating skeletal muscle
Recurrent seizures progressing to status epilepticus
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Progressive cardiac (dilated cardiomyopathy) and respiratory muscle involvement determine prognosis and are the leading causes of death, so both are monitored.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which investigation is definitive for diagnosing Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Genetic testing of the dystrophin gene
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: A markedly raised CK supports the diagnosis, but genetic testing of the dystrophin gene is definitive; muscle biopsy shows absent dystrophin.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which treatment is used to slow progression in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Corticosteroids slow progression in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. They also cause weight gain, growth suppression, vertebral fractures and adrenal suppression, so every boy needs a steroid emergency card and sick-day rules and must never stop them abruptly. Overall management is supportive and multidisciplinary.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A 30-year-old man cannot release his grip after a handshake and is slow to open his eyes after screwing them shut. He has ptosis, frontal balding and bilateral cataracts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Myotonia (delayed relaxation — an inability to release the grip), with distal/facial weakness, ptosis, frontal balding and cataracts, is characteristic of myotonic dystrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which systemic complication of myotonic dystrophy most importantly requires ECG monitoring?
options: Diabetes mellitus, which is part of the endocrine picture
Cataracts, which are an early and characteristic finding
Frontal balding, a recognised part of the phenotype
Cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias, which may need a pacemaker
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias, which may need a pacemaker
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy causes cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias, a leading cause of death, so ECG monitoring and sometimes a pacemaker are needed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Myotonic dystrophy is a trinucleotide-repeat disorder. Which feature does this explain, where onset is earlier and disease more severe down the generations?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy (CTG repeat in DMPK) shows anticipation — earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations as the repeat expands.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient has proximal muscle weakness, normal sensation and a very high CK, with no fasciculations. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: The lower motor neurone (anterior horn cell)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Proximal weakness with normal sensation and a very high CK points to a myopathy/dystrophy. Fasciculations with mixed UMN/LMN signs and a CK that is at most mildly raised would suggest MND, and fatigability the neuromuscular junction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A 20-year-old man is still walking but has slowly progressive proximal weakness and a raised CK; genetic testing shows an in-frame dystrophin mutation. Even with mild skeletal weakness, what must be monitored?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Becker muscular dystrophy (in-frame dystrophin mutation) is milder in skeletal terms, but dilated cardiomyopathy still occurs and can be significant, so cardiac surveillance is essential.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the calves appear enlarged. What is the basis of this 'pseudohypertrophy'?
options: Replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Calf pseudohypertrophy in DMD is due to replacement of degenerating muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, not true muscle growth.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient with fatigable weakness that worsens through the day, with ptosis and diplopia but a normal CK, is unlikely to have a muscular dystrophy. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy presenting atypically late
Myotonic dystrophy with early bulbar involvement
Myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder
Becker muscular dystrophy with ocular involvement
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy of adult onset
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia and a normal CK is myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder. Note that a normal CK does not by itself exclude every dystrophy — it is normal or only mildly raised in myotonic dystrophy too; it is the fatigability and ocular involvement that make this myasthenia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A mother is a known carrier of the Duchenne dystrophin mutation. What is the risk to each of her sons?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: In X-linked recessive inheritance, each son of a carrier mother has a 50% chance of being affected (and each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A 29-year-old woman develops subacute loss of vision in one eye over a few days, with pain on eye movement and reduced colour vision; there is a relative afferent pupillary defect. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis to consider?
