options: Acute angle-closure glaucoma with a red, painful eye and haloes
Central retinal artery occlusion from a carotid embolus
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis
Migraine with a prolonged and predominantly visual aura
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Painful subacute unilateral visual loss with reduced colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect is optic neuritis — the classic first presentation of MS. Note that standard-dose oral prednisolone must not be used: it does not improve the visual outcome and increases the recurrence rate.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: What is required to diagnose multiple sclerosis (McDonald criteria)?
options: Lesions disseminated in space AND time
A single episode of optic neuritis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Lesions disseminated in space AND time
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: MS requires dissemination in space (≥2 CNS sites) and time (≥2 episodes, or MRI/CSF evidence); a single attack in one site is a clinically isolated syndrome.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A young patient has impaired adduction of the left eye with nystagmus of the right (abducting) eye on lateral gaze. What is this sign, and what does it suggest?
options: A third-nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
A sixth-nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a lesion of the MLF
Horner's syndrome from a lesion in the sympathetic chain
Ocular myasthenia gravis with fatigable extraocular weakness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a lesion of the MLF
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus is an INO (MLF lesion); bilateral INO in a young person is highly suggestive of MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient with MS reports an electric-shock sensation running down the spine whenever they flex their neck. What is this called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Lhermitte's sign — an electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion — reflects dorsal column demyelination in MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient with MS notices their symptoms transiently worsen after a hot bath or exercise. What is this phenomenon?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Uhthoff's phenomenon is transient worsening of MS symptoms with heat (hot bath, exercise, fever); it is not a true relapse.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which is the commonest disease course of multiple sclerosis?
options: Primary progressive MS, in which disability accrues from onset
Secondary progressive MS, which follows a relapsing phase
Clinically isolated syndrome that never evolves any further
A radiologically isolated syndrome found incidentally on MRI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Relapsing-remitting MS is the commonest pattern (~85%), with discrete relapses and remissions and no progression in between. Most eventually transition to secondary progressive disease; primary progressive MS accounts for ~10–15% from the outset.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which statement best defines an MS relapse?
options: New symptoms lasting >24 hours, with no infection or fever
Any neurological symptom lasting a few minutes and then settling
Symptoms that occur only in the presence of a fever or infection
A fixed, permanent neurological deficit present from birth
A severe headache with photophobia and neck stiffness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: New symptoms lasting >24 hours, with no infection or fever
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: A relapse is new neurological symptoms lasting >24 hours in the absence of infection/fever; heat- or infection-related worsening (a 'pseudorelapse') does not count.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: An MRI brain in suspected MS shows ovoid periventricular white-matter lesions radiating perpendicular to the ventricles. What is this appearance called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Periventricular demyelinating plaques oriented perpendicular to the ventricles are 'Dawson's fingers', characteristic of MS on MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A lumbar puncture is performed in suspected MS. Which CSF finding supports the diagnosis?
options: Oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not in serum
Oligoclonal bands present equally in CSF and serum
A neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not in serum
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Oligoclonal IgG bands in the CSF but not the serum indicate intrathecal inflammation and support MS (they can substitute for dissemination in time).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient has an MS relapse causing disabling weakness. Infection has been excluded and a specialist advises treating. What does NICE recommend?
options: Interferon-beta started that day to bring the relapse under control
Oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days
Plasma exchange, which is first-line for every disabling relapse
Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily, tapered over the next 3 months
No treatment at all, since steroids alter the long-term course
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: NICE offers oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days. IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days is the alternative where oral steroids have failed or were not tolerated, or where the person needs admission for a severe relapse or for monitoring. A lower dose must not be substituted. Steroids shorten the relapse but do not change long-term disability; plasma exchange is for steroid-refractory relapses.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: What is the role of disease-modifying therapy in relapsing-remitting MS?
options: To cure the disease and halt demyelination permanently
To abort an acute relapse more quickly than steroids do
To treat spasticity and the associated painful spasms
To reduce relapse frequency and slow disability accrual
To correct the vitamin D deficiency underlying the disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: To reduce relapse frequency and slow disability accrual
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: DMTs reduce relapse frequency and slow progression, and early effective treatment reduces long-term disability. They do not abort acute relapses — that is what steroids are for — and they are started and monitored by a specialist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: Which disease-modifying therapy is the main option shown to benefit primary progressive MS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Ocrelizumab is the main disease-modifying therapy shown to help primary progressive MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient has severe optic neuritis and a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, with poor recovery between episodes. What should be considered rather than MS?
options: Guillain–Barré syndrome, which also causes ascending weakness
Vitamin B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder or MOG-antibody disease
Neurosarcoidosis with cranial nerve and meningeal involvement
Lyme disease with a painful radiculitis and facial palsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder or MOG-antibody disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Severe or bilateral optic neuritis, a longitudinally extensive myelitis and poor recovery point away from MS. Test aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies: both NMOSD and MOG-antibody disease are treated differently, and some MS disease-modifying drugs make them worse.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient has a progressive myelopathy with sensory ataxia and both dorsal column and pyramidal signs. Which reversible mimic of MS should be excluded with a blood test?
options: Hypothyroidism, which can cause a reversible cerebellar syndrome
Copper deficiency, which mimics subacute combined degeneration
HIV infection, which causes a vacuolar myelopathy
Hypercalcaemia, causing proximal weakness and confusion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration — dorsal column plus pyramidal signs — and is a reversible mimic of MS. Copper deficiency and HIV produce very similar myelopathies and are the other two to remember. In any acute myelopathy, exclude structural cord compression with urgent MRI first.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A young woman has a first episode of optic neuritis with a normal brain MRI and no other lesions. How is this best classified?
options: Definite multiple sclerosis, since optic neuritis is diagnostic
A clinically isolated syndrome, which may progress to MS
Primary progressive MS, given the absence of prior relapses
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder with an isolated attack
A migraine variant producing a prolonged monocular visual aura
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.answer: A clinically isolated syndrome, which may progress to MS
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: A single attack in a single site without dissemination in space/time is a clinically isolated syndrome; it may or may not progress to MS.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient with MS has troublesome limb stiffness and spasticity affecting mobility. Which is an appropriate first-line symptomatic treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Spasticity in MS is treated symptomatically with baclofen (or gabapentin) and physiotherapy; amantadine is for fatigue and anticholinergics for bladder symptoms.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.question: A patient with a severe MS relapse shows no improvement after a full course of high-dose corticosteroids. What is the next appropriate step?
options: Repeat the identical steroid course again immediately
Start baclofen to treat the resulting spasticity instead
Give high-dose vitamin D and review again in three months
Switch to a long-term oral prednisolone maintenance dose
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mu.explanation: Plasma exchange is used for severe MS relapses that have not responded to a full course of high-dose corticosteroids. It is a specialist decision.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A 60-year-old man has 8 months of progressive weakness. Examination shows wasting and fasciculations in the hands with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars in the legs; sensation and eye movements are entirely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Mixed UMN (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) and LMN (wasting, fasciculations) signs with NO sensory loss and spared eye movements is the near-unique signature of motor neurone disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Which set of signs represents lower motor neurone involvement?
options: Muscle wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone and reduced reflexes
A sensory level and sphincter disturbance
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Muscle wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone and reduced reflexes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: LMN signs are wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia and hyporeflexia; spasticity, hyperreflexia and upgoing plantars are UMN signs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A patient with MND presents predominantly with dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech and a wasted, fasciculating tongue. Which subtype does this represent, and what is its prognostic significance?
options: Primary lateral sclerosis; the slowest course of all the subtypes
Progressive muscular atrophy; a pure lower motor neurone picture
Progressive bulbar palsy; the worst prognosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; the commonest subtype overall
These are not features of motor neurone disease at all
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Progressive bulbar palsy; the worst prognosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech and a wasted fasciculating tongue are progressive bulbar palsy, which carries the worst prognosis. Primary lateral sclerosis (pure UMN) has the best prognosis, often more than 10 years; progressive muscular atrophy is pure LMN and sits in between.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Which feature most reliably distinguishes MND from myasthenia gravis?
options: Both cause weakness, but only MND causes any muscle wasting
MND causes fatigable weakness that worsens through the day
MND is associated with prominent distal sensory loss
MND spares the extraocular muscles; myasthenia involves them
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: MND spares the extraocular muscles; myasthenia involves them
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Extraocular involvement is the discriminator: ptosis and diplopia are typical of myasthenia gravis and are essentially never the presentation of MND. Fatigability belongs to myasthenia; fasciculations belong to MND; neither condition causes sensory loss.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A patient with suspected MND has weakness but also reports a sensory level and bladder disturbance. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose MND and start riluzole without further investigation
MRI of the spine, to exclude cervical cord compression
Start non-invasive ventilation for the respiratory weakness
Give intravenous immunoglobulin for multifocal motor neuropathy
Reassure and review him again in twelve months' time
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: MRI of the spine, to exclude cervical cord compression
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: A sensory level and bladder disturbance are red flags AGAINST MND, which is pure motor and spares the sphincters until late. Cervical myelopathy is the mimic that produces mixed UMN and LMN signs with sensory and sphincter involvement, and it is treatable — so image the cord.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Electromyography in MND characteristically shows which pattern?
options: Reduced numbers of action potentials with increased amplitude
Conduction block with slowing of motor conduction velocity
Myotonic discharges with a waxing and waning frequency
A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
A completely normal study with no denervation changes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Reduced numbers of action potentials with increased amplitude
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: EMG in MND shows fewer but larger motor units (reduced number of action potentials with increased amplitude), reflecting denervation and reinnervation; motor conduction is normal.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Riluzole is offered to a patient with ALS. What is its mechanism and expected benefit?
options: A glutamate release inhibitor that extends survival by about 3 months
An anticholinesterase that markedly and rapidly improves muscle strength
A corticosteroid that halts progression of the underlying disease
A dopamine agonist that improves the associated tremor and rigidity
An antiviral that treats the retroviral cause of the condition
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: A glutamate release inhibitor that extends survival by about 3 months
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Riluzole is a glutamate release inhibitor, reducing excitotoxicity. Be precise about the benefit: it extends survival, or the time to mechanical ventilation, by around 3 months. It does not slow symptomatic progression or improve strength. Monitor LFTs because it is hepatotoxic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A patient with MND has worsening breathlessness and orthopnoea. FVC is 45% predicted. What is indicated?
options: Long-term oral corticosteroids to reduce airway inflammation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for a presumed chest infection
Long-term oxygen therapy delivered through nasal cannulae
A course of inspiratory muscle training physiotherapy alone
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: An FVC below 50% predicted is a threshold for referral for NIV, which improves both survival and quality of life. Note the trap in option 4: respiratory failure in MND is ventilatory, not a problem of oxygenation, so oxygen alone worsens CO2 retention and must not be given without specialist advice.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A patient with MND is losing weight and struggling to swallow. FVC is 55% predicted. What is the correct approach to nutrition?
options: Encourage larger oral meals and high-calorie supplements only
Long-term parenteral nutrition as the first-choice route
Refer for gastrostomy now, rather than waiting for it to worsen
A pureed diet with thickened fluids and no other intervention
No intervention, since nutrition does not influence prognosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Refer for gastrostomy now, rather than waiting for it to worsen
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Gastrostomy should be discussed early and acted on without delay, because late placement — once respiratory function has fallen — carries substantially higher procedural risk. Route follows respiratory function: PEG while it is preserved, RIG once FVC is below about 50% predicted.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: What is the usual cause of death in motor neurone disease, and the typical timescale?
options: Sudden cardiac death, typically within weeks of the diagnosis
Respiratory failure or pneumonia, usually within 2–4 years
A massive ischaemic stroke within a few months of onset
Progressive renal failure developing over several decades
Refractory status epilepticus in the terminal phase
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Respiratory failure or pneumonia, usually within 2–4 years
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Patients with MND typically die of respiratory failure or pneumonia, usually within 2–4 years of onset.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Which combination of findings would argue AGAINST a diagnosis of MND?
options: Wasting and fasciculations together with brisk reflexes
Progressive painless weakness of one limb spreading over months
Dysarthria and dysphagia with a wasted, fasciculating tongue
Prominent sensory loss with sphincter and eye involvement
Upgoing plantars with hyperreflexia and increased limb tone
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Prominent sensory loss with sphincter and eye involvement
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: MND is pure motor, eye-sparing and sphincter-sparing; sensory loss, sphincter disturbance or abnormal eye movements should prompt a search for a mimic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: A patient has purely upper motor neurone signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) with a very slow course and no LMN features. Which MND subtype is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Pure UMN signs with the slowest course are primary lateral sclerosis; pure LMN signs would be progressive muscular atrophy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Which single examination combination is regarded as the hallmark of MND?
options: A wasted, fasciculating limb with brisk reflexes and normal sensation
Glove-and-stocking sensory loss with symmetrically absent reflexes
Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with a decremental EMG response
A resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity and reduced arm swing
A sensory level at T10 with a spastic bladder and brisk reflexes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: A wasted, fasciculating limb with brisk reflexes and normal sensation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: The coexistence of LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations) and UMN signs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) with preserved sensation is the hallmark of MND.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.question: Which aspect of care should be introduced early in MND, and why?
options: Aggressive immunosuppression, to slow the immune-mediated damage
Prophylactic antibiotics for life, to prevent aspiration pneumonia
Palliative care and advance care planning, while capacity allows
Routine deep brain stimulation, before the disease progresses
Long-term corticosteroids, to preserve remaining muscle bulk
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.answer: Palliative care and advance care planning, while capacity allows
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mo.explanation: Palliative care and advance care planning are introduced early, not at the end — ventilation wishes, an advance decision to refuse treatment, DNACPR and preferred place of death all need deciding while the person has capacity. That matters especially here, because up to half of people with MND develop cognitive or behavioural change.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A 19-year-old student has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and photophobia but is fully orientated. A flatmate had similar symptoms. Which process does this picture point to?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Meningism — headache, neck stiffness and photophobia — with preserved higher function points to meningitis (inflamed meninges); altered brain function would suggest encephalitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A previously well 24-year-old develops fever with confusion, personality change and a seizure over two days, but no neck stiffness. Which diagnosis and immediate treatment are most appropriate?
options: Encephalitis (likely HSV); IV aciclovir plus antibiotic cover
Bacterial meningitis; IV ceftriaxone alone with no antiviral
A functional or psychiatric illness; refer him to psychiatry
A complex migraine with aura; give a triptan and reassess
A first unprovoked seizure; arrange outpatient EEG and MRI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Encephalitis (likely HSV); IV aciclovir plus antibiotic cover
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Altered brain function — confusion, personality change, seizures — points to encephalitis, most importantly HSV, so IV aciclovir is started empirically without waiting for the PCR. But you cannot separate meningitis from encephalitis at the bedside, so a febrile encephalopathic patient gets antibiotics as well until you know: cover both.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A lumbar puncture in a septic, febrile patient shows turbid CSF with markedly raised neutrophils, very high protein and a low CSF:blood glucose ratio. What does this indicate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Turbid CSF with neutrophil predominance, high protein and low glucose is the classic picture of bacterial meningitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: CSF from a patient with meningitis is clear with a lymphocytosis, normal glucose and only mildly raised protein. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Bacterial meningitis, with a partially treated picture
Tuberculous meningitis with a fibrin web on standing
A subarachnoid haemorrhage with xanthochromic CSF
Cryptococcal meningitis in an immunocompromised host
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: A clear, lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose and near-normal protein is typical of viral meningitis, commonly enteroviral. Be careful with the reverse inference, though: very early bacterial meningitis — and Listeria in particular — can give a lymphocytic CSF, so a lymphocyte predominance does not by itself exclude bacterial disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A patient with a subacute meningitis has CSF showing a fibrin web, lymphocytes, very high protein and low glucose. Which cause does this most suggest?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: A fibrin web with a lymphocytic, high-protein, low-glucose CSF is characteristic of TB (or fungal) meningitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A 70-year-old with confusion and neck stiffness is diagnosed with bacterial meningitis. Beyond IV ceftriaxone, what should be added and why?
options: Vancomycin, to cover meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Metronidazole, to cover anaerobic organisms in the CSF
Gentamicin, to cover Pseudomonas and other Gram negatives
Flucloxacillin, to cover Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: From the age of 60, Listeria becomes a risk that cephalosporins do not cover, so IV amoxicillin is added. The same applies to babies under 3 months, in pregnancy, and in the immunocompromised.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A child has fever and a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash that does not fade under a glass. What is the immediate pre-hospital action?
options: Give IM benzylpenicillin and arrange urgent transfer, unless it would delay it
Give oral paracetamol and arrange a review the following morning
Wait to see whether the rash blanches before taking any action
Perform a lumbar puncture at home to confirm the diagnosis first
Give an oral antihistamine and refer routinely to dermatology
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Give IM benzylpenicillin and arrange urgent transfer, unless it would delay it
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: A non-blanching rash suggests meningococcal septicaemia — a life-threatening emergency. Give IM or IV benzylpenicillin (under 1 year 300 mg, 1–9 years 600 mg, 10 years and over 1.2 g) and transfer urgently. The critical caveat is that giving it must never delay the transfer.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: During examination of a patient with suspected meningitis, passive neck flexion causes involuntary flexion of the hips and knees. What is this sign?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Brudzinski's sign is involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion; Kernig's is pain on knee extension with the hip flexed — both are signs of meningeal irritation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis has a GCS of 8 and new focal neurological signs. What is the correct sequence?
options: Lumbar puncture first, then start the antibiotics once CSF is obtained
Withhold antibiotics until both the CT and the lumbar puncture are done
Start antibiotics only if the CT head is reported as abnormal
Blood cultures, antibiotics immediately, then CT before any LP
Lumbar puncture now, with antibiotics held pending the CSF result
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Blood cultures, antibiotics immediately, then CT before any LP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: A GCS of 9 or less, or new focal neurology, means imaging before lumbar puncture — but antibiotics come first. Take blood cultures, give the antibiotics, then image. Most patients with suspected bacterial meningitis need no scan before LP at all; this patient does.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: What is the first-line empirical hospital antibiotic for suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult?
options: Oral benzylpenicillin, given as a stat dose in the department
Oral amoxicillin, with a switch to IV if there is no response
IV aciclovir, with antibiotics added only if cultures grow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: IV ceftriaxone is first-line empirical treatment, started within an hour. Amoxicillin is added from the age of 60, in pregnancy, in the immunocompromised and in every baby under 3 months, to cover Listeria. Cefotaxime replaces ceftriaxone in neonates who are jaundiced, acidotic, pre-term or on calcium-containing infusions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A 30-year-old has bacterial meningitis with a non-blanching purpuric rash and meningococcus is confirmed. What is the position on dexamethasone?
options: Give it with the first antibiotic dose, as in all bacterial meningitis
Do not routinely give corticosteroids in meningococcal disease
Give it, but only once the antibiotics have been running for 24 hours
Give a single high dose to prevent sensorineural hearing loss
Give it only if the patient develops a cranial nerve palsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Do not routinely give corticosteroids in meningococcal disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Dexamethasone is given in bacterial meningitis over 3 months of age, with the greatest benefit in pneumococcal disease. Meningococcal disease is the exception: corticosteroids are not routinely given, as they do not help and have been associated with higher mortality. The only steroid role there is low-dose replacement in septic shock unresponsive to high-dose vasoactive drugs.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A patient is diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. What is required regarding close contacts?
options: Notify public health; give close contacts single-dose ciprofloxacin
No action is needed, as person-to-person spread does not occur
Admit every household contact for intravenous antibiotic treatment
Give all contacts a three-month course of oral penicillin V
Isolate the contacts for three weeks without any drug treatment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Notify public health; give close contacts single-dose ciprofloxacin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Meningococcal disease is notifiable, and close contacts receive chemoprophylaxis — a single dose of ciprofloxacin, suitable at any age including pregnancy, ideally within 24 hours (rifampicin is the alternative). Contacts are also offered vaccination where the serogroup is vaccine-preventable. Note that contacts of pneumococcal, group B streptococcal or viral meningitis need no prophylaxis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: Which is the commonest long-term complication of bacterial meningitis, warranting routine follow-up?
options: Blindness from bilateral optic nerve infarction during the illness
Parkinsonism from basal ganglia damage in the acute phase
A peripheral neuropathy affecting all four limbs symmetrically
Cranial diabetes insipidus from posterior pituitary involvement
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest complication of bacterial meningitis, so audiology follow-up is routine (and dexamethasone helps reduce it).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A patient with fulminant meningococcal septicaemia develops shock with adrenal haemorrhage. What is this syndrome called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage complicating severe meningococcal septicaemia, causing adrenal failure and shock.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A patient with suspected HSV encephalitis has an MRI. Which finding would be most characteristic?
options: Normal appearances that exclude the diagnosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: HSV encephalitis characteristically involves the temporal lobes, seen as oedema/hyperintensity on MRI; CSF HSV PCR is the diagnostic test.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: Regarding the diagnostic test for HSV encephalitis, which statement is correct?
options: A single negative CSF HSV PCR reliably excludes it at any stage
Blood cultures are the definitive diagnostic test for HSV
Only a brain biopsy can establish the diagnosis with certainty
CSF HSV PCR is diagnostic but can be negative very early
EEG is the definitive test and should precede any treatment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: CSF HSV PCR is diagnostic but can be negative very early
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: CSF HSV PCR is the diagnostic test but can be falsely negative very early in the illness, so empirical IV aciclovir (10 mg/kg 8-hourly) is started immediately and continued if HSV is confirmed — 14 days in the immunocompetent, 21 days if immunocompromised.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: A young woman develops psychiatric symptoms, seizures and a movement disorder, with an encephalitic picture and negative viral PCR. Which diagnosis should be considered, and what does it prompt?
options: Bacterial meningitis; add amoxicillin for Listeria cover
A prolonged migraine aura; start a triptan and reassess
A functional neurological disorder; refer to psychiatry
A first presentation of temporal lobe epilepsy; start an antiepileptic
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is a key non-infective cause presenting with psychiatric features, seizures and movement disorder; it is treated with immunotherapy (steroids/IVIG) and a search for an underlying tumour.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.question: Which clinical feature best steers you towards encephalitis rather than meningitis?
options: Neck stiffness on passive flexion of the neck
Photophobia with a severe frontal headache
Altered brain function — confusion, personality change or seizures
A non-blanching purpuric rash over the trunk and limbs
A positive Kernig's sign with pain on knee extension
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.answer: Altered brain function — confusion, personality change or seizures
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Me.explanation: Altered brain function — confusion, personality change, seizures, focal deficits — points to encephalitis, whereas neck stiffness, photophobia, rash and Kernig's sign point to meningitis. The two overlap as meningoencephalitis, so if in doubt cover both.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A 48-year-old has recurrent attacks of severe rotational vertigo lasting about an hour, each with nausea, ringing and a sense of fullness in the left ear, and fluctuating hearing loss on that side. Between attacks she is well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Episodic vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is the classic triad plus aural fullness of Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops). Attacks shorter than 20 minutes suggest BPPV or a TIA; attacks running well beyond 12 hours, especially with headache or photophobia, suggest vestibular migraine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: What is the underlying pathophysiological abnormality in Ménière's disease?
options: Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth)
Otoconia displaced into a semicircular canal
A vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle
Reactivation of varicella-zoster in the geniculate ganglion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: Endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Ménière's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops — excess endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth, disrupting cochlear and vestibular function.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A 60-year-old has brief spells of vertigo lasting under a minute, triggered each time by rolling over in bed or looking up, with no hearing loss or tinnitus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Ménière's disease, given the recurrent rotational attacks
Labyrinthitis following a recent upper respiratory infection
Acoustic neuroma compressing the vestibulocochlear nerve
Vestibular migraine, given the recurrent stereotyped spells
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Brief, positionally triggered vertigo lasting seconds with no hearing loss is BPPV; Dix-Hallpike is positive and the Epley manoeuvre is the treatment.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient has acute, constant vertigo lasting several days after a recent viral upper respiratory infection, with no hearing loss or tinnitus. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Prolonged (days) acute vertigo after a viral illness without hearing loss is vestibular neuronitis; adding hearing loss would make it labyrinthitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient with CONTINUOUS acute vertigo has a HINTS examination. Which pattern is reassuringly peripheral rather than central?
options: Gaze-evoked nystagmus in all directions with limb ataxia
A normal head impulse test with direction-changing nystagmus on gaze
Vertical nystagmus with a skew deviation on cover-uncover testing
A normal head impulse test together with a skew deviation
An abnormal head impulse, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: An abnormal head impulse, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: HINTS is valid ONLY in the acute vestibular syndrome — continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus, present at the moment you examine — which is why the stem specifies continuous vertigo. It is uninterpretable in episodic or positional vertigo such as BPPV. The reassuringly peripheral pattern is an ABNORMAL head impulse (a corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus and no skew. A normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, or a skew deviation each point central. A 'peripheral' result never overrules other neurological signs or new hearing loss — AICA infarction causes vertigo with sudden deafness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient with acute vertigo also has limb ataxia, diplopia and a normal head impulse test. What must be urgently excluded?
options: Ménière's disease with an unusually prolonged attack
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the posterior canal
Otitis externa with secondary vestibular irritation
A simple vasovagal faint with post-episode unsteadiness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Persistent vertigo with other neurology (ataxia, diplopia) and a normal head impulse points to a central cause — a posterior circulation stroke must be excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: Which investigation is most useful to confirm and characterise the hearing loss of Ménière's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Audiometry confirms a sensorineural pattern of hearing loss (typically low-frequency and fluctuating early), the key test in Ménière's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and episodic vertigo is referred. Why is an MRI often arranged?
options: To exclude an acoustic neuroma and central causes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: To exclude an acoustic neuroma and central causes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: MRI is used to exclude an acoustic neuroma (a cause of unilateral SNHL) and central pathology before settling on a diagnosis of Ménière's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: What is the most appropriate treatment for an acute attack of Ménière's vertigo with vomiting?
options: Oral corticosteroids continued for a six-week course
Long-term daily betahistine, started during the acute attack
Intratympanic gentamicin given immediately at presentation
A short course of prochlorperazine, given buccally or intramuscularly
The Epley manoeuvre performed at the bedside straight away
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: A short course of prochlorperazine, given buccally or intramuscularly
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: An acute Ménière's attack with vomiting is treated with a vestibular sedative/antiemetic — prochlorperazine, given BUCCALLY or INTRAMUSCULARLY because the patient cannot reliably absorb an oral dose. Keep it to a short course, a maximum of about 7 days: longer use delays central vestibular compensation and worsens the chronic imbalance. Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine, so warn about extrapyramidal effects. Betahistine is prophylaxis, not acute treatment; intratympanic gentamicin is a refractory specialist option; and the Epley treats BPPV.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: Which combination is first-line for reducing the frequency of Ménière's attacks?
options: Betahistine plus a low-salt diet (± reduced caffeine/alcohol)
Intratympanic gentamicin plus endolymphatic sac surgery
Aspirin plus a high-intensity statin for vascular risk
The Epley manoeuvre plus a course of oral antibiotics
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: Betahistine plus a low-salt diet (± reduced caffeine/alcohol)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Prophylaxis is betahistine (the usual UK choice, given as a trial) with lifestyle measures — a low-salt diet and reduced caffeine/alcohol. Diuretics are not routinely used in the UK: they are unlicensed for this and there is no good evidence of benefit.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient with disabling Ménière's disease refractory to medical therapy is offered intratympanic gentamicin. What is the key risk to counsel about?
options: Acute kidney injury requiring monitoring of renal function
Permanent facial nerve palsy from injury to the chorda tympani
Ototoxicity with a risk of hearing loss (it ablates vestibular function)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: Ototoxicity with a risk of hearing loss (it ablates vestibular function)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Intratympanic gentamicin ablates vestibular function but is ototoxic, carrying a risk of hearing loss — an important counselling point in refractory disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: What specific driving advice should be given to a patient with active Ménière's disease?
options: Notification is needed only for a bus or lorry licence
They should stop driving for four weeks but need not notify the DVLA
They may keep driving provided a companion travels with them
They may continue to drive as long as they carry their medication
They must inform the DVLA and stop driving until symptoms are controlled
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.answer: They must inform the DVLA and stop driving until symptoms are controlled
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: The DVLA must be told of any liability to sudden, unprovoked or unprecipitated disabling giddiness. A Group 1 (car) driver must stop driving and notify, and may be relicensed once symptoms are satisfactorily controlled; Group 2 (bus and lorry) standards are stricter, but notification is not limited to Group 2. By contrast, vertigo that is provoked and positional (BPPV) and is controlled does not usually require notification.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.question: A patient with long-standing Ménière's disease describes sudden falls to the ground without warning or loss of consciousness. What is this feature called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Mé.explanation: Sudden falls without warning (drop attacks) in later Ménière's disease are Tumarkin crises, thought to arise from sudden otolithic dysfunction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A non-contrast CT head shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection that does not cross the suture lines. Which type of intracranial haemorrhage is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Extradural haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A biconvex/lens shape that respects (does not cross) suture lines is an extradural haemorrhage, reflecting the dura's tight attachment at the sutures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A non-contrast CT head shows a crescent-shaped (concave) collection that spreads across the suture lines. Which type of intracranial haemorrhage is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subdural haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A crescent (concave) collection that crosses sutures is a subdural haemorrhage (bridging-vein bleed); extradurals are biconvex and do not cross sutures.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Which intracranial haemorrhage classically arises from rupture of the bridging veins?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subdural haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Subdural haemorrhage results from tearing of the bridging veins (venous), typically in the elderly, alcoholic or anticoagulated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient presents with a sudden 'worst-ever' thunderclap headache and neck stiffness, with blood seen in the sulci and basal cisterns on CT. Which haemorrhage is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A thunderclap headache with meningism and blood in the sulci/basal cisterns is a subarachnoid haemorrhage, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A 22-year-old is struck on the temple during a rugby match, is briefly knocked out, then gets up and seems fine. An hour later he becomes drowsy with a worsening headache and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Extradural haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A young adult with temporal trauma, a lucid interval and then rapid deterioration is the classic story of an extradural haemorrhage (middle meningeal artery).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A head-injured patient's CT shows a hyperdense biconvex (lens-shaped) collection over the temporal lobe that does not cross the suture lines. Which vessel is most likely responsible?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: The middle meningeal artery
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A biconvex collection that respects sutures is an extradural haemorrhage, classically from the middle meningeal artery after a temporal fracture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with a rapidly expanding extradural haematoma develops a fixed, dilated pupil on the same side as the bleed. What is the mechanism?
options: Uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve
Direct trauma to the globe sustained in the original injury
Occlusion of the central retinal artery on the affected side
Transection of the optic nerve within the optic canal
A Horner's syndrome from carotid dissection in the neck
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: An ipsilateral fixed dilated 'blown' pupil results from uncal herniation compressing CN III — a sign of impending coning and a surgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: What is the definitive management of a symptomatic extradural haemorrhage with a deteriorating GCS?
options: Lumbar puncture, to relieve the raised intracranial pressure
Conservative management with observation and serial CT scans
Urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A symptomatic, deteriorating extradural haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent craniotomy, evacuation and control of the middle meningeal artery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: The middle meningeal artery, the source of most extradural haemorrhages, is vulnerable at which anatomical site?
options: The occiput, close to the confluence of the venous sinuses
The foramen magnum, at the base of the posterior fossa
The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, in the floor of the anterior fossa
The mastoid process, behind and below the external ear
The pterion, where four skull bones meet over the temple
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: The pterion, where four skull bones meet over the temple
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: The middle meningeal artery runs beneath the pterion, the thin bone at the temple, so a fracture there readily tears it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A head-injured patient with a suspected extradural haemorrhage has a GCS of 7. Beyond urgent imaging and neurosurgical referral, what is the immediate airway priority?
options: Give oral analgesia and observe him on the ward for four hours
Intubate to protect the airway, with C-spine control
Perform a lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure
Nurse him flat and give fluids to increase cerebral perfusion
Await spontaneous recovery of the GCS before any intervention
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Intubate to protect the airway, with C-spine control
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less mandates intubation for airway protection, with C-spine control and careful avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension, which cause secondary brain injury. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated where there is a space-occupying haematoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated in a patient with an extradural haemorrhage?
options: The CSF obtained would not yield any diagnostically useful information
It would almost always introduce infection and cause a meningitis
It would dislodge the haematoma and provoke further arterial bleeding
Removing CSF below a mass risks coning
It is far too painful to perform in an acutely head-injured patient
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Removing CSF below a mass risks coning
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: With a space-occupying haematoma and raised ICP, LP risks a pressure gradient causing coning, so it must be avoided.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Which set of signs indicates impending herniation ('coning') in a patient with an expanding extradural haematoma?
options: Rising BP, bradycardia, irregular breathing and a fixed dilated pupil
Falling blood pressure with a tachycardia and rapid shallow breathing
Bilateral small reactive pupils with a stable GCS and normal reflexes
Fever, neck stiffness and photophobia with a normal conscious level
A collapsing pulse with a wide pulse pressure and warm peripheries
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Rising BP, bradycardia, irregular breathing and a fixed dilated pupil
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Cushing's reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) with an ipsilateral blown pupil signals raised ICP and impending herniation — a surgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Why is extradural haemorrhage classically seen in young adults rather than the elderly?
options: The middle meningeal artery is absent in most elderly patients
Young adults have considerably thicker skulls at the temple
The dura is more firmly adherent to the skull in the elderly
Elderly patients essentially never sustain temporal bone fractures
Blood clots very much faster in the young than in the elderly
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: The dura is more firmly adherent to the skull in the elderly
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: In the elderly the dura adheres more tightly to the skull, making extradural stripping/bleeding less likely; hence extradural haemorrhage is commoner in young adults.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: An extradural haematoma is evacuated within a few hours of injury in a patient whose GCS had begun to fall. Why is the outlook often good?
options: Because the underlying brain is usually uninjured
Because arterial bleeds stop spontaneously once the clot forms
Because the dura protects the cortex from any lasting damage
Because a lucid interval indicates that no herniation occurred
Because extradural bleeds rarely raise the intracranial pressure
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Because the underlying brain is usually uninjured
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: In an extradural haemorrhage the brain itself is often undamaged — the harm comes from compression. Relieve it before herniation and the outcome is excellent, which is why the lucid interval is so dangerous: 'talk and die' is a preventable death.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A 78-year-old on apixaban falls and hits her head. GCS is 15, there is no focal deficit and she has not vomited. What does NICE advise?
options: No CT is needed, as she has no clinical indication for imaging
Consider a CT head within 8 hours of the injury
Discharge her with head-injury advice and GP review
Admit for 24 hours of neurological observation without imaging
Arrange an outpatient MRI head within the next two weeks
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Consider a CT head within 8 hours of the injury
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Being on an anticoagulant is itself an indication to consider imaging: NICE advises considering a CT head within 8 hours for anyone on an anticoagulant, or an antiplatelet other than aspirin alone, who has had a head injury but no other indication for a scan — or within 1 hour if they present more than 8 hours after the injury. This rule catches exactly the patient whose trivial head injury becomes a subdural.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: An 82-year-old man on warfarin is brought in with three weeks of fluctuating confusion, unsteadiness and a mild headache. His family recall he slipped and bumped his head about a month ago. CT shows a hypodense crescent-shaped collection over one hemisphere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Chronic subdural haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Insidious fluctuating decline in an elderly, anticoagulated patient after trivial/forgotten trauma, with a hypodense (old blood) crescent on CT, is a chronic subdural haemorrhage.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A CT head shows a crescent-shaped (concave) collection that spreads across the suture lines but stops at the midline. Which vessel/structure is the source?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: The bridging veins
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A crescent collection crossing sutures (but not the midline) is a subdural haemorrhage from torn bridging veins (venous).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: On CT, a subdural collection appears hypodense (dark). What does this indicate about the bleed?
options: It is a hyperacute arterial bleed
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: It is chronic (old, liquefied blood)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Hypodense (dark) blood indicates a chronic subdural haemorrhage; acute blood is hyperdense (bright), and acute-on-chronic is mixed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma in an elderly patient is best managed with which procedure?
options: Craniotomy and evacuation of a solid clot
Burr-hole drainage of the liquefied collection
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Burr-hole drainage of the liquefied collection
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Chronic subdural blood is liquefied and drains well through burr holes, often with dramatic improvement; solid acute clots need craniotomy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with major head trauma has a hyperdense crescent-shaped collection with midline shift and a falling GCS. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Craniotomy and evacuation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: An acute (hyperdense) symptomatic subdural with mass effect requires craniotomy and evacuation, as the fresh clot is solid; burr holes are for chronic liquefied collections.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A 4-month-old infant presents with reduced consciousness; CT shows bilateral subdural collections and fundoscopy reveals retinal haemorrhages, with no clear history of trauma. What must be strongly considered?
options: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces
Abusive head trauma; initiate safeguarding immediately
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Abusive head trauma; initiate safeguarding immediately
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Bilateral subdural haemorrhages with retinal haemorrhages and no adequate trauma history in an infant are a red flag for abusive head trauma (non-accidental injury), mandating safeguarding and a skeletal survey.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Why are elderly and alcoholic patients particularly predisposed to subdural haemorrhage after minor trauma?
options: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins, so they tear
Their middle meningeal arteries become progressively enlarged
They have a congenitally absent or markedly thinned dura mater
Their skulls fracture far more readily on even minor impact
They commonly harbour berry aneurysms on the Circle of Willis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins, so they tear
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Cerebral atrophy in the elderly and alcoholics stretches the bridging veins taut, so they tear with minor or forgotten head trauma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: An anticoagulated patient on warfarin has an acute subdural haemorrhage. Which is the most appropriate reversal strategy?
options: Platelet transfusion alone, with no clotting-factor replacement
Protamine sulfate, given as a slow intravenous infusion
Prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K
Tranexamic acid alone, as a bolus then an infusion
Idarucizumab, given as two sequential intravenous boluses
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Warfarin is reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K. Idarucizumab is the specific antidote for dabigatran; apixaban and rivaroxaban are reversed with PCC. Reversing the coagulopathy is a priority in any intracranial haemorrhage.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Which vessel type and structure classically bleed in a subdural haemorrhage?
options: Venous — the dural venous sinus wall
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Venous — the bridging veins
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Subdural haemorrhage is a venous bleed from torn bridging veins; the middle meningeal artery is the extradural source.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A confused 79-year-old on aspirin has become progressively more drowsy over six weeks. Why is chronic subdural haemorrhage a 'can't-miss' diagnosis here?
options: It is a treatable cause of decline that mimics dementia or stroke
It always progresses to coning within a few days of presentation
It is invisible on CT and can only be diagnosed at post-mortem
It occurs almost exclusively in young adults after major trauma
It resolves spontaneously and so needs no specific intervention
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: It is a treatable cause of decline that mimics dementia or stroke
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Chronic subdural haemorrhage presents with insidious confusion and decline and is easily mistaken for dementia, stroke or delirium — yet burr-hole drainage often reverses it. Remember that in the subacute phase the collection can be isodense to brain and easily overlooked, particularly if bilateral, when there is no midline shift.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: How do the CT densities of acute versus chronic subdural haemorrhage differ?
options: Acute is hypodense (dark); chronic is hyperdense (bright)
Both appear identical on CT at every stage
Acute is calcified; chronic is cystic
Acute is hyperdense (bright); chronic is hypodense (dark)
Density does not vary with age of the bleed
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Acute is hyperdense (bright); chronic is hypodense (dark)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Fresh (acute) blood is hyperdense/bright, and old (chronic) blood is hypodense/dark; acute-on-chronic bleeds are mixed — density indicates the age of the bleed. Between the two, in the subacute phase (roughly 3 days to 3 weeks), the collection passes through being isodense to brain and is easily missed.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A subdural collection is noted to cross the cranial suture lines but stops at the falx in the midline. How does this pattern compare with an extradural haemorrhage?
options: Subdural crosses sutures but not the midline; extradural the reverse
Both types of collection cross sutures and cross the midline freely
Subdural respects the suture lines in exactly the way an extradural does
Extradural crosses suture lines but is always stopped at the midline
Neither collection respects any anatomical boundary within the skull
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subdural crosses sutures but not the midline; extradural the reverse
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Subdural blood crosses sutures but is limited at the midline by the falx; extradural blood is limited by the dural attachment at sutures but can cross the midline.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A 52-year-old woman collapses with the sudden onset of the 'worst headache of her life', maximal within seconds, at the back of her head, followed by neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A thunderclap (sudden, severe, worst-ever) occipital headache with meningism is a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient presents 3 hours after a thunderclap headache. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
options: MRI with contrast the next day
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Urgent non-contrast CT head
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Urgent non-contrast CT is first-line and is ~100% sensitive within 6 hours of onset; a normal scan in that window effectively excludes SAH.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with a thunderclap headache has a normal non-contrast CT performed 20 hours after onset, but clinical suspicion of SAH remains. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge him with simple analgesia and GP follow-up in a week
Lumbar puncture at 12 hours or more after onset, for xanthochromia
Immediate craniotomy without any further diagnostic investigation
Start nimodipine empirically and observe him on the ward overnight
Repeat the non-contrast CT head in one week's time as an outpatient
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Lumbar puncture at 12 hours or more after onset, for xanthochromia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: When CT is done beyond 6 hours (or is negative with ongoing suspicion), LP ≥12 hours after onset looking for xanthochromia distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: On CSF analysis after a suspected SAH, which finding distinguishes a true subarachnoid haemorrhage from a traumatic lumbar puncture?
options: A markedly raised opening pressure recorded at the time of the tap
A high white cell count with a neutrophil predominance in the CSF
Completely clear, colourless CSF in all three sequential bottles
A low CSF glucose relative to the paired plasma glucose sample
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Xanthochromia on spectrophotometry
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Xanthochromia — yellow discoloration from bilirubin formed over ≥12 hours — indicates true SAH, whereas a traumatic tap gives blood without xanthochromia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with SAH has a painful third-nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil, ptosis and a 'down-and-out' eye. Which aneurysm is most likely responsible?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm classically compresses CN III, producing a painful third-nerve palsy (dilated pupil, ptosis, down-and-out eye).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: What is the commonest site of the berry aneurysm responsible for spontaneous SAH?
options: The internal carotid artery in the neck
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: The anterior communicating artery
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Berry aneurysms arise at Circle of Willis branch points; the commonest site is the anterior communicating artery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with aneurysmal SAH is started on nimodipine. What does it achieve, and how is it given?
options: It prevents rebleeding; give it once the aneurysm is secured
It reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia; 60 mg enterally 4-hourly for 21 days
It lowers intracranial pressure; give it as an intravenous bolus
It reverses the coagulopathy; give a single dose on admission
It prevents seizures; continue it for six months after discharge
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: It reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia; 60 mg enterally 4-hourly for 21 days
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Nimodipine reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia and improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH. It is given 60 mg enterally, 4-hourly, for 21 days, started within 4 days (96 hours) of the bleed. Hypotension is the dose-limiting effect. It does not treat or prevent rebleeding — that is what securing the aneurysm early does.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: In SAH, rebleeding carries a high mortality. When is the risk highest, and what is the key intervention?
options: Days 3 to 14; give nimodipine, which prevents the rebleed itself
Within the first 24 hours; secure the aneurysm early
After three weeks; start long-term anticoagulation at that point
The risk is not time-dependent; observation alone is appropriate
Only after discharge home; no inpatient intervention alters it
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Within the first 24 hours; secure the aneurysm early
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Rebleeding risk is highest in the first 24 hours, so the aneurysm is secured early (endovascular coiling first-line, or clipping); nimodipine prevents vasospasm, not rebleeding.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with confirmed SAH deteriorates with a new focal deficit on day 6. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Vasospasm causing delayed cerebral ischaemia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm typically occurs on days 3–14; nimodipine helps prevent it, and it is treated with euvolaemia and blood-pressure support.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: What is the first-line method of securing a ruptured aneurysm in most patients with SAH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Endovascular coiling
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Endovascular coiling is first-line in most cases (less invasive, better outcomes); surgical clipping is used when the aneurysm is unsuitable for coiling.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A 35-year-old with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension presents with a thunderclap headache. Which diagnosis should be prioritised?
options: A tension-type headache brought on by uncontrolled hypertension
Cluster headache, given the abrupt onset and severity of the pain
Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm
Acute sinusitis with referred pain over the vertex of the skull
Benign exertional headache, which can also start abruptly
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: ADPKD is associated with berry aneurysms; a thunderclap headache in this context should be treated as SAH until excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: A patient with SAH develops increasing drowsiness a few days after the bleed, and CT shows dilated ventricles. What complication has most likely developed?
options: Rebleeding from the aneurysm that has not been fully secured
Vasospasm causing delayed cerebral ischaemia in a watershed zone
Medication-overuse headache from the opioid analgesia given
A secondary bacterial meningitis introduced at the time of coiling
Hydrocephalus, from blood obstructing CSF flow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Hydrocephalus, from blood obstructing CSF flow
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: Blood in the subarachnoid space can block CSF flow/absorption, causing hydrocephalus, which may need an external ventricular drain or shunt.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.question: Which electrolyte disturbance should be monitored for after a subarachnoid haemorrhage?
options: Hyperkalaemia, from the tissue injury caused by the bleed
Hypercalcaemia, from immobilisation on the neurosurgical unit
Hypermagnesaemia, from the calcium channel blocker prescribed
Hyperphosphataemia, from the acute kidney injury that follows
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.answer: Hyponatraemia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__In.explanation: SAH commonly causes hyponatraemia via SIADH or cerebral salt wasting, so serum sodium is monitored; SAH can also cause ECG changes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A 28-year-old obese woman has several weeks of daily headache worse in the mornings, transient greying of vision on standing, and a whooshing noise in her ears. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema; MRI brain with venography is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: A young obese woman with raised-ICP headache, bilateral papilloedema, transient visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus, with normal imaging/venography, has IIH — a diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A patient with suspected IIH undergoes lumbar puncture after normal imaging. Which combination of findings supports the diagnosis (modified Dandy criteria)?
options: Raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmH₂O) with normal CSF composition
Low opening pressure with high CSF protein
Raised opening pressure with a high CSF white cell count
Normal opening pressure with low CSF glucose
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Raised CSF opening pressure (>25 cmH₂O) with normal CSF composition
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: IIH requires a raised CSF opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF composition (and normal imaging); a high white cell count or low glucose would suggest meningitis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A young woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill presents with headache and papilloedema. Which key mimic of IIH must be excluded, and how?
options: Giant cell arteritis; temporal artery biopsy
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; MR/CT venography
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; MR/CT venography
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis shares the demographic (young woman, COCP, pregnancy) and presents identically, so venography is essential before diagnosing IIH.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A 19-year-old woman being treated for severe acne develops headaches and blurred vision with papilloedema. Which medication is a recognised precipitant of IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Retinoids (isotretinoin) and tetracyclines used for acne are classic drug precipitants of IIH in young women; the causative drug should be stopped.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: In the management of IIH, what is the single overriding treatment goal?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: The papilloedema of IIH threatens sight, so the overriding priority is protecting vision, monitored with serial visual fields.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: Which is the first-line drug treatment for IIH, and what is its mechanism?
options: Prednisolone; an anti-inflammatory that reduces meningeal inflammation
Acetazolamide; a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production
Propranolol; a beta-blocker that reduces cerebral blood flow and pressure
Sumatriptan; a triptan causing cranial vasoconstriction and pain relief
Levodopa; dopamine replacement that restores normal CSF dynamics
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Acetazolamide; a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, reduces CSF production and is first-line (typically 250–500 mg twice daily, titrated as tolerated); topiramate is an alternative but carries MHRA pregnancy-prevention restrictions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: Which intervention is the key disease-modifying step in IIH and may even be curative?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Weight loss is the key disease-modifying step in IIH — a sustained loss of around 10% of body weight can resolve papilloedema and can be curative; the causative drug should also be stopped.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A patient with suspected IIH is booked for a lumbar puncture. What must be done first, and why?
options: A temporal artery biopsy, to exclude giant cell arteritis as the cause
Start acetazolamide before any test, so pressure is falling by the time of LP
A therapeutic LP immediately, to relieve the pressure before imaging is done
Neuroimaging (MRI + MR venography), to exclude a mass and venous thrombosis
Nothing further — proceed straight to lumbar puncture at the bedside
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Neuroimaging (MRI + MR venography), to exclude a mass and venous thrombosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Imaging must precede LP to exclude secondary causes (mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis); once imaging is normal, LP is safe and diagnostic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A patient with IIH has deteriorating vision on serial perimetry despite weight loss and maximal acetazolamide. Which is an appropriate next step?
options: Reassurance and repeat review in a year
Surgery — optic nerve sheath fenestration or a CSF shunt
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Surgery — optic nerve sheath fenestration or a CSF shunt
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Sight-threatening or refractory IIH warrants surgery — optic nerve sheath fenestration (to protect the optic nerve) or CSF diversion (VP/lumboperitoneal shunt); venous sinus stenting is an option in selected stenosis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: Which auditory symptom is characteristically reported by patients with IIH?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Pulsatile tinnitus (a whooshing sound synchronous with the pulse) is a characteristic symptom of IIH.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A patient with IIH reports brief episodes of vision 'greying out' for a few seconds when she stands up or bends over. What are these episodes called, and what do they reflect?
options: Transient visual obscurations, reflecting papilloedema/raised ICP
Amaurosis fugax, reflecting emboli arising from the internal carotid
Occipital seizures arising from the visual cortex on standing
Retinal migraine, reflecting vasospasm of the retinal circulation
Posterior vitreous detachment causing brief shadowing of vision
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: Transient visual obscurations, reflecting papilloedema/raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Transient visual obscurations — brief greying of vision with posture change — are typical of papilloedema/raised ICP in IIH and signal threat to vision.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: A patient with IIH develops horizontal diplopia due to a sixth nerve palsy. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is a false-localising sign of raised ICP
It localises a lesion to the brainstem
It indicates a cavernous sinus tumour
It excludes the diagnosis of IIH
It indicates impending brain herniation from a mass
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: It is a false-localising sign of raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: A CN VI (abducens) palsy is a false-localising sign of raised ICP in IIH and does not indicate a focal structural lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: Which feature helps distinguish IIH clinically from a space-occupying brain lesion?
options: No focal deficit other than a CN VI palsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: No focal deficit other than a CN VI palsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: In IIH there should be no focal neurological deficit apart from a CN VI palsy (a false localising sign); any other focal sign, drowsiness or a seizure points towards a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis. Papilloedema, headache and raised pressure occur in both.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.question: Topiramate is sometimes chosen over other agents in IIH. Besides lowering ICP, what additional benefit makes it useful?
options: It raises the seizure threshold usefully here
It improves the pulsatile tinnitus directly
It increases CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi
It causes weight loss, addressing a key driver of IIH
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.answer: It causes weight loss, addressing a key driver of IIH
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Id.explanation: Topiramate promotes weight loss, a useful dual benefit given obesity's central role in IIH. But it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women and girls able to have children unless a pregnancy prevention programme is in place (MHRA) — which matters in this typically young female population. Acetazolamide remains first-line.
