conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A 40-year-old presents with morning headaches, vomiting and papilloedema. MRI shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle, due to a tumour blocking the cerebral aqueduct. What type of hydrocephalus is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: A block within the ventricular system (aqueduct) with dilatation upstream of it is obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus; the fourth ventricle is spared because it lies below the block.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A patient with obstructive hydrocephalus and raised ICP is referred. Why is a lumbar puncture contraindicated here?
options: Removing CSF from below the block risks coning/tonsillar herniation
It would not obtain any CSF
It always causes a permanent CSF leak
LP cannot measure pressure in hydrocephalus
It would worsen the papilloedema irreversibly only
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.answer: Removing CSF from below the block risks coning/tonsillar herniation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: In obstructive hydrocephalus, lowering pressure below the block creates a pressure gradient that risks coning (herniation), so LP is avoided.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A 74-year-old has a 6-month history of a shuffling, wide-based 'magnetic' gait, urinary incontinence and mild cognitive decline. CT shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to any sulcal atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: The triad of gait disturbance, incontinence and dementia ('wet, wobbly, wacky') with ventriculomegaly without sulcal atrophy is normal pressure hydrocephalus — a potentially reversible cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A patient with normal pressure hydrocephalus is offered a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Which symptom is most likely to improve?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: Gait is typically the earliest and most shunt-responsive feature of NPH; a positive tap test (transient gait improvement after large-volume LP) predicts a good response.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A 4-month-old infant has a rapidly increasing head circumference, a bulging anterior fontanelle, irritability and eyes that appear to look downward ('sunsetting'). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Benign familial macrocephaly with no pathology
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: In infants the open sutures allow head enlargement; a bulging fontanelle, increasing head circumference and 'sunset eyes' (upward gaze palsy) indicate hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A patient develops acute obstructive hydrocephalus and a falling conscious level from an obstructing posterior fossa tumour. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention to relieve the pressure?
options: Immediate lumbar puncture to drain CSF
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: Acute hydrocephalus with raised ICP is managed with an external ventricular drain to reduce pressure quickly; LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: Two weeks after recovering from bacterial meningitis, a patient develops hydrocephalus. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi (communicating hydrocephalus)
Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus tumour
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.answer: Impaired CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi (communicating hydrocephalus)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: Meningitis (and subarachnoid haemorrhage) 'clog' the arachnoid villi, impairing CSF absorption and causing communicating (non-obstructive) hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: Which is the first-line imaging investigation in suspected hydrocephalus?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: CT head is first-line, showing ventricular enlargement, loss of the sulcal pattern and periventricular lucency (transependymal CSF exudation); MRI adds detail on the level and cause of obstruction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A young patient has obstructive hydrocephalus from aqueduct stenosis. Which surgical option creates an alternative CSF drainage route that bypasses the block?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: ETV creates a new drainage route (bypassing the obstruction) and is an alternative to a VP shunt in obstructive hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: Acetazolamide is sometimes said to reduce CSF production. What is its mechanism?
options: It increases CSF absorption at the arachnoid villi
It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF secretion by the choroid plexus
It osmotically draws water out of the brain
It is a loop diuretic acting on the kidney only
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.answer: It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF secretion by the choroid plexus
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production by the choroid plexus. Note that it is NOT recommended in hydrocephalus — with furosemide it was shown to increase shunt rates and disability, and definitive treatment is CSF diversion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A child with a long-standing ventriculoperitoneal shunt presents with recurrent morning headaches, vomiting and drowsiness. What should be suspected first?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: Returning raised-ICP symptoms in a shunted patient mean a blocked shunt until proven otherwise — a neurosurgical emergency needing urgent CT and immediate discussion with the on-call neurosurgeon. A normal CT does not exclude it. (Over-drainage causes the opposite: a postural headache worse on standing, with a risk of subdural haematoma.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A patient reports a headache that is worse first thing in the morning and on coughing or bending forward, with associated vomiting. Which underlying problem does this pattern most suggest?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: A morning headache worse on coughing/bending with vomiting is the classic pattern of raised intracranial pressure, as seen in hydrocephalus.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: In a patient with suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus, a large-volume lumbar puncture transiently improves the gait. What does this 'tap test' indicate?
options: A good likely response to ventriculoperitoneal shunting
That the CSF pressure is dangerously high
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.answer: A good likely response to ventriculoperitoneal shunting
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: In NPH, transient gait improvement after a large-volume LP (tap test) predicts a good response to VP shunting.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.question: A patient with raised intracranial pressure is found to have a new sixth cranial nerve palsy causing horizontal diplopia. How is this sign best interpreted?
options: It localises a lesion precisely to the abducens nucleus
It indicates a primary orbital tumour
It is unrelated to intracranial pressure
It is a false-localising sign of raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.answer: It is a false-localising sign of raised ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hy.explanation: A CN VI (abducens) palsy is a classic false-localising sign of raised ICP, owing to the nerve's long intracranial course, and does not pinpoint the lesion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A 42-year-old man is brought by his wife because of two years of increasing irritability, low mood and, more recently, fidgety involuntary movements of his hands and face. His late father had a similar illness in his 40s. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: A middle-aged adult with a positive family history, personality/mood change and chorea is the classic picture of Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: Huntington's disease is caused by which genetic mechanism?
options: A CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.answer: A CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Huntington's disease is the archetypal CAG trinucleotide-repeat disorder, with an expanded repeat in HTT on chromosome 4 producing a toxic huntingtin protein.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A family notices that Huntington's disease has appeared at progressively younger ages in each generation, especially when inherited from the father. What is this phenomenon called?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Anticipation — earlier onset and greater severity down the generations as the repeat expands — is characteristic of trinucleotide-repeat disorders and tends to occur through the paternal line.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A woman whose father has genetically confirmed Huntington's disease asks about her own risk. What is the chance she has inherited the disease-causing allele?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk of inheriting the expanded allele.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: Which region of the brain degenerates in Huntington's disease, accounting for the chorea?
options: The hippocampus, with neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaque deposition
The substantia nigra pars compacta, losing pigmented dopaminergic neurons
The striatum (caudate and putamen), losing indirect-pathway medium spiny neurons
The cerebellar vermis, producing a wide-based gait and truncal ataxia
The subthalamic nucleus alone, sparing the rest of the basal ganglia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.answer: The striatum (caudate and putamen), losing indirect-pathway medium spiny neurons
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Degeneration of the striatum — especially GABAergic medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway — disinhibits the thalamus, producing chorea; caudate atrophy is seen on MRI.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: How does the movement disorder of Huntington's disease differ mechanistically from that of Parkinson's disease?
options: Neither condition involves the basal ganglia; both arise in the cerebellar pathways
Both conditions result in too little movement, differing only in their age of onset
Huntington's is a pure rest tremor, indistinguishable from that of Parkinson's disease
Both are caused by an excess of dopamine acting within the striatum of the basal ganglia
Huntington's causes excess movement from indirect-pathway loss; Parkinson's too little
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.answer: Huntington's causes excess movement from indirect-pathway loss; Parkinson's too little
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Loss of the indirect pathway in Huntington's disinhibits movement (hyperkinetic chorea), the opposite imbalance to the hypokinetic state of Parkinson's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A 38-year-old at-risk individual requests predictive genetic testing for Huntington's disease. What is the most important element of the process?
options: Testing immediately without discussion, so as to reduce the patient's anxiety
Structured pre- and post-test counselling, in an adult who requests it themselves
Testing only once symptoms have appeared, and never before that point
Screening all of the at-risk relatives at the same time, without their consent
A brain biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before any genetic testing is arranged
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.answer: Structured pre- and post-test counselling, in an adult who requests it themselves
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Predictive testing needs structured pre- and post-test genetic counselling. It is offered only to adults with capacity who request it themselves, never to asymptomatic children, and the counselling must cover the implications for untested relatives, reproductive options, and UK insurance — HD is the only condition insurers may ask about, for life cover above 500,000 pounds.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A patient with Huntington's disease has troublesome chorea affecting daily function. Which drug is most appropriate to reduce the chorea?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Tetrabenazine, a dopamine-depleting agent, is used for troublesome chorea in Huntington's disease. It can cause or worsen depression and suicidal ideation and is contraindicated in untreated depression or active suicidality, so screen for depression first — an antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone, sulpiride) is often preferred where mood or psychotic symptoms coexist.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: What is the common cause of death in Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Progressive dysphagia leads to aspiration and pneumonia, the common cause of death; life expectancy is roughly 15–20 years from symptom onset.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: An 11-year-old develops acute involuntary, dance-like movements a few weeks after a sore throat, with no family history of neurological disease. Which cause of chorea is most likely?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Sydenham's chorea follows group A streptococcal infection (rheumatic fever) in children — distinct from the autosomal dominant, mid-life Huntington's disease.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.question: A 24-year-old presents with chorea, deranged liver function and a brownish ring at the corneal margin. Which diagnosis should be considered rather than Huntington's disease?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Hu.explanation: Young age with liver disease and Kayser–Fleischer rings points to Wilson's disease; Huntington's typically presents in mid-life with a family history and lacks these features.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A 62-year-old man reports a hand tremor that makes writing and holding a cup of tea difficult; it disappears when his hands are resting in his lap. It affects both hands equally, his father had the same problem, and he notices it settles after a glass of wine. Examination shows no bradykinesia or rigidity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: A bilateral, symmetrical postural/action tremor that is absent at rest, alcohol-responsive, familial and without other neurology is essential tremor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: Which single feature best discriminates essential tremor from the tremor of Parkinson's disease?
options: Essential tremor is worse on action, whereas Parkinson's tremor is worse at rest
Essential tremor has a pill-rolling quality
Essential tremor is always accompanied by rigidity
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.answer: Essential tremor is worse on action, whereas Parkinson's tremor is worse at rest
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: The best discriminator is timing: essential tremor is an action/postural tremor (worse when using the hands); Parkinson's is a rest tremor (worse when still).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A patient with a bilateral action tremor has a positive family history. What pattern of inheritance is most typical of essential tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Essential tremor is often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so a positive family history is common and supportive.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A 55-year-old woman with a suspected essential tremor is investigated. Which is the most important reversible condition to exclude with a blood test?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Hyperthyroidism is a key reversible cause of tremor; thyroid function tests are part of excluding mimics, along with a drug/caffeine review.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A 24-year-old presents with a tremor and is being assessed for essential tremor. Which diagnosis must specifically be considered in a young patient with a tremor?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Wilson's disease should be considered in a young person with a tremor; copper studies (caeruloplasmin, urinary/serum copper) help exclude it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A patient's tremor worsens as their finger approaches your target finger, and they also have nystagmus and past-pointing. Which type of tremor is this, and what does it localise to?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: A tremor that worsens on approaching a target, with nystagmus and past-pointing, is a cerebellar intention tremor — distinct from the postural/action tremor of essential tremor.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A retired teacher with essential tremor finds it socially embarrassing and functionally limiting. She has no respiratory or cardiac history. What is the most appropriate first-line drug treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Propranolol is first-line for essential tremor when treatment is warranted: start 40 mg two to three times daily, usual maintenance 80–160 mg daily. Avoid it in asthma, bradycardia, heart block or uncontrolled heart failure, where primidone is the alternative.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A 58-year-old man with troublesome essential tremor also has poorly controlled asthma. Which first-line agent is most appropriate?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Primidone is a first-line alternative to propranolol and is preferred when a beta-blocker is contraindicated, as in asthma. Start at 62.5 mg at night and titrate slowly over 4–6 weeks — the low night-time start is what avoids its notorious acute first-dose reaction.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: Regarding management principles in essential tremor, which statement is most appropriate?
options: Levodopa is first-line, since essential tremor is a movement disorder
All patients should be treated with a drug as soon as the diagnosis is made
Long-term daily alcohol is a recommended treatment given the alcohol response
Treat only if the tremor causes functional or psychosocial impairment
Deep brain stimulation is offered as the initial treatment in most patients
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.answer: Treat only if the tremor causes functional or psychosocial impairment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Essential tremor is treated only when it impairs function or causes psychosocial distress; many patients require just reassurance, caffeine reduction and a drug review.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A patient with severe essential tremor remains disabled despite propranolol, primidone and topiramate. Which is the most appropriate next option?
options: Deep brain stimulation (thalamic/VIM) or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
Regular botulinum toxin to the limbs as first choice
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.answer: Deep brain stimulation (thalamic/VIM) or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: For drug-refractory, disabling essential tremor, deep brain stimulation (thalamic VIM) or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy are the appropriate escalations.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.question: A patient with essential tremor mainly has a quavering voice and a 'yes-yes' head tremor that drug treatment has not helped. Which targeted option may be considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Es.explanation: Botulinum toxin is an option for head and voice tremor in essential tremor when it is the predominant, drug-resistant problem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of a unilateral throbbing headache lasting about a day, associated with nausea and a strong dislike of light, during which she lies still in a dark room. Between attacks she is well and her examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Migraine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A unilateral, throbbing, disabling headache with nausea and photophobia lasting 4–72 hours, during which the patient lies still, is typical of migraine.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 45-year-old man describes a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds ('like being hit on the head'), with neck stiffness. What must be excluded first?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A thunderclap headache is a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Get an urgent non-contrast CT: if it is done within 6 hours of onset and reported as normal by a radiologist, no lumbar puncture is routinely needed. If the CT was done beyond 6 hours and is negative with ongoing suspicion, do an LP at least 12 hours after onset, looking for xanthochromia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 68-year-old woman has a new persistent temporal headache, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and jaw pain on chewing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Giant cell arteritis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A new headache in someone over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication is giant cell arteritis. Send ESR and CRP — but start high-dose steroid on clinical suspicion, before the results and before the temporal artery biopsy, because vision can be lost within hours.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient reports a headache that is worse on waking and when bending or coughing, with vomiting; fundoscopy reveals papilloedema. What does this most suggest?
options: A primary tension-type headache with pericranial tenderness
A typical migraine attack with prominent nausea and vomiting
Cluster headache, occurring in bouts with autonomic features
A sinus headache from frontal or maxillary sinus congestion
Raised intracranial pressure — a tumour, or IIH
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Raised intracranial pressure — a tumour, or IIH
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Headache that is worse on waking/Valsalva, with vomiting and papilloedema, suggests raised intracranial pressure — image the brain.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 24-year-old describes seeing expanding zig-zag lines and a shimmering blind spot in one visual field that build up over about 15 minutes and resolve within the hour, followed by a throbbing headache. How is this best described?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Migraine with aura
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Fully reversible visual symptoms evolving over 5–20 minutes and lasting less than an hour, followed by headache, is migraine with aura.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A woman with typical episodic migraine has a normal neurological examination and no red-flag features. What is the most appropriate investigation strategy?
options: Urgent CT head, as every new migraine needs imaging first
MRI brain with contrast, arranged routinely for reassurance
Lumbar puncture to measure the CSF opening pressure
No neuroimaging; diagnose clinically and keep a diary
An EEG to exclude an underlying seizure disorder
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: No neuroimaging; diagnose clinically and keep a diary
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Typical migraine with a normal examination and no red flags requires no imaging — the diagnosis is clinical.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient presents early in a migraine attack. According to NICE, what is the most appropriate first-line acute treatment?
options: A triptan plus an NSAID (or paracetamol), taken early
A strong opioid such as codeine, taken at the first symptom
Regular prophylactic propranolol, started during the attack
Oral morphine, titrated against the severity of the pain
A benzodiazepine to settle the associated photophobia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: A triptan plus an NSAID (or paracetamol), taken early
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: First-line acute treatment is a triptan combined with an NSAID or paracetamol, taken early; opioids are avoided.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A migraine patient is very nauseated. In addition to a triptan and an NSAID, which adjunct is most appropriate, and which drug should be avoided?
options: Add an opioid for the pain; antiemetics should be avoided
Add a benzodiazepine for the nausea; avoid all NSAIDs
Add metoclopramide or prochlorperazine; avoid opioids
Add regular codeine for the nausea; avoid triptans here
Add a corticosteroid for the nausea; avoid paracetamol
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Add metoclopramide or prochlorperazine; avoid opioids
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: An antiemetic (metoclopramide/prochlorperazine) treats nausea and aids drug absorption; opioids are ineffective and cause medication-overuse headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 55-year-old man with stable angina asks for a triptan for his migraines. What is the correct advice?
options: Prescribe sumatriptan as normal, with a review in three months
Prescribe a double dose to overcome reduced responsiveness
Combine the triptan with a beta-blocker to offset the risk
Triptans are contraindicated by his ischaemic heart disease
Prescribe a nasal triptan, which avoids systemic absorption
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Triptans are contraindicated by his ischaemic heart disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Triptans cause vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and previous stroke or TIA. The route does not change this — the effect is systemic.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 26-year-old woman with migraine WITH aura requests the combined oral contraceptive pill. What is the correct advice?
options: It is safe and is the first-line contraceptive choice for her
It is acceptable provided she also has a triptan to hand
It can be used as long as her migraine attacks are infrequent
It will reduce her migraine frequency, so it is positively helpful
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Contraindicated (UKMEC 4); use progestogen-only or non-hormonal
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception multiplies ischaemic stroke risk and is UKMEC 4 — an absolute contraindication.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 30-year-old man with asthma has migraine on about 6 disabling days a month and needs prophylaxis. What is the correct approach?
options: Propranolol is the ideal choice and his asthma is not a concern
No prophylaxis is warranted at this attack frequency at all
Amitriptyline is contraindicated in migraine and must be avoided
Avoid propranolol in asthma; amitriptyline or topiramate instead
Verapamil is the preferred preventive at this attack frequency
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Avoid propranolol in asthma; amitriptyline or topiramate instead
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline are the three preventive options to consider, with no single first-line agent. Propranolol is avoided in asthma, leaving amitriptyline or topiramate here. Around 4 or more migraine days a month is the usual practical trigger for offering prophylaxis.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 25-year-old woman who might become pregnant is considering topiramate for migraine prophylaxis. What is the key concern?
options: It is entirely safe in pregnancy and needs no special precautions
Contraindicated in pregnancy; needs a pregnancy prevention programme
It has no clinically important interactions with contraception
The restrictions on topiramate apply only to male patients
It is the recommended first-line preventive during pregnancy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Contraindicated in pregnancy; needs a pregnancy prevention programme
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Topiramate is contraindicated in pregnancy for migraine prophylaxis, and contraindicated in women and girls able to have children unless all the conditions of a pregnancy prevention programme are met. In-utero exposure carries a 2–3 times higher risk of intellectual disability, autism and ADHD, and topiramate also reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient with chronic migraine has been taking sumatriptan on 12–15 days each month and now has a daily headache. What is the most likely explanation and the appropriate management?
options: A new brain tumour — arrange urgent CT
Medication-overuse headache — withdraw the overused drug
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Medication-overuse headache — withdraw the overused drug
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Frequent triptan use (>=10 days/month) causes medication-overuse headache; management is withdrawal of the overused drug.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A young woman has a migraine in which the aura includes weakness of one arm that fully resolves. What is essential before attributing this to migraine?
options: Nothing further — treat it as an ordinary migraine with aura
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle control
Give a strong opioid to abort this more severe attack type
Reassure and discharge her without further assessment today
Exclude stroke/TIA — motor aura mimics cerebrovascular disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Exclude stroke/TIA — motor aura mimics cerebrovascular disease
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Motor weakness (hemiplegic migraine) mimics a stroke; exclude cerebrovascular disease first, and the aura should be fully reversible.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient with disabling migraine has failed adequate trials of propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline. Which is an appropriate next step?
options: High-dose long-term opioids, taken daily for prevention
A CGRP monoclonal antibody or a gepant, under specialist care
Lifelong daily triptans, taken every morning as prophylaxis
There are no further preventive options available to her
Combined hormonal contraception to stabilise her hormones
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: A CGRP monoclonal antibody or a gepant, under specialist care
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: After at least three failed preventives, specialists may use CGRP monoclonal antibodies or gepants (and botulinum toxin for chronic migraine).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 35-year-old office worker has a bilateral, non-throbbing, 'tight band' headache without nausea, photophobia or aura, occurring on stressful days and relieved by simple analgesia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Tension-type headache
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A bilateral, pressing 'tight band' headache without migrainous features is a tension-type headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A useful bedside discriminator between cluster headache and migraine is the patient's behaviour during an attack. Which statement is correct?
options: The cluster patient is restless and paces; the migraine patient lies still
Both conditions cause the patient to lie completely still and quiet
Both cause the patient to pace around and be unable to settle
Migraine patients are characteristically the more agitated of the two
Behaviour is identical in the two and is of no discriminatory value
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: The cluster patient is restless and paces; the migraine patient lies still
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Cluster headache patients are restless and agitated, whereas migraine patients prefer to lie still in the dark — a classic discriminator.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A woman has a first, thunderclap-onset headache in pregnancy with focal neurological signs. Which must be excluded?
options: Migraine with aura and tension-type headache, the commonest causes
Subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pre-eclampsia
Cluster headache, which is commoner during pregnancy than outside it
Medication-overuse headache from analgesia taken through the pregnancy
Acute bacterial sinusitis with orbital or intracranial extension
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pre-eclampsia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Any thunderclap headache is a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise. Pregnancy adds two more: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (pregnancy is prothrombotic) and pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. Focal signs make urgent imaging and a blood-pressure and urine check mandatory.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 35-year-old man has bouts of excruciating, strictly unilateral pain behind the right eye lasting about an hour, several times a day for the past two weeks. During attacks the right eye is red and watering with a droopy lid, and he paces the room unable to keep still. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Cluster headache
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Severe unilateral peri-orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features, restlessness and a clustering pattern is cluster headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A man in a known cluster bout presents with an acute attack. What is the most appropriate acute treatment?
options: Oral sumatriptan together with regular paracetamol and rest
Regular verapamil, given at the onset of each individual attack
A strong opioid, titrated against the severity of the attack
Oral ibuprofen alone, taken as early in the attack as possible
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: High-flow 100% oxygen plus subcutaneous sumatriptan
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Acute cluster headache is treated with high-flow 100% oxygen and a subcutaneous/intranasal triptan; oral triptans and simple analgesics are too slow.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Why is an oral triptan not used to abort a cluster attack?
options: The attacks are too short for oral absorption to act in time
Oral triptans are contraindicated in every headache disorder
Oral triptans provoke rebound cluster attacks within hours
They worsen the autonomic features of lacrimation and ptosis
They cause a hypertensive crisis when given during a bout
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: The attacks are too short for oral absorption to act in time
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A cluster attack peaks within minutes, so an oral drug cannot be absorbed in time. Subcutaneous sumatriptan — the formulation licensed for cluster headache — or a nasal triptan is used instead, alongside high-flow oxygen.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient with recurrent cluster bouts is started on preventive treatment. Which agent is first-line, and what monitoring is required?
options: Verapamil; monitor the ECG for heart block / PR prolongation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Verapamil; monitor the ECG for heart block / PR prolongation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Verapamil is first-line prophylaxis during a bout; ECG monitoring is required because of the risk of heart block/PR prolongation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which cluster of examination findings, ipsilateral to the pain, is characteristic of cluster headache?
options: Bilateral papilloedema with enlarged blind spots on field testing
A fixed dilated pupil with ptosis and a down-and-out eye
A bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression by a tumour
Miosis, ptosis, a red watering eye and nasal congestion
Facial sensory loss over the cheek in the maxillary division
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Miosis, ptosis, a red watering eye and nasal congestion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: The ipsilateral autonomic signature (miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion) is characteristic of cluster headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: With which patient group is cluster headache most associated?
options: Men who smoke, with onset in their 20s–40s
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Men who smoke, with onset in their 20s–40s
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Cluster headache is commoner in men and smokers, typically presenting in the 20s–40s.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient has very frequent, short-lived unilateral headaches with autonomic features that are completely abolished by indomethacin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Paroxysmal hemicrania
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Complete responsiveness to indomethacin, with shorter and more frequent attacks, indicates paroxysmal hemicrania (another trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient's cluster bout is proving difficult to control while verapamil is being titrated. Which is a recognised way to help 'break' the bout?
options: A short course of oral prednisolone, or an occipital nerve block
A long course of high-dose opioids until the bout has settled
Regular daily oral triptans taken throughout the whole bout
Combined hormonal contraception to stabilise the hormonal trigger
Lifelong lithium, started as the first measure at presentation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: A short course of oral prednisolone, or an occipital nerve block
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A short prednisolone course (or an occipital nerve block) can break a bout while verapamil takes effect.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: What lifestyle advice is specifically important during a cluster bout, and what should be considered at first presentation?
options: Avoid caffeine only, and never image a patient with cluster headache
Strict bed rest during attacks, plus a routine EEG at presentation
Avoid alcohol during the bout; consider MRI at first presentation
Avoid all exercise during a bout, and perform a lumbar puncture
Maintain a high fluid intake, and arrange a carotid Doppler scan
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Avoid alcohol during the bout; consider MRI at first presentation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Alcohol characteristically triggers attacks during a bout, so it is avoided; MRI is considered at first presentation or if features are atypical, to exclude a secondary cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 38-year-old office worker describes a dull, pressing headache 'like a tight band' around the whole head most days for months. It is mild-to-moderate, not throbbing, and does not stop her working or worsen when she climbs stairs; there is no nausea, visual disturbance or eye watering. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Tension-type headache
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A bilateral, band-like, non-pulsatile, mild-moderate headache that is not aggravated by activity and lacks nausea, aura and autonomic features is tension-type headache — the 'featureless' primary headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which single feature most reliably separates tension-type headache from migraine?
options: Tension-type headache is always strictly unilateral in distribution
Tension-type headache is not worsened by activity; migraine is
Tension-type headache characteristically lasts longer than migraine
Tension-type headache is typically preceded by a visual aura
Migraine is always bilateral and band-like in its distribution
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Tension-type headache is not worsened by activity; migraine is
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TTH is bilateral, pressing/non-pulsatile and unaffected by activity; migraine is (often unilateral) throbbing, disabling and worsened by activity, with nausea/photophobia ± aura.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 42-year-old man reports a daily bilateral pressure headache for 4 months. He has been taking codeine-containing tablets and paracetamol on most days for it. Which diagnosis must be actively considered, and what is the key management principle?
options: Cluster headache; start high-flow oxygen and a subcutaneous triptan
Migraine; start a daily triptan taken first thing every morning
Giant cell arteritis; start high-dose steroids and check the ESR
Medication-overuse headache; withdraw the overused analgesia
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; start acetazolamide today
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Medication-overuse headache; withdraw the overused analgesia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A chronic daily headache in someone using regular symptomatic analgesia is medication-overuse headache; the treatment is to stop the overused analgesic, not escalate it.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: In medication-overuse headache, how should the offending drugs be withdrawn?
options: Stop all the overused drugs abruptly for at least a month
Withdraw everything gradually over the course of several months
Stop the opioids abruptly but taper the simple analgesics slowly
Continue all the analgesia and add a prophylactic agent alongside
No withdrawal is needed provided a preventive drug is started
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Stop all the overused drugs abruptly for at least a month
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: NICE advises stopping ALL overused acute headache medication abruptly rather than gradually, for at least 1 month — simple analgesics, triptans and opioids alike. Warn the patient the headache usually worsens for a week or two first. Consider specialist referral or inpatient withdrawal for people on strong opioids, with relevant comorbidities, or in whom previous attempts have failed, and review at 4–8 weeks.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient has episodic tension-type headaches roughly once a fortnight. What is the most appropriate acute treatment?
options: Subcutaneous sumatriptan, given as early in the attack as possible
A regular daily opioid to keep the headaches under control
Reassurance plus a simple analgesic — paracetamol or ibuprofen
High-flow 100% oxygen through a non-rebreathing mask at onset
Prophylactic amitriptyline, started immediately at this frequency
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Reassurance plus a simple analgesic — paracetamol or ibuprofen
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Episodic TTH is managed with reassurance and a simple analgesic (aspirin/paracetamol/NSAID); opioids are avoided and acute analgesia limited to <15 days/month.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 45-year-old woman has a band-like pressure headache on 20 or more days a month for over 6 months. Red flags are absent and she uses analgesia on fewer than 10 days a month. Which preventive treatment does NICE recommend?
options: A course of up to 10 sessions of acupuncture over 5–8 weeks
Propranolol, titrated up to the maximum tolerated dose
Topiramate, with a pregnancy prevention programme in place
Sodium valproate, at a low dose taken at night
Verapamil, with ECG monitoring before and during treatment
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: A course of up to 10 sessions of acupuncture over 5–8 weeks
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: For chronic tension-type headache, the only prophylaxis NICE recommends is a course of up to 10 sessions of acupuncture over 5–8 weeks, alongside addressing triggers and lifestyle. Low-dose amitriptyline is widely used in practice but is off-label here and is not a NICE recommendation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: How is tension-type headache classified by attack frequency?
options: Episodic (<15 days/month) vs chronic (≥15 days/month for >3 months)
There is no recognised frequency classification
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Episodic (<15 days/month) vs chronic (≥15 days/month for >3 months)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TTH is episodic when it occurs on <15 days/month and chronic when on ≥15 days/month for >3 months; chronic TTH overlaps with medication-overuse headache.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which examination finding is most consistent with (though not specific to) tension-type headache?
options: Ipsilateral ptosis with a red, watering eye and nasal congestion
A thickened, tender, pulseless temporal artery on palpation
Bilateral papilloedema with blurring of the disc margins
Pericranial tenderness with an otherwise normal examination
A fixed dilated pupil with impaired accommodation on that side
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Pericranial tenderness with an otherwise normal examination
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Pericranial tenderness may be present in TTH; the remainder of the neurological examination is normal. Autonomic signs suggest cluster, temporal-artery signs suggest GCA, and papilloedema suggests raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A student asks how to counsel a patient newly diagnosed with tension-type headache after red flags and medication overuse have been excluded. What is the most appropriate emphasis?
options: Reassurance that it is benign, an explanation, and no over-investigation
An urgent MRI brain, arranged specifically in order to reassure her
Immediate referral to neurosurgery for an opinion on the headache
Starting a strong opioid to give her rapid and reliable relief
Lifelong daily triptan use to suppress the headaches completely
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Reassurance that it is benign, an explanation, and no over-investigation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TTH is benign; reassurance and explanation are central, avoiding unnecessary imaging once red flags and medication-overuse headache are excluded.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which set of triggers is most classically associated with tension-type headache?
options: Bright light and specific dietary tyramine only
Alcohol during a discrete 'bout' with facial flushing
Stress, poor sleep, skipping meals, dehydration and poor posture
Sudden neck extension in a hairdresser's chair
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Stress, poor sleep, skipping meals, dehydration and poor posture
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TTH is classically linked to stress, fatigue, poor sleep, skipping meals, dehydration and poor posture; the other options point towards other headache syndromes.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient with frequent 'tension' headaches is found to be taking ibuprofen or a triptan on more than 15 days each month. Regarding future acute analgesia for their headaches, what advice best prevents recurrence of the problem?
options: Take analgesia at the first hint of any headache, every single day
Switch entirely to regular daily codeine for better control
Use a combination analgesic every day as a preventive measure
Keep triptans under 10 days a month and analgesics under 15
Take a triptan prophylactically each morning before work
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Keep triptans under 10 days a month and analgesics under 15
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: The two thresholds differ: triptans, opioids, ergots and combination analgesics must be kept to fewer than 10 days a month, and simple analgesics such as ibuprofen and paracetamol to fewer than 15. Avoid opioids altogether. Regular daily or prophylactic symptomatic analgesia is precisely what causes the problem.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 68-year-old woman describes sudden bursts of severe, stabbing 'electric-shock' pain in her right cheek and jaw, each lasting a few seconds, triggered by touching her face, chewing or a cold breeze. She is completely pain-free between attacks and neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Trigeminal neuralgia
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Paroxysmal, seconds-long, electric-shock unilateral facial pain in a trigeminal distribution, triggered by innocuous stimuli with pain-free intervals and a normal exam, is classic trigeminal neuralgia.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with bilateral trigeminal neuralgia and, on examination, has reduced facial sensation. Which underlying diagnosis should this particularly prompt you to investigate for?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Multiple sclerosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Young age, bilateral pain and sensory loss are red flags for secondary TN; ~2–4% of TN is due to an MS plaque on the trigeminal root, so MS should be investigated (MRI).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient has the characteristic paroxysmal shock-like facial pain of trigeminal neuralgia. Which is the most appropriate first-line drug treatment?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Carbamazepine
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia; the pain is neuropathic, so standard analgesics, NSAIDs and opioids are ineffective.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 70-year-old man with trigeminal neuralgia is started on carbamazepine. Two weeks later he is confused and lethargic. Which adverse effect should be checked for first?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Hyponatraemia (SIADH)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Carbamazepine can cause hyponatraemia via SIADH; it is a recognised cause of confusion/lethargy and should be checked with serum sodium.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Why are standard analgesics and opioids not used to treat trigeminal neuralgia?
options: They cause a rebound facial pain that worsens with continued use
They are contraindicated in all older adults with facial pain
They directly trigger the paroxysms of pain in this condition
The pain is neuropathic, so it needs an anticonvulsant instead
They work only when combined with a regular NSAID alongside
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: The pain is neuropathic, so it needs an anticonvulsant instead
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TN pain is neuropathic; it responds to sodium-channel-blocking anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine rather than to conventional analgesics or opioids.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which single feature most reliably distinguishes trigeminal neuralgia from cluster headache?
options: Trigeminal neuralgia is bilateral whereas cluster headache is unilateral
TN lasts seconds and is touch-triggered; cluster lasts 15 min–3 hours
Trigeminal neuralgia produces a red, watering eye and nasal congestion
Cluster headache is pain-free between attacks whereas TN is not
Both conditions characteristically last for several hours at a time
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: TN lasts seconds and is touch-triggered; cluster lasts 15 min–3 hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: TN paroxysms last seconds and are touch-triggered; cluster attacks last 15 min–3 h with ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 55-year-old with new trigeminal neuralgia is being worked up. What is the most appropriate investigation to exclude a secondary cause?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: MRI brain
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: MRI brain is used to exclude secondary causes — neurovascular compression, MS plaques and tumours (e.g. cerebellopontine angle lesions) — especially where red flags are present.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: In classic trigeminal neuralgia, what is the usual underlying cause?
options: Compression of the trigeminal root near the pons by a vascular loop
A demyelinating plaque in the pons at the root entry zone
An acoustic neuroma compressing the nerve in the cerebellopontine angle
Giant cell arteritis affecting the superficial facial vessels
Reactivation of varicella-zoster within the trigeminal ganglion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Compression of the trigeminal root near the pons by a vascular loop
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Classic TN is usually caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal root by an aberrant artery/vein, leading to demyelination and abnormal firing.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient with classic trigeminal neuralgia and MRI-confirmed neurovascular compression has pain refractory to carbamazepine and several other agents. Which procedure offers the best long-term relief?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Microvascular decompression
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Microvascular decompression is the procedure of choice for refractory classic TN with neurovascular compression, giving the best long-term relief; ablative/radiosurgical options are reserved for those unfit for, or declining, MVD.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 45-year-old woman with trigeminal neuralgia cannot tolerate carbamazepine because of dizziness and diplopia. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add a regular opioid alongside a reduced dose of carbamazepine
Stop all treatment and reassure her that it will settle in time
Start high-dose prednisolone to suppress the paroxysms of pain
Arrange urgent microvascular decompression as the next step
Refer to a specialist — nothing else is started outside one
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Refer to a specialist — nothing else is started outside one
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: If carbamazepine fails or is not tolerated, refer to a specialist. NICE is explicit that no drug other than carbamazepine should be started for trigeminal neuralgia outside a specialist setting, and surgery — most often microvascular decompression — is considered for refractory cases.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A frail 78-year-old with refractory classic trigeminal neuralgia is not fit for a craniotomy. Which treatment option is most appropriate?
options: Stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife) or a percutaneous ablative procedure
Immediate microvascular decompression regardless of fitness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife) or a percutaneous ablative procedure
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: For patients unfit for or declining microvascular decompression, ablative/percutaneous procedures (radiofrequency, glycerol, balloon) or stereotactic radiosurgery (gamma knife) are appropriate options.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A man is assessed after a road traffic collision. He opens his eyes only to a painful stimulus, uses inappropriate words, and localises to a painful stimulus. What is his GCS?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Eyes to pain = 2, inappropriate words = 3, localises to pain = 5, giving a total GCS of 10.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A head-injured patient has a GCS of 7. Which is the most appropriate immediate airway management?
options: Definitive airway protection with endotracheal intubation
High-flow oxygen via a non-rebreathe mask, then observe
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and monitor
Place in the recovery position and reassess in 30 minutes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Definitive airway protection with endotracheal intubation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less means the airway is unprotected — the patient should be intubated ('GCS 8, intubate').

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: During GCS assessment, a patient reaches up towards and above the clavicle in response to a supra-orbital painful stimulus. Which motor score is this?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: 5 — localises to pain
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Purposeful movement towards the stimulus (bringing the hand above the clavicle) is localising = motor score 5.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A comatose head-injured patient extends and internally rotates both arms in response to a painful stimulus. How is this best interpreted?
options: Decorticate (flexor) posturing, which is worse than extension
Decerebrate (extensor) posturing, which is worse than decorticate flexion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Decerebrate (extensor) posturing, which is worse than decorticate flexion
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Extension is decerebrate posturing (motor score 2) and is worse than decorticate flexion, reflecting deeper brainstem involvement.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 40-year-old who fell has clear fluid dripping from the nose, bruising over the mastoid process, and blood behind the eardrum. Per NICE, what imaging is indicated?
options: No imaging is required if the GCS is 15
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: CT head within 1 hour
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: These are basal skull fracture signs (CSF rhinorrhoea, Battle's sign, haemotympanum), which mandate CT head within 1 hour.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient who struck his head is now fully alert (GCS 15) but has vomited three times since the injury. What does NICE advise?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: CT head within 1 hour
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: More than one episode of vomiting after head injury is a 'CT within 1 hour' criterion.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 68-year-old pedestrian struck by a car had a brief loss of consciousness but now has a GCS of 15 and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate imaging plan?
options: Admit for 24 hours with no imaging
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: CT head within 8 hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Loss of consciousness plus a risk factor (age >=65 and/or a dangerous mechanism) meets the 'CT within 8 hours' criteria.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 72-year-old woman on apixaban trips and bumps her head. GCS is 15, there was no loss of consciousness, her examination is normal, and there is no other CT indication. What does recommend?
options: No CT — reassure her and discharge with head-injury advice today
CT head only if she later develops symptoms or her GCS drops
Consider a CT head within 8 hours of the injury
Skull X-ray, to look for a fracture before deciding on a CT
MRI head within 24 hours, as it is more sensitive than CT
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Consider a CT head within 8 hours of the injury
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: NICE advises considering a CT head within 8 hours for someone on an anticoagulant, or an antiplatelet other than aspirin alone, who has had a head injury with no other indication for a scan — or within 1 hour if they present more than 8 hours after the injury. Note this is a 'consider' recommendation, and a low-risk patient may reasonably be managed without a scan after shared decision making.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A young man is struck on the side of the head, is briefly knocked out, recovers and talks normally, then rapidly deteriorates and loses consciousness. CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Extradural haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A lucid interval followed by deterioration, with a biconvex bleed (middle meningeal artery), is an extradural haematoma — a neurosurgical emergency.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: An 80-year-old on warfarin presents with two weeks of increasing confusion and unsteadiness after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the cerebral convexity. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Subdural haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A crescent-shaped collection in an elderly/anticoagulated patient with an insidious course is a (chronic) subdural haematoma.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A head-injured patient's observations change to a blood pressure of 190/100 mmHg, a heart rate of 44/min, and irregular breathing. What does this indicate?
options: Cushing's reflex, indicating raised ICP and impending herniation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Cushing's reflex, indicating raised ICP and impending herniation
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular respiration is Cushing's reflex — a late, ominous sign of critically raised ICP.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A deteriorating head-injured patient develops a unilateral fixed, dilated pupil. What is the most likely cause?
options: Uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Uncal herniation compressing the third cranial nerve
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A fixed, dilated ('blown') pupil reflects third-nerve compression from uncal (transtentorial) herniation.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which single observation is the most important indicator that a head-injured patient is deteriorating?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: A falling GCS
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A falling GCS is the most important sign of neurological deterioration.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: In managing a severe head injury, why are hypoxia and hypotension avoided so aggressively?
options: They only lower the GCS artefactually
They have no proven effect on outcome
They worsen secondary brain injury and outcome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: They worsen secondary brain injury and outcome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Hypoxia and hypotension worsen secondary brain injury, so meticulous airway, oxygenation and circulatory support are essential.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A 30-year-old presents within 90 minutes of a head injury with a GCS of 11 and no evidence of extracranial bleeding. Which intervention should be considered?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Intravenous tranexamic acid
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: For a head injury with GCS <=12 and no active extracranial bleeding, IV tranexamic acid within 2 hours is recommended; corticosteroids are harmful in traumatic brain injury.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient on warfarin (INR 3.5) is found to have a traumatic intracranial haemorrhage on CT. What is the most appropriate reversal?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Warfarin-associated intracranial bleeding is reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K (PCC acts faster than FFP).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Which of the following is a sign of a basal skull fracture?
options: Battle's sign (bruising over the mastoid process)
A boggy scalp haematoma over the vertex
A subconjunctival haemorrhage with a visible posterior margin
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Battle's sign (bruising over the mastoid process)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Battle's sign, 'panda' eyes, haemotympanum and CSF otorrhoea/rhinorrhoea indicate a basal skull fracture.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: Why does even a small expanding intracranial haematoma become life-threatening?
options: The blood itself is directly toxic to the surrounding neurones
It invariably provokes seizures within the first hour of injury
The skull is a fixed box, so an expanding mass raises the ICP
It always ruptures into the ventricles and causes hydrocephalus
It lowers the systemic blood pressure and starves the brain
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: The skull is a fixed box, so an expanding mass raises the ICP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: By the Monro-Kellie doctrine, the fixed cranial volume means an expanding mass raises ICP, leading to herniation and brainstem compression.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient on apixaban has a head injury. The CT head is normal, the GCS is 15 and there are no other concerns. What does NICE advise?
options: Admit for 24 hours of neurological observation despite the normal scan
Discharge with written head-injury advice and a responsible adult
Repeat the CT head at 8 hours before any decision about discharge
Admit and reverse the apixaban with prothrombin complex concentrate
Admit for 48 hours, as delayed bleeding peaks on the second day
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Discharge with written head-injury advice and a responsible adult
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Being on an anticoagulant is NOT by itself an indication for admission. NICE reviewed this specifically and found no clinically important excess of delayed bleeding, and noted that admitting on that basis alone could harm an already vulnerable group. With a normal CT, a GCS of 15 and no other admission criterion, the patient goes home with written head-injury advice and a responsible adult.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A young adult with a minor head injury has a GCS of 15, a normal CT, and a responsible adult at home. What is essential before discharge?
options: A course of prophylactic antibiotics to cover any skull fracture
Written head-injury advice with clear return criteria
A follow-up MRI head arranged for the following week
Prescribed opioid analgesia for the post-traumatic headache
Two weeks of strict bed rest in a darkened, quiet room
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Written head-injury advice with clear return criteria
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Discharge with WRITTEN head-injury advice and a responsible adult — return if there is worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, weakness, visual change or a seizure. Note that being on an anticoagulant is not by itself a reason to admit once the CT is normal and the GCS is 15.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A rugby player is briefly dazed and confused after a head clash, with headache and patchy amnesia; his CT is normal. Weeks later he still has headaches, dizziness and poor concentration. Which two diagnoses does this describe?
options: A slowly expanding chronic subdural haematoma
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Concussion, followed by post-concussion syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: Concussion is a transient functional disturbance and a clinical diagnosis — most concussed patients never meet the CT criteria, so imaging is neither required nor able to exclude it; persistent symptoms over weeks constitute post-concussion syndrome (supportive care, graded return).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.question: A patient has a GCS of 10 following a head injury. How is the severity classified?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.answer: Moderate
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__He.explanation: A GCS of 9–12 is a moderate head injury (mild 13–15; severe 8 or less).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A 2-year-old boy has a brief, self-limiting generalised seizure at the height of a viral fever and recovers completely within minutes. He is developmentally normal, and there is no evidence of CNS infection. What is the diagnosis?
options: Newly diagnosed epilepsy requiring antiseizure medication
A simple febrile convulsion — a provoked seizure, not epilepsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: A simple febrile convulsion — a provoked seizure, not epilepsy
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: A fever-provoked seizure in a neurologically normal child aged 6 months to 5 years, without CNS infection, is a febrile convulsion — a provoked seizure, not epilepsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A 3-year-old has a generalised febrile seizure lasting about 8 minutes; she recovers fully and has no further seizure in the next 24 hours. How is this best classified?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Simple = duration <15 minutes, generalised, no recurrence within 24 hours, and complete recovery.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A paediatric registrar is teaching about febrile convulsions. Which single feature would make a febrile seizure 'complex'?
options: Occurring at the peak of the fever rather than at its onset
Being 2 years old at the time of the first seizure
A family history of febrile convulsions in a sibling
Focal features, lasting more than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours
A clear viral trigger such as a coryzal upper respiratory illness
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: Focal features, lasting more than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Complex = at least one of: focal features, duration of more than 15 minutes (no upper limit), recurrence within 24 hours or within the same illness, or incomplete recovery within 1 hour. Febrile status epilepticus (>30 min) is a prolonged complex seizure, not a separate category.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: Febrile convulsions characteristically occur within a specific age range. Which is correct?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Febrile convulsions typically occur between 6 months and 5 years; outside this range, scrutinise more carefully for another cause.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A 14-month-old has a febrile seizure and remains drowsy afterwards, with a bulging fontanelle and a non-blanching petechial rash. What is the priority?
options: Reassure the parents and discharge with antipyretic advice
Immediate empirical IV ceftriaxone — do not delay antibiotics for an LP
Start regular prophylactic antiseizure medication straight away
Give antipyretics alone and observe on the paediatric ward
Arrange an outpatient EEG and paediatric follow-up
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: Immediate empirical IV ceftriaxone — do not delay antibiotics for an LP
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: A bulging fontanelle, a non-blanching rash and failure to recover mandate emergency treatment for meningitis/meningococcal disease. Antibiotics are given immediately; the lumbar puncture is DEFERRED here because of the signs of raised intracranial pressure and the non-blanching rash.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: In which child presenting with a febrile seizure is lumbar puncture most clearly indicated?
options: A well 4-year-old, fully recovered, with obvious otitis media
A 3-year-old with a confirmed UTI who has fully recovered
A 2-year-old who had a brief simple seizure and is now playing normally
A 10-month-old who remains drowsy and is not recovering as expected
Any child who has a fever, regardless of other features
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: A 10-month-old who remains drowsy and is not recovering as expected
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Lumbar puncture is for suspected meningitis/encephalitis — complex features, red flags, or failure to recover, with a much lower threshold under 18 months because the signs are unreliable. It is deferred if there is shock, a non-blanching rash or raised intracranial pressure, and must never delay antibiotics.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A previously well 3-year-old has a typical simple febrile convulsion in the context of a clear viral upper respiratory infection and recovers fully. Which investigation strategy is most appropriate?
options: Lumbar puncture in every child who has had a seizure with a fever
Routine EEG and CT head of the brain in every case of febrile seizure
No specific investigations beyond the fever source, with a urine dip for UTI
Routine MRI brain to look for an underlying structural abnormality
Prolonged inpatient EEG monitoring to exclude an epilepsy syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: No specific investigations beyond the fever source, with a urine dip for UTI
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: A simple febrile convulsion needs no routine EEG, imaging or bloods — just identify the fever source (and a urine dip for occult UTI).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: The parents of a child who has had febrile convulsions ask whether regular paracetamol will prevent further episodes. What is the correct advice?
options: Give regular paracetamol to prevent future seizures
Give prophylactic ibuprofen at the first sign of illness to prevent seizures
Antipyretics improve the child's comfort but do NOT prevent febrile convulsions
Alternate paracetamol and ibuprofen specifically to prevent seizures
Antipyretics are contraindicated in these children
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: Antipyretics improve the child's comfort but do NOT prevent febrile convulsions
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Antipyretics are for comfort only; they do not prevent febrile convulsions.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: A child with a history of prolonged febrile seizures is to be provided with a home rescue medication. Which is appropriate?
options: Oral phenytoin taken at the onset of every fever
Regular daily sodium valproate as ongoing prophylaxis
Intravenous lorazepam administered at home by the parents
Oral carbamazepine taken during every febrile illness
Buccal midazolam (first choice) if a seizure lasts over 5 minutes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: Buccal midazolam (first choice) if a seizure lasts over 5 minutes
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Buccal midazolam is the UK first choice for home rescue, with rectal diazepam if it is unsuitable or unavailable, given if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes. Routine daily antiepileptics are not indicated.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: The parents of a child who has just had a first simple febrile convulsion ask about the chance of it happening again. What is the approximate recurrence risk?
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: The recurrence risk is roughly 1 in 3 — higher if the child was under 18 months at the first seizure, with a family history of febrile convulsions, a lower peak temperature, or a short fever before the seizure. (Complex features raise the risk of later epilepsy, not of recurrence.)

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: Parents are worried that a simple febrile convulsion means their child will develop epilepsy. What is the correct information about later epilepsy risk?
options: It is only slightly above the general-population risk (about 1-2%)
It is the same as after an episode of status epilepticus
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: It is only slightly above the general-population risk (about 1-2%)
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: After a simple febrile convulsion the absolute epilepsy risk is about 1–2%, against roughly 0.5–1% in the general population. It is higher with complex febrile convulsions, neurodevelopmental problems, or a family history of epilepsy.

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.question: Which child with a febrile convulsion most clearly warrants admission to paediatrics?
options: A well 3-year-old with a recognised simple recurrence who has fully recovered
A first febrile convulsion, complex features, unwell child, or age under 18 months
Any child who happens to have a fever, whatever the circumstances
Only children older than 5 years at the time of the seizure
None — all febrile convulsions are managed entirely at home
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.answer: A first febrile convulsion, complex features, unwell child, or age under 18 months
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Fe.explanation: Admit for a first febrile convulsion, complex features, diagnostic uncertainty, an unwell child, age under 18 months, no identified focus for the fever, or a child currently or recently on antibiotics (which can mask meningitis).

conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.question: A 41-year-old man presents with 4 days of weakness that began in both feet and has ascended to his thighs and hands. Ten days ago he had bloody diarrhoea after a barbecue. Examination shows symmetrical flaccid weakness (3/5 legs, 4/5 arms) with absent reflexes throughout, normal sensation and no sensory level. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A first presentation of multiple sclerosis
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.answer: Guillain-Barre syndrome
conditions__NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY__Gu.explanation: Ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness with areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness (likely Campylobacter) is classic GBS; absent reflexes and no sensory level argue against a cord lesion.
